1.title: What is on the resource disc
1.gist: This opening page explains that the facilitator kit is a set of printable PDFs plus two meditation audio tracks, one narrated and one music-only. It matters because the audio is meant as an optional on-ramp that settles a group before any session begins.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Starting with a short relaxation lowers physiological arousal, and a calmer nervous system is better at the slow, reflective thinking that worksheets ask for. It also marks a threshold: the group room becomes a different space from the unit outside.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In a correctional setting, closed eyes can feel unsafe. Offer an eyes-open option, such as softly gazing at the floor, and frame the exercise as a skill athletes use, not as something soft.

ask: What would tell you that an opening ritual is helping your group focus rather than just using up time?
How might guided relaxation land differently for someone with a trauma history, and how would you adjust?

5.title: What Living in Balance is
5.gist: The page introduces Living in Balance as a manualized program for substance use disorders, usable as a main treatment or an add-on, with short worksheet-driven sessions. Knowing its design helps you decide when to run a full session and when to split it into shorter parts.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Manualized treatment trades some flexibility for consistency: every facilitator delivers roughly the same active ingredients, which is what makes a program testable at all. The art is staying faithful to the core while adapting examples to the people in front of you.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Worksheet-heavy programs assume a certain reading level. In many prison groups literacy varies widely, so reading aloud, pairing members, or using drawings can keep the material from quietly excluding people.

ask: Where is the line between adapting a manual and drifting so far that you are no longer delivering it?
Which parts of a session do you think are the true active ingredients, and which are packaging?

terms.d: A therapy delivered from a written protocol so that different counselors provide essentially the same intervention.

6.title: The theory the program stands on
6.gist: This page lays out the program's foundation: a biopsychosocial view of addiction, motivational enhancement and the stages of change, and cognitive-behavioral tools such as functional analysis and skills training. It tells you why the worksheets keep asking members to notice gaps between goals and actions.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Highlighting the gap between what someone values and what they do is a core move of motivational interviewing (Miller & Rollnick). People tend to argue for change more when they hear themselves name that gap, rather than when someone lectures them about it.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Functional analysis comes from behavioral psychology: a behavior persists because of what triggers it and what it pays off. It is close to asking, like a detective, what job the drug was doing in this person's life.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Motivational and cognitive-behavioral approaches are among the best-supported treatments for substance use disorders, though effects are typically moderate and no single approach clearly outperforms the others across studies.

ask: If several different therapies produce similar outcomes, what does that suggest about what actually helps people change?
How would you run a functional analysis with someone who insists their use had no benefits at all?

terms.d: The view that illness and recovery arise from biological, psychological, and social factors acting together.
Mapping the triggers, thoughts, feelings, and payoffs that surround a behavior to understand why it continues.

7.title: Three curricula, starting with Core
7.gist: The page explains that the program has three linked curricula and lists the twelve Core Program sessions that cover early-recovery basics. It matters because the Recovery Management sessions you teach assume members have had, or can catch up on, that Core foundation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Before a Recovery Management session, quickly check which Core ideas the group already owns, such as triggers or cravings. A one-minute recap can prevent a later session from building on sand.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Sequencing from basic education to deeper personal work mirrors scaffolding in learning theory: people take on harder material once simpler concepts feel familiar and safe.

ask: What happens to learning when someone joins a sequenced program halfway through?
Which Core topic do you think your members most need before tackling the advanced sessions?

8.title: The Recovery Management menu
8.gist: This page introduces the twenty-five Recovery Management sessions, which go deeper into specific life areas such as peer support, health, family, money, and sexuality. The key message is that counselors can pick sessions to match each client's needs instead of running all of them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Choosing topics by individual need echoes the need principle of the Risk-Need-Responsivity model (Andrews & Bonta): interventions work better when they target the problems actually driving someone's difficulties.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: List three members you serve and, for each, pick the two sessions here you would prioritize. Notice whether your picks follow their needs or your own comfort with the topic.

ask: How would you decide which sessions to offer when a group's needs are very mixed?
Which topic on this list do you suspect is most under-taught in reentry work, and why?

9.title: Later sessions and dual recovery
9.gist: The page finishes the Recovery Management list and introduces the Co-occurring Disorders curriculum for people who face both addiction and a mental health condition. It matters because many people in correctional treatment carry both, and the two interact.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Co-occurring mental health and substance use problems are common among incarcerated people. Integrated care, treating both together rather than in separate silos, is generally recommended by treatment guidelines.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A counselor can easily mistake untreated depression, trauma, or psychosis for poor motivation. Knowing when to refer for psychiatric assessment is as important as delivering the curriculum.

ask: What signs would make you suspect a member's resistance is actually an untreated mental health problem?
Why might treating addiction and mental illness separately fail even when both treatments are good?

terms.d: Having a substance use disorder and a mental health disorder at the same time.

10.title: Tailoring with mini-tracks
10.gist: This page says sessions can be adapted for culture, gender, and sexual orientation, and describes three mini-tracks that bundle sessions for anger, trauma and violence, and peer support. It gives you ready-made pathways when a group shares one dominant need.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Adapting delivery to the person reflects the responsivity principle in RNR: the same content works better when it fits a person's learning style, culture, and readiness.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Trauma material in a prison group needs extra care: set clear limits on disclosure, warn members before hard content, and have a plan for someone who becomes overwhelmed.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A track first written for women may need real rethinking for men, who are often less likely to name victimization. Simply swapping pronouns rarely does the job.

ask: What would a genuinely culturally adapted session look like, beyond translating the words?
How do you balance a group's shared mini-track with members whose main need is different?

11.title: Where it runs and claimed results
11.gist: The page describes the many settings where the program is used, including jails and prisons, its origins in a federally funded cocaine-treatment study, and summary claims of reduced use and better retention. It gives you the program's evidence pitch, which deserves a critical read.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Publishers' summaries tend to present the strongest numbers. Before accepting a claim of effectiveness, ask about sample size, how many people dropped out, and what the comparison group received.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Keeping people in treatment matters: across addiction research, longer retention is consistently linked with better outcomes. Retention gains are a meaningful result even when other effects are modest.

ask: If a program keeps people longer, is that because it works better or because it is more engaging? Does the difference matter?
What would you want to know before telling a parole officer this program is evidence-based?

12.title: Inside the original study
12.gist: This page details the evaluation: two outpatient sites, mostly justice-referred cocaine users, randomly assigned to this program or a Twelve Step group, with self-reported drug use tracked. Reading the design lets you judge how much weight the outcomes can carry.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Only about a quarter of participants completed the end and follow-up assessments. With so much missing data, the people who stayed may differ from those who left, so the results could look better than reality.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Random assignment is the strongest tool against bias because it spreads unmeasured differences evenly across groups. Its power is weakened, though, when most participants drop out before measurement.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Write one sentence describing this study the way a skeptical journal reviewer would, then one the way a marketer would. The distance between them is a lesson in reading evidence.

ask: How might self-reported drug use be biased among people referred by the justice system?
Why is comparing a program to an active treatment, like a Twelve Step group, a harder test than comparing it to nothing?

terms.d: Loss of participants from a study over time, which can distort results if those who leave differ from those who stay.

13.title: Small sample, satisfied buyers
13.gist: The page admits the study was too small to generalize, then turns to a satisfaction survey of organizations that bought the program. It shows the gap between evidence of outcomes and evidence that people liked a product.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A survey mailed to buyers with a very low return rate mostly hears from enthusiasts. Satisfaction among purchasers says little about whether clients actually changed, so treat it as marketing rather than outcome data.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: This is the classic self-selection problem from statistics: who answers a survey shapes what it finds. The same bias distorts online product reviews and polls with voluntary participation.

ask: What is the difference between a program being liked and a program working, and can one exist without the other?
How would you design a fair test of whether this curriculum helps your own groups?

terms.d: The share of people asked who actually answer a survey; low rates raise the risk of biased results.

14.title: What users say they like
14.gist: This page reports high satisfaction ratings and favorable comments from counselors and programs using the curriculum. It shows what practitioners value: ease of use, structure, and a safe way to discuss sensitive subjects.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Structure helps groups feel safe. A predictable format reduces anxiety and gives members a frame for difficult conversations, which may be part of why counselors praise it.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Counselors' beliefs about client relapse prevention are perceptions, not measurements. A useful habit as a scientist-practitioner is noticing when a claim is about opinion rather than observed outcomes.

ask: Which of these praised features actually change client outcomes, and which mainly make the counselor's job easier?
How could ease of use become a trap that leads to mechanical delivery?

15.title: Session goals begin: Session 1
15.gist: After closing the comments, the page starts listing learner objectives for each session, beginning with Session 1 on terms, the nature of substance use disorders, self-assessment, and effects on brain and body. These objectives are your checklist for what a session should achieve.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Turn objectives into a closing check: ask members to name one thing they now understand that they did not an hour ago. It shows you what landed and gives them a sense of progress.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Many objectives say understand, which is hard to observe. Educators often prefer action verbs such as explain, identify, or compare because you can actually see whether learning happened.

ask: How would you know, by observation, that a member truly understands the diagnostic criteria rather than repeating them?
Why might self-assessment be more persuasive than being told you have a disorder?

16.title: Goals for drugs and triggers
16.gist: The page lists goals for Session 2 on drug classes and their effects and Session 3 on triggers, cravings, and the steps from trigger to relapse. Together they move members from knowing about drugs to knowing about their own patterns.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Cue reactivity explains much of this: places, people, and moods paired with past use come to trigger craving on their own, a form of conditioning. Knowing this makes cravings feel less mysterious and more manageable.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Drug education alone rarely changes behavior; people often know the risks already. Its value comes when it connects to personal triggers and skills, which is why Session 3 follows Session 2.

ask: Why does information about drug harms so often fail to change behavior?
How would you explain conditioned craving to someone who believes it shows a lack of willpower?

terms.d: Craving and bodily arousal triggered by reminders that were repeatedly paired with past substance use.

17.title: Goals for sobriety plans and alcohol
17.gist: This page covers goals for Session 4, which frames sobriety and relapse as processes with warning signs and decisions, and Session 5 on alcohol and tobacco. It shows the program treating relapse as something that unfolds before the first drink.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt and Gordon's relapse prevention model describes small, seemingly irrelevant decisions that gradually move a person toward a high-risk situation. Spotting those early choices is easier than resisting at the last moment.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Tobacco is often ignored in addiction treatment, yet it kills many people in recovery. Ask members how they view smoking compared with their main drug; the answers can be revealing.

ask: What is gained by treating relapse as a process rather than an event?
Why do you think tobacco is often left out of recovery conversations?

18.title: Goals for spirituality and sex
18.gist: The page lists goals for Session 6 on spirituality and a Higher Power, and Session 7 on how alcohol and drugs affect sex. Both touch private parts of life that substances often take over.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: William James, in The Varieties of Religious Experience, treated spiritual change as a psychological event worth studying. His work influenced the founders of Alcoholics Anonymous.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Spirituality can alienate atheist or non-Christian members. Framing it as meaning, purpose, and connection to something beyond the self keeps the door open for everyone.

ask: How can a counselor talk about spirituality without imposing their own beliefs?
Why might sex and substance use become so tightly linked that one triggers the other?

19.title: Goals for stress sessions
19.gist: This page covers goals for Session 8 on stress and emotional well-being, including defense mechanisms and stages of stress response, and Session 9 on practical stress reduction, support, and relaxation. It reflects how often stress precedes relapse.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The three stages of stress echo Hans Selye's general adaptation syndrome: alarm, resistance, and exhaustion. Chronic stress keeps people stuck in resistance, wearing them down over time.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The Relaxation Response was named by Herbert Benson, who described it as the physiological opposite of fight-or-flight. It can be triggered by simple breathing or repetition.

ask: Which stressors in prison are truly outside a person's control, and how should coping differ for those?
Why might isolation be both a symptom and a cause of relapse?

20.title: Goals for emotions and anger
20.gist: The page lists goals for Session 10 on depression, guilt, fear, and forgiveness, and Session 11 on recognizing anger, its suppression and displacement, and assertive communication. These are the emotions most likely to send someone back to using.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Psychologists often distinguish guilt, which focuses on a behavior, from shame, which focuses on the self. Guilt can motivate repair, while shame tends to lead to hiding and relapse.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Displacing anger onto a safer target is one of the defense mechanisms described in the psychoanalytic tradition. It is a useful lens for a member who explodes at a cellmate after a hard phone call.

ask: When is guilt useful in recovery and when does it become harmful?
Why might assertiveness be risky in a prison setting, and how would you adapt the skill?

21.title: Relapse basics and Session 13 goals
21.gist: This page finishes the Core list with Session 12 on relapse prevention basics, then begins the Recovery Management goals with Session 13 on self-help groups, secrecy, trust, and alternatives to Twelve Step programs. It previews the first session you will deliver from this book.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Thought-stopping, listed here, has weak support and can backfire. Research on thought suppression by Daniel Wegner showed that pushing a thought away can make it return more often; acceptance or redirection may work better.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Addiction often thrives in secrecy, while recovery depends on being known by others. That is why Session 13 links isolation, honesty, and trust.

ask: If suppressing a thought can backfire, what should a member do with a craving thought instead?
Why might offering alternatives to Twelve Step groups increase participation in mutual help overall?

terms.d: Interrupting an unwanted thought, often by saying stop; a technique with limited and mixed evidence.

22.title: Goals for Steps and sexual health
22.gist: The page lists goals for Session 14 on the demands of each of the Twelve Steps, Session 15 on sexually transmitted diseases, and Session 16 on HIV testing, spread, risk, and treatment. It pairs a spiritual program with frank health education, both relevant to reentry.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: HIV and hepatitis C are more common in prison populations than in the general public, partly because of injection drug use. Release is a key moment for linking people to testing and ongoing care.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Health sessions go better when members are invited to bring questions anonymously, for example on slips of paper. Embarrassment and myths about transmission are common, and anonymity lowers the cost of asking.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: HIV treatment has transformed: with effective antiretroviral therapy, people can live long lives, and an undetectable viral load prevents sexual transmission. Older stigma often lags behind this science.

ask: Why might people who have taken many risks with drugs underestimate their own HIV risk?
How does stigma about a disease shape whether people get tested?

23.title: Goals for body and sleep
23.gist: This page lists goals for Session 17 on nutrition, balanced eating, and exercise, and Session 18 on common health problems and insomnia in early sobriety. It reminds facilitators that recovery happens in a body that substances have depleted.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Sleep problems are common in early recovery and are linked to relapse risk. Poor sleep weakens emotional control and impulse control, the very capacities sobriety relies on.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Exercise reliably improves mood and reduces anxiety for many people, and it is being studied as a support in addiction treatment. Results for preventing relapse are promising but still mixed.

ask: How might prison routines and environments make healthy sleep and nutrition harder, and what can members realistically control?
Why might physical health goals feel more achievable to some members than emotional ones?

24.title: Goals for problem solving and beliefs
24.gist: The page lists goals for Session 19 on step-by-step problem solving and Session 20 on how irrational beliefs and an inner critic create stress, along with focusing on strengths and acceptance. These are the most directly cognitive-behavioral sessions in the book.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Disputing irrational beliefs comes from Albert Ellis's rational emotive behavior therapy: it is often our beliefs about an event, not the event itself, that drive our distress. Beck's cognitive therapy makes a related point about automatic thoughts.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Accepting what cannot be changed echoes the Serenity Prayer and, long before it, the Stoic Epictetus, who taught separating what is within our control from what is not.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Problem-solving training has decent support for reducing stress and depression and is a common component of correctional cognitive programs.

ask: When does labeling a belief irrational help a member, and when might it feel dismissive of real injustice?
Why might problem-solving skills fade under stress, and how could you practice them so they hold up?

terms.d: In REBT, a rigid, demanding thought, such as I must never be disrespected, that produces needless distress.

25.title: Goals for needs and family
25.gist: This page lists goals for Session 21 on levels of human needs and healthy relationships, and Session 22 on dysfunctional family rules and roles, forgiveness, and reconciliation. It moves the program from the self toward the people around it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Levels of needs come from Abraham Maslow's hierarchy. Critics note that people often pursue belonging or meaning even when basic needs are unmet, so the order is not as fixed as the pyramid suggests.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Roles such as the hero, scapegoat, or lost child come from family-systems writing on alcoholic families, notably Sharon Wegscheider-Cruse. They are useful metaphors rather than diagnoses with strong research behind them.

ask: How might the prison environment itself shape which needs a person focuses on?
When is forgiveness healthy, and when could pressure to forgive harm someone?

26.title: Goals for parents and parenting
26.gist: The page lists goals for Session 23 on parenting styles and how one's mother and father continue to shape adult life, and Session 24 on child development stages and healthy parenting. Many members are both wounded children and parents separated from their own kids.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Attachment theory, from John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth, holds that early relationships shape expectations about whether others will be reliable. These patterns can change later through new, consistent relationships.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Diana Baumrind's parenting styles, authoritative, authoritarian, and permissive, are a classic framework. Warmth combined with clear limits is generally linked with better child outcomes.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Talking about parents can open deep wounds. Make it clear members can share as much or as little as they want, and watch for anyone who goes quiet.

ask: How do you help a member understand a parent's influence without excusing the harm or locking them into blame?
What could parenting from prison realistically look like?

27.title: Goals for school, work, money
27.gist: This page lists goals for Session 25 on education, job choice, résumés, interviews, and workplace triggers, and the start of Session 26 on budgeting and financial goals. These are the practical anchors of reentry.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Stable employment is widely associated with lower reoffending, and education in prison is linked with better post-release outcomes. Employment is one of the central eight risk and need factors in Andrews and Bonta's work.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prepare members for how to discuss a conviction in an interview: brief, honest, focused on change. Role-playing that moment often lowers anxiety more than any handout.

ask: Which barriers to employment after release can a member influence, and which are structural?
Why might workplace triggers be underestimated by someone leaving prison?

28.title: Goals for credit and sexual abuse
28.gist: The page lists goals for Session 27 on insurance, consumer credit, scams, and compulsive borrowing, and Session 28 on confusing sexual messages, rape, other sexual assault, and how childhood sexual abuse can echo into adult life. The second topic requires extra care.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Histories of childhood sexual abuse are common among people with substance use disorders, in both women and men. Substances are often used to numb trauma symptoms.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Before Session 28, know your facility's reporting rules and referral options. Disclosures of abuse, including abuse in custody, need a planned response, not improvisation.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Men's victimization is frequently overlooked. Using language that clearly includes men as possible survivors can make it safer for them to recognize their experience.

ask: How does shame about victimization differ for men and women, and how should that shape your approach?
What does it mean to be trauma-informed when a group covers abuse?

29.title: Goals for compulsive sexuality
29.gist: This page lists goals for Session 29 on how people talk about sex, early misinformation, intimacy, and how compulsive sexual behavior develops alongside substance use. It treats sexual compulsion as a parallel recovery issue.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Whether compulsive sexual behavior should be viewed as an addiction is debated. The World Health Organization's ICD-11 lists compulsive sexual behaviour disorder as an impulse-control disorder, while DSM-5 does not include it as a diagnosis.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Any behavior that quickly relieves distress can become a go-to coping strategy. When one is removed, another may grow, which is sometimes called substitution.

ask: How would you distinguish compulsive sexual behavior from a value judgment about someone's sex life?
Why might stopping drugs increase other compulsive behaviors for some people?

30.title: Goals for loss and grief
30.gist: The page lists goals for Session 30 on what addiction took, including relationships, jobs, and decision-making, and what recovery takes away, like rituals of use, plus Session 31 on grief reactions and growth. It frames recovery itself as a kind of loss.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The famous stages of grief come from Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's work with dying patients. Later research suggests people rarely move through neat stages; grief tends to come in waves.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Naming what one lost by quitting, like the rituals, the friends, the excitement, can feel taboo. Yet unmourned losses fuel nostalgia, which can drive relapse.

ask: What might members grieve about giving up drug use that they are reluctant to say aloud?
How is grief complicated for someone who cannot attend a funeral because they are incarcerated?

31.title: Goals for spiritual growth
31.gist: This page lists goals for Session 32 on how spirituality relates to personality change since getting sober, and on types of meditation and how to practice them. It treats recovery as a change in who a person is, not just what they do.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Mindfulness-based relapse prevention, developed by Sarah Bowen, G. Alan Marlatt and colleagues, has shown some benefit in reducing relapse. As with most mindfulness research, results vary and study quality is uneven.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Personality was once thought fixed after early adulthood, but longitudinal studies show traits continue to shift, often becoming more conscientious and emotionally stable with age.

ask: Is personality change in recovery a cause of staying sober or a result of it?
How might meditation be adapted for a loud, crowded housing unit?

32.title: Goals for advanced relapse prevention
32.gist: The page lists goals for Session 33: triggers, building a protective wall across physical, emotional, relational, and spiritual life, personal weak spots, and learning to trust others for help. It turns relapse prevention into a whole-life structure.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Relapse prevention theory stresses self-efficacy, a person's confidence in coping with high-risk situations, a concept from Albert Bandura. Each successful coping experience strengthens it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Trust is a hard sell in prison, where it can be dangerous. Separate trusting everyone from choosing a few people worth testing slowly, and ask what earns trust.

ask: Why might a member who has been betrayed often see self-reliance as a strength rather than a risk?
What would a wall against relapse look like for someone leaving prison with no stable housing?

terms.d: A person's belief that they can successfully perform a behavior or handle a situation.

33.title: Goals for medication and the Steps
33.gist: This page lists goals for Session 34: what medication-assisted treatment is, medications for alcohol and opioid addiction, active Twelve Step participation, and finding meetings that accept people on medication. It bridges two approaches that have sometimes clashed.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Medications such as methadone and buprenorphine are strongly linked with lower overdose deaths in opioid use disorder. The weeks after release from prison carry a very high overdose risk.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some mutual-help members view medication as not truly clean. That stigma can push people off effective treatment, so knowing which meetings are welcoming matters.

ask: How would you respond to a member who says people on methadone are just trading one drug for another?
Why is the period right after release so dangerous for overdose?

terms.d: Using approved medications alongside counseling and support to treat substance use disorders.

34.title: Goals for pain and opioids
34.gist: The page lists many goals for Session 35 on chronic pain and opioids: the pain-addiction cycle, rating pain, multi-part treatment including CBT and physical therapy, careful opioid use, and planning for flare-ups. It addresses a common trap where real pain and addiction feed each other.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Pain is shaped by the brain as well as the body: fear, mood, and attention can amplify or dampen it. This is why CBT and other psychological approaches can reduce suffering even when the injury remains.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: People with addiction histories are sometimes denied adequate pain care. The goal is careful, monitored treatment, not automatic refusal, which can push people toward street drugs.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Validate pain first. A member who feels disbelieved will not hear anything about coping skills.

ask: How do you hold both truths, that someone's pain is real and that opioids may be risky for them?
Why might multi-part pain treatment work better than a single medication?

35.title: Goals for chronic disease
35.gist: The page lists goals for Session 36: understanding chronic diseases and their risk factors, how comorbid conditions and their treatments interact, working with providers, and using diet, exercise, support groups, and health journals. It treats addiction itself as one chronic condition among others.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Comparing addiction to diabetes or hypertension is a common framing: all involve relapse, long-term management, and behavior change. Relapse rates for these illnesses are roughly comparable, which challenges the idea that addiction treatment fails more often.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask a member to name one chronic illness in their family and how that person manages it. Then ask which of those habits might also protect recovery.

ask: What does the chronic-disease framing gain, and what might it lose about personal responsibility and social causes?
How would comorbid illness change the relapse-prevention plan for an older member?

terms.d: Two or more health conditions present in the same person at the same time, often influencing each other.

36.title: Goals for older adults
36.gist: This page lists goals for Session 37: substance use among older adults, how lifelong use affects them now, medication misuse, losses tied to retirement and health, and finding new meaning and activities. It speaks to an aging prison population.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The prison population in the United States is aging, and older incarcerated people often have more chronic illness. Alcohol remains the most commonly misused substance among older adults generally.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Erik Erikson described the late-life tension between integrity and despair: looking back on life and either making peace with it or feeling it was wasted. Recovery can be a path toward integrity even late in life.

ask: How might a long sentence change what losses and meaning look like for an older member?
Why might medication misuse in older adults be missed by both families and doctors?

37.title: Dual diagnosis: how drugs affect minds
37.gist: The page begins the Co-occurring Disorders goals with Session 38: how substances and withdrawal can trigger, mask, mimic, or induce mental health symptoms, including psychosis and depression. It explains why diagnosis during active use is so tricky.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Clinicians often wait for a period of abstinence before diagnosing an independent mental disorder, because intoxication and withdrawal can produce symptoms that clear on their own. Some symptoms, however, persist and need treatment regardless.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A member who says they became paranoid on methamphetamine is describing a known effect, not a personal failing. Normalizing it can open a frank talk about risk.

ask: How would you help a member tell whether their anxiety comes from withdrawal or from an underlying disorder?
Why could masking symptoms with substances make someone believe they do not need help?

38.title: Goals for co-occurring basics and care
38.gist: This page lists goals for Session 39 on the features of addiction and common mental disorders, and Session 40 on a full treatment program, assessments, services, and medications. It builds a shared vocabulary for dual recovery.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Calling these disorders independent brain diseases is a simplification. Many researchers see addiction as involving brain changes while also being shaped by environment, choice, and social conditions.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Diagnostic manuals like DSM-5 classify by symptoms rather than causes. That makes them useful for communication but means two people with the same label can have very different problems.

ask: What are the benefits and risks of telling members that their addiction is a brain disease?
How might assessment feel to someone who has been evaluated mainly to determine punishment?

39.title: Goals for phases and Double Trouble
39.gist: The page lists goals for Session 41 on recovery from co-occurring disorders as a phased biopsychosocial process, and Session 42 on the Double Trouble in Recovery version of the Steps. It adapts familiar recovery ideas for people facing two conditions.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Phase models remind counselors that early recovery needs stabilization, while later recovery can tackle identity and relationships. Pushing deep work too early can overwhelm someone still struggling with symptoms.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Double Trouble in Recovery is a peer fellowship for people with both mental illness and addiction, adapting the Twelve Steps so members can openly discuss psychiatric medication and symptoms.

ask: What would tell you that a member is ready to move from stabilization to deeper work?
Why might standard Twelve Step meetings feel unwelcoming to someone with a psychiatric diagnosis?

40.title: Goals for peer groups and psych meds
40.gist: This page lists goals for Session 43 on how mutual-help groups build hope, reduce shame, and work for people with co-occurring disorders, and Session 44 on psychiatric medications and how to talk with prescribers. It emphasizes being an informed participant in one's own care.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Mutual-help participation is associated with better recovery outcomes, partly through changes in social networks and confidence. A large Cochrane review in 2020 found AA and Twelve Step facilitation generally performed as well as or better than other treatments for alcohol abstinence.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Coach members to prepare two or three questions before a prescriber visit. In prison, appointments are short, so preparation can be the difference between being heard and being rushed.

ask: How do peer groups produce change that professional treatment cannot?
What makes it hard for members to tell a doctor the truth about side effects or substance use?

41.title: Goals for support and decisions
41.gist: The page lists goals for Session 45 on building a recovery support system, home groups, sponsors, and healthy friends, and Session 46 on recovery as small steps and turning off addictive thinking. Both focus on daily choices that keep recovery going.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Social network research suggests that adding even one sober person to someone's circle can shift their recovery. Network support approaches, tested in trials like Project MATCH, target exactly this.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to draw their circle: themselves in the center, then people who help recovery, people who threaten it, and empty spaces. The empty spaces become goals.

ask: What does addictive thinking sound like in your members' own words?
How would you help someone build a support system if most people they know still use?

42.title: Seeking help, then the mini-tracks
42.gist: This page lists goals for Session 47 on choosing treatment systems that fit one's combination and severity of problems, then details Mini-Track 1, which bundles stress, anger, relapse basics, and beliefs sessions for emotional management. It shows how to build a focused program from parts.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Matching treatment to severity reflects the quadrant model, which sorts people by low or high mental health severity and low or high substance severity. Each quadrant suggests a different setting and intensity of care.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: An anger track works best when members do not feel labeled as angry people. Framing it as emotional skill training, like learning to drive in bad weather, keeps defensiveness down.

ask: Why might anger in a correctional group sometimes be a reasonable response that still needs managing?
What would you add to Mini-Track 1 if you were designing it from research?

43.title: Trauma and mutual-support tracks
43.gist: The page details Mini-Track 2, which combines stress, emotion, anger, relapse, beliefs, and sexual abuse sessions for survivors of trauma, and Mini-Track 3, which combines spirituality, self-help, and Twelve Step sessions. It gives two more ready-made paths through the curriculum.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Integrated trauma and addiction programs, such as Lisa Najavits's Seeking Safety, have been tested in correctional settings. They tend to emphasize present-focused coping before any detailed retelling of trauma.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Sequencing matters: placing the sexual abuse session after skills sessions gives members tools before facing hard material. Reversing that order could increase distress.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pick one member you know well and ask which track would serve them best. Then ask why you chose it: is it their need or what is easiest to deliver?

ask: What safeguards would you need before running a trauma track in a prison?
Why might peer support tracks be especially valuable right before release?

44.title: Contact information and references
44.gist: This short page lists where to get more information and the references behind the program, including works by Carroll on cognitive-behavioral treatment of cocaine addiction and Miller on motivation. It points to the scientific roots of the curriculum.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Kathleen Carroll's manual for cognitive-behavioral treatment of cocaine use, published by NIDA, describes functional analysis and coping skills training. It is a good primary source for understanding the CBT elements in this program.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Choose one reference and read its summary. Checking a program's sources is a scientist-practitioner habit that keeps marketing claims honest.

ask: How old are these references, and what has changed in addiction science since?
Which source would you read first to deepen your delivery of this program?

45.title: Federal registry review begins
45.gist: This page starts a federal evidence-registry report that summarizes the program, lists measured outcomes such as retention, drug use, and crime, and notes it was tested in outpatient and correctional settings. It is an outside view of the evidence.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The registry that produced this report, SAMHSA's National Registry of Evidence-based Programs and Practices, was discontinued in 2018 amid criticism of its review standards. Its listings remain useful history but are not current endorsements.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Being listed in a registry meant a program met review criteria, not that it outperformed alternatives. Read the outcome details rather than the badge.

ask: What would make a program evidence-based in your own eyes?
Why might listing seven outcomes create an impression of strength even if few differ between groups?

terms.d: Teaching people about their condition and recovery as part of treatment.

46.title: Study details and retention results
46.gist: The page describes the main randomized trial with six conditions and reports that this program and enhanced groups kept clients longer, with higher completion than usual group therapy alone. Retention is the program's strongest evidence.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Usual group therapy met twice weekly for shorter sessions, while this program met five times a week. More available contact could explain much of the retention difference, not just better content.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Early dropout is common in addiction treatment, and many people leave in the first week. Anything that helps people survive that first stretch increases their chance of benefiting.

ask: What features of a program might reduce dropout in the first week?
How would you test whether content or dose explains better retention?

terms.d: A study that assigns participants by chance to different treatments so differences in outcomes can be attributed to the treatment.

47.title: Exposure and cocaine outcomes
47.gist: This page reports that clients in the program's conditions attended far more sessions, and that weekly cocaine use dropped sharply from intake to the year-later follow-up across everyone. It also notes no significant differences between conditions on drug use.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Since all six groups were combined for drug use outcomes, the decline cannot be credited to this program specifically. Improvement over time can also come from regression to the mean or simply from people entering treatment at a low point.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Regression to the mean is the tendency for extreme measurements to move toward average on retesting. People often enter treatment at their worst, so some improvement is expected regardless.

ask: If all treatments improved outcomes equally, what argument remains for using this one?
How would you explain regression to the mean to a group in plain words?

terms.d: The tendency for unusually high or low scores to be closer to average when measured again.

48.title: Dose and alcohol findings
48.gist: The page shows that clients who stayed longer and attended more sessions were less likely to be regular cocaine or alcohol users a year later, and regular alcohol use fell overall. It links staying in treatment with better results.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: This is correlation, not causation. People who stay longer may already be more motivated or stable, so retention could be a marker of readiness rather than the cause of improvement.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The report notes the effect of each extra session was very small, while heavy use at intake strongly predicted later use. Where someone starts often matters more than any single treatment variable.

ask: How would you separate the effect of treatment from the effect of motivation in this data?
What does it mean for your work that baseline severity predicts outcomes so strongly?

terms.d: A measure comparing the odds of an outcome in one group with the odds in another; 1 means no difference.

49.title: Other drugs and crime outcomes
49.gist: This page reports declines in weekly use of other drugs and in drug-related illegal activity at follow-up, with those still using or offending more likely to have left treatment early. Non-drug crime fell slightly but not significantly.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The pattern that drug-related crime fell more than other crime fits the idea that some offending is driven by addiction itself. Offending rooted in criminal thinking or peers may need separate targets, such as those in CBI-style programs.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Crime here was self-reported and not checked against arrest records. Self-reports of illegal acts can be biased, especially when people fear consequences.

ask: Why might drug treatment alone reduce drug-related crime but not other crime?
How does this support combining substance use treatment with criminal thinking work?

50.title: Drug sales and research quality
50.gist: The page reports a drop in drug sales at follow-up, describes the study population as mostly Black adults, and introduces six criteria reviewers used to rate research quality. It shifts from results to how trustworthy those results are.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Reliability means a measure gives consistent results; validity means it measures what it claims to. A measure can be reliable but invalid, like a scale that is always five pounds off.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Run one of your group's tools through the six criteria: is it reliable, valid, delivered with fidelity, missing data, confounded, analyzed properly? It is a quick way to think like a reviewer.

ask: How might the population studied limit how well these results apply to your groups?
Which of the six criteria do you think is most often weak in correctional program research?

terms.d: How closely a program is delivered as designed.
An outside factor linked to both treatment and outcome that can create a false appearance of effect.

51.title: Ratings, strengths, weaknesses
51.gist: This page shows the reviewers' ratings, with fidelity scored lowest, and lists strengths such as random assignment and checked self-reports, and weaknesses including no fidelity monitoring and confounded treatment exposure. It is a candid outside critique of the evidence.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Low fidelity ratings mean no one checked whether counselors delivered the program as written. Without that, it is hard to know what was actually tested.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This page is a reason to take the program's fidelity scorecard seriously. Your own consistency is part of what makes the evidence meaningful in your setting.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Treatment exposure being built into the design is like comparing two gyms by how often members visit when one gym is open twice as many days. The comparison is unfair from the start.

ask: What would it take to monitor fidelity in your setting without making it feel like surveillance?
How should weaknesses like these change the confidence you express to clients or staff?

52.title: Dissemination readiness and costs
52.gist: The page rates how ready the program is for wide use, praising organized materials and a fidelity tool while noting limited guidance on implementation and quality assurance, then lists costs and states no replications were identified. It completes the outside review.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: No replications is a serious gap. In science, findings from a single trial are fragile until repeated by other teams in other settings.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Implementation science studies why proven programs fail in real settings: staff turnover, poor training, and lack of support. A good program delivered badly may help no one.

ask: Why does replication matter so much, especially for programs used in prisons?
What obstacles to implementation do you see in your own facility?

terms.d: Repeating a study, often by different researchers, to see whether the results hold.

53.title: Quick start: opening a session
53.gist: The page lays out a six-step group format and details the first two steps: a brief check-in and an optional relaxation exercise using a repeated word and gentle return to the breath. It gives every session a predictable, calming start.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The relaxation steps closely follow Herbert Benson's Relaxation Response: a quiet setting, a repeated word, and a passive attitude toward distractions. Benson drew this from studying meditation practices.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Suggesting om may feel foreign or religious to some members. Offering neutral words like calm, or a word from their own language, keeps everyone included.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The instruction not to worry about success matters: trying hard to relax tends to backfire. Gently returning attention is itself the exercise, not a failure.

ask: What does a good check-in reveal that the rest of the session might miss?
How would you adapt a ten-minute relaxation for a group that keeps laughing or talking?

54.title: Quick start: running and closing
54.gist: This page covers the remaining steps: a session overview, reading and discussing the content, optional videos, role-plays and visualizations, and a closing summary. It shows that most of the session time goes to guided discussion, not lecture.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Role-play builds skills through behavioral rehearsal, a method Bandura's social learning theory supports: people learn by doing and by watching peers model new behavior, then getting feedback.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Reading aloud every section can drain energy. Rotate readers, pause for quick reactions, and cut repetitive passages so discussion gets the most time.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: End your next session by asking each member for a single word that captures what they are taking away. It is a fast summary and shows you what landed.

ask: What makes a role-play feel real rather than silly in a prison group?
How would you balance following the format with responding to what the group brings that day?

55.title: Fidelity scorecard: delivery checklist
55.gist: The page introduces a scorecard for counselors or supervisors to rate session delivery, starting with a checklist of preparation and format steps, from room setup through the closing summary. It turns the session format into something you can observe and improve.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: In correctional program research, quality of delivery matters: well-implemented programs tend to produce larger reductions in reoffending than poorly delivered versions of the same model.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Score yourself on one recent session, then ask a colleague to score you on the next. The gap between the two ratings is often the most useful information.

ask: Which checklist items do you tend to skip when time is short, and what might that cost?
How could a fidelity tool be used to support counselors rather than police them?

56.title: Fidelity scorecard: quality of interaction
56.gist: This page rates how the counselor interacts: energy, nonjudgmental rapport, checking understanding, cultural relevance, motivational interviewing, CBT, reinforcement, and checking for triggers and emotional impact before members leave. It captures the skills that separate delivery from reading a script.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The therapeutic alliance, the bond and shared goals between counselor and client, is one of the most consistent predictors of outcome across therapies. These items largely measure alliance-building behaviors.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Checking for triggers at the end matters more in prison, where members return to a unit with no one to process with. A two-minute grounding close can prevent a hard evening.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Ratings like enthusiasm or effective MI use are subjective. Without clear examples of what a three versus a four looks like, two raters may score the same session differently.

ask: Which of these nine items do you believe matters most for outcomes, and why?
What signs would show that a member left a session more distressed than they arrived?

terms.d: The collaborative bond between counselor and client, including agreement on goals and tasks.

59.title: Session 13 opens: self-help groups
59.gist: The session introduces self-help groups such as AA and NA, plus alternatives to the Twelve Steps, in three parts: what groups do, Twelve Step fellowships, and alternative programs. It sets up peer support as a core recovery resource after release.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Engagement with mutual-help groups after treatment is linked with better abstinence outcomes. The benefit seems to grow with active involvement, not just attendance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members attended meetings because a court ordered it. Ask what that was like before selling the benefits; mandated attendance often leaves resentment that needs airing.

ask: How might coerced attendance at meetings affect later voluntary involvement?
Why would offering alternatives up front make the session more persuasive?

60.title: What the session asks of members
60.gist: This page explains members will examine secrecy, isolation, trust, and honesty, explore Twelve Step features like the Serenity Prayer, and weigh alternatives, then starts Part 1 on how peers empower one another. It frames sharing as the engine of these groups.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Irvin Yalom described therapeutic factors in groups, including universality, the relief of discovering others share your struggle, and instillation of hope from seeing others improve. Self-help groups run largely on these factors.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The helper therapy principle, described by Frank Riessman, suggests that helping others benefits the helper too. Service roles in recovery groups put this into practice.

ask: Which of Yalom's group factors can you deliberately strengthen in your own sessions?
How does the prison code against showing weakness conflict with the logic of self-help groups?

terms.d: The relief of realizing others share your problems, one of the healing factors in group therapy.

61.title: Secrecy, shame, and going it alone
61.gist: The page explains that shame drives people with addiction to hide it and try to quit alone, a common reason attempts fail, and Exercise 1 asks members whether they kept their use secret and how it isolated them. It invites personal reflection on hiding.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Shame pushes people to hide, and hiding cuts them off from the help that would reduce shame. Breaking secrecy interrupts that loop, which is why disclosure in a safe group can be so powerful.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In a correctional group, members may have good reasons for secrecy, like legal risk. Debrief by separating hiding from people who could help from protecting yourself from people who could harm.

ask: How do you tell healthy privacy from isolating secrecy?
Why might people believe they can quit alone even after many failed tries?

62.title: Still isolated? Recovery is one process
62.gist: The worksheet continues by asking whether members still feel isolated, then the text argues that addiction and recovery follow similar paths regardless of drug. The focus therefore shifts from the specific substance to the shared process of getting sober.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Many addictions share core features: craving, loss of control, and continued use despite harm. This shared pathway is why groups can mix people with different drugs of choice.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Recovery is not identical across drugs. Opioid use disorder has effective medications, and alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal can be medically dangerous, so specific differences still matter.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prison can be crowded and lonely at once. When debriefing the isolation question, invite members to notice that feeling alone in a full unit is common, not strange.

ask: What do people lose when their recovery story is defined only by their drug of choice?
How is isolation in prison different from isolation during active use?

63.title: Addiction and recovery as processes
63.gist: Exercise 2 asks members to explain how both addiction and recovery unfold over time rather than in one decision. It plants the idea that sobriety is built daily, not won once.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Prochaska and DiClemente's stages of change describe movement from precontemplation through action to maintenance, often with recycling back. Seeing change as a cycle makes setbacks less of a verdict on the person.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members often describe getting arrested as the moment they quit. Debrief by asking what came before and after that moment, so they see a longer story with choices on both sides.

ask: If recovery is a process, what counts as success on any given day?
How might the event view of quitting set someone up for shame after a lapse?

terms.d: A model describing change as moving through precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, and maintenance.

64.title: How AA began and works
64.gist: The page tells how two men in the 1930s discovered that helping each other kept them sober, founding AA, its Big Book, and Steps later adapted to other drugs and behaviors. It stresses that fellowships have no leaders, dues, or rolls, only a desire to stop.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: AA's founders, known as Bill W. and Dr. Bob, met in Akron, Ohio, in 1935. Bill had been influenced by the Oxford Group, a Christian movement, which helps explain the program's spiritual language.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The discovery that one alcoholic talking to another helped both is an early example of what later research calls helper therapy: giving support strengthens the giver's own commitment.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Leaderless groups vary widely in quality. Without professional oversight, some meetings can be welcoming and wise while others carry bad advice or predatory members.

ask: Why might people who share a problem help each other in ways professionals cannot?
What does anonymity protect, and what might it cost a group?

65.title: What fellowship means
65.gist: Exercise 3 asks members what the word fellowship means to them and what they gain from others' support in recovery. It moves them from hearing about groups to imagining being in one.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking people to name advantages in their own words is a motivational technique: self-generated reasons are more persuasive than ones handed to them. Miller and Rollnick call this eliciting change talk.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In prison, fellowship may first evoke gangs or crews. Use that: ask what loyalty and belonging gave them there, and what a sober version of belonging would need.

ask: How is fellowship in recovery different from belonging to a crew, and what do they share?
What would make a member willing to accept support from strangers?

66.title: Many kinds of Twelve Step groups
66.gist: The page explains that Twelve Step programs are one kind of self-help and lists fellowships for different drugs, for families like Al-Anon, for behaviors such as gambling and debt, and for people with dual diagnoses. It shows the format is widely adaptable.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Al-Anon, founded in the early 1950s with Lois W., Bill W.'s wife, among its founders, recognizes that addiction harms the whole family. It offers families their own recovery rather than just ways to fix the drinker.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name one person in their life who might benefit from a family group like Al-Anon or Nar-Anon. It widens recovery beyond the self.

ask: Why would a format built for alcohol transfer to gambling, eating, or debt?
What does it say about addiction that families need their own recovery groups?

67.title: Meeting types and first steps
67.gist: This page describes speaker, topic, Step, and Big Book meetings, notes each group has its own personality, and explains how to attend a first meeting: go with someone, arrive early, stay late, and introduce yourself. It makes the unknown feel concrete.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Shopping for a meeting is a key message. Many people quit after one bad meeting; normalize trying several before judging the whole program.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Run a quick mock first meeting: one member plays a newcomer, another greets them. Rehearsal lowers the anxiety that keeps people from walking through the door.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Arriving early and staying late is about building social ties, not the meeting content. Research suggests relationships formed in groups are a key reason they help.

ask: What barriers would make a newly released member skip a first meeting?
How could you connect members with a meeting before their release date?

68.title: Spiritual, not religious, not therapy
68.gist: The page explains that Twelve Step groups describe themselves as spiritual rather than religious and are peer support rather than therapy, then Exercise 4 offers multiple-choice items on why meetings work and what counts as a good reason not to go. It addresses common objections head-on.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Many people find the God language in the Steps religious, and some US courts have ruled that mandating AA attendance can violate the separation of church and state. Acknowledging this honestly builds credibility.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The second question has a built-in answer, none of the above. Debrief by letting members argue the other options first; their objections are real and deserve a response, not a correction.

ask: Is the distinction between spiritual and religious convincing to you? Why or why not?
How do you respect a member's objection to groups while still encouraging support?

69.title: Honesty and the hard shell
69.gist: The text explains that addiction teaches people to fake it behind a hard shell, which protects but blocks growth, and that meetings only help if one is honest. Exercise 5 asks members how strong their defenses are and how they blocked honesty.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The shell metaphor resembles what sociologist Erving Goffman called front-stage performance: managing how others see us. In prison, the front stage may be constant and survival-driven.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Do not ask members to drop their shell in the unit, where it may protect them. Frame honesty as choosing safe places to take it off.

ask: How might a member's shell be both a survival skill and a recovery barrier?
What would a gradual path to honesty look like in a group that just formed?

70.title: Gains and losses of dishonesty
70.gist: The worksheet continues by asking whether members need honesty from others, and what lying gained and cost them. It sets up a personal cost-benefit look at deception.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Weighing what lying gained and lost is a decisional balance, a motivational interviewing tool. Naming the real benefits first makes the costs feel less like a lecture and more like their own conclusion.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect members to say they want others' honesty but find their own hard. Point out the double standard gently, as something everyone shares rather than an accusation.

ask: Why do people often demand more honesty from others than they give?
What would you say to a member who claims lying kept them alive?

terms.d: Weighing the pros and cons of a behavior and of changing it, to clarify motivation.

71.title: Learning to trust again
71.gist: The page defines trust as believing someone is truthful and reliable plus expecting good from them, notes addiction trains lying and cheating, and describes drugs forming a triangle in relationships. Exercise 6 begins by asking how use broke trust in oneself and others.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Psychologist Erik Erikson put trust versus mistrust as the first stage of development. Many members learned early that people were unreliable, and addiction deepened that lesson.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Trust rebuilds through small, repeated, kept promises. One grand gesture rarely repairs it; consistency over time does.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The triangle image works well on a whiteboard: two people with the drug in the middle. Ask members who else was in their triangles.

ask: What does trusting oneself mean for someone who has broken many promises to themselves?
How can a person tell whether someone has earned trust?

72.title: What earns trust, and a trap
72.gist: The worksheet asks what members expect before trusting others, what builds trust both ways, and whether they have threatened relapse when not trusted. That last question exposes a common way people punish others by hurting themselves.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Saying I might as well use if you treat me like a user is a cognitive distortion: it shifts responsibility for one's choice onto another person's distrust. It mirrors victim stance thinking described in criminal thinking work by Yochelson and Samenow.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Validate the hurt of not being trusted before naming the trap. Then ask who pays if they act on that threat.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members write one small, checkable promise they can keep this week. Trust becomes a skill they practice rather than a feeling they wait for.

ask: Why does being distrusted feel like permission to use for some people?
How long should family members reasonably take to trust someone again?

73.title: The Serenity Prayer
73.gist: The page presents the Serenity Prayer used at many meetings, and Exercise 7 asks members what it means to them and whether they live by it. It introduces the core idea of sorting what can and cannot be changed.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The prayer is generally credited to theologian Reinhold Niebuhr in the twentieth century. AA adopted it in the 1940s, and it spread far beyond recovery circles.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The prayer maps onto modern coping research: problem-focused coping for what can change and emotion-focused coping or acceptance for what cannot. Matching the strategy to the situation is linked with better adjustment.

ask: How do you know the difference between something you cannot change and something you are afraid to change?
Can the prayer's ideas work for a member who does not believe in God?

74.title: Acceptance, courage, and sponsors
74.gist: The worksheet asks members to list what they cannot change and what they have courage to change, then introduces sponsors as guides through the confusing early months of recovery. It links personal reflection to a concrete support step.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members serving long sentences may list their sentence as the thing they cannot change. Help them find what is still in play: how they spend the time, who they become, what relationships they keep.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Having a sponsor early in Twelve Step involvement is associated with better abstinence outcomes in several studies, though motivated people may be more likely to seek sponsors in the first place.

ask: What would courage look like for someone who cannot leave prison for years?
How would you help a member choose a sponsor wisely?

75.title: What sponsors do and who to pick
75.gist: The page lists a sponsor's roles, answering questions, listening, suggesting solutions, keeping confidences, and pushing for help after a slip, and describes a good sponsor: years sober, stable, active in the program, respected, and not a romantic interest. It turns a vague idea into a selection guide.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A sponsor is a living model of recovery. Bandura's work shows people learn by watching someone similar succeed, so a sponsor who shares one's background can be especially persuasive.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The same-sex rule assumes everyone is heterosexual. For gay, lesbian, or bisexual members the point is avoiding romantic interest, which may mean a different choice than the rule suggests.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In prison, members may be wary of anyone who wants to know their secrets. Talk about how to test a potential sponsor's confidentiality slowly.

ask: What would make a sponsor relationship unhealthy, and how would a newcomer notice?
Can someone in prison have a sponsor, and what would that look like?

terms.d: An experienced member of a Twelve Step group who guides a newer member through the program.

76.title: True or false: sponsor basics
76.gist: Exercise 8 offers true-or-false statements about sponsors, on choosing one of the same sex, how quickly to find one, and whether they give advice, each with space to explain. It checks understanding while inviting members' own reasoning.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking people to explain a true-or-false answer turns recognition into reasoning. The explanation reveals misunderstandings that a checkmark would hide.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The item on taking as long as you want is a good debate starter. Some will argue rushing leads to a poor choice; others that waiting leaves you unsupported when you most need it. Both have a point.

ask: Why might a newcomer delay asking someone to be their sponsor?
What is the difference between advice and guidance, and which should a sponsor offer?

77.title: Boundaries, then secular alternatives
77.gist: The worksheet ends with whether sponsors lend money or housing, then Part 3 explains that some people are uncomfortable with the Higher Power, notes agnostic AA meetings, and introduces secular groups focused on responsibility and sober networks. It presents alternatives as partners rather than rivals.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies comparing secular groups with AA suggest that involvement in any mutual-help group is linked with better outcomes. Fit and participation may matter more than which philosophy a group follows.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The money and housing question is about boundaries. Ask what happens to a support relationship when it becomes a financial one.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Twelve Step meetings far outnumber alternatives, especially in prisons and small towns. Recommending an alternative is only useful if a member can actually reach one, online or in person.

ask: Why might mixing support and money damage a sponsor relationship?
How would you help a member who rejects AA but has no alternative nearby?

78.title: Your view of a Higher Power
78.gist: The page names three alternatives, SMART Recovery, Women for Sobriety, and Secular Organizations for Sobriety, and Exercise 9 asks members how they feel about the term Higher Power and what specifically makes them uneasy. It gives space for doubt without judgment.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will describe their Higher Power as the group, nature, or their children. Treat each as valid; the point is something larger than one's own craving.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Philosophers distinguish theism, belief in God, from broader spirituality, a sense of meaning or connection. Members may have strong views on one and none on the other.

ask: What does a Higher Power do psychologically for someone in recovery?
How might a member's religious upbringing, including painful experiences with religion, shape their answer?

79.title: Secular Organizations for Sobriety
79.gist: The page describes SOS, founded by James Christopher as an alternative to AA, with confidential meetings, one day at a time, admitting the problem, and a sole focus on sobriety. Exercise 10 asks how treating spirituality as separate from sobriety would affect members.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: SOS keeps much of AA's structure while removing the spiritual layer. That suggests some of what helps in AA may be the social and ritual elements rather than the theology.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members who reject God whether they had dismissed groups altogether. Learning that a secular path exists can reopen a door they had closed.

ask: Which parts of AA would you guess are doing most of the helping?
Can sobriety and personal growth really be separated?

80.title: Sobriety first, and SMART Recovery
80.gist: The worksheet asks what making sobriety the top priority means, then introduces SMART Recovery: CBT-based tools, self-reliance, no addict labels, no sponsors, and the expectation that people eventually move on from meetings. It offers a skills-focused option.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: SMART Recovery draws on Albert Ellis's rational emotive behavior therapy and on motivational interviewing. Ellis was involved in its early development.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Making sobriety the top priority can sound selfish to people with children or parents depending on them. Reframe it: without sobriety, the other priorities are at risk.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Not requiring the label addict reflects concern that labels can become fixed identities. Others find naming the problem freeing. Both views have defenders.

ask: What are the risks and benefits of calling oneself an addict for life?
Why might a CBT-based group appeal to members who distrust spiritual language?

81.title: Self-reliance versus a Higher Power
81.gist: Exercise 11 asks members to weigh the benefits and drawbacks of SMART Recovery's self-reliance and whether its therapy-based methods appeal to them. It invites a genuine comparison rather than a single right answer.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-reliance builds self-efficacy, while surrender to a Higher Power can relieve the exhausting sense of fighting alone. Different people need different balances, and the same person may need both at different times.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members who pride themselves on independence may favor self-reliance. Ask whether going it alone has worked before, linking back to the earlier talk on isolation.

ask: Is self-reliance the opposite of seeking support, or can it include it?
Which members of your group might do best in SMART, and why?

82.title: Women for Sobriety
82.gist: The page describes Women for Sobriety, created by Jean Kirkpatrick to empower women rather than burden them with guilt, using Thirteen Statements and positive self-introductions. Exercise 12 asks why a program designed for women might be useful.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Women often enter addiction with different paths, such as higher rates of trauma, and face stronger stigma, particularly as mothers. Gender-responsive treatment developed partly from these differences.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In a men's group, this page can open a conversation about what men need from recovery. What would a program designed for men's specific struggles look like?

ask: What might a guilt-focused approach do to someone already overwhelmed by shame?
How could positive self-statements help, and when might they ring false?

83.title: The past, amends, and session close
83.gist: The worksheet asks members to weigh the Twelve Step practice of reviewing the past and making amends against Women for Sobriety's view that the past is gone, then the summary recaps isolation, trust, honesty, and the range of self-help options. It ends with a real philosophical choice.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: This echoes an old debate: whether healing requires facing the past, as in Freud's tradition, or focusing on the present and future, as in many cognitive and solution-focused approaches. Most current therapies blend both.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For members whose crimes harmed others, the past cannot simply be left behind. Distinguish not dwelling in shame from taking responsibility, which still matters.

ask: Can a person take responsibility for the past without being defined by it?
When might making amends do more harm than good?
