84.title: Role-play: late from work
84.gist: This role-play shows a man six months sober who keeps coming home late, his frightened wife confronting him, an angry clash over trust, and his sponsor inviting him to a meeting that conflicts with their dinner. It puts the session's themes of trust and support into motion.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The scene shows how early recovery strains families: the person in recovery wants credit for change, while the family still carries fear from years of lies. Both reactions make sense.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Cross-gender role-plays may not be possible in single-sex prison groups. Let members play either role, or have one member narrate the wife's lines.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pause the scene right before he storms out and ask the group for three different things he could say instead. Then replay the best one.

ask: Why does distrust feel so unfair to someone working hard on recovery?
What would John need to hear to stay calm in this moment?

85.title: Role-play debrief questions
85.gist: The role-play continues with discussion questions asking about the couple's strengths and the problems that could undermine them. It pushes the group to see both resources and risks in the same relationship.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking about strengths first reflects a strengths-based approach: people engage more when their resources are noticed, not just their deficits.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members may side strongly with one partner. Gently ask the group to argue the other side, which builds empathy and perspective-taking.

ask: What strengths might a family bring to recovery even after years of harm?
How could both partners seeking their own support groups help the relationship?

86.title: Contacts for alternative groups
86.gist: The page lists contact details for Secular Organizations for Sobriety, SMART Recovery, Women for Sobriety, and Dual Recovery Anonymous. It gives members a practical way to follow up on the session's alternatives.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Contact details in printed manuals go out of date. Before handing this out, check current information, and note that several of these groups now offer online meetings.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Help a member about to be released write down one group they will contact in the first week and when. A specific plan beats a general intention.

ask: How might online meetings change access for members after release?
What would stop a member from contacting a group after leaving prison?

87.title: Session 14 opens: the Twelve Steps
87.gist: The session introduces the Twelve Steps used by AA and NA, in two parts: what each Step asks, and the principles by which they work. It moves from knowing about meetings to understanding the program's actual content.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Anthropologist Gregory Bateson wrote a well-known essay on AA arguing that the alcoholic's pride in self-control is part of the problem, and that admitting defeat changes the person's whole relationship with drinking.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members have heard the Steps recited without anyone explaining them. Ask who has worked any Steps before; their experience can make the session more vivid than the text.

ask: Why might a program built on surrender attract people whose lives have been shaped by control and violence?
What would you need to know to present the Steps fairly to a skeptic?

88.title: Step One: admitting powerlessness
88.gist: The page explains the Steps came from what worked for early AA members, are practiced continually rather than finished, and begins Step One, admitting powerlessness and unmanageability, framed as humility. It tackles the hardest idea first.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some critics, including feminist and trauma-informed writers, argue that powerlessness can be harmful for people who have been oppressed or abused. Others read it narrowly, as powerlessness over the drug only, not over one's whole life.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: There is a paradox here: admitting limited control over a substance can increase control over the rest of life, because a person stops relying on willpower in moments where it fails and builds other supports.

ask: How do you reconcile Step One's powerlessness with relapse prevention's emphasis on self-efficacy?
What would powerlessness mean to someone who already feels powerless inside prison?

89.title: Relief in not being to blame
89.gist: The text says admitting powerlessness can bring relief, since failure was not simply a lack of willpower, and Exercise 1 asks how members were powerless and whether it helps to know others were too. It reframes defeat as release.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Attribution theory helps here: blaming failure on a fixed flaw in oneself leads to hopelessness, while seeing it as caused by a condition that can be treated invites action. The Step offers a less shaming explanation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will hear not your fault as an excuse for crimes. Separate the compulsion to use from responsibility for what one did, both of which can be true.

ask: Can someone be powerless over a substance and still responsible for their actions?
Why might shared powerlessness feel comforting rather than discouraging?

90.title: Unmanageability and Step Two
90.gist: The worksheet asks how life became unmanageable, then Step Two is explained: the craziness of addictive behavior, the hope that life can be restored, a greater Power's role, and how restoration happens, often after several attempts. It shifts from defeat to hope.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Many people who achieve lasting recovery have tried to quit several times before. Multiple attempts are a common path, not proof that someone cannot succeed.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The old line, often wrongly attributed to Einstein, that insanity is repeating the same thing and expecting different results, captures Step Two's idea of insanity. It is about behavior, not mental illness.

ask: What does restored to sanity mean for someone who never had a stable normal to return to?
How can hope be offered without sounding naive to people with many failed attempts?

91.title: Insanity, healing, a greater Power
91.gist: Exercise 2 asks members to describe their own crazy addiction-driven behavior, whether they believe healing is possible, and what a Power greater than themselves means to them. It joins honest self-review with hope.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Stories of crazy behavior can drift into war stories that glorify use. Steer the debrief toward what the behavior cost and what it reveals about the compulsion.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Hope is a measurable factor in change. C. R. Snyder's hope theory describes it as having both goals and believable pathways to reach them, not just a good feeling.

ask: How do you tell a member's war story apart from honest reflection?
What answers might a non-religious member give to the Power question that still fulfill the Step?

terms.d: Retelling past drug use in a way that glamorizes it, which can trigger craving in listeners.

92.title: Step Three: letting go of control
92.gist: The page explains Step Three as choosing to stop battling problems with willpower alone and turning one's will over to a Higher Power, which eases obsessing over the uncontrollable. Exercise 3 asks what happened when members tried to control their lives while using.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, developed by Steven Hayes, makes a similar point in secular terms: struggling to control unwanted thoughts and urges often makes them stronger, while accepting them frees energy for valued action.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members may see giving up control as dangerous, since in prison losing control can mean losing safety. Clarify that the Step is about letting go of what you never truly controlled.

ask: What is the difference between giving up control and giving up responsibility?
Why might effort and willpower make cravings worse?

93.title: Step Four: the moral inventory
93.gist: The text completes the control question, then explains Step Four as a searching look at one's behavior, attitudes, and beliefs, showing how addiction twists normal desires into harm and naming pride, greed, lust, anger, selfishness, envy, and laziness. It asks for unflinching self-examination.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The list of failings closely echoes the seven deadly sins of Christian tradition. AA's inventory carries forward a very old practice of examining conscience.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The inventory resembles a cognitive review: examining attitudes and beliefs that drive behavior. It overlaps with the thinking reports used in CBI programs.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: An inventory focused only on defects can deepen shame. Many sponsors also encourage listing strengths, which keeps the process honest rather than punishing.

ask: How would you keep an inventory from becoming self-punishment?
What would a searching inventory look like for someone with a history of violence?

94.title: How using bent your thinking
94.gist: Exercise 4 asks how attitudes toward others changed while using, whether thinking shifted after stopping, and for examples of normal feelings becoming exaggerated and hurtful. It helps members see the drug's effect on character, not just behavior.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Substances can impair the prefrontal cortex, which supports judgment and empathy, while sharpening the drive for reward. This gives a biological angle to why people acted in ways they now regret.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask for one concrete example rather than general statements. A specific moment, like a broken promise to a child, carries more insight than I was selfish.

ask: How can members tell which harmful traits came from using and which existed before?
What risks come from blaming all past behavior on substances?

95.title: Step Five: telling someone
95.gist: The page asks whether self-examination is hard, then explains Step Five: admitting wrongs to God, oneself, and another person, a safety valve that relieves the pain and loneliness of the inventory and opens forgiveness. It is traditionally done with a sponsor or clergy.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: James Pennebaker's research on expressive writing found that putting painful experiences into words can improve mood and even physical health for some people. Disclosure seems to help people make sense of what happened.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Remind members that disclosures in a correctional setting have limits on confidentiality. Some admissions are better saved for a sponsor or clergy outside the group.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Confession appears across religions, from Catholic confession to Jewish practices of repentance. Step Five borrows an ancient human technology for releasing guilt.

ask: Why does telling another person relieve guilt in ways that private reflection may not?
What safeguards should someone in prison consider before doing a Fifth Step?

96.title: Who could hear your Fifth Step
96.gist: Exercise 5 asks whether members have felt relief after sharing something personal and whether they have someone in mind for the Fifth Step, and how to approach or find that person. It turns an abstract Step into a practical plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Recalling a past experience of relief from sharing is a form of evidence gathering: it reminds members that vulnerability has helped them before, which lowers the fear of trying again.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members will say no one comes to mind. Brainstorm safe options available inside, such as a chaplain or a long-sober peer, and outside after release.

ask: What qualities make someone safe to hear a confession?
How does the lack of trusted people in a member's life affect their recovery plan?

97.title: Step Six: willing to change
97.gist: The page explains Step Six as recognizing defects, believing they can be removed, and being willing to let them go, repeatedly and without expecting perfection, while affirming that having faults does not make someone bad. Exercise 6 asks how members feel about changing who they are.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Separating the person from the behavior reduces shame and supports change. Shame says I am bad; guilt says I did something bad, and only the second points toward repair.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Carol Dweck's research on mindsets suggests people who see traits as changeable are more likely to persist. Step Six assumes exactly this kind of growth view of character.

ask: Why is willingness to change harder than wanting to change?
How might a lifelong identity, like being tough, feel threatened by Step Six?

98.title: Progress, not perfection; Step Seven
98.gist: The worksheet asks what progress, not perfection means to members, then Step Seven is introduced: humbly asking for shortcomings to be removed, which requires moving past the self-reliance learned while using. Humility returns as the theme.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Perfectionism is a known risk factor for relapse: one mistake can feel like total failure, triggering the abstinence violation effect described by Marlatt. Progress, not perfection is a direct antidote.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Humility can sound like weakness in a prison culture. Reframe it as accurate self-knowledge: knowing exactly what you can and cannot do alone.

ask: How is humility different from low self-esteem?
When has self-reliance helped your members survive, and when has it hurt them?

terms.d: The tendency after a slip to feel total failure and give up, making a full relapse more likely.

99.title: What humility means
99.gist: Exercise 7 asks members to define humility in their own words and connect it to defects of character. It invites a personal meaning for a word that recurs across the Steps.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Psychologists studying intellectual humility describe it as recognizing the limits of one's knowledge and being open to correction. It is linked with better learning and relationships, not with weakness.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect some to equate humility with being humiliated, something many have experienced in custody. Separate the two clearly: humiliation is imposed, humility is chosen.

ask: How can someone practice humility in an environment that punishes looking weak?
Is humility a feeling, a belief, or a behavior?

100.title: Step Eight: the list of harms
100.gist: The page explains Step Eight as listing those one has harmed and becoming willing to make amends, dealing with the past so it stops controlling the present, not to wallow in guilt. Exercise 8 asks how much guilt members carry and what it does to them.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Restorative justice, associated with Howard Zehr, focuses on repairing harm rather than only punishing it. Step Eight shares that logic: accountability means facing the people affected.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Unresolved guilt can act like a background stressor that drives the urge to numb. Turning guilt into a list with possible actions makes it something to work on rather than something to carry.

ask: How would you help a member whose list includes people they harmed through crime, not just through use?
When does guilt motivate change and when does it paralyze?

101.title: Step Nine: making direct amends
101.gist: The worksheet asks if addicted behavior differs from one's normal self, then explains Step Nine: making direct amends wherever possible unless that would harm them or others, as the start of healthier relationships. Exercise 9 asks whether facing those harms is hard.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Direct amends can be impossible or unlawful in correctional settings, for example when no-contact orders exist with victims. Living amends, changing how one behaves, and indirect amends are important alternatives.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The idea that addicted behavior is not one's real self can help reduce shame, but it can also be used to dodge responsibility. Encourage members to own both the behavior and the change.

ask: What does making amends look like when contact would hurt the other person?
Is there a risk that amends serve the person apologizing more than the person harmed?

102.title: When amends worked or failed
102.gist: The worksheet asks about advantages of amends and whether members have sincerely made one, whether it helped, and why it may have failed. It treats past attempts as learning material.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Research on apologies suggests that effective ones acknowledge specific harm, accept responsibility, and offer repair. Apologies that include excuses or demand forgiveness often fail.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to compare a sorry, I was high with an amends that names the harm and offers change. Let the group identify what makes the second land differently.

ask: Why might an amends fail even when it is sincere?
What should a person do when someone refuses to accept their amends?

103.title: Step Ten: daily inventory
103.gist: The page explains Step Ten as continuing the inventory into the present, noticing wrongs and admitting them promptly before bad feelings build. Exercise 10 asks why ongoing self-awareness matters after stopping and whether admitting mistakes is hard.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The Stoic philosopher Seneca described reviewing his day each night to examine his conduct. Step Ten builds the same habit into recovery.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Prompt admission prevents small conflicts from becoming resentments, which AA literature names as a major relapse danger. It is maintenance rather than repair.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Teach a nightly three-question review: where was I wrong, where did I do well, what will I do differently tomorrow. It takes two minutes and can be done on a bunk.

ask: Why is it often harder to admit a small mistake than to confess a big past one?
How could a daily inventory become anxious rumination instead of a helpful habit?

104.title: Step Eleven: prayer and meditation
104.gist: The text explains Step Eleven as using prayer, described as talking to a Higher Power, and meditation, described as listening, to understand how to stay sober and stay aware of something beyond oneself. Exercise 11 asks members about their experience with either.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Meditation practices have shown modest benefits for stress, anxiety, and craving in various studies. Results depend on the practice and on how consistently it is done.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members prayed only in crisis, often asking to get out of trouble. Ask how a regular practice might differ from crisis prayer.

ask: What might meditation offer someone in a noisy, stressful prison environment?
Why might prayer help some people even if one doubts that anyone is listening?

105.title: Step Twelve: service now
105.gist: The page explains Step Twelve as service, sharing what has worked and applying the principles throughout life, and Exercise 12 asks how members can practice service today rather than waiting. It turns the last Step into an immediate action.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies by Maria Pagano and colleagues found that helping other alcoholics, especially through AA service, was associated with lower relapse rates. Helping others seems to protect the helper.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to name one act of service possible this week on the unit, such as helping someone write a letter. Recovery starts to look like action, not just talk.

ask: How might service help someone in prison feel like they have value?
Can helping others become a way to avoid one's own problems?

106.title: How the Steps work: admitting it
106.gist: Part 2 presents the Steps as a road map rather than rules, summarizes seven core principles, and begins with admitting the problem, the need for help, and true feelings, noting how culture discourages this, especially for men. It explains why meetings use self-introductions.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Research on masculinity norms shows men often avoid seeking help to protect a tough image. In prison, these norms are amplified, so admitting feelings carries real social risk.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Instead of pushing members to name feelings directly, ask what their body did or what they wanted to do. That route often feels safer and still leads to emotion.

ask: How do you invite emotional honesty in a culture that treats it as weakness?
Which of the seven principles do you think matters most for people in reentry?

107.title: Labels, feelings, and fellowship
107.gist: Exercise 13 asks how members feel about calling themselves an addict or alcoholic and whether they find it hard to talk about feelings, then the text explains fellowship works because shared pain and goals bond people and end isolation. It links identity with belonging.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Person-first language, like a person with a substance use disorder, has gained ground in clinical writing because labels can increase stigma. In meetings, the label may serve as a badge of honesty. Context changes its effect.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Do not force anyone to use the label. Ask what the word means to them and what it would mean to say it out loud.

ask: Does identifying as an addict support recovery or limit a person's sense of who they can become?
How might a person's own terms for themselves change over the course of recovery?

108.title: Hope and sober friendships
108.gist: The text explains that meeting people further along in recovery builds hope and that fellowship extends to sober friendships, and Exercise 14 asks how members related to friends while using and what they expect from sober people. It focuses on rebuilding a social life.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Social learning theory suggests people adopt the norms of those they spend time with. Shifting from a using network to a sober one changes what feels normal.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members fear sober life will be boring. Brainstorm concrete sober activities that offer excitement or meaning, such as sports, music, or learning a trade.

ask: Why might people struggle to imagine having fun without substances?
How can someone leave old friends without feeling like a traitor?

109.title: Surrender as leaving the fight
109.gist: The page reframes surrender not as defeat in war but as walking away from an unwinnable fight with addiction and relying on something larger, whether the fellowship or God. Exercise 15 asks when trying to control a situation caused problems.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Martial arts like judo and aikido teach using an opponent's force rather than meeting it head-on. Surrender works similarly: stop pushing against craving and redirect energy toward what helps.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The war metaphor can resonate with members who have fought their whole lives. Ask what surrender meant on the street, and what it might mean here instead.

ask: Is there a difference between surrendering and giving up? Where is the line?
Why might some members resist surrender more than any other principle?

110.title: Letting go and taking inventory
110.gist: The worksheet asks when letting go of control led to good results, then explains inventory as honestly examining defects such as grudges, anger, or dishonesty, often survival habits from addiction, and discussing them with someone who sees more clearly. It stresses that change needs another person's view.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Many defects were once adaptive: lying, hypervigilance, or aggression may have helped people survive the street or prison. Recognizing their past function makes it easier to let them go without shame.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Psychologists describe blind spots in self-perception: others often judge some of our traits, like arrogance, more accurately than we do. This supports the Step's call for an outside view.

ask: How can a survival skill become a liability after release?
Who would be a reliable outside observer for someone with few trusted relationships?

111.title: Naming defects, then facing the damage
111.gist: Members list their own character defects and predict how each could sabotage recovery; the page then opens the theme of restitution. It bridges Steps 4-7 (self-inventory) and Steps 8-9 (amends), separating loss of control from responsibility.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Holding someone responsible while acknowledging diminished control is the same move CBT makes: you are not to blame for every urge, but you own the choices that follow. That framing lowers shame enough for honest inventory to happen.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In custody, 'defects' can sound like the language of a disciplinary report. Ask members to name a defect as a strategy that once protected them (e.g., distrust kept them safe on the street) before naming its cost now.

ask: Where is the line between explaining a behavior by addiction and excusing it?
Could a defect list reinforce a criminal or addict identity rather than loosen it? How would you prevent that?

terms.d: Twelve Step term for a recurring trait, such as resentment or dishonesty, that fuels harm and relapse.
Repairing or compensating for harm done to others.

112.title: Regret, apology, and what happened next
112.gist: Members recall something they wish they had not said or done and an apology they made, noting the outcome. It grounds the abstract idea of amends in their own history before Step 9 work is asked of them.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Restorative justice, used in some courts and prisons, shares the Twelve Step intuition: repair is about relationships, not only punishment. Both treat the harmed person's experience as central, not the offender's relief.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect stories where an apology went badly or was rejected. Debrief by separating the act of making amends from controlling the response; the second is never guaranteed, and that is why Step 9 warns against amends that injure others.

ask: Is guilt (I did a bad thing) or shame (I am bad) more useful for motivating amends, and what does the research on each suggest?
When might a direct apology from someone incarcerated do more harm than good to a victim?

terms.d: Actively making right a wrong, beyond saying sorry, through changed behavior or repair.

113.title: Helping others to see yourself clearly
113.gist: The page explains service, the principle behind Step 12, and asks members how helping someone felt and how being asked for help would feel. It reframes members from takers of help into people with something to offer.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on the 'helper therapy principle' (Riessman) and studies of AA members who sponsor or do service suggest that helping others is associated with better abstinence outcomes, though people who help may also differ in other ways.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Psychologists call this decentering: stepping outside the loop of one's own problem. Rumination narrows attention; attending to someone else's struggle widens it and often reveals solutions one could not see from inside.

ask: Can service become a way of avoiding one's own work? How would you spot that in a member?
Why might being needed matter so much for people whose identity has been reduced to an inmate number?

terms.d: Twelve Step practice of helping the group or other members, from setting up chairs to sponsoring.

114.title: One day at a time, both directions
114.gist: The page presents 'one day at a time' as a cure for two opposite problems: rushing to fix everything and despairing over small progress. Members then examine how dwelling on the past has cost them something in the present.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The slogan echoes Stoic advice (Seneca, Marcus Aurelius) to live in the present and mindfulness-based relapse prevention (Bowen, Marlatt and colleagues), which trains attention on the current moment rather than on regret or dread.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For someone facing years of sentence, 'today' can feel like the only honest time scale. Ask what a single sober, decent day inside looks like concretely, then have them name one action for today only.

ask: How does 'one day at a time' differ from simple avoidance of long-term planning?
Why might proximal goals work better than distal ones for building self-efficacy (Bandura)?

115.title: Spirituality is not the same as religion
115.gist: After a last question on future worries, the page distinguishes religion (specific beliefs about superhuman powers) from spirituality (awareness of something larger than oneself). It widens 'Higher Power' to include the group or recovery itself, lowering a barrier for nonreligious members.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Many atheists and agnostics still find the Steps' God language exclusionary, which is why secular alternatives such as SMART Recovery exist. Courts in the US have ruled that coerced attendance at religious-flavored programs can raise First Amendment concerns.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: William James, in The Varieties of Religious Experience, treated conversion-like change as a psychological event. Bill W. was influenced by James, and the 'spiritual awakening' of Step 12 owes something to that view.

ask: If the Higher Power can be 'the group', what is the active ingredient: belief, belonging, or accountability?
How would you honor a devout Muslim member and a firm atheist in the same discussion?

terms.d: In the Twelve Steps, whatever a person sees as greater than themselves, from God to the recovery group.

116.title: Not the center of the world
116.gist: The page argues that relying on a power beyond yourself both admits you are not the center of things and lifts the burden of believing you are. Members then write what spirituality means to them and how it differs from religion.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Yochelson and Samenow described criminal thinking patterns such as grandiosity and the sense of being uniquely entitled. Surrendering centrality targets exactly that pattern, which is why the Steps can fit cognitive-behavioral corrections work.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to recall a time they felt small in a good way, under a night sky, in a crowd, at a birth. Have them describe the body sensation. This 'awe' experience is a nonreligious doorway into the page's idea.

ask: Is there a difference between humility and low self-esteem, and could this page be misread as the second?
Research on awe (Keltner) suggests it shrinks self-focus. Could awe be cultivated in a prison setting?

117.title: Your own meaning of a greater power
117.gist: A final question asks members what relying on a greater power means to them personally, followed by the Session 14 summary of the Steps, how they work, and spirituality. It is the session's personal close.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Kelly and colleagues' research on AA suggests much of its benefit works through social mechanisms, such as changes in social networks and confidence, more than spiritual ones, although spirituality seems to matter more for some members.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Close by having each member say one sentence about what they will keep from the session. Short verbal commitments in front of peers tend to stick better than silent written ones.

ask: If AA's effects are mostly social, what does that imply for how you present spirituality?
What would a reentry plan need so that the 'power greater than yourself' exists on the outside, not just in group?

118.title: The Twelve Steps, in AA's original wording
118.gist: This reference page reprints AA's Twelve Steps as published in the Big Book. It lets members see the full sequence the session has been interpreting, from admitting powerlessness to carrying the message.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The Steps were written by Bill Wilson around 1938 and drew on the Oxford Group, a Christian movement emphasizing confession, restitution, and sharing. Many steps map onto those older practices.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Read as psychology, the Steps form a cycle: accept the problem, find support, take inventory, disclose, repair, maintain, and help others. Each phase has parallels in modern therapy, such as acceptance in ACT and exposure through disclosure.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The 'powerless' framing troubles some clinicians and feminist critics, who argue it may not suit people whose problem is having had too little power, such as trauma survivors. Some groups rewrite the Steps for that reason.

ask: Which step do you think is hardest for justice-involved men and women, and why?
How might Step 1's powerlessness coexist with the self-efficacy that relapse prevention tries to build?

119.title: Session 15 opens: sexually transmitted diseases
119.gist: The session introduction explains it will cover what STDs are, how they spread, symptoms, treatment, and safer sex. Its two parts and objectives frame a health topic that is highly relevant for people leaving custody.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Substance use raises STD risk through disinhibition, sex traded for drugs or money, and shared equipment. Treating STD education inside a recovery curriculum reflects that the two problems travel together.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Sexual health topics can trigger joking, bravado, or silence, especially in single-gender units. Name that openly at the start and set a norm of using clinical words, which lowers embarrassment.

ask: Why might a health-education session belong in a substance use program rather than in medical services?
What group norms would you need for members to speak honestly about sexual risk?

120.title: What STDs are and why early care matters
120.gist: The page asks members to assess their own sexual risk, previews glossary terms, and defines STDs as infections from bacteria and viruses spread through body fluids. It stresses that most are curable when treated early, while untreated ones can do lasting damage.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Public health research consistently finds higher rates of STDs, HIV, and hepatitis C among incarcerated people than in the general population, which is why correctional settings are considered key sites for testing and treatment.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Current public health usage often prefers 'sexually transmitted infections' (STIs), since many infections cause no disease symptoms. The manual's older terminology is still widely understood.

ask: How does the 'silent infection' problem (no symptoms) change the logic of testing?
What barriers keep people newly released from getting tested, and which can a counselor reduce?

terms.d: Sexually transmitted infection; the newer term for STD, used because many infections cause no symptoms.

121.title: Five shared traits of STDs
121.gist: The page lists what most STDs have in common: often curable early, dangerous if ignored, frequently symptomless yet contagious, and passable to a fetus. It links long-term substance use to weaker immunity and riskier sex, then checks understanding with true/false items.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Alcohol myopia theory (Steele and Josephs) explains part of the link: intoxication narrows attention to immediate cues like arousal, while distant ones like infection risk fade. Risk is a thinking problem as much as a knowledge problem.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The third true/false item targets the most dangerous myth: no symptoms means no infection. Spend the debrief there; ask who has ever assumed a partner was clean because they looked healthy.

ask: If people already know condoms prevent infection, why does knowledge alone change behavior so little?
How would you explain asymptomatic spread using an analogy members would remember?

terms.d: Having an infection without noticeable signs, while still able to pass it on.

122.title: Warning signs, and chlamydia up close
122.gist: The page lists common STD symptoms for everyone, for women, and for men, then begins the disease-by-disease tour with chlamydia, the most frequently reported bacterial STD in the US, and its complications such as infertility.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Chlamydia remains among the most commonly reported notifiable infections in the US, and because many cases are silent, public health agencies recommend routine screening for younger sexually active women rather than waiting for symptoms.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A symptom checklist can turn into anxious self-diagnosis or jokes. Redirect: the point is not to diagnose yourself but to know that any of these means get tested, and that silence does not mean safety.

ask: Why might screening policies focus on young women when men carry and spread chlamydia too?
What does a list of 'women only' and 'men only' symptoms leave out for transgender members?

terms.d: A pregnancy that implants outside the uterus, usually in a fallopian tube; a medical emergency.

123.title: Silent chlamydia, gardnerella, and genital warts
123.gist: The page notes most chlamydia cases show no symptoms, then describes gardnerella (a bacterial vaginal infection) and genital warts caused by the papilloma virus, with their treatments. It keeps reinforcing that early care makes treatment easier.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: This material is dated in places. Gardnerella is now usually described as bacterial vaginosis, which is linked to sex but not classed as a classic STD. And the HPV vaccine, which prevents the types causing most genital warts and many cancers, is not mentioned.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: HPV is the clearest case of an STD tied to cancer: certain strains cause most cervical cancers and many throat and anal cancers. Vaccination programs have sharply cut infection rates in countries that adopted them early.

ask: When a manual's medical facts are outdated, how should a facilitator correct them without undermining trust in the whole program?
Should adults leaving prison be offered HPV vaccination, and who would pay for it?

terms.d: Human papillomavirus; a very common sexually spread virus causing warts and some cancers, preventable by vaccine.

124.title: Gonorrhea's limits and herpes' persistence
124.gist: The page explains gonorrhea lives only in warm, moist membranes, so it does not spread from toilet seats, and describes its silent spread and complications. It then introduces herpes, a viral infection that cannot be cured because the virus hides inside human cells.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The antibiotics listed for gonorrhea are out of date. Gonorrhea has become resistant to several drug classes over the decades, and current US guidance relies on an injectable cephalosporin (ceftriaxone). Members should follow a clinician, not this list.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Debunking the toilet-seat myth has a psychological job: it removes a face-saving excuse. When infection can only come from intimate contact, people must think honestly about their own behavior and partners.

ask: What does antibiotic resistance teach about finishing medication courses, and how does that parallel adherence in recovery?
Why do myths like toilet-seat transmission survive even when they are easy to disprove?

terms.d: When bacteria evolve so that drugs that once killed them no longer work.

125.title: Herpes stages, and yeast infections
125.gist: The page describes how herpes spreads, even without sores, its flu-like onset and blisters, risks to newborns, and antiviral treatment that eases but does not cure it. It then introduces moniliasis, a fungal yeast infection triggered by conditions like pregnancy or antibiotics.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some figures here, such as newborn death rates and cervical cancer risk, reflect older research; modern antivirals and delivery care have changed outcomes. Also, yeast infections are not usually considered STDs, though they appear in many such lists.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Herpes carries heavy stigma, often worse than the medical reality for most adults. If a member discloses it, model calm: it is common, manageable with medication, and disclosure to partners is an act of respect, not confession.

ask: How does stigma around an infection affect whether people get tested and tell partners?
What parallels do you see between managing a chronic incurable virus and managing addiction as a chronic condition?

126.title: Urethritis and syphilis's first stages
126.gist: The page covers nongonococcal urethritis, an infection of the urine tube treated with antibiotics, then syphilis, caused by a spirochete bacterium. It describes the painless primary sore and the secondary rash, both of which can vanish while the disease continues.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Syphilis shaped history: it devastated Europe after the 1490s, and the Tuskegee study (1932-1972), in which Black men were left untreated, became a landmark ethics scandal that still fuels medical mistrust in Black communities.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Syphilis is a lesson in false reassurance: the sore goes away, so people assume they are healed. Addiction works similarly when a period of control is mistaken for cure.

ask: How might the history of Tuskegee shape how some members hear advice to get tested?
Why does a painless symptom tend to be more dangerous than a painful one?

terms.d: The firm, painless sore that marks the first stage of syphilis.
A spiral-shaped bacterium; the type that causes syphilis.

127.title: Syphilis's late damage and trichomoniasis
127.gist: The page finishes syphilis with its latent and late stages, when untreated infection can damage organs and the brain, and notes it is curable at any stage though damage stays. It then describes trichomoniasis, a common parasite infection that rarely shows symptoms in men.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: US syphilis rates, once near elimination around 2000, have risen substantially since, including congenital syphilis in newborns. Public health officials link part of the rise to drug use, especially methamphetamine, and to gaps in testing.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Before penicillin, late syphilis filled psychiatric hospitals as 'general paresis'. Its discovery as an infectious cause of madness was a milestone in showing that some mental illness has biological roots.

ask: What does the rise of syphilis alongside methamphetamine use suggest about integrating STD testing into addiction treatment?
How would you explain irreversible damage to a member who believes a cure erases all consequences?

128.title: Testing knowledge, then lowering the risk
128.gist: After noting Flagyl's alcohol warning, members answer true/false items on treatments and herpes spread. Part 2 then begins: STDs spread through any sexual contact, and fewer partners means lower risk.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The claim that metronidazole (Flagyl) plus alcohol can be fatal is stronger than the evidence. Patients are still advised to avoid alcohol because of possible nausea and flushing, but recent reviews question how common or severe the reaction is.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The alcohol warning is a teaching opportunity for this population: many medicines interact with alcohol and drugs. Ask members which prescriptions they will leave custody with and whether they know the interactions.

ask: How do true/false formats help or hurt learning compared with explaining in one's own words?
How should a counselor handle a manual's medical claim that seems exaggerated?

129.title: Monogamy, barriers, and safer sex basics
129.gist: The page explains that a mutually faithful, infection-free couple carries no STD risk, asks members to list risk-reducing actions, and introduces the basics of safer sex: condoms, dental dams, lubricants, and female condoms. Other birth control does not stop infection.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is harm reduction: meeting people where their behavior is rather than demanding abstinence. Many recovery programs embrace it for sexual health even while asking for abstinence from substances, a tension worth noticing.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members brainstorm risk-reduction ideas, then sort them into what depends on me alone and what depends on a partner's honesty. The second pile shows why testing and communication matter as much as condoms.

ask: Is it consistent to promote harm reduction for sex but abstinence for drugs? Defend either side.
What makes monogamy a weaker safeguard in practice than on paper?

terms.d: Approaches that lower the damage of risky behavior without requiring that the behavior stop.
A thin latex sheet used as a barrier during oral sex.

130.title: Which condoms work and what ruins them
130.gist: The page warns against animal-skin condoms, which let viruses pass, and oil-based lubricants, which damage latex, and notes the spermicide nonoxynol-9 can actually raise HIV risk. A short multiple-choice check follows.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Large trials in the 1990s and 2000s found nonoxynol-9 did not protect against HIV and could irritate tissue, raising risk; the WHO advised against it for HIV prevention. It is a striking case of a well-meant intervention backfiring.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Since this manual was written, HIV prevention has changed: PrEP, a daily or injectable medication, greatly reduces HIV infection risk for people at high exposure. It does not protect against other STDs.

ask: What does the nonoxynol-9 story teach about trusting intuition over trial data in treatment?
Why should information about PrEP reach people at release, and who in reentry services should deliver it?

terms.d: Pre-exposure prophylaxis; HIV-negative people take HIV medication to prevent infection.

131.title: A ladder of sexual risk
131.gist: This handout sorts sexual activities into safe, probably safe, and unsafe categories, and ends with sharing needles and drug equipment. It gives members a graded map instead of an all-or-nothing rule.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Graded risk lists respect adult choice and fit the stages-of-change view: someone not ready to abstain may be ready to move one rung down the ladder. Small, real steps beat perfect, ignored rules.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note that injection equipment sits on the unsafe list. It is the moment to link sexual and drug risk, and to mention needle exchange and naloxone as reentry resources, since overdose risk peaks shortly after release.

ask: Why might a ladder of risk change behavior more than a list of prohibitions?
What risks are missing from this list that members might face after release?

132.title: Checkups when symptoms stay silent
132.gist: The page urges sexually active adults outside monogamous relationships to get checked regularly, even without symptoms, and explains special risks to women and newborns. Members describe whether they get checkups and whether STDs are tested.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members have little history of preventive care; medicine meant emergency rooms. Ask what got in the way before: cost, fear, distrust, being high. Then link to concrete reentry steps such as Medicaid enrollment and free health department clinics.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Routine screening flips the logic of illness from waiting for pain to looking for silence. Relapse prevention works the same way: check warning signs before a crisis, not after.

ask: Why do people avoid tests whose results could help them? What role does fear of knowing play?
How could STD testing be built into a reentry plan so it is automatic rather than voluntary?

133.title: Session 15 wrap-up
133.gist: The summary recaps identifying and treating STDs and reducing the risk of catching or spreading one. It frames sexual health as part of a healthier recovery rather than a separate medical topic.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Before closing, ask each member to name one concrete health action for release week, such as a clinic visit or test. Implementation intentions (Gollwitzer), specifying when and where, raise follow-through compared with vague goals.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Recovery models like SAMHSA's working definition list health as one of four dimensions of recovery, alongside home, purpose, and community. This session puts that dimension into practice.

ask: What would tell you this session changed behavior, not just knowledge?
Which piece of this session is most likely to be forgotten by release, and how could you make it stick?

134.title: Role-play: the testing talk before marriage
134.gist: An engaged couple role-play the conversation about past partners, HIV risk, condoms, and testing, followed by discussion prompts for the group. It moves the session from facts to the harder skill of saying them out loud to someone you love.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Role-play builds self-efficacy through rehearsal, which Bandura identified as a powerful source of confidence. People rarely do in real life what they have never once practiced saying.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect gendered pushback on the condom questions, such as asking means accusing. Freeze the scene and have the observers suggest one better line, then replay it. Swapping roles between members can also build empathy.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The scenario assumes a heterosexual couple and prescribes genders for volunteers. Adapt it freely so members of any orientation can see themselves, which matters given that men who have sex with men face the highest HIV rates.

ask: What makes a disclosure conversation feel like a trial instead of an act of care?
How would you run this role-play in an all-male unit without it becoming a joke?

135.title: STD glossary, first half
135.gist: The glossary condenses the session's terms, from chlamydia through moniliasis, with a line on causes and treatment for each. It is a quick review sheet for members.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A few entries reflect older medicine, for example the treatment notes for gardnerella and gonorrhea. Treat this as a vocabulary aid, and send medical questions to a clinician.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Turn the glossary into a matching game: read a definition aloud and have pairs name the infection. Retrieval practice, recalling rather than rereading, is one of the most reliable findings in learning research.

ask: How would you adapt this glossary for members with limited reading levels?
Which three terms would you insist every member leaves knowing, and why?

136.title: STD glossary, second half
136.gist: The rest of the glossary defines urethritis, STDs in general, syphilis, and trichomoniasis. It reinforces the key message that many are curable but some leave lasting damage.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Plain-language glossaries support health literacy, a strong predictor of how well people manage their health. Low health literacy is common in correctional populations, which makes clear definitions practical, not decorative.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members which word they had never heard before today. Naming gaps without shame normalizes asking questions of doctors later.

ask: What is the difference between learning a term and being able to use it with a doctor?
How might low health literacy interact with distrust of institutions in this population?

137.title: Session 16 opens: focus on HIV/AIDS
137.gist: The introduction presents HIV/AIDS as the most dangerous STD and a global health issue, outlines two parts (understanding the disease; risk reduction and treatment), and lists objectives including judging one's own risk.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: HIV has changed from a near-certain death sentence in the 1980s to a manageable chronic condition for people with steady treatment access, one of modern medicine's major turnarounds.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some older members lived through the early AIDS years and lost people. Allow room for that grief and for lingering fear or stigma before teaching facts.

ask: How has the shift from fatal to chronic changed the stigma around HIV, if at all?
Why might this session matter more for someone leaving prison than for the general public?

138.title: Facing the fear of testing
138.gist: The page lists Part 2 objectives and asks members to review past and present behavior and confront fears about being tested. It frames attention to physical health as part of sobriety, then previews a dense immunology glossary.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Avoiding a test is classic avoidance coping: it reduces anxiety now and raises danger later, the same short-term relief, long-term cost pattern that sustains substance use.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The glossary is heavy with immune-system jargon. Pick five words that matter for decisions (HIV, AIDS, antibody, opportunistic infection, window period) and let the rest wait.

ask: What does someone fear more, the virus or the knowledge of having it?
How can you make a test feel like taking control rather than awaiting a verdict?

terms.d: An infection that takes hold because the immune system is weakened, such as some pneumonias in AIDS.

139.title: What HIV is and how testing works
139.gist: The page defines HIV and AIDS, names sex and shared injection equipment as main routes, and stresses you cannot tell by looking. It cites CDC advice for routine screening and explains antibody and RNA tests.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The testing details are dated. Current US labs mostly use combined antigen/antibody tests that detect infection earlier, and the Western blot has been dropped from the standard confirmation sequence. Rapid and home tests are also widely available.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: HIV is a retrovirus: it writes its genetic code into the host's DNA, which is why it persists for life. That biology explains why treatment controls it rather than clearing it.

ask: Why does the CDC recommend testing everyone once, rather than only people who report risk?
How should you update members when the manual's testing information has been overtaken?

terms.d: A protein the immune system makes to target a specific invader; many HIV tests look for it.

140.title: The window period and who is at risk
140.gist: The page explains the window period, when an infected person may test negative but can still transmit, and how untreated HIV progresses to AIDS. It then identifies injection drug use and addiction-linked sexual behavior as major risks.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Since this was written, a key finding has reshaped HIV care: people on treatment who keep an undetectable viral load do not transmit HIV sexually. Health agencies summarize this as Undetectable equals Untransmittable (U=U).

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The page notes risk lies in behaviors more than identities. That shift moves the focus from who you are to what you do, which is both less stigmatizing and more actionable.

ask: How might U=U change both stigma and motivation to stay on medication?
Why is the window period especially relevant at intake and at release?

terms.d: Time after infection before a test can detect it; the person may still pass the virus on.
Amount of virus in the blood; treatment aims to make it undetectable.

141.title: US HIV numbers and who bears them
141.gist: This sheet presents CDC figures, mostly from around 2010-2012, on how many Americans live with HIV, how many are unaware, and how unequally new infections fall across sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, and drug injection.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The figures are over a decade old; read them as historical snapshot, not current data. The overall pattern of racial and sexual-minority disparities has persisted, but numbers have shifted.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Disparities like these are usually explained by structural factors such as access to care, stigma, incarceration, and the density of infection within networks, rather than by individual behavior alone.

ask: How does incarceration itself contribute to HIV disparities in Black and Latino communities?
How would you present group statistics without members hearing them as statements about their worth?

142.title: A private risk check, and transmission routes
142.gist: Members answer yes/no questions about needle sharing, sex between men, partners with HIV, and past STDs; any yes means talk to a health professional. The page then lists how HIV spreads, including shared works and childbirth.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Questions about sex between men are sensitive in custody, where disclosure can carry real danger. Make clear answers are private, not to be shared aloud, and the purpose is self-assessment only.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A yes/no screen works by lowering the bar: one yes is enough to act. It sidesteps the human tendency toward optimism bias, believing bad outcomes happen to other people.

ask: How would you protect confidentiality when the worksheet itself could be read by others in a cell block?
Why is sharing cookers or cotton underestimated as a risk compared with sharing needles?

terms.d: Street term for drug injection equipment such as cookers, cotton, and water.

143.title: Myths about catching HIV
143.gist: After a true/false check on routes, the page lists everyday contacts that do not spread HIV: sharing dishes, food, toilets, pools, hugging, kissing, insect bites. It advises only against sharing razors and toothbrushes.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Fear of casual contact in the 1980s led to children being barred from school, such as Ryan White. Myth-busting is not trivia; it protects people living with HIV from exclusion.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In close prison quarters, fear of a cellmate with HIV can be intense. Use this list to defuse it, and steer members toward concrete precautions (no shared razors, no tattoo needles) rather than avoidance of people.

ask: Why do misconceptions about casual transmission persist after decades of education?
How would you respond if a member says he refuses to share a cell with someone HIV-positive?

144.title: Telling partners: notification methods
144.gist: A true/false check on blood, mosquitoes, and toilet seats is followed by an explanation of partner notification: why partners must be told, and three approaches, patient referral, physician referral, and a combination.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Partner notification sits on an ethical fault line between confidentiality and duty to warn. Public health practice tries to protect partners without exposing the patient, often by notifying without naming the source.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to write the first sentence they would say to a past partner. Then ask what would make it easier to have a clinic do it. Comparing the two shows why multiple notification routes exist.

ask: When does a person's right to privacy end and another's right to know begin?
How does shame shape whether someone notifies partners, and what could reduce it?

145.title: Risk lies in behavior: first protections
145.gist: The page completes notification methods and opens Part 2 by shifting from risk groups to risky behaviors. It begins listing protections: never share needles or other injection gear, and use latex condoms properly.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Syringe service programs are among the best-supported HIV prevention measures; research consistently links them to lower HIV and hepatitis C transmission without increasing drug use.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Bleach disinfection, recommended here, is a fallback; health agencies treat it as far less reliable than always using new sterile syringes. Members should know where free syringes are available after release.

ask: Does teaching safer injection conflict with an abstinence-based program, or complement it?
Why did moving from risk groups to risk behaviors matter for prevention and for stigma?

146.title: Looking back at past precautions
146.gist: The page finishes the risk-reduction list, warns people with HIV or who inject drugs not to donate blood or organs, and asks members why drug use raises risk and whether the precautions they took while using were enough.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The second question invites a hindsight review without demanding confession. It mirrors a relapse-prevention chain analysis: trace the moments where judgment slipped, so the same links can be spotted next time.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will say they never worried because they felt invincible. Treat that as data, not bravado: invulnerability beliefs are common in young adults and are a known driver of risk taking.

ask: How can you get honest answers to a question that may feel like admitting past danger to others?
What other drug-related risks besides needles and disinhibition might members name, and which would surprise you?

147.title: Male condom use, step by step
147.gist: This handout gives ten practical rules for male condoms: latex only, water-based lubricant, check dates, store cool, use once, apply correctly from start to finish, and remove carefully. It turns safer sex into concrete skills.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Condom failure is mostly user error, such as late application, slipping, or wrong lubricant, rather than product defects. That is why correct-use training matters as much as handing condoms out.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some correctional rules forbid condoms or demonstration items. Teach the steps verbally and emphasize the two most common mistakes, putting it on late and using oil-based products.

ask: Why does skills training tend to beat information alone for health behaviors?
What would make men in this group actually carry condoms after release?

148.title: Female condoms and how HIV attacks
148.gist: The page lists ten rules for female condoms, then explains HIV's effect: it targets T cells, the white blood cells that coordinate defense, gradually breaking down the immune system, often without symptoms for years.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: T helper cells are like a band's conductor: they signal other immune cells when to act. HIV infects and depletes them, so the whole orchestra loses coordination even though the players remain.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Female condoms give the receptive partner direct control over protection, which matters when a partner refuses male condoms. Control over protection is a power issue as much as a medical one.

ask: How does putting protection in the receptive partner's hands change the dynamics described in the next role-play?
Why might a disease that is silent for years be harder to fight socially than one that is immediately visible?

terms.d: White blood cells that direct and carry out immune responses; HIV targets the helper type.

149.title: Early symptoms and drug combinations
149.gist: The page lists possible early HIV symptoms, checks that HIV attacks white rather than red cells, and introduces treatment: no cure, but several drug classes used together in combination therapy.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Combination therapy works because the virus mutates rapidly; one drug alone breeds resistance, but hitting several targets at once makes escape unlikely. It is evolution used against the virus.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Since the mid-1990s, combination antiretroviral therapy has transformed survival. Today many people who start treatment early and stay on it have a life expectancy approaching that of people without HIV.

ask: What does combination therapy suggest by analogy about using several recovery supports at once?
What happens to HIV care continuity at release, and where are the gaps?

terms.d: A combination of medicines that suppresses HIV so the immune system can recover.

150.title: Antiretrovirals and an AIDS awareness test
150.gist: The page explains that antiretroviral drugs suppress HIV, sometimes to undetectable levels, without eliminating it, and urges seeing a doctor quickly if exposure is suspected. A true/false awareness test begins.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Since this edition, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) has become standard: antiretrovirals started soon after a possible exposure, ideally within hours and no later than about 72 hours, can prevent infection. That gives 'contact your doctor immediately' new urgency.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Item 5 names homosexual men as a risk group, though the session earlier stressed behaviors over identities. Point out the tension and ask members which framing they find more accurate.

ask: Why is 'undetectable' different from 'cured', and why does that distinction matter for adherence?
How might quick access to PEP be arranged for people in the first weeks after release?

terms.d: Post-exposure prophylaxis; HIV drugs taken right after possible exposure to prevent infection.

151.title: Session 16 wrap-up
151.gist: The awareness test finishes with items on casual contact, symptomless spread, and shared works, and the summary recaps how HIV affects the body, how it is treated, and how changing behavior lowers risk in sobriety.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Go over the test aloud and let members argue answers before you settle them. Explaining reasoning to peers deepens learning more than marking answers correct.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: HIV's story is a public health success built on activism: groups like ACT UP pushed for faster drug approval and patient voice in research. Patients organizing changed science, a hopeful model for recovery communities.

ask: Which item on the test do you predict members will get wrong most often, and why?
What would make health knowledge from a prison group survive the chaos of release?

152.title: Role-play: when a condom offer turns ugly
152.gist: In this scene, a partner offers a condom and the other reacts with anger, takes it as an accusation, and storms out. Members discuss what went well and what went wrong, practicing how to handle defensiveness around protection.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Carlos hears the request as an attack on his identity, a classic cognitive distortion of personalizing. CBT would have him notice the thought that she thinks I'm dirty and test it against the evidence.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask the men which line Carlos could have said instead and replay it. Also note what Margarita did well: she held her boundary and left when respect broke down. Both skills deserve applause.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Like the earlier role-play, this one assigns fixed genders. You can flip roles so the man is the one asking, which challenges assumptions about who resists protection.

ask: How is Carlos's reaction connected to masculinity norms common in prison culture?
What is the difference between Margarita setting a boundary and punishing Carlos?

153.title: From HIV to AIDS: four stages
153.gist: This appendix describes the path from exposure to AIDS: window period, seroconversion with flu-like symptoms, a long asymptomatic phase, and a symptomatic phase. AIDS is defined by a very low T4 count or specific infections.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The window period figures here are older; modern tests usually detect infection within weeks, not up to a year. And modern antiretrovirals are far better tolerated than the page's warning about dangerous side effects suggests.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The long silent phase is why HIV spread so widely before it was recognized in 1981: people felt healthy for years while transmitting. Silent periods are where epidemics, and relapses, gain ground.

ask: How would you explain seroconversion to someone in plain words in under thirty seconds?
What does a CD4 count measure, and why is it a better marker than how someone feels?

terms.d: When the body starts producing detectable antibodies after infection.
Number of helper T cells in blood; below 200 signals AIDS.

154.title: Where to get more information
154.gist: The page lists hotlines and agencies for HIV, drug abuse, and sexual health information, including the CDC, NIDA, SAMHSA, the Red Cross, and the American Sexual Health Association. It gives members a route beyond the group.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Phone numbers and websites change; some services listed have been merged or renamed since printing. Verify current numbers before members rely on them after release.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Rather than handing out a list, help each member pick one resource and write it on their release plan. One chosen contact beats ten unused ones.

ask: What barriers stop people from calling a hotline, even when they have the number?
Which local Miami resources would be more useful to your members than national hotlines?

155.title: HIV glossary: immune system basics
155.gist: The first glossary page defines AIDS, antibodies, antigens, B cells, dendritic cells, ELISA, lymphocytes, and related immune-system terms. It supports the session's explanation of how HIV harms the body.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Lymphocytes remembering which invaders to attack is the basis of vaccines: the immune system learns once and responds faster later. Learning in the brain and in the immune system share this logic of memory.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pick four terms and have members act them out as a story: the antigen breaks in, the dendritic cell raises the alarm, the T helper calls B cells, B cells make antibodies. A physical story beats a list.

ask: Which of these terms do members actually need to make decisions, and which are enrichment?
How might immune memory serve as a metaphor for building recovery skills?

156.title: HIV glossary: from lymphokines to Western blot
156.gist: The second glossary page defines lymphokines, opportunistic infections, phagocytes, suppressor and helper T cells, syndrome, virus, and the Western blot confirmation test.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The Western blot entry reflects older practice; it is no longer part of the standard US confirmation algorithm. The term remains useful mainly for reading older materials.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: A syndrome is a cluster of symptoms that occur together before the cause is known. AIDS was named a syndrome in 1982, before HIV was identified as its cause in 1983-84.

ask: What does the word 'syndrome' reveal about how medicine names things it does not yet understand?
Are there conditions in addiction treatment still described as syndromes for the same reason?

157.title: Session 17 opens: nutrition and exercise
157.gist: The introduction states the session will cover healthy eating and physical activity and why both matter for sobriety. Objectives include how addiction distorts eating, essential nutrients, a balanced diet, and types of exercise.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Physical self-care is a lifestyle balance strategy in Marlatt's relapse prevention: when daily life holds rewarding, healthy 'wants', the pull toward substances as the only reward weakens.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members have little control over prison food. Frame the session around what they can choose now, such as commissary, portions, and movement, and what they will control after release.

ask: How would you make nutrition relevant to people who cannot choose their meals?
Why might physical health be a less threatening entry point to change than emotional topics?

158.title: How drugs wreck the body's fuel supply
158.gist: The page asks members to examine eating habits and begin an exercise plan, explains that a balanced diet supports recovery, and describes how stimulants, PCP, inhalants, and alcohol can cause weight loss by suppressing appetite or speeding metabolism.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Chronic heavy drinking often causes deficiencies, notably thiamine (vitamin B1), whose lack can lead to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, a serious memory disorder. Nutrition in early recovery is a medical issue, not just a lifestyle tip.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Alcohol supplies calories but few nutrients, often called empty calories. A heavy drinker can be both overweight and malnourished at the same time.

ask: Why might weight gain in early recovery be both a healthy sign and a relapse risk?
What role could hunger play as a trigger mistaken for craving?

terms.d: Vitamin B1; often depleted by heavy drinking, and needed for brain function.
Calories from food or drink that supply energy but little nutritional value.

159.title: Appetite shifts after quitting
159.gist: The page adds that marijuana can cause weight gain and junk-food binges, and that long, heavy use poses the highest nutritional risk. Members reflect on whether their appetite rose after stopping and whether they ate junk food while using.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Sugar and highly palatable food activate the same reward circuitry that drugs do, though far more weakly. Some people in early recovery swap one reward for another, which is understandable but worth watching.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Commissary culture runs on chips, noodles, and candy, which double as currency. Ask what a snack means beyond hunger: comfort, trade, boredom relief. The answer points to the real need.

ask: Is substituting sugar for drugs in early recovery a problem or a reasonable harm-reduction step?
How can you tell physical hunger from emotional hunger or craving?

160.title: The body's toolkit of nutrients
160.gist: The page introduces the main nutrients, vitamins, minerals like salt, calcium, and iron, water, fats, fiber, and carbohydrates, explaining each one's role. It suggests a short course of multivitamins after long-term heavy use.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Vitamins were discovered through deficiency diseases: scurvy in sailors (vitamin C) and beriberi in rice-eating populations (thiamine). Many vitamins were identified by noticing what was missing, a neat parallel to finding what recovery lacks.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to name one item they ate today and guess its main nutrient. Quick guessing games make the categories usable rather than abstract.

ask: Why might a supplement be justified for people leaving long-term heavy use but not for most others?
What nutritional gaps are most likely in a prison diet, and what could members do about them?

161.title: Good carbs, bad carbs, and protein
161.gist: The page argues carbohydrates belong in the diet, contrasting whole grains, fruit, vegetables, and legumes with added sugars and refined grains. It links protein to rebuilding the amino acids that neurotransmitters are made from, then quizzes members on minerals.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Neurotransmitters such as dopamine and serotonin are built from amino acids in food (tyrosine and tryptophan). The page's point is real, but eating protein supports the brain's supply generally; it is not a direct way to repair drug-related brain changes.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some recovery programs market amino acid supplements as cures for craving. Evidence for such claims is limited and mixed, so a plain balanced diet is the safer message.

ask: Why are simple explanations like 'protein replaces lost neurotransmitters' appealing, and what do they risk?
How would you explain the glycemic swing of sugar to a member who notices mood crashes in the afternoon?

terms.d: Building blocks of protein; some are raw material for brain chemicals.
Grain with bran and germ removed, like white rice; less fiber and nutrients.

162.title: Too little or too much: nutrition disorders
162.gist: After quiz items on carbs and fiber, the page explains nutritional disorders: deficiencies, such as protein-calorie malnutrition seen in famine and addiction, and excesses, such as obesity and tooth decay from refined sugar.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Dental damage is common in heavy methamphetamine use and among people with long periods of neglected care. For many reentry clients, dental pain also drives requests for opioids, linking teeth and relapse.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Both too little and too much harm health, a balance theme that echoes the program's title. Many biological systems work on a curve where the middle is healthiest.

ask: Why might malnutrition and obesity coexist in the same low-income neighborhoods?
How could dental care fit into a reentry relapse-prevention plan?

terms.d: Tooth decay, largely driven by frequent sugar exposure.

163.title: A day's eating and the grain foundation
163.gist: Members log what they eat in a typical day, then the page introduces USDA MyPlate food groups, beginning with whole grains as the base of a nutritious diet. It distinguishes whole grains from refined ones.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members compare their logged day to the food groups and circle the missing one. Self-monitoring is one of the most consistent ingredients in successful behavior change programs, from diet to drinking.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Inside, the 'typical day' is set by the facility menu. Encourage members to also log a typical day before incarceration; that is the pattern they will likely return to.

ask: Why does writing down what you eat change behavior even without other advice?
How do national guidelines handle cultural food traditions, such as Latin American or Caribbean diets?

164.title: Daily amounts: grains, fruit, vegetables
164.gist: The page gives USDA daily amounts by age and sex for grains, fruit, and vegetables, and highlights fiber in skins, vitamin C in citrus and berries, vitamin A and calcium in dark greens, and the heart benefits of produce.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Large observational studies consistently link higher fruit and vegetable intake with lower cardiovascular risk, though people who eat more produce also differ in other habits, so exact effect sizes are debated.

deeper.label: In the room
