deeper.text: Cup and ounce amounts are hard to visualize. Translate them: a cup is about a fist, an ounce of grain is roughly one slice of bread.

ask: What would make fresh produce accessible to someone newly released with little money?
Why might people trust traditional food wisdom over USDA charts, and is that reasonable?

165.title: Proteins and dairy, the smart choices
165.gist: The page covers the protein group, nuts and legumes, red and processed meats, poultry, seafood, and eggs, with advice to limit saturated fat and sodium. It begins the dairy group, which includes calcium-rich milk foods.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The World Health Organization's cancer agency classified processed meat as carcinogenic to humans in 2015, mainly for colorectal cancer. Dietary cholesterol limits have been relaxed in recent US guidelines, though saturated fat advice remains.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Beans and rice, a staple across Latin America, provide complementary amino acids. Traditional diets often solved nutrition problems long before science explained them.

ask: Why does nutrition advice seem to change so often, and how should that affect how you present it?
What protein options are both cheap and healthy for someone on a tight reentry budget?

terms.d: Fat mostly from animals, solid at room temperature; raises LDL cholesterol.

166.title: Dairy, oils, and eating every group
166.gist: The page finishes dairy and introduces plant and fish oils as a source of essential fats, giving daily amounts. Members then report whether they regularly eat from every food group, with examples.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members may be lactose intolerant, which is very common among people of African, Latin American, and Asian descent. Mention fortified alternatives so the guideline does not feel irrelevant.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking for examples rather than a bare yes keeps answers honest. Concrete recall is harder to fake than general self-description.

ask: How do guidelines built around dairy fit populations where lactose intolerance is the norm?
What makes checklist questions vulnerable to socially desirable answers?

167.title: Filling the gaps on your plate
167.gist: Members explain why they skip any food groups and how they might add them, guided by two simple slogans: half your grains whole, and half your plate fruits and vegetables.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Simple rules of thumb (heuristics) are easier to follow than gram counts. The half-plate rule is a good example of turning complex science into a decision someone can make in a cafeteria line.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to design one realistic plate from what is served at the facility today. Planning within real constraints builds problem-solving skills the program targets later.

ask: Which barriers to healthy eating are about knowledge, and which are about money, access, or habit?
How do simple slogans support behavior change compared with detailed information?

168.title: Moving enough, and what calories are
168.gist: The page sets the adult activity target, about 150 minutes of moderate or 75 of vigorous aerobic exercise weekly, and urges choosing enjoyable activities. It explains calories as energy and the balance between intake and use.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Exercise reliably improves mood and reduces anxiety and depression symptoms in many studies. Research on exercise as an addiction treatment add-on is promising but more mixed, with some trials showing reduced craving and others little effect.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Calories in versus calories out is true as physics, but appetite, sleep, stress, and medication all shape both sides. Weight is not purely a willpower equation.

ask: Why might exercise help some people in recovery more than others?
How could exercise be used as a coping response to cravings, and what would make it stick?

169.title: Ideal weight formulas and the fat question
169.gist: The page explains the Hamwi formula for an ideal weight range by height and sex, notes BMI as a screening tool, and begins explaining dietary fat: necessary in moderation, calorie dense, and harmful when saturated.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The Hamwi formula was a quick clinical rule of thumb, not derived from large outcome studies. BMI also misjudges muscular people and varies in accuracy across ethnic groups. Both are rough screens, not verdicts.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members compute their range with the formula and then discuss: how does seeing a number feel? Notice whether it brings motivation or shame, and talk about which actually helps change.

ask: How might weight numbers interact with body image and eating disorders, which are underdiagnosed in men?
Why do simple formulas persist in medicine even when better tools exist?

terms.d: Body mass index; weight relative to height, used to screen weight categories.

170.title: Your fats: what you ate and swaps
170.gist: The page distinguishes saturated and unsaturated fats and links saturated fat to cholesterol and heart disease. Members list fatty foods from the past day and name a favorite high-fat food and a possible substitute.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Substitution works better than prohibition: the brain resists losing a reward but accepts replacing it. Relapse prevention uses the same move, filling the space a drug occupied rather than leaving it empty.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect members to defend favorite foods passionately. Don't fight it; ask what makes it a favorite (memory, family, comfort) and whether a version could be kept with fewer costs.

ask: Why does replacing a behavior tend to work better than simply stopping it?
What food memories carry emotional weight for members, and how might those connect to family themes in later sessions?

171.title: Cooking fats, cholesterol, and family history
171.gist: Members consider how they cook and how to cut fat, then the page explains cholesterol, its role in clogging arteries leading to heart attack and stroke, and asks about family history of heart disease.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Family history is an important heart disease risk factor, reflecting both shared genes and shared habits. Recent US guidelines have relaxed the focus on dietary cholesterol itself, putting more weight on saturated fat and overall diet.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Family history questions echo how addiction runs in families too, through genes and environment. Members may notice the parallel: inheritance raises risk, but it is not destiny.

ask: How would you separate genetic risk from shared family habits when a member says heart disease runs in his family?
Can talking about inherited risk motivate change, or does it feed fatalism?

terms.d: Hardening and narrowing of arteries from fatty deposits on their walls.

172.title: Salt and the silent killer
172.gist: The page advises a doctor visit for family heart risk, explains how salt contributes to high blood pressure, a symptomless condition common among African Americans, and offers tips to cut salt. Members tally salted snacks and alternatives.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Instant noodle seasoning packets are a major salt source in commissary diets. A concrete swap, such as using half the packet, is more likely to happen than abstract advice.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Hypertension disparities among Black Americans are linked to stress, neighborhood food access, and discrimination, not only salt and genes. Researchers sometimes call cumulative stress damage 'weathering' (Geronimus).

ask: What does calling high blood pressure a silent killer teach about risks that cannot be felt?
How could a facility support blood pressure checks for members with high risk?

terms.d: Chronically high blood pressure; raises risk of stroke, heart attack, and kidney disease.

173.title: Salt habits and sugar's hidden names
173.gist: Members check whether they salt food automatically and whether they've adapted to salty tastes. The page then turns to sugar: empty calories, possible mood swings, its many disguised names, and advice to cut back gradually.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Taste preferences adapt: studies suggest that after several weeks of lower salt intake, food tastes salty enough with less. The same habituation likely works for sweetness, which offers hope that cravings for flavor fade.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The popular idea of a 'sugar rush' has weak support; reviews of controlled trials find sugar does not reliably lift mood and may even lower alertness soon after. Whether sugar is truly addictive in humans is still debated.

ask: What does taste adaptation suggest about how quickly a 'new normal' can form in recovery?
Why might calling sugar addictive be both helpful and misleading for this population?

174.title: Sweet cravings and the crash
174.gist: Members examine when they crave sweets and why, whether they notice a lift and then a slump after sugar, and which healthy foods they enjoy. It builds self-observation around food and mood.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Craving sweets at certain times, after stress, late at night, when bored, maps onto cue reactivity: the brain links settings and moods with rewards. Recognizing the cue is the first step of any craving plan, food or drug.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Use the third question to end on strengths. Asking for favorite healthy foods shifts the tone from deficit to what members already like, which tends to make change plans more realistic.

ask: How might noticing food cravings serve as low-stakes practice for noticing drug cravings?
Could a strong sugar crash be partly expectation, and how would you test that?

175.title: Caffeine is a drug too
175.gist: The page names caffeine as a stimulant with effects like tension, insomnia, and faster heart rate, and warns that quitting brings withdrawal. It suggests cutting down to ease stress and sleep in early recovery, then asks about members' own caffeine use.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Caffeine withdrawal, with headache, fatigue, and low mood, is recognized in DSM-5. Moderate caffeine is considered safe for most adults, but it can worsen anxiety and sleep, both common problems in early recovery.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Recovery culture is famous for coffee and cigarettes at meetings. Asking why people accept these substances while banning others opens a useful discussion about how society decides what counts as a drug.

ask: Where would you draw the line between a harmless habit and a dependence when it comes to caffeine?
How might poor sleep in early recovery raise relapse risk, and what part could caffeine play?

176.title: Practical ways to cut sugar and fat
176.gist: This tip sheet lists four goals, less processed sugar, less fat, more nonsugar carbs, less salt, and gives concrete fat- and sugar-cutting techniques: lean protein, trimming fat, broiling or roasting, skimming soups, and using vegetable oils.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some advice reflects the low-fat era. Current guidance focuses on fat type and whole foods rather than fat amount, and egg yolks are less restricted than before. Low-fat processed foods often add sugar.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members who will cook for themselves after release. For many, a family member does it; the tip sheet may be most useful taken home to that person.

ask: Why did nutrition science swing between low-fat and low-carb messages, and what does that teach about certainty?
Which single tip here would change the most for a typical member, and why?

177.title: More complex carbs, less salt
177.gist: The tips continue with ways to raise complex carbohydrates, such as beans, whole grains, meatless meals, and to cut salt by reading labels. A true/false check tests ideas about protein, meat, fat types, and organ meats.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Rice and beans, a meatless meal on this list, is a daily staple in Nicaraguan and Cuban cooking. Healthy eating can be framed as returning to traditional foods rather than adopting a foreign diet.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The first true/false item targets a common misconception, that fat and protein are the same thing. Clearing up category confusions often changes choices more than adding new facts.

ask: How would you adapt this tip sheet for a Hispanic or Caribbean food culture?
Which item on the quiz do you think members get wrong most, and what does that reveal?

178.title: Exercise and borrowed brain chemistry
178.gist: Part 2 opens by explaining that exercise naturally boosts brain chemicals, while stimulants drive the same chemicals much harder, leaving the brain 'running low' in the crash. Regular exercise is presented as a way to rebalance body and mood after quitting.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The 'borrowing' metaphor simplifies a real process: repeated drug surges lead the brain to adapt, for example by reducing dopamine receptor activity, so ordinary pleasures feel flat. This is related to what researchers call anhedonia in early recovery.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Exercise does not simply refill depleted chemicals. Its benefits likely come from many paths, including stress hormones, sleep, sense of mastery, and social contact. The metaphor is useful but not literal.

ask: How would you explain anhedonia to a member who says nothing feels good since he got clean?
What are the risks of teaching a simplified brain metaphor as if it were literal fact?

terms.d: Reduced ability to feel pleasure; common in early recovery and depression.
A chemical messenger that carries signals between nerve cells.

179.title: Exercise highs versus drug highs
179.gist: Members recall any exercise 'high' and compare it with the feeling of drinking or using. The page then introduces four exercise types, starting with isometric work, which builds strength without movement.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The 'runner's high' was long credited to endorphins; more recent research also points to the endocannabinoid system, the body's own cannabis-like chemicals. The science is still developing, especially in humans.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The comparison question is gold for debrief. Members often say the exercise feeling is earned, lasts longer, and has no guilt afterward. Write their answers on the board; it is their own case for change.

ask: What does 'earned' versus 'unearned' reward mean psychologically, and why might it matter in recovery?
Could exercise itself become compulsive? Where is the line?

180.title: Isotonic, isokinetic, aerobic
180.gist: The page describes isotonic (weights, push-ups), isokinetic (machine-based), and aerobic exercise (sustained activity raising oxygen needs), and claims aerobic exercise best restores neurotransmitter balance. Members recall whether they exercised while using.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Research since this was written suggests resistance training also reduces depressive symptoms, with meta-analyses finding meaningful effects. Aerobic exercise is not the only mood-helpful type.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many incarcerated men lift weights, partly for status and protection. Validate that, then add the case for cardio: heart health, sleep, and a lower resting heart rate, which tends to help with anxiety.

ask: Why might someone have exercised hard while using, and does that challenge the idea that addiction means total neglect of the body?
What does the yard's exercise culture reveal about identity and safety in prison?

181.title: Building a weekly aerobic routine
181.gist: Members report current exercise and their reasons for not doing more. The page recommends at least twenty minutes of aerobic activity three times a week, suggests mixing activities, and lists options from basketball to sustained dancing.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The page stresses enjoyment. Self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan) predicts that activities done for intrinsic enjoyment last longer than those done out of duty or guilt.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have each member schedule three twenty-minute slots this week inside the facility's real routine, naming day, time, and activity. Specific plans close the gap between intending and doing.

ask: Why does this page's twenty-minute minimum differ from the 150 minutes cited earlier, and how would you reconcile them for members?
Which reasons for not exercising are real barriers and which are rationalizations, and how can you tell?

182.title: Everyday movement and a stronger heart
182.gist: The page lists supporting habits like stairs, walking, and stretching, quizzes members on which activities are not aerobic, and explains how aerobic exercise strengthens the heart, lowers resting heart rate, and reduces heart disease and blood pressure.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Aerobic exercise tends to raise HDL, the 'good' cholesterol that helps clear fat from arteries, which is likely the protective substance the page means. Effects vary between people.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: A lower resting heart rate reflects more efficient work. Recovery has a similar logic: practiced coping skills let a person handle the same stress with less strain.

ask: What small daily movements are possible in a facility where stairs and errands are limited?
How might tracking resting heart rate give members visible proof of progress?

terms.d: High-density lipoprotein; 'good' cholesterol that carries fat away from arteries.

183.title: Heart risk in your own family
183.gist: Members explore family history of heart disease and whether they know their blood pressure or have been told to exercise. It turns general heart facts into a personal health inventory.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members have never had a regular doctor and do not know their numbers. Treat 'I don't know' as a useful answer and help them plan to ask medical staff for a blood pressure check.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Perceived personal risk is a core element of the Health Belief Model: people change when they see a threat as relevant to them and believe action will help. Family history makes the threat personal.

ask: When does personalizing risk motivate, and when does it trigger denial?
What would a minimal health checklist for reentry include?

184.title: Exercise as a natural antidepressant
184.gist: The page explains that aerobic exercise boosts brain chemicals regulating mood, sleep, and appetite, eases depression common in substance use disorders, normalizes sleep, and lifts self-esteem. A quick quiz checks the key ideas.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Reviews of trials find exercise reduces depressive symptoms, with effects in some analyses comparable to standard treatments for mild to moderate depression. Study quality varies, so it is best seen as a strong supplement, not a replacement for care.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The quiz implies only aerobic exercise affects mood; current evidence suggests strength training and yoga help too. Correct this during the debrief.

ask: Why might exercise work for depression through mastery and routine as much as chemistry?
How would you motivate a depressed member for whom getting off the bunk is the hardest step?

185.title: Back strength, immunity, and your fitness
185.gist: The page notes core exercises can prevent back pain and regular exercise can reduce illness and raise stamina. Members rate their physical condition, say whether they want to improve, and name exercises they enjoy.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Back pain is a common reason people first receive opioid prescriptions. Strengthening and movement-based approaches are now first-line advice for many back problems, which makes this tip quietly relevant to relapse prevention.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to rate fitness from one to ten, then ask why it isn't lower. This motivational interviewing move draws out strengths and reasons for change rather than defensiveness.

ask: Why does asking why not lower work better than asking why so low?
How could pain management without opioids be built into a reentry plan?

186.title: Why exercise belongs in recovery
186.gist: A final question asks members why exercise matters in recovery, followed by the Session 17 summary linking diet and exercise to mental and physical health, lower stress, and well-being.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking members to state the reason in their own words produces change talk, which in Miller and Rollnick's motivational interviewing is linked to later behavior change more than a counselor's arguments.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Close with a round where each person names one food change and one movement change for the coming week. Pairing commitments makes the session feel like a plan, not a lecture.

ask: What would count as evidence, a month from now, that this session made a difference?
How do self-care habits connect to identity change in recovery, from 'user' to 'someone who takes care of himself'?

187.title: Session 18 opens: physical wellness
187.gist: The introduction invites members to face health problems ignored while using and to get them treated, and flags insomnia as a common early-sobriety problem. Two parts cover physical problems and insomnia.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Substances often mask symptoms: opioids hide pain, alcohol hides anxiety, stimulants hide fatigue. Early sobriety can feel like getting sicker when it is actually the body reporting problems that were there all along.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Normalize that many members avoided doctors because of cost, fear of judgment, or warrants. Ask what would make medical visits feel safe after release.

ask: Why might people interpret new symptoms in early recovery as proof that sobriety is harmful?
How does health avoidance connect to the avoidance patterns that sustain addiction?

188.title: Balance between neglect and worry; anemia
188.gist: The page calls addiction biopsychosocial and advises a middle path: neither ignore real symptoms nor panic over every ache, since health anxiety is common early on. It then defines anemia and its symptoms, such as fatigue and breathlessness.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The biopsychosocial model, introduced by George Engel in 1977, argued medicine must look at biology, mind, and social context together. Addiction treatment adopted it to move beyond seeing addiction as either pure disease or pure moral failure.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Reading symptom lists makes some people sure they have everything, a phenomenon familiar to medical students. Name it with humor up front so anxious members can relax enough to learn.

ask: What does the biopsychosocial model let you do as a counselor that a purely medical or purely moral model would not?
How can you tell health anxiety from appropriate concern in a member who keeps asking about symptoms?

terms.d: View that biological, psychological, and social factors together shape health and illness.
Too few healthy red blood cells or too little hemoglobin to carry enough oxygen.

189.title: Types of anemia and getting checked
189.gist: The page describes iron-deficiency, B12-related (pernicious), and hemolytic anemia including inherited sickle-cell disease, notes treatments differ, and asks members about family history and whether they have had a blood test.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Pernicious anemia is usually an autoimmune problem in absorbing B12 rather than a dietary lack, and it is more common in older adults than the page implies. Heavy drinking can also cause anemia through poor diet and bleeding.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The sickle-cell trait persists in populations with a history of malaria because one copy offers some protection against it. It is a classic example of evolution trading one risk for another.

ask: Why might fatigue from anemia be mistaken for depression or laziness in early recovery?
What does the sickle-cell story teach about how a trait can be both protective and harmful?

terms.d: The protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen.

190.title: Gut troubles in early recovery
190.gist: The page explains that constipation alternating with diarrhea is common early in recovery, recommends fiber, fluids, and exercise over laxatives and antidiarrheal drugs, and quizzes members on the best fixes.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Opioids slow the gut, so withdrawal often swings it the other way. Advising against antidiarrheals also has a recovery reason: loperamide is an opioid that some people misuse in very high doses, which can cause dangerous heart rhythms.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Bodily topics invite jokes; let a bit of laughter happen. Humor reduces embarrassment, and members who laugh are more likely to report symptoms to medical staff later.

ask: Why might a recovery program advise against an over-the-counter drug that is safe for most people?
What other ordinary medicines carry hidden risks for people with substance use disorders?

191.title: Cancer risk and regular checkups
191.gist: The page defines cancer as uncontrolled cell growth, notes alcohol, drugs, smoking, diet, and chemicals raise risk, and urges regular exams and telling doctors about family history. Members check their own family history and exposures.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Alcohol is classified by the WHO's cancer agency as a carcinogen, linked to mouth, throat, esophagus, liver, breast, and colorectal cancers. Combined drinking and smoking raises some cancer risks more than either alone.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Tobacco is often the substance most likely to kill people in addiction treatment, yet programs historically ignored it. Many now offer smoking cessation alongside other treatment.

ask: Why have addiction programs often treated nicotine as acceptable while banning other drugs?
How would you raise cancer risk without triggering fatalism in members who have smoked for decades?

terms.d: Something that can cause cancer.

192.title: How plaque becomes decay and gum disease
192.gist: The page explains that plaque, formed from saliva, bacteria, and food, hardens into calculus and produces acid that erodes enamel, causing cavities. It also covers gingivitis, bleeding gums, and the causes of bad breath.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Gum disease is linked in research to heart disease and diabetes, likely through chronic inflammation, though whether it causes them is still debated. The mouth is not separate from the rest of the body.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Teeth matter for reentry: visible decay affects job interviews and self-esteem. Frame dental care as part of how members present themselves to the world, not just hygiene.

ask: How do appearance and stigma, such as damaged teeth, affect employment after release?
Why might dental neglect be one of the most visible lasting marks of addiction?

terms.d: Inflammation of the gums, often with bleeding; the early stage of gum disease.

193.title: Dental care then and now
193.gist: Members compare how much they cared for their teeth while using with their care now. The page then sets out dental hygiene basics: brushing after meals and before bed, fluoride toothpaste, soft brushes, and regular cleanings.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Current American Dental Association advice is to brush twice a day for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste and clean between teeth daily. The page's four-times-a-day rule is stricter than most dentists now recommend.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Comparing then and now gives members a visible measure of progress. Noticing small improvements builds the sense of self-efficacy that bigger changes depend on.

ask: Why might self-care tasks like brushing collapse first during active addiction?
How would you correct a manual's outdated advice without making members distrust the rest?

194.title: Flossing and a quick dental quiz
194.gist: The page argues flossing is as essential as brushing because it reaches plaque between teeth and at the gum line, notes early bleeding usually stops, and checks understanding with a short quiz.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on flossing alone is weaker than many assume; reviews have found limited high-quality evidence, partly because trials are hard to run. Dentists still recommend cleaning between teeth by floss or interdental brushes.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name one daily habit that takes under two minutes and pays off for decades. Flossing is a model for tiny keystone habits that support identity change.

ask: What does the flossing evidence debate teach about the difference between 'no evidence' and 'evidence of no effect'?
How do tiny habits connect to the larger structure of a recovery routine?

195.title: Diabetes: when sugar can't be used
195.gist: The page explains how insulin moves glucose into the liver and muscles, and how diabetes results when the body makes too little insulin or cannot use it. It lists symptoms from thirst to coma and stresses early detection by blood test.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Low blood sugar can mimic intoxication, with confusion and slurred speech, and people with diabetes have been mistaken for drunk by police. Knowing this matters in corrections and on the street.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Type 2 diabetes, the most common form, is strongly linked to weight and inactivity, and lifestyle programs have been shown in large trials to cut the risk of developing it in high-risk adults.

ask: How might antipsychotic medications, common in correctional populations, interact with diabetes risk?
Why do people with diabetes and substance use disorders face extra danger when drinking?

terms.d: A hormone that lets cells take in sugar from the blood for energy.

196.title: Diabetes checks and recovery headaches
196.gist: Members note family history of diabetes and testing, then the page explains that headaches are common in early recovery from stress, hunger, or poor sleep. It urges finding the cause before reaching for pills and seeing a doctor if headaches are severe.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Pausing to identify a headache's cause before medicating is a small version of a core recovery skill: noticing discomfort, naming it, and choosing a response instead of reflexively reaching for a substance.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Frequent use of pain relievers can itself cause rebound headaches, called medication overuse headache. The page's caution about pills is sound, beyond the addiction concern.

ask: What is the difference between avoiding all medication and using medication wisely in recovery?
How can urge surfing for cravings apply to physical pain like headaches?

197.title: Headache coping and hepatitis
197.gist: Members describe when headaches strike and better coping options. The page then introduces hepatitis, liver inflammation from viruses or alcohol and drugs, noting injection drug use spreads the serious types and vaccines exist for A and B.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: This text is dated. Hepatitis C, very common among people who inject drugs, is now curable in most cases with short courses of direct-acting antiviral pills. Also, the commonly recognized viral types are A through E; 'F' and 'G' are not standard.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask whether members have been tested for hepatitis C and B. Many correctional systems now offer testing and treatment; a cure may be within reach before release.

ask: How does the existence of a cure for hepatitis C change the message you would give members who inject drugs?
Why might people avoid testing even for a disease that is now curable?

terms.d: Inflammation of the liver, most often from viruses or alcohol.
Yellowing of the skin and eyes from liver problems.

198.title: Hepatitis quiz and blood pressure risks
198.gist: A short quiz checks how hepatitis spreads and what it affects. The page then explains hypertension, high blood pressure at rest, and its risk factors, including obesity, stress, smoking, heavy drinking, stimulants, and salt.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Several risk factors here, smoking, alcohol, stimulants, chronic stress, are also central to addiction. Recovery can lower blood pressure simply by removing these, a concrete health payoff worth naming.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Chronic stress keeps the body's fight-or-flight system switched on. Incarceration and poverty create exactly this kind of sustained stress, which helps explain health disparities beyond individual choices.

ask: How would you show members that quitting substances improves measurable health numbers?
What sources of chronic stress after release could keep blood pressure high even in sobriety?

199.title: Silent pressure and how it's treated
199.gist: The page stresses that high blood pressure usually has no symptoms, so testing is the only way to know, and lists its damage to brain, heart, kidneys, and eyes. Treatments include weight loss, exercise, stress reduction, quitting smoking and drinking, less salt, and medication.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: If the facility allows, arrange for members to learn their blood pressure, then revisit it in a month. A number they track themselves is more motivating than a warning they hear.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members may resist blood pressure medication as being 'on pills'. Distinguish medicines that treat a condition from substances used to change mood; the same distinction comes up with medications for addiction.

ask: How does resistance to taking blood pressure pills mirror stigma about medications for addiction?
Why are symptomless conditions so hard to treat, and what keeps people taking their medicine?

200.title: Heart attack signs and your risk
200.gist: The page describes heart attack symptoms, such as crushing chest pain spreading to the arm or jaw, and triggers including stress, exertion, and drug use. Members check whether they have risk factors and want to reduce them.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Cocaine use is a well-known trigger for heart attacks, even in young people with no other risk factors, because it constricts arteries and raises heart rate and blood pressure.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Women, older adults, and people with diabetes often have less classic symptoms, such as shortness of breath, nausea, or fatigue, instead of crushing chest pain. Teach the full range.

ask: Why do many people delay calling for help during a heart attack, and how is that like delaying help in a relapse?
How could you make risk checklists feel like a plan rather than a verdict?

201.title: Choosing a first step; obesity's risks
201.gist: Members name which heart risk they would work on first. The page then explains that weight gain in early recovery is normal but can become obesity, which raises risks for hypertension, stroke, heart disease, diabetes, some cancers, sleep apnea, and arthritis.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The claim that many obese people simply don't burn calories off oversimplifies; genetics, sleep, stress, medication, and appetite hormones all play roles. Weight stigma itself is linked to poorer health and avoiding doctors.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The opening question, what to work on first, is a choice point. Let members pick one risk factor only; choosing a single target respects autonomy and avoids the overwhelm that kills change plans.

ask: How do you discuss weight in a way that motivates without shaming?
Why might weight gain in early recovery threaten sobriety, especially for people who used stimulants to stay thin?

202.title: Calculating your ideal weight range
202.gist: The page repeats the Hamwi formula for estimating ideal weight by height and sex, with BMI noted as a screen. Members calculate their own range and check whether they are overweight or more than 20 percent above it.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: This formula appeared in the previous session too; here it becomes a personal calculation. Remind members it gives a rough range, and that muscle, frame, and age change what is healthy for any one person.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pair members to do the arithmetic together. Mental math in a practical context builds numeracy, and peers can soften the moment of seeing an uncomfortable number.

ask: What are the benefits and risks of having members calculate their own weight targets in a group?
Would waist size or fitness be a better target than weight for this population?

203.title: Weight goals and tuberculosis
203.gist: Members decide whether to work on weight. The page then explains tuberculosis, an airborne bacterial lung infection, its symptoms, and screening with a skin test or blood test, followed by a short true/false check.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Prisons and jails have historically had higher TB rates than the community because of crowding and poor ventilation, which is why intake TB screening is standard in US correctional facilities.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Most infected people have latent TB: the bacteria are held in check and not contagious. Treating latent TB prevents later active disease, a clear example of preventive rather than reactive care.

ask: Why does a positive TB skin test not mean someone is contagious, and how would you explain that to an anxious member?
What makes institutions like prisons breeding grounds for infectious disease?

terms.d: TB infection held dormant by the immune system; no symptoms, not contagious, but can activate later.

204.title: Insomnia's role in recovery
204.gist: Part 2 explains that insomnia is common during detox and early recovery and occasionally even years later, and that poor sleep makes people more vulnerable to relapse triggers. Members describe their sleep problems while using and now.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Sleep problems in early recovery predict relapse in several studies of alcohol use disorder. Sleep disturbance can persist for months after quitting alcohol, longer than many people expect.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prison sleep is shaped by lights, noise, counts, and hypervigilance. Acknowledge that some insomnia here is environmental and adaptive, not just withdrawal, before offering strategies.

ask: How does sleep loss weaken self-control, and what does that suggest about relapse timing?
Which sleep problems in custody can members actually change, and which must they tolerate?

terms.d: Persistent difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting restful sleep.

205.title: Sleepless nights during detox
205.gist: Members explore how sleep problems feed and interfere with addiction. The page then explains detox insomnia comes with agitation and anxiety, feels worse than it is, may need medical supervision, and warns some sleep medicines are addictive.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Worrying about not sleeping keeps the brain alert, which prevents sleep, a loop CBT for insomnia targets directly. Catastrophic thoughts about sleep are one of its main treatment targets.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is recommended as the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia by major medical bodies, ahead of medication, and has been studied in people with alcohol use disorder with encouraging results.

ask: Why might sedative sleep medicines be especially risky for this population?
How does the page's warning that insomnia feels worse than it is apply to cravings too?

terms.d: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia; structured techniques that change sleep habits and thoughts.

206.title: What helps you sleep; how drugs disrupt it
206.gist: The page reassures that the worst detox symptoms usually pass within about a week. Members list their sleep techniques and whether they need help, then the page explains how stimulants block sleep and alcohol helps sleep come but ruins its quality.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Alcohol suppresses REM sleep early in the night and then produces a rebound with fragmented, restless sleep later. Many drinkers believe it helps them sleep because they notice only the first half.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to share one sleep technique that works for them and collect them on the board. Peer-generated strategies tend to be more realistic for the facility than textbook tips.

ask: Why do people keep believing alcohol helps them sleep despite their own bad nights?
How would you distinguish expected detox insomnia from something that needs medical attention?

terms.d: Rapid eye movement sleep; the stage linked to vivid dreams and emotional processing.

207.title: Stages of sleep deprivation
207.gist: The page describes escalating effects of sleep loss, from irritability and short attention to microsleeps and, after days awake, paranoia and hallucinations, worse when drugs are involved. Members recall their longest time without sleep and how it felt.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Paranoia and hallucinations after days awake are well known from stimulant binges. Some of what looks like drug-induced psychosis is partly sleep-deprivation psychosis, and both often resolve with rest and abstinence.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Questions about the longest time awake often bring vivid war stories from binges. Allow brief accounts, then pivot to what they cost. Avoid letting the stories glamorize use.

ask: How might sleep deprivation have shaped decisions that led to arrests for some members?
How do you let members tell using stories without the group drifting into euphoric recall?

terms.d: A brief, involuntary lapse into sleep lasting seconds, often without awareness.

208.title: Lingering insomnia and the excuse trap
208.gist: The page says insomnia can recur for weeks after stopping, especially after depressants like alcohol, heroin, and marijuana, and warns people may overinterpret it and use it as a reason to take a sedative. Members examine their worry about sleep.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Using insomnia to justify a sedative is a seemingly irrelevant decision in Marlatt's relapse model: a choice that looks reasonable but sets up relapse. Labeling the pattern helps members catch it.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The page calls these episodes short, but for some people, particularly after heavy alcohol use, sleep can stay disturbed for months. Members should hear that persistence is not failure and can be treated.

ask: What distinguishes a legitimate request for sleep help from an apparently irrelevant decision toward relapse?
How might a counselor and medical staff coordinate on sleep complaints?

terms.d: A small choice that seems harmless but moves someone closer to a relapse situation.

209.title: A steady sleep schedule protects recovery
209.gist: Members examine whether insomnia has ever led them to use. The page then urges a regular schedule of seven to eight hours, especially on emotionally hard nights, and telling a counselor, sponsor, or doctor about sleep problems.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: A consistent wake time anchors the body's circadian clock more than a consistent bedtime. Sleep scientists often advise getting up at the same time even after a bad night, which builds sleep pressure for the next one.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Sleep is when strong feelings, grief, guilt, fear about release, often surface. Teach a short grounding routine members can use on their bunk, such as slow breathing with a longer exhale.

ask: Why might emotions that were numbed by substances show up most strongly at night?
How does telling someone about sleep problems function as relapse prevention?

210.title: Your plan for better rest
210.gist: Members write how good sleep would help their recovery and list techniques to break poor sleeping habits. It turns the session's sleep information into a personal plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Classic sleep hygiene and stimulus control (Bootzin) include: use the bed only for sleep, get up if awake too long, keep a fixed wake time, and avoid caffeine late. Stimulus control is one of the better-supported parts of CBT-I.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members build a five-minute wind-down routine from what is possible in their housing unit, then try it for a week and report back. A tested routine beats a list of ideas.

ask: Which sleep hygiene rules are impossible in a prison setting, and what alternatives fit?
How could you evaluate whether sleep improvement affects other recovery outcomes in your groups?

211.title: A step-by-step plan against insomnia
211.gist: The page gives a first-line plan, no naps, bed only for sleep and intimacy, regular bedtime, get up if not sleepy within about half an hour, fixed alarm, and a backup plan: earlier worrying, afternoon exercise, a controlled environment, no late caffeine or sweets, and relaxation.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: These steps closely match stimulus control and sleep scheduling, the behavioral core of CBT-I. Trials suggest the benefits of CBT-I tend to last longer after treatment ends than those of sleep medication.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Leaving the room is impossible in a cell. Adapt: sit up, read under allowed light, or do a quiet breathing exercise, then lie down again. Also suggest a 'worry time' earlier in the day, writing worries down before evening count.

ask: Why does getting out of bed when awake work, even though it feels like losing sleep?
Which steps would you prioritize for a member with nightmares related to trauma, where standard rules may not be enough?

terms.d: Retraining the brain to link bed with sleep by leaving it when awake.

212.title: Session 18 wrap-up
212.gist: The summary recaps physical problems members may have ignored while using and the insomnia common in early sobriety. Some conditions need medical treatment, while others like insomnia respond to behavior change, all in service of staying sober.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The session divides problems into ones that need professionals and ones members can manage themselves. That distinction mirrors the Serenity Prayer's split between what can and cannot be changed, applied to the body.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Close by asking each member to name one health question to bring to medical staff. Writing it down before an appointment raises the chance it actually gets asked.

ask: How might better physical health change a member's confidence in tackling psychological work?
What would a health section of a reentry plan look like if you designed it?

213.title: Session 19 opens: problem solving
213.gist: The introduction says the session addresses problems that piled up during addiction and new ones in sobriety, and offers a six-step method. Three parts cover life problems, the steps, and techniques like prioritizing and brainstorming.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Structured problem-solving training comes from D'Zurilla and Goldfried's work in the early 1970s and became problem-solving therapy. It is a component of many cognitive-behavioral programs for justice-involved adults.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Reentry concentrates problems: housing, ID, debt, supervision rules, family, jobs. Research on scarcity (Mullainathan and Shafir) suggests that juggling many urgent problems itself drains the mental bandwidth needed to solve them.

ask: Why might teaching a structured method matter more for people under heavy stress than for people with stable lives?
What reentry problems will members face that no six-step method can solve alone?

214.title: How addiction lets problems pile up
214.gist: After Part 3's objectives, the page explains that addiction adds problems to normal life and describes a typical pattern: distorted thinking hides problems, responsibility is denied, using takes priority, and problems are ignored until they accumulate.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Avoidance gives immediate relief and is reinforced each time, while costs arrive later. Behavioral psychology calls this negative reinforcement, and it explains why ignoring a problem can become as habitual as using.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The pattern centers individual distortions. For many members, problems also piled up through poverty, policing, and lack of resources. Acknowledge both to keep the account honest and avoid pure self-blame.

ask: How do you hold members accountable for avoidance without ignoring structural causes?
Where does denial end and genuine lack of awareness begin?

terms.d: A behavior grows stronger because it removes something unpleasant, like anxiety.

215.title: Blame, neglect, and escape
215.gist: Members reflect on times they blamed others for problems they caused, ignored problems because of drinking or drug use, and tried to forget problems that overwhelmed them. It makes the avoidance pattern personal.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Blaming others is a common cognitive distortion targeted in criminal thinking curricula, sometimes called externalizing or the victim stance. Yochelson and Samenow highlighted this pattern in their work on criminal thinking.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect members to answer yes easily to the second and third questions but resist the first. Model it by noting how common blame is for everyone, and ask for a small, low-stakes example to start.

ask: Why is admitting blame harder than admitting avoidance?
How can externalizing protect self-esteem in the short run while preventing change?

216.title: Why problems feel harder early in recovery
216.gist: Members rate their current problem-solving. The page explains that early recovery brings poor concentration, little practice with daily problems, and even new problems created by recovery, so help from sponsors, counselors, family, and sober friends matters. Members list problems they need help with.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on early abstinence shows that attention, memory, and planning often improve over weeks to months, especially after heavy alcohol use. Expecting a gradual return of these abilities helps members be patient with themselves.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Seeking help is itself a problem-solving skill. Social support is consistently linked with better recovery outcomes, partly because it supplies the planning capacity a stressed person lacks.

ask: What problems can recovery itself create, such as losing using friends, and how should they be addressed?
Why might asking for help feel dangerous to someone who learned self-reliance in prison?

217.title: Choosing helpers and unhelpful reactions
217.gist: Members name one or two people they could ask for help and why. The page then lists unhelpful responses to problems in sobriety: feeling problems are new, being overwhelmed, exaggerating, using problems as an excuse to relapse, and guilt and shame.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Exaggerating severity is catastrophizing, a distortion Beck and Ellis both described. Ellis's term 'awfulizing' captures how turning a bad situation into an unbearable one makes action feel pointless.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking why they chose a helper reveals whether the person is truly safe and sober. Gently probe: would this person help you solve the problem or help you forget it?

ask: How do guilt and shame differ in their effect on problem solving?
What makes a person a good helper for a problem, beyond loyalty?

terms.d: Treating a problem as far worse or more permanent than the evidence supports.

218.title: Your unhealthy reactions to problems
218.gist: Members identify their own unhealthy ways of responding to problems, how those responses feel, and how they would like to respond differently. It moves from recognizing the pattern to wanting change.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Linking reactions to feelings makes the cost visible. In CBT terms, members connect a situation, their response, and the emotional consequence, the groundwork for choosing a different response.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members score how they felt an hour after their usual unhealthy response, and a day after. Short-term relief versus longer-term cost is often clearest when time is made explicit.

ask: Why do people repeat responses that leave them feeling worse?
How does a desired change become a plan rather than a wish?

219.title: Willingness: the starting point
219.gist: The page argues good problem solving starts with willingness: to accept problems exist, to believe solutions exist, to examine them, to find solutions, and to change yourself. Members check whether they are willing to examine and solve problems and change.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Problem-solving research separates orientation from skill. D'Zurilla and Nezu found that a positive problem orientation, seeing problems as solvable challenges, predicts outcomes as much as technique does. Willingness is that orientation.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Seligman's research on learned helplessness showed that repeated uncontrollable setbacks teach people to stop trying even when control returns. Belief that a solution exists counteracts that learned passivity.

ask: How would you work with a member whose experience has taught him that problems rarely get solved?
Is willingness something a person can choose, or must it be built through small successes?

terms.d: Giving up after repeated uncontrollable failure, even when change becomes possible.

220.title: Neither catastrophize nor avoid
220.gist: Members finish the willingness checks, then the page calls for balance: avoid both worst-case thinking and avoidance. Using an unpaid bill as an example, it urges contacting the business or making a token payment, and stresses solving rather than dwelling.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Rumination, replaying a problem without acting, feels like work but usually deepens low mood. Research by Nolen-Hoeksema linked rumination to depression; shifting to concrete steps interrupts it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The bill example fits reentry well: court fines, fees, and child support often go unpaid until a warrant appears. Help members role-play the phone call to a clerk or creditor; rehearsing it makes it doable.

ask: What is the difference between thinking a problem through and ruminating on it?
Why might a small token payment change both the creditor's response and the person's own sense of control?

terms.d: Repetitive, passive dwelling on problems and feelings without moving toward action.

221.title: Do problems pile up on you?
221.gist: Members check whether they let problems sit and accumulate, then name the problem-solving weak spots they want to fix. It closes Part 1 by turning the idea of avoidance into a personal admission before the step model arrives.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Avoidance is negatively reinforced: putting a problem off brings instant relief, so the delay habit gets stronger even as the problem grows. In addiction the substance often served the same relief function, which is why procrastination and use tend to travel together.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members will say no to question 1 to look competent. Normalize it first by naming something you yourself put off, then ask what the pile looked like the month before their arrest. Concrete timelines get more honest answers than abstract yes/no boxes.

ask: Is procrastination in this population better framed as a skill deficit, an emotion-regulation strategy, or both, and does the answer change your intervention?
What problems are structurally impossible to solve from inside a cell, and how do you keep this exercise from producing helplessness?

terms.d: A behavior grows stronger because it removes something unpleasant, such as the dread of facing a bill.

222.title: Steps one and two: name it, own it
222.gist: Part 2 opens a six-step problem-solving method, starting with defining the problem narrowly and then taking ownership of one's part in it. It separates owning from self-blame, a distinction that decides whether members engage or shut down.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This mirrors D'Zurilla and Goldfried's social problem-solving model, where a precise problem definition is the step people most often skip. A vague problem like my life is a mess offers no handle; a specific one like I owe two months of child support does.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The owning-versus-blaming split echoes the Stoic division between what is up to us and what is not. Responsibility looks forward to what can change; blame looks backward to assign guilt. Shame research suggests the second tends to freeze people rather than move them.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect members to hear own it as admit you are a bad person. Draw two columns on the board: what I did that fed this, and what I can do next. Leave out a column for who I am.

ask: Where does owning the problem end and appropriately naming systemic causes such as poverty or racism begin?
Why might stripping feelings out of a problem definition help, and when could it backfire?

terms.d: Stating a problem in concrete, observable terms narrow enough that a specific action could address it.

223.title: Brainstorm before you judge
223.gist: After reflecting on ownership, members learn step three: list every possible solution, even weak or untried ones, and borrow ideas from others. It pushes against the rigid, single-option thinking that often keeps people repeating the same failed moves.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Separating idea generation from evaluation, known as deferred judgment, comes from Osborn's brainstorming work. Studies broadly support generating many options for individuals, though group brainstorming often produces fewer ideas than people working alone and then pooling.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Give the group a stuck scenario and a hard rule: ten solutions in three minutes, no comments allowed. Include at least two absurd ones on purpose. The silly ones loosen thinking and often contain a usable seed.

ask: How might criminal thinking patterns like a closed channel limit the solution list, and how would you spot that live?
Is asking others how they solved it always safe advice for someone whose network is mostly people still using?

terms.d: Holding off criticism of ideas until a full list exists, so evaluation does not kill options too early.

224.title: Weigh outcomes, then commit
224.gist: Steps four and five ask members to predict the results of each option against short- and long-term goals, then build a concrete plan with how, when, where, who, and a backup. This is where impulsive choosing gets slowed into deliberate choosing.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Consequential thinking is a core target in correctional CBT because many offending choices weigh only the next hour. Holding short- and long-term outcomes side by side counters what behavioral economists call delay discounting, the tendency to value immediate rewards far more than later ones.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Gollwitzer's research on implementation intentions, plans phrased as if X happens then I will do Y, shows they reliably raise follow-through compared with goals alone. The page's how-when-where plan is a close cousin.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to turn their plan into one if-then sentence. If my cousin offers me a ride to the old block, then I will say I already have a ride. Specific beats sincere.

ask: Delay discounting is steeper in people with addictions; is that a cause, a consequence, or both?
What makes a backup plan protective rather than a built-in excuse to drop plan A?

terms.d: An if-then plan linking a specific situation to a specific action, which makes following through more automatic.

225.title: Learn from what happened
225.gist: The sixth step urges members to retry what works and drop what keeps failing, then asks whether they have used these steps before or have their own. It invites members to recognize skills they already have.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The six steps form a loop much like the scientific method or the plan-do-study-act cycle in quality improvement: a plan is a hypothesis, the outcome is data. Framing a failed plan as data rather than proof of worthlessness protects against the abstinence violation effect.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 2 is gold. Many members solved hard problems on the street, such as logistics, negotiation, and reading people. Name those as real skills aimed at the wrong goals, and ask how they could be redirected.

ask: When is persistence wise and when is it the stubbornness the page warns against? What signal tells them apart?
How does a strengths-based framing like the Good Lives Model fit with a risk-focused curriculum?

terms.d: Marlatt's term for the all-or-nothing reaction to a slip, where one lapse feels like total failure and invites full relapse.

226.title: Apply it to a real problem, part one
226.gist: Members pick a current problem and work the first two steps on it: define it precisely, then trace how it started, who was involved, and how long it has lasted. It moves the method from theory to the member's own life.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Skills generalize best when practiced on personally relevant material; social learning theory holds that rehearsal on real stakes, with feedback, builds self-efficacy more than abstract examples. The ownership questions also function like a mini functional analysis.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Steer members toward a problem that is medium-sized and partly in their control. A first attempt at getting my children back may overwhelm; how to answer my daughter's letter is workable and still meaningful.

ask: What risks come with asking how many people were involved for a member whose problem includes co-defendants or victims?
How would you debrief a member who picks a problem they cannot influence at all while incarcerated?

terms.d: Bandura's term for a person's belief that they can carry out a specific action successfully.

227.title: Options and realistic forecasts
227.gist: Continuing the personal problem, members list past, failed, and suggested solutions, then forecast outcomes realistically, avoiding both fearful catastrophizing and wishful fantasy. It trains balanced prediction, a core cognitive skill.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The page names two classic thinking traps: catastrophizing, from Beck's cognitive distortions, and magical optimism. Both distort forecasts. Gilbert and Wilson's work on affective forecasting shows people generally misjudge how future outcomes will feel, which is another reason to test predictions against evidence.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: For each solution, have the member write a worst case, a best case, and a most likely case. Then ask: what would your most level-headed friend predict? The third column is the one to plan on.

ask: How do you tell realistic pessimism, rooted in real barriers after release, from a cognitive distortion?
Why might asking what has changed since a solution failed be the most useful question on this page?

terms.d: Jumping to the worst possible outcome and treating it as likely, which spikes anxiety and blocks action.

228.title: Plan it, try it, review it
228.gist: Members finish their worked problem by picking the best solution, laying out who, what, when, where, and how with a backup, and later reviewing what worked best and worst. It completes the full loop on one real issue.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Revisit question 6 in a later session rather than leaving it blank. Bringing the plan back after a week makes the review real and shows the group that follow-up is part of the method, not an extra.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Linear step models assume time, information, and control that people facing release may not have, such as housing waitlists or parole rules. Pair the plan with honest talk about what depends on others, so a stalled plan is not read as personal failure.

ask: What would an after-action review look like if borrowed from the military and adapted for a recovery group?
How specific does a plan need to be before it is likely to be carried out?

terms.d: A structured debrief asking what was planned, what happened, why, and what to do differently next time.

229.title: Triage: which ticket gets paid first
229.gist: Part 3 adds practical tools, starting with prioritizing, using the image of a big pile of fines with different costs and deadlines. Members then list problems that need attention soon, a direct antidote to the overwhelm that leads to giving up.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Emergency medicine calls this triage, and Eisenhower's urgent-versus-important grid is a familiar version. Sorting turns a cloud of dread into a ranked list, which is easier on working memory and on mood.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Feeling swamped by many problems can slide into learned helplessness, Seligman's term for giving up after repeated uncontrollable setbacks. Ranking problems restores a sense of control, which is protective against both depression and relapse.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Update the example to fit the room: a parole check-in versus a commissary debt. Ask what happens if each is ignored for a month. The cost of delay is a quick way to rank.

ask: Do urgent problems crowd out important ones for people in early recovery, and what does that cost over a year?
Is learned helplessness the right lens here, or does it underplay real structural barriers?

terms.d: Sorting problems by severity and urgency so the most pressing ones get handled first.
Giving up trying after repeated experiences of not being able to control outcomes.

230.title: Shrink big problems into small ones
230.gist: Members finish ranking by naming problems that can wait, then learn to break a complex problem into smaller parts and solve them one at a time. It makes large reentry tasks feel doable.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Breaking goals into proximal subgoals has support from Bandura and Schunk's studies, where near-term targets raised both performance and self-efficacy compared with distant goals alone. Small wins build momentum.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The proverb on this page is usually credited to the Tao Te Ching, attributed to Laozi. Twelve Step culture says the same thing as one day at a time, and project managers call it a work breakdown structure.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pick one big goal, like getting a job after release, and have the group shout out sub-steps until each one could be done in a single day. Count the steps; the length itself is reassuring.

ask: Can chunking ever hide the big picture, so someone completes steps without asking whether the goal is right?
Why might naming problems that can wait reduce anxiety even before anything is solved?

terms.d: A near-term, small target on the way to a larger goal, which gives quicker feedback and motivation.

231.title: Chunk the problem that scares you
231.gist: Using a legal problem broken into lawyer-referral steps as a model, members name a current overwhelming problem, say why it feels so big, and split it into smaller problems. It converts dread into a first move.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Overwhelm is partly a cognitive-load problem: a vague, many-sided task exceeds what working memory can hold, so the mind defaults to avoidance. Writing the parts down offloads them to paper and frees attention for one piece at a time.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask why it feels overwhelming before asking for steps. Members often reveal the real blocker, such as shame about calling a lawyer or not reading well. That emotional barrier is often the first sub-problem worth naming.

ask: What is the smallest step that still counts as real progress, and who should decide that, you or the member?
How could a counselor tell when breaking things down has become a way to stall?

terms.d: The amount of mental effort a task demands of working memory at one time.

232.title: Asking for help as strength
232.gist: Members check whether their sub-steps need further splitting, then the page reframes asking for help as mature rather than weak, noting that people often enjoy helping and that mistakes others made are also lessons. It targets a code of self-reliance common in prison culture.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Prison codes often prize never showing need, since vulnerability can be dangerous inside. Help-seeking research also finds masculine norms of self-reliance predict lower use of support. The page is asking members to switch codes between environments, which is a real skill, not a simple attitude fix.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The helper therapy principle, named by Riessman, holds that helping others benefits the helper. Studies of AA service and sponsorship broadly link helping others with better sobriety outcomes, though causation is hard to pin down.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask who has been asked for help by someone and how it felt. Most will say respected or trusted. Then flip it: what stops you from giving someone that same feeling?

ask: Is it fair to tell people that asking for help is safe when, inside a facility, it sometimes truly is not?
Why might learning from someone who failed teach more than learning from someone who succeeded?

terms.d: The idea that people who help others with a shared problem gain benefits themselves, such as purpose and confidence.

233.title: Find someone who has been there
233.gist: Members name a problem where they need help, choose a person with relevant experience and explain why, and identify what kind of help they want, from ideas to simply being heard. It builds a concrete support map.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Social support research distinguishes types: informational (advice), instrumental (practical aid), and emotional (listening). Question 3 teaches members to ask for the right type, which reduces the classic frustration of wanting to vent and getting a lecture.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Watch for members who list someone still active in use or crime as their expert. Do not shame it; ask whether that person solved the problem in a way the member wants to copy. It opens a useful conversation about recovery capital.

ask: How does recovery capital, the resources a person can draw on, shape who can realistically answer question 2?
When might a professional be a better choice than a peer who has been there, and vice versa?

terms.d: The personal, social, and community resources a person can draw on to start and sustain recovery.

234.title: A fifteen-minute brainstorm with a partner
234.gist: For moments of being stuck, the page lays out a timed brainstorm with a trusted helper: state the problem aloud, say ideas freely, write them down, then sort the good from the poor. Members begin by naming a problem they are stuck on.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Stating a problem aloud has a cousin in software engineering called rubber duck debugging: explaining the issue to someone, even a toy, often surfaces the answer. Speaking forces a vague worry into sequence and words.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Getting stuck often reflects functional fixedness, Duncker's term for seeing objects or options only in their usual role. A time box and a no-judgment rule lower the pressure that keeps people locked in that fixed view.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Model it live with a volunteer and a stopwatch. Write every idea, including jokes. Fifteen minutes feels long; most groups run dry at five, and the best ideas often show up right after that lull.

ask: Why might ideas that come after the first dry spell be more original?
Who in a reentry setting counts as trusted enough for this, and what if a member can name no one?

terms.d: A mental block where people see an object or option only in its familiar use, missing new solutions.

235.title: Brainstorming you already do
235.gist: Members find everyday situations that already resemble brainstorming and decide which kinds of problems and which helpers suit it. It shows them the tool is familiar, not a classroom invention.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prompts that work well: planning a family gathering, figuring out a budget with a partner, or a crew working out a job site problem. Members often discover that the group talk they already do in the dorm is brainstorming.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Brainstorming suits open-ended problems with many possible answers. It is a poor fit for problems that need facts, like a legal deadline, where the better move is asking someone who knows. Help members match the tool to the problem.

ask: What makes a problem a good candidate for brainstorming versus expert advice?
How might group dynamics, such as status inside the unit, quietly shape whose ideas get written down?

236.title: Score the pros and cons
236.gist: When several solutions compete, members list benefits and risks for each and may score them from 0 to plus 10 and 0 to minus 10. The first question asks whether they face such a choice now.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Benjamin Franklin described a similar method he called moral or prudential algebra, listing pros and cons over several days and crossing off items of equal weight. The page's numbers are a lighter version of decision analysis.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Decisional balance is also a classic motivational interviewing tool. Miller and Rollnick later cautioned that working through pros and cons of change can deepen ambivalence for people not yet committed, so it fits best when choosing among options rather than deciding whether to change.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Score one choice two ways: once thinking only of tonight, once thinking of a year from now. Watch how the numbers shift. That gap is the short-term pull the group needs to see.

ask: Do numbers make a decision more rational or just make gut feelings look objective?
How would you weigh a risk that is unlikely but catastrophic, like a parole violation, on a simple 0 to minus 10 scale?

terms.d: Listing and weighing the pros and cons of options, used in MI to explore ambivalence about change.

237.title: Everyday risk-benefit thinking
237.gist: Members recall times they weighed benefits and risks informally and explain how doing it on purpose could help. It closes the toolkit by linking a formal method to instincts they already use.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Kahneman's dual-process idea separates fast, intuitive thinking from slow, deliberate thinking. Most informal risk judgments are fast. The worksheet helps members recognize when to switch to slow mode, especially under craving or anger.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members did sharp risk-benefit math in illegal activity, such as weighing the odds of getting caught. Acknowledge the skill, then ask what was left off those lists, often family, health, and time.

ask: Why do craving and anger make slow, deliberate thinking harder to access?
Is a member who is skilled at street risk analysis at an advantage or a disadvantage for this exercise?

terms.d: The idea that people use both fast, automatic judgment and slow, effortful reasoning.

238.title: Session 19 wrap-up
238.gist: The summary reviews the session: past problem-solving struggles, the six-step plan applied to a real problem, and the tips on prioritizing, chunking, asking for help, brainstorming, and weighing options. It ties daily problem solving directly to staying sober.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Problem-solving therapy, developed by D'Zurilla and Nezu, has good evidence for depression and some support in substance use and correctional programs. Gains depend heavily on practice outside sessions, not on knowing the steps.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The claim that every problem has a solution is motivating but not literally true. Some losses can only be accepted. That is a good bridge into the next session on beliefs, where accepting what cannot change appears.

ask: Which of the session's tools would you expect members to still use six months after release, and why?
How would you measure whether problem-solving skill actually improved, rather than just worksheet completion?

terms.d: A structured CBT approach that teaches people to define problems, generate options, decide, act, and review.

239.title: Session 20 opens: beliefs shape stress
239.gist: This introduction to Attitudes and Beliefs previews three parts: why beliefs matter, disputing irrational beliefs, and building a positive self-attitude. It signals a turn from fixing outer problems to examining the thinking that colors them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The session draws on Albert Ellis's rational emotive behavior therapy and Beck's cognitive therapy, both holding that our interpretation of events, more than the events alone, drives emotion. That idea traces back to Epictetus, whom Ellis cited directly.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will hear your thinking is the problem as dismissing real injustice. Say early that the goal is not to pretend bad things are fine but to stop adding avoidable pain on top of them.

ask: Where is the line between a belief being irrational and a belief being a fair read of a harsh environment?
How does this session's focus on inner beliefs complement the outward problem solving of Session 19?

terms.d: Rational emotive behavior therapy, Ellis's approach of identifying and disputing rigid, irrational beliefs that drive distress.

240.title: Stressors versus stress
240.gist: After listing objectives for parts 2 and 3, the page begins Part 1 with the half-full glass and a key split: stressors are outside demands, stress is the inner reaction. Seeing the gap between them is the doorway to every later skill.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model says stress arises from appraisal: judging whether a demand threatens you and whether you can cope. Two people facing the same demand can appraise it differently and feel very different stress.

deeper.label: Connection
