deeper.text: Hans Selye, who popularized the word stress in biology, borrowed it from engineering, where stress is the load on a material. The page's split mirrors that: the load is outside, the strain is inside.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some stressors, such as solitary confinement or chronic poverty, are harmful to almost anyone regardless of attitude. Keep the appraisal message honest so it does not imply members can think their way out of every hardship.

ask: If appraisal drives stress, why do chronic stressors still wear people down even when they cope well?
What does the courage the page mentions actually require of a member?

terms.d: An outside demand, such as a person, event, or rule, that asks something of you.
Your judgment of what a situation means for you and whether you can handle it.

241.title: Same court order, two reactions
241.gist: Members define stress and stressor, then read about two women given the same order to attend NA: one resents it and feels stress, the other welcomes it and feels relief. The difference lies in what each believes about her use.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The two women sit at different stages of change in Prochaska and DiClemente's model: one precontemplative, one preparing for action. Their reactions show that readiness, not just thinking style, colors how mandated treatment lands.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on coerced or mandated treatment broadly finds outcomes can be comparable to voluntary treatment, partly because people often build internal motivation once inside. Results vary, and perceived coercion may matter more than legal status.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Most of your members are mandated too. Ask openly: who here is more like the first woman? Honest answers give you a live reading of the room's motivation.

ask: Can a counselor ethically try to change a mandated member's appraisal of their own treatment?
What would motivational interviewing do with the woman who resents the order?

terms.d: The stage of change where a person does not yet see a problem or intend to change.

242.title: Event, belief, feeling: the ABC chain
242.gist: The page lays out a three-step chain of stressor event, belief, and emotional consequence, applies it to the resentful woman, and checks comprehension with quick multiple-choice questions. It gives members the session's core diagnostic tool.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is Ellis's ABC model: Activating event, Belief, Consequence. Ellis later added D for disputing and E for a new effective outlook, which is exactly where Part 2 is heading. Teaching the letters now makes the later steps feel like a natural continuation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The quiz is easy on purpose; use it as a warm-up. Then ask a harder question aloud: is the belief that NA is a waste of time irrational, or just a different opinion? It previews the line between disagreeing and distorting.

ask: Do feelings ever come before beliefs, as some emotion researchers argue, and what would that mean for the ABC model?
Is anger at a court order always a C caused by an irrational B, or can it be a fitting response?

terms.d: Ellis's frame: an Activating event meets a Belief, which produces an emotional and behavioral Consequence.

243.title: Change the belief, change the feeling
243.gist: The page explains that the two women's different beliefs about having a problem, needing help, and NA's value produced their different feelings. Members then pick a stressful event of their own and imagine how other beliefs might have changed how they felt.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Epictetus wrote that people are disturbed not by things but by their views of things; Shakespeare's Hamlet says nothing is good or bad but thinking makes it so. The idea is ancient, and CBT gave it a testable method.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Gross's research on cognitive reappraisal shows that reinterpreting a situation tends to lower negative emotion without the physical costs of suppressing it. Reappraisal is among the better-supported emotion-regulation strategies, though it works less well when stress is extreme.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rewrite their stressful event in one sentence from the view of someone who would barely care. Then from someone who would be devastated. The event stays the same; only the lens moves.

ask: If beliefs about whether NA can help drive feelings, how might early positive experiences in a group change those beliefs?
When is reappraisal the wrong tool, for instance when action is needed instead?

terms.d: Reinterpreting the meaning of a situation to change its emotional impact.

244.title: The tyranny of should and must
244.gist: The page separates rational from irrational, self-defeating beliefs and flags warning words like should, must, always, and never. Members dissect a first example where not understanding something becomes proof of stupidity.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Ellis called rigid demands musturbation and saw them as the root of much distress: turning a preference into an absolute requirement. Beck's list adds labeling, where one event becomes a fixed identity, as in I must be stupid.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Literacy and learning disabilities are common in correctional groups, so this example can hit close to home. Normalize it: many smart people struggle with dense reading. Ask what else could explain trouble understanding, like noise, fatigue, or how the material is written.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to swap must for I would prefer and say the sentence again. Notice how the emotional temperature drops while the goal stays.

ask: Can should statements ever be healthy, as in moral commitments, and how would you tell those apart from irrational demands?
How might school experiences shape the I must be stupid belief in this population?

terms.d: Turning a single behavior or mistake into a global judgment of who you are.

245.title: Is total control of emotions possible?
245.gist: Members finish the stupidity example, then take on a second belief: that one ought to control emotions completely and is weak otherwise. They are asked why it is irrational and what rational reasons explain imperfect control.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Emotions arise partly from fast brain systems, such as threat responses involving the amygdala, before deliberate thought catches up. Control is about what we do with feelings, not whether they show up. DBT, from Linehan, builds skills around exactly this distinction.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Wegner's white bear studies found that trying hard to suppress a thought tends to make it return more. Demanding total emotional control can backfire the same way, which is useful for members who pride themselves on never feeling.

ask: In prison, showing emotion can carry real risk; how do you teach acceptance of feelings without making members unsafe?
Is the goal emotional control, emotional regulation, or emotional acceptance, and how do these differ?

terms.d: The ways people influence which emotions they have, when, and how they experience and express them.

246.title: The need for everyone's approval
246.gist: After closing the emotion-control item, members examine a belief from a conflict at an NA meeting: that they must agree with everyone or be rejected. They test whether universal agreement is possible.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Ellis listed the need for love and approval from virtually everyone as a core irrational belief. It drives people-pleasing, which in recovery can mean saying yes to offers they should refuse simply to avoid conflict.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Link it to refusal skills: who has used because saying no felt like losing a friend? Members often see the connection between approval-seeking and relapse faster than any lecture could make it.

ask: How do cultural values around harmony or respect for elders affect what counts as an irrational need for approval?
What is the difference between healthy belonging and the approval demand Ellis described?

terms.d: A pattern of putting others' wishes first to avoid disapproval, often at one's own expense.

247.title: Change is impossible for me
247.gist: Members test whether disagreement really brings rejection, then take on a treatment-defeating belief: the program is interesting but change is impossible because of long habit. They examine whether anyone is locked into the same behavior forever.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Carol Dweck's fixed versus growth mindset maps neatly onto this belief. Neuroscience adds that the brain stays plastic through adulthood; habits are learned and can be relearned, though change takes repetition and time.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This is sustain talk in MI terms. Rather than arguing, reflect it and look for the exception: tell me about one thing you used to do that you no longer do. Every member has one, even something small.

ask: Is I can't change a belief to dispute, or a sign of low self-efficacy that needs success experiences rather than logic?
How strong is the evidence for growth-mindset interventions, given that later replications found smaller effects than early studies?

terms.d: In MI, statements that favor keeping things the same, as opposed to change talk.

248.title: One mistake becomes never right
248.gist: The final practice belief turns forgetting homework into never doing anything right and not being ready for treatment. Members test the overgeneralization and whether one slip says anything about readiness.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is overgeneralization, one of Beck's distortions: a single event stretched into a rule with words like never. It also shows the shame spiral, where embarrassment becomes an exit door from treatment.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The pattern previews the abstinence violation effect: one slip gets read as proof of failure, which invites giving up altogether. Practicing the dispute on forgotten homework builds the muscle for the far higher stakes of a lapse.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to count how many things they did right today before arriving. The list, even if it is woke up and came to group, breaks the never with evidence.

ask: Why might shame push people out of treatment while guilt can pull them toward repair?
How would you respond if a member forgot their work and then used this very page's logic to excuse it?

terms.d: Drawing a sweeping conclusion from one event, often using words like always and never.

249.title: Disputing: a husband's hidden fears
249.gist: Part 2 introduces disputing irrational beliefs and tells the story of a man sixty days clean who feels angry, guilty, and worthless when his wife starts Nar-Anon and therapy, fearing she will leave. Speaking up reveals she is caring for herself.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The man's beliefs show personalization, assuming her choices are about him, and mind reading, assuming her intentions without asking. His fix was behavioral: checking the belief by speaking honestly. Reality testing is one of the strongest disputes.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Family systems ideas help here: when one person in a family changes, others often feel threatened even by healthy change. Nar-Anon and Al-Anon exist because addiction affects everyone close to the person using.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask the group what the man risked by admitting his fears. Many will say looking weak. Point out that saying it out loud is the very thing that ended his suffering.

ask: How could a partner's recovery work actually threaten the relationship, and is the man's fear entirely irrational?
Why do people so often reach for anger when the underlying feeling is fear of abandonment?

terms.d: Assuming that events or others' actions are about you when they may not be.
Questioning a belief's evidence, logic, and usefulness to weaken it.

250.title: Break the story into its parts
250.gist: Members analyze the husband's story by naming his stressors, his irrational beliefs, and the feelings those beliefs produced. It is guided practice on someone else's case before members turn to their own.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Practicing on a third party first lowers defensiveness. It is easier to spot distortion in someone else, a pattern social psychologists sometimes call the bias blind spot. Once the skill is sharp, members are more ready to aim it inward.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect members to split the beliefs into several: she will leave, I am worthless, I do not deserve love, this is my fault. Write them separately. Distinct beliefs need distinct disputes.

ask: Why might people more easily see distorted thinking in others than in themselves?
Which of the husband's beliefs carries a grain of truth, and how should a dispute handle that grain?

terms.d: The tendency to notice biases in other people more readily than in oneself.

251.title: From his case to yours
251.gist: Members finish the husband example by asking how he could recognize his beliefs as irrational and how different beliefs would change his feelings, then begin disputing their own recent stressful event. The handoff from example to self is the key move.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Classic disputing asks three kinds of questions: evidence (is it true?), logic (does it follow?), and pragmatic (does believing it help me?). Teaching all three gives members options when one line of attack does not land.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have members choose a recent, moderate event rather than their worst trauma. Disputing works best when emotion is present but manageable; deep wounds need a different pace.

ask: Which type of dispute, evidence, logic, or usefulness, do you expect would land best with your members, and why?
How would you tell a member is disputing for real rather than reciting the right answer?

252.title: Write your own dispute
252.gist: Members complete their personal ABC analysis: what they believed, how they felt, how they could argue against the belief, and what calmer feeling a different belief would bring. It is the full disputing cycle on paper.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: After writing the dispute, have members read it aloud in the voice of a respected coach or elder. Hearing a dispute in a trusted voice often makes it more believable than reading it silently.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Written disputes can stay intellectual: members may know a belief is irrational yet still feel it. Ellis called this the gap between intellectual and emotional insight. Repetition and acting against the belief tend to close it.

ask: What would a behavioral experiment look like to test the belief a member writes here?
Why might the less stressful feeling in question 5 need to be realistic rather than positive?

terms.d: A planned real-life test of a belief to gather evidence about whether it holds.

253.title: Meet the inner critic
253.gist: Part 3 explains that addiction and fresh awareness of harm done can sink self-esteem, and introduces the internal critic, a harsh voice that judges unfairly yet tries in a clumsy way to protect. Understanding its purpose comes before fighting it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Paul Gilbert's compassion-focused therapy frames harsh self-criticism as a threat-protection system: attacking yourself first can feel safer than being attacked by others. Internal Family Systems, from Richard Schwartz, likewise treats critical parts as protectors with good intentions and bad methods.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Programs that chase self-esteem have a mixed record; Baumeister's reviews found high self-esteem does not reliably cause better behavior. Self-compassion, as Kristin Neff describes it, may be a sturdier target because it does not depend on feeling better than others.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members with real harm on their record may think a positive self-attitude means letting themselves off the hook. Say plainly that accountability and self-worth can live together, and that self-hatred rarely produces repair.

ask: If the critic protects, what exactly does it protect against for someone in prison?
Is self-esteem or self-compassion the better treatment target for people who have caused serious harm?

terms.d: A habitual harsh inner voice that judges and blames you, often unfairly.
Treating yourself with the kindness you would give a friend who is struggling.

254.title: What your critic is guarding
254.gist: A table pairs typical critic lines with their hidden purposes, such as dodging challenges, embarrassment, or disappointment, or gaining sympathy. Members name their three most common self-criticisms and how each protects them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Telling yourself you will fail before you try is close to self-handicapping, studied by Berglas and Jones: if you do not try, failure cannot prove you lack ability. It protects self-image now at the cost of growth later.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to give their critic a name and a face, like a coach who only yells. Externalizing the voice, a narrative therapy move associated with Michael White, makes it easier to talk back to.

ask: Why might the seek-sympathy purpose be the hardest for a member to admit?
How is a protective function different from a payoff in criminal thinking frameworks?

terms.d: Creating obstacles or excuses before a task so that failure can be blamed on them rather than on ability.

255.title: Healthy versus harsh self-criticism
255.gist: Members note how their critic hurts them, then learn that some self-criticism is healthy, like recognizing you were mean to a coworker, while sweeping verdicts are destructive. A challenge test asks for evidence that the criticism is true or exaggerated.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: June Tangney's research on guilt and shame fits this split: guilt focuses on the act and tends to motivate repair, while shame focuses on the whole self and tends to drive hiding or lashing out. Shame-proneness has been linked with worse outcomes after release, guilt-proneness with better.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have members rewrite a harsh line into a healthy one: from I am a total loser to I lied to my sister and I want to fix it. The second is more painful in a useful way and points toward action.

ask: How does the guilt-versus-shame distinction change how you deliver feedback to members?
Can a healthy self-criticism slide into the harsh kind, and what are the signs?

terms.d: A painful feeling that the whole self is bad, often leading to hiding or anger.
Feeling bad about a specific act, which tends to motivate making amends.

256.title: Putting the critic on trial
256.gist: A worked example shows a man applying the challenge test to never doing anything right: he finds no evidence it is true and realizes he ignores his good actions. Members then list three recurring self-criticisms and dispute the first.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The man discovers a filter: he counts mistakes and discounts successes. Beck called this mental filtering and disqualifying the positive. Negativity bias, the brain's tendency to weigh bad information more than good, makes the filter feel natural.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Run it like a courtroom: one member plays prosecutor for the critic, another defense attorney with evidence. Many members know courtroom roles well, and the frame makes evidence-seeking vivid.

ask: What if a member finds real evidence for a self-criticism, such as a pattern of hurting family? How should the challenge test handle that?
Why does negativity bias exist, and when was it useful?

terms.d: Focusing on negative details while ignoring positive ones, so the whole picture looks darker.

257.title: Your deepest self-criticism
257.gist: Members dispute their second and third criticisms, then turn to the one self-criticism they cling to most, even while sensing it causes problems. It moves from surface beliefs toward core beliefs.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Beck's model layers thinking: automatic thoughts on top, intermediate rules beneath, and core beliefs such as I am unlovable at the bottom. Core beliefs feel like facts rather than thoughts, which is why they are the hardest to shift.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Deep self-criticisms may tie to trauma or childhood messages. Watch for distress and allow members to choose a belief they can work with safely in a group. Note who may need individual follow-up.

ask: Why might a core belief persist even when a person holds plenty of contrary evidence?
When should this work happen in group, and when does it belong in individual sessions?

terms.d: A deep, broad conviction about oneself, others, or the world, often formed early in life.

258.title: How the belief controls you
258.gist: Members examine what is unrealistic or exaggerated about their strongest self-criticism and trace how it controls and harms them. Naming the costs builds motivation to loosen its grip.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking about consequences is a pragmatic dispute: rather than debating truth, it asks what the belief costs. Acceptance and commitment therapy, from Steven Hayes, leans on the same idea, asking whether a thought is workable rather than whether it is true.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members draw a line from the belief to three things it stopped them from doing. Seeing the doors it closed often hits harder than logic does.

ask: Is asking whether a belief is useful a stronger lever than asking whether it is true? For whom?
What does it mean for a belief to control someone, in plain behavioral terms?

terms.d: An ACT term for judging thoughts or actions by whether they move you toward what matters.

259.title: Would you say this to a friend?
259.gist: Members ask whether the belief helps or hurts them, whether any proof supports it, and how they would talk another person out of the same idea. The last question flips the perspective to unlock kinder reasoning.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Psychologists call it Solomon's paradox: people reason more wisely about others' problems than their own. Studies by Grossmann and Kross found that taking a distanced view, even speaking of yourself in the third person, improves balanced reasoning.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Pair members up and have each argue the other's case. Hearing someone else dismantle your belief is often more convincing than doing it yourself.

ask: Why does psychological distance improve reasoning, and how could members create it in a heated moment?
What does it suggest about the critic that most members would never speak to a friend this way?

terms.d: Viewing your situation from an outside perspective to think about it more calmly and wisely.

260.title: Take stock of your strengths
260.gist: The page argues that being in treatment is itself a strength and asks members to name strengths in relationships and personality. It balances the session's work on flaws with deliberate attention to assets.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Strengths-based approaches, including the Good Lives Model by Ward, argue rehabilitation works better when it builds valued abilities rather than only cutting risk. Outcome evidence is still developing, but it fits well with RNR principles.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Positive psychology, led by Martin Seligman and Christopher Peterson, catalogued character strengths like perseverance, humor, and loyalty. Giving members that vocabulary helps those who struggle to name anything good about themselves.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: If a member says they have no strengths, ask the group to name one they have seen. Peer-observed strengths are harder to dismiss than self-reported ones.

ask: Can a strength like loyalty also be a risk factor, for example loyalty to an old crew?
How might a focus on strengths change a member's response to risk-focused programming?

terms.d: A rehabilitation approach that helps people build fulfilling, prosocial ways to meet basic human needs.

261.title: Strengths, then the Serenity Prayer
261.gist: Members name emotional and physical health strengths, then the page introduces the Serenity Prayer as a balance between growing where you can and accepting what you cannot change. It sets up the session's final skill, acceptance.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The prayer is usually credited to theologian Reinhold Niebuhr, from the 1930s or 1940s, and AA adopted it soon after. The Stoic Epictetus taught a similar split between what is up to us and what is not, nearly two thousand years earlier.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For members who are not religious, the prayer can be framed as a three-part decision rule: accept, change, discern. The wisdom part, knowing the difference, is the hard skill and worth most of the discussion.

ask: How do you know the difference between what can and cannot be changed when you are incarcerated?
Can acceptance become resignation, and what keeps the two apart?

terms.d: A short prayer, central in Twelve Step groups, asking for acceptance, courage to change, and wisdom to tell them apart.

262.title: Letting go of what you can't change
262.gist: The page divides unchangeable things into external ones like laws and broken promises, and internal ones like personality traits, diagnoses, and fears. Members name one of each and how they could stop fighting it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Radical acceptance in Linehan's DBT means fully acknowledging reality without approving of it. Fighting what cannot change adds suffering on top of pain. Acceptance frees energy for the parts that can be influenced.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Listing psychiatric diagnoses and fears as unchangeable is too strong. Many symptoms improve with treatment, and anxieties often respond well to exposure. Help members accept having a condition while still working on how much it limits them.

ask: Which fears on a member's list are truly fixed, and which have just never been treated?
How does accepting a broken promise from a family member differ from forgiving them?

terms.d: A DBT skill of fully acknowledging reality as it is, without approving of it, to reduce added suffering.

263.title: Kindness to self, and wrap-up
263.gist: Members plan how to be good to themselves when struggling with an internal limit, and the summary recaps the session: beliefs shape reactions, irrational beliefs add stress, and the inner critic can be weakened. It closes a cognitive arc from event to self-image.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Self-compassion research, led by Kristin Neff, links it to lower anxiety and depression and to more motivation after failure, not less. Studies in addiction populations are fewer but point in a similar direction.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to write one sentence they will say to themselves the next time the critic shows up, in plain words they would actually use. Keep it on a card in their pocket for the week.

ask: Which skill from this session would hold up best under the pressure of a craving, and which would fade first?
How would you tell whether members are changing beliefs or just learning the vocabulary of change?

264.title: Role-play: a slip and two fears
264.gist: A role-play script follows a man two years in recovery who hides his nerves at a party, drinks, craves cocaine, then commits to ninety meetings in ninety days, while his partner blames herself and fears he is escaping her. It shows irrational beliefs on both sides of a couple.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The man's slip follows Marlatt's relapse chain: a high-risk situation, unspoken emotion, no coping response, and then using to manage feelings. His quick return to meetings is the opposite of the abstinence violation effect; he treats the slip as a lapse, not a collapse.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Cast volunteers who are comfortable performing, and give the partner role equal weight; groups tend to focus only on the person using. Afterward, ask both actors what they felt in role before asking the audience anything.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Her self-blame echoes patterns common among adult children of alcoholics, who often learned to feel responsible for a parent's drinking. That family history is a clue the script plants on purpose.

ask: What should the man have said at the party, in one sentence, to change the whole chain?
Whose irrational beliefs are harder to dispute here, his or hers, and why?

terms.d: A lapse is a brief slip in use; a relapse is a return to the old pattern of use.
A Twelve Step suggestion to attend ninety meetings in ninety days to steady early or shaken recovery.

265.title: Debriefing the couple's role-play
265.gist: Discussion questions ask whether the partner's stressors are real, what her irrational beliefs are, which Twelve Step activity could help her, and what the man could tell her about struggling to share feelings at high-risk times. It turns performance into analysis.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 1 is subtle: her stressors are real, since a partner's slip is genuinely stressful, but her beliefs that she caused it and that he is fleeing her add avoidable pain. Draw that line clearly; it models validating feelings while disputing beliefs.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have the man's actor deliver question 4 as a real statement to her. Then let her respond in role. Members get to rehearse the exact conversation the scene skipped.

ask: How does Al-Anon's idea that you did not cause, cannot control, and cannot cure another's drinking work as a ready-made dispute?
What risks come with role-playing relationship conflict in a group where members have histories of domestic violence?

terms.d: A Twelve Step fellowship for family and friends of people with drinking problems.

266.title: Session 21: what people need to thrive
266.gist: This introduction to Human Needs and Social Relationships previews three parts: human needs, social relationships, and an introduction to parenting. It frames addiction as something that reorders priorities so real needs go unmet.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The session builds on Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs, from survival through safety, belonging, and esteem toward self-actualization. Recovery is framed as climbing back up after addiction pulled everything down to a single drive.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Parenting appears in Part 3, and for incarcerated parents it is often the most charged topic. Mention it early so members can prepare, and be ready for grief about lost time with children.

ask: Why might a session on needs come right after one on beliefs in this curriculum's sequence?
How does incarceration itself affect each level of needs?

terms.d: Maslow's model ranking human needs from physical survival up to growth and self-fulfillment.

267.title: Levels of need and the cost of using
267.gist: After previewing objectives on relationships and parenting, Part 1 introduces levels of needs: survival, safety, belonging, and esteem, leading toward full potential. Members are told they will examine how use disrupted relationships and priorities.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Maslow's ordered pyramid is popular but loosely supported. Cross-cultural research suggests people pursue needs like belonging and respect even when basic needs are unmet, and the order varies. Use it as a map, not a law.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Maslow himself never drew the famous pyramid; it was added later by others. His later work also placed self-transcendence above self-actualization, a link to the spiritual themes of Twelve Step recovery.

ask: If needs are not strictly ordered, what does that mean for a man in prison who seeks respect before safety?
How would you explain the gap between basic needs and full potential to someone facing a long sentence?

terms.d: Maslow's term for becoming the fullest version of yourself and using your abilities well.

268.title: Hunger first: biological needs
268.gist: Members recall which basic needs they neglected while using, then learn that biological needs like food and water override everything else when unmet, as a hungry child cannot focus on learning. It sets up the comparison between drug drive and survival drive.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on school meal programs broadly links reliable food with better attention and behavior in children. Adults under food insecurity likewise show more stress and poorer decision making, which matters for people leaving prison with few resources.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question answers will often include sleep, eating, hygiene, and medical care. Ask which of those is still shaky now. Unmet basic needs after release are real relapse risks, not side issues.

ask: How does scarcity, as Mullainathan and Shafir describe it, narrow attention in ways that resemble craving?
What basic needs are reliably met inside prison but at risk on release day?

terms.d: Not having reliable access to enough nutritious food.

269.title: When a drug feels like hunger
269.gist: The page explains that in addiction the drive for substances outranks other needs yet can never be fully satisfied. Members consider whether their use felt like thirst or hunger and how it differed from real biological needs like air or water.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Drugs act on the same dopamine reward circuits that drive eating and other survival behaviors. Berridge and Robinson's incentive-sensitization theory proposes that drugs inflate wanting even as liking fades, which explains why the craving is never satisfied.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Question 2 opens a philosophical door: a real need is satisfied by its object, while addiction grows with feeding. Buddhist thought calls this kind of endless thirst tanha, often translated as craving.

ask: What is the scientific difference between a need and a learned drive, and does it matter to someone in withdrawal?
If wanting and liking can split apart, what does that predict about pleasure in early recovery?

terms.d: The pull a cue or reward has on attention and desire, which drugs can greatly amplify.

270.title: Safety: rent money and lost jobs
270.gist: Safety needs like stable housing, work, and steady food come next, and the page notes how addiction trades them away, such as spending rent on drugs. Members describe whether they felt secure while using and what they feared losing.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Housing First programs, which offer housing without requiring sobriety first, show strong results for keeping people housed. Effects on substance use itself are more mixed. For reentry, unstable housing is linked with higher reincarceration risk.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For many members, danger while using was literal: violence, robbery, police. Let them name it. Then ask what safety looks like now and after release, since the answers shape realistic relapse plans.

ask: Is lost housing a consequence of addiction, a cause of relapse, or both, and how would you study which?
How does the meaning of safety differ for someone raised in chronic danger?

terms.d: An approach that provides stable housing first, without preconditions, and then offers support services.

271.title: Belonging: the using crowd versus real friends
271.gist: Members reflect on threats to their living conditions, then learn that social needs, chiefly love and affection, come next. Using circles often run on exploitation and leave a void in recovery, which healthy, mutual relationships in self-help groups can fill.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Bruce Alexander's Rat Park experiments suggested rats in rich social settings drank less morphine water than isolated rats. Replications were mixed, but the idea that connection protects against addiction has wider support, including studies tying AA's benefits partly to changes in social networks.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Calling all using-era relationships exploitative can feel untrue to members who had real loyalty there. Acknowledge that some bonds were genuine, then ask whether they can survive the member's recovery.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what members will lose socially by getting sober. Grief over the old crowd is a hidden relapse driver, and naming it lets you plan for it.

ask: How does the shift from a using network to a recovery network happen when release puts someone back in the same neighborhood?
Is a trauma bond a kind of addiction, as the page suggests, or a different phenomenon?

terms.d: Replacing using contacts with people who support recovery, one way self-help groups appear to work.

272.title: Who were your friends before?
272.gist: Members map their friendships before addiction, whether using acquaintances replaced old friends, and how comfortable they feel with the social side of Twelve Step groups. It surfaces both lost connections and present barriers.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Social learning theory and differential association, from Sutherland in criminology, hold that people learn behaviors and attitudes from those they spend time with. Peer associates are one of the strongest predictors of both use and offending in the RNR literature.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members draw three circles: friends before use, during use, and now. Arrows show who moved, who stayed, and who faded. The picture often shows a lost sober friend worth reaching out to.

ask: Why might shared activities like sports or work make sober friendships easier to rebuild than shared feelings?
What makes Twelve Step social life uncomfortable for some members, and which concerns are fair?

terms.d: In RNR, peers who support crime or use; one of the central risk factors for reoffending.

273.title: Twelve marks of a healthy bond
273.gist: After asking when members felt truly accepted, the page presents Janet Woititz's twelve issues of healthy relationships and starts with vulnerability: letting down barriers and allowing someone to affect your feelings. It begins a long self-inventory.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Woititz is best known for her book on adult children of alcoholics, so her list grew out of families shaped by drinking. Brené Brown's later research popularized vulnerability as a source of connection rather than weakness.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In prison, letting down barriers can be unsafe. Frame vulnerability as something chosen carefully: with whom, when, and how much. Safe vulnerability is a skill of discernment, not total openness.

ask: How do you invite vulnerability in a group where members may be exploited for showing it outside group?
Which of the twelve issues would you expect most members to rate lowest, and why?

terms.d: Willingness to be emotionally open and affected by others, despite the risk of being hurt.

274.title: Understanding and empathy
274.gist: The inventory continues with understanding, grasping what others mean by their words and actions, and empathy, letting yourself feel what others feel. Members rate how much each shows up in their relationships.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Researchers split empathy into cognitive empathy, knowing what someone feels, and affective empathy, feeling it with them. Some people can read others well yet feel little, a pattern relevant in correctional work, since reading people without caring can be used to manipulate.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Paul Bloom has argued that emotional empathy can be biased toward people like us and can cloud judgment, favoring compassion instead. Useful nuance for members who say they feel too much and get overwhelmed.

ask: How would you tell, in group, whether a member's empathy is cognitive, affective, or both?
Can victim-impact work build empathy, or does it mostly build guilt? What would the difference look like?

terms.d: Understanding what another person thinks or feels, without necessarily sharing the feeling.
Actually feeling an emotional response that matches another person's state.

275.title: Compassion and respect
275.gist: The relationship inventory moves to compassion, caring about what concerns the other person, and respect, treating them as having value. Members rate both in their own relationships.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Kant's principle of treating people as ends in themselves, never merely as means, is a crisp definition of respect. It also names exactly what went wrong in many using relationships, where people became tools for getting drugs or money.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: John Gottman's couples research found contempt, the opposite of respect, to be among the strongest predictors of relationships breaking down. Eye-rolling and mockery do more damage than open anger.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Respect is a loaded word in prison, often meaning fear or deference. Ask members to define the respect they get on the yard and the respect described here. The contrast is the lesson.

ask: Can someone feel compassion for a person they do not respect, or the reverse?
How does the prison meaning of respect help or hurt reentry relationships?

terms.d: Treating someone as beneath you, through mockery or disdain; highly damaging to relationships.

276.title: Trust and acceptance
276.gist: Members examine trust, how much they let someone know private things about them, and acceptance, whether they are okay with themselves and others as they are. Both questions point inward as much as outward.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Erik Erikson placed trust versus mistrust as the first stage of psychosocial development, rooted in infancy. Attachment research suggests early care shapes adult expectations of whether others are reliable, though later relationships can revise those patterns.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Carl Rogers held that unconditional positive regard, accepting a person without conditions, helps them change. Acceptance of the person is not acceptance of every behavior, a useful distinction for families of people with addiction.

ask: Is trust something given or earned, and does the answer change after a betrayal like active addiction?
Why might the page pair accepting yourself with trusting others?

terms.d: Rogers's term for accepting and valuing a person fully, without requiring them to earn it.

277.title: Honesty and talking it through
277.gist: Members examine honesty, whether relationships rest on truth or on games, and communication, whether they can speak freely about what matters and be understood. These two items often expose the biggest gaps left by addiction.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Eric Berne's Games People Play described repeating hidden-agenda patterns in relationships. Naming games, such as playing victim to get sympathy, helps members see dishonesty that is not quite lying.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Addiction requires constant concealment, so many members lied by reflex. Normalize that honesty is a muscle that has wasted, not a trait they lack. Ask for one small truth they told this week that cost them something.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Teach a quick I-statement formula: I feel, when, because, and I would like. Have pairs use it to raise a minor real issue. Short structure makes hard talk safer.

ask: When does tact become dishonesty, and when does brutal honesty become cruelty?
Why do many recovering people describe secrets as relapse fuel?

terms.d: Expressing a feeling or need from your own view, such as I feel worried, rather than blaming.

278.title: Compatibility and integrity
278.gist: Members consider compatibility, how much shared likes and beliefs matter, and personal integrity, being honest with themselves and staying true to who they are around others. Integrity links the list back to self-respect.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on couples suggests similarity in values and attitudes predicts satisfaction modestly, while how partners handle differences matters more. Compatibility is less about matching and more about managing mismatch well.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask whether members acted like different people with different crowds while using. Shapeshifting to fit in is the opposite of integrity, and recognizing it helps them spot pressure to slide back.

ask: Is integrity consistency across situations, or staying loyal to values even when you act differently?
Can two people with very different beliefs build a healthy relationship, and what would it require?

terms.d: Being whole and consistent, so your actions match your values across situations.

279.title: Consideration, then esteem needs
279.gist: The inventory ends with consideration for the other person's needs, credited to Woititz's book on adult children of alcoholics. The page then turns to esteem: role models, encouragement, and praise for reached goals, which Twelve Step groups provide repeatedly.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Bandura named mastery experiences, actually achieving goals, as the strongest source of self-efficacy, with modeling and encouragement close behind. Twelve Step chips and anniversaries turn small milestones into public mastery experiences.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Esteem that depends on others' praise can be fragile. Researchers such as Jennifer Crocker have argued that contingent self-worth swings with feedback. Pair outside praise with members learning to notice their own progress.

ask: Why might realistic goals build more esteem than ambitious ones in early recovery?
What happens to esteem built on group praise when a member leaves the group or moves away?

terms.d: Succeeding at a task yourself, the most powerful way to build belief in your abilities.

280.title: Goals lost and goals renewed
280.gist: Members reflect on goals they could not reach while using, goals set since treatment, old goals worth reviving, and what self-esteem and praise feel like to them. It reconnects them to pre-addiction ambitions.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Revived goals are powerful: a trade, a GED, coaching kids. Ask what age they were when they set it. The answer often points to a time before addiction that holds an intact self worth reconnecting to.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to recall a specific compliment that stuck with them for years. Discuss why it stuck. It shows how much recognition matters and how rarely many received it.

ask: Why might praise feel uncomfortable or suspicious to members who rarely received it?
How do you help a member revive a goal without setting up a crash if release barriers block it?

281.title: What reaching your potential means
281.gist: The page introduces Maslow's self-actualization as becoming the best version of yourself regardless of job, skill, or intelligence. Members define their potential and name what blocks them from reaching it.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Viktor Frankl, who survived Nazi camps, argued in Man's Search for Meaning that people can find meaning even in extreme confinement. He also critiqued self-actualization as a goal, saying it comes as a side effect of devotion to something beyond oneself.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members with long sentences may hear potential as something for others. Frankl's example opens a different frame: potential can be lived inside, in how one treats others and uses time.

ask: Is Frankl right that self-actualization cannot be pursued directly?
How does defining potential relative to one's own abilities protect against comparing oneself to others?

terms.d: Frankl's therapy approach centered on finding meaning as the main human motivation.

282.title: The traits that make growth possible
282.gist: Members discuss whether reaching potential is rare and name someone who has, then read a list of growth qualities: tolerating uncertainty, accepting self and others, caring, humor, deep ties, creativity, healthy solitude, and holding inner opposites. These are drawn from Maslow's picture of self-actualizing people.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Holding opposites within yourself echoes Carl Jung's idea of integrating the shadow, the parts of ourselves we deny. Recovery literature says something similar about accepting defects alongside strengths.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Maslow drew his traits from a small set of admired people he chose himself, including Lincoln and Einstein, so the list reflects his values as much as data. Treat it as an inspiring portrait rather than a scientific profile.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Tolerating uncertainty is especially relevant: release dates, housing, and family reactions are all unknown. Intolerance of uncertainty is linked with anxiety, and drugs once offered fast certainty about how one would feel.

ask: Which listed quality is most at odds with prison survival, and how can members hold both?
Why might healthy solitude be harder in recovery than in active use?

terms.d: Difficulty coping with not knowing what will happen, linked with worry and anxiety.

283.title: Natural traits and hard-won ones
283.gist: Members sort the growth qualities into those that come naturally, those they built with effort, and those that remain hardest, and explore why. It invites honest self-assessment without shame.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Personality research, such as studies on the Big Five traits, shows traits are fairly stable but do shift over adulthood, often toward more agreeableness and conscientiousness. Deliberate practice can move traits modestly, supporting the page's idea of effort-built qualities.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask about the hard-won ones first. Stories of effort teach the group more than stories of natural talent, and they model that growth is possible.

ask: Which of these qualities might addiction have masked rather than destroyed?
How would you know if a member's growth on this list was real after release, not just in group?

terms.d: A widely used model describing personality as five broad traits, such as openness and conscientiousness.

284.title: Rebuilding your social life
284.gist: Part 2 explains that addiction damaged relationships but recovery allows repair, including learning to balance dependence and independence, leading and following, closeness and solitude. Members begin by naming the important people in their lives and why they matter.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Prison visitation research generally finds that people who receive visits have lower reoffending rates after release. Family contact appears protective, though the people with the strongest ties may differ in other ways too.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The page's balances echo Aristotle's golden mean, where virtue sits between two extremes: not isolated nor enmeshed, not domineering nor passive. Living in Balance is, in a sense, an Aristotelian title.

ask: Which of the page's balances is hardest for people coming out of prison, and why?
How might a member's list of important people change between now and six months after release?

terms.d: Aristotle's idea that a virtue lies in the balanced middle between excess and deficiency.

285.title: Social strengths, gaps, and goals
285.gist: Members list their social strengths, areas to improve, and top social goals. It turns the relationship themes into a short personal plan.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push for specific goals: call my brother monthly beats be a better brother. Then ask what could stop the call and what they would do then. Specificity is where the plan becomes real.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rank their goals by how scared they feel about each. The scariest is often the most important, and naming the fear makes it easier to address.

ask: What social skills do people sometimes lose during long incarceration, and how could they be practiced inside?
How do you balance reconnecting with family against the risk of reconnecting with family members who still use?

286.title: What mattered more than the drug?
286.gist: Members list steps toward their social goals, then read that addiction competes with relationships and often wins, while recovery means rediscovering bonds built on growth and shared enjoyment. They ask whether any relationship ever outranked their use.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A yes to question 1 is a powerful resource; it is often a child or grandparent. Ask what that relationship gave them that drugs could not. That person may be the core of their reasons for staying sober.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Behavioral economics frames addiction as choice shaped by available alternatives: when rewarding alternatives like close relationships are scarce, drugs win more often. Community reinforcement approaches, developed by Azrin and later Meyers, work by making sober life more rewarding.

ask: If a relationship mattered more than drugs yet use continued, what does that say about how addiction works?
How does the alternative-rewards view change what a reentry plan should prioritize?

terms.d: A behavioral treatment that builds rewarding sober activities, work, and relationships so they compete with use.

287.title: Why we hide our feelings
287.gist: Members name healthy relationships built in sobriety, then the page explains how hiding hurt, anger, sadness, and even love blocks understanding and problem solving. Fear of embarrassment or looking weak often keeps the real self hidden.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Gross and John's research found habitual suppression of emotion is linked with poorer social connection and less closeness, while sharing builds intimacy. Hiding feelings tends to make conversations feel guarded to both sides.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Men in many cultures are taught that crying signals weakness, a pattern some writers call the boy code. That training starts young and often deepens in prison, where showing pain can be dangerous.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Notice the page includes positive feelings. Many members find appreciation harder to say than anger. Ask who they love but have not told recently.

ask: Why might expressing love feel riskier than expressing anger for some men in your groups?
How would you separate healthy privacy from harmful emotional hiding?

terms.d: Holding back the outward expression of feelings, which tends to keep the feeling going inside.

288.title: Your first time sharing in group
288.gist: Members remember how they felt the first time they spoke about feelings in a meeting, what they feared would happen, whether it did, and how they felt afterward. It shows that imagined consequences rarely match reality.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is a natural exposure experiment: predicting disaster, doing the feared thing, then comparing the result with the prediction. Disconfirmed predictions are how anxiety shrinks, a core idea in exposure-based therapy.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: James Pennebaker's research on expressive writing found that putting difficult experiences into words can improve mood and some health markers. Effects are generally modest and vary, but the direction supports the value of speaking up.

ask: Why does a prediction that fails to come true lose power only if the person notices it failed?
What would you do if a member's fear of sharing did come true, for example gossip outside group?

terms.d: Facing a feared situation safely so the fear can decrease through experience.

289.title: Holding back versus blowing up
289.gist: The page argues that revealing true feelings is risky but necessary for growth, and names two failed patterns from active use: walling off feelings or exploding with built-up emotion. Members ask if they are waiting for a safe time and what the worst outcome of sharing could be.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Bottling then exploding is a known cycle: suppressed emotion builds pressure until it bursts out of proportion. The healthy middle, steady assertive expression, sits between passive and aggressive styles.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to answer the worst-case question, then the most likely case, then what they would do if the worst happened. Having a coping plan for the worst case often makes the risk bearable.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members' outbursts led to violence and charges. Treat this page with care, and connect it to anger management skills so members see a path between silence and harm.

ask: Why might waiting for a safe time become a permanent delay?
How does the passive-aggressive-assertive spectrum apply to people raised where assertiveness was punished?

terms.d: Expressing your feelings and needs directly and respectfully, without passivity or aggression.

290.title: Interdependence: I need you, you need me
290.gist: The page contrasts society's praise of independence with recovery's model of interdependence, marked by honest talk, joint choices, working together, trust, and mutual care. Early recovery may take more than it gives, and members define what independence means to them.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The Southern African idea of ubuntu, often rendered as a person is a person through other people, captures interdependence. Many collectivist cultures, including much of Latin America, value it naturally, which may help some members see this as a return home rather than a new rule.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Healthy interdependence differs from codependence, where one person's sense of worth hinges on managing another. The page's list of qualities is a useful test: are decisions shared, or is one person carrying everything?

ask: How does the American ideal of self-reliance interact with mandated treatment that tells people to depend on others?
Where is the line between interdependence and codependence in a family affected by addiction?

terms.d: A relationship where people rely on each other in a balanced, mutual way.
An unhealthy pattern of focusing on another's needs or problems at the expense of one's own.

291.title: Asking for help, being asked
291.gist: Members compare how it feels to ask for help with how it feels to be asked, and define interdependence in their own words. The contrast usually shows that being asked feels good, which undercuts fear of burdening others.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies by Flynn and Bohns found people underestimate how willing others are to help when asked directly. Most people say yes more often than askers predict.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Put the two answers side by side on the board. If being asked feels like trust, then asking is offering someone that feeling. This often reframes asking from taking to giving.

ask: Why do people systematically underestimate others' willingness to help?
How does giving help to others in recovery, as in Step 12, change the giver's sense of interdependence?

292.title: What siblings taught you
292.gist: The page explains how growing up with siblings, cousins, or none can shape trust, cooperation, competition, honesty, and openness. Members name the sibling experiences that most influenced them.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Siblings do shape behavior; for example, older siblings' substance use is linked with younger siblings' use. But large recent studies have found birth order itself has little effect on personality, despite its popularity.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Literature is full of sibling rivalries that shaped lives, from Cain and Abel to the Karamazov brothers. These stories can help members talk about siblings indirectly when direct talk feels too raw.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members raised younger siblings, functioning as parents. That role often brings both strength and resentment. Ask who took care of whom growing up.

ask: How can an older sibling's addiction or incarceration shape a younger sibling's path?
Why might the effects of siblings be about specific relationships rather than birth position?

terms.d: When a child takes on adult caregiving roles, such as raising siblings or caring for a parent.

293.title: Your relational style, traced home
293.gist: Members connect having or not having siblings to how they relate now: trusting or wary, cooperative or competitive, solving problems alone or with others, open or closed. It links family history to present patterns.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Family systems theory, associated with Murray Bowen, sees each person's style as shaped by roles in the family. Roles like hero, scapegoat, or lost child are often used in addiction family work, though they are clinical shorthand rather than research categories.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name the role they played in their family in one word. Then ask whether they still play it in the unit. The overlap is often striking.

ask: How fixed are relational styles learned in childhood, and what changes them in adulthood?
What are the risks of using family role labels with members?

terms.d: Patterned positions family members take, such as caretaker or scapegoat, especially in stressed families.

294.title: People, places, and the group's rules
294.gist: The page notes that swapping old friends for using ones signals addiction while the reverse signals good recovery, and that every group carries unspoken rules shaping behavior. Staying close to using friends is named a top relapse cause, and members recall who they associated with before addiction.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Social norms theory explains how groups shape behavior through expectations people rarely notice. In a using group, the hidden rule may be that leaving early or refusing a hit is disloyal, which makes refusal feel like betrayal.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Telling people to cut off all using contacts is simple to say and hard to live, especially when they are family or the only people in the neighborhood. Reentry planning works better when it helps members manage contact rather than only demanding it end.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to write down two unspoken rules of their old crowd. Then ask which of those rules they are still following inside.

ask: How would you help a member whose only housing after release is with a family member who uses?
What unspoken rules of prison culture might follow members into recovery groups?

terms.d: Shared, often unstated expectations about how members of a group should behave.

295.title: Before, during, now: your people
295.gist: Members describe the people they associated with during addiction and the people they spend time with now in recovery. Together with the previous page, it creates a three-point timeline of their social world.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to score each period from one to ten on how much those people wanted good things for them. The numbers make the trajectory concrete and often show progress members had not noticed.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For members inside, the now answer may be other members of the unit. Discuss honestly which of those ties will help after release and which are prison-only alliances.

ask: How could you help members build sober contacts in the community before their release date?
What does it mean for recovery when the people in the now column are mostly paid professionals?

296.title: What parenting actually involves
296.gist: Part 3 defines parenting broadly: prenatal care and staying in recovery during pregnancy, daily care and safety, love and attention, allowing others' care, nurturing, and learning children's developmental stages. It widens the role beyond biology to include relatives and friends who raise children.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Parental incarceration is counted among the adverse childhood experiences linked with later health and behavior problems. That makes parenting work during incarceration a prevention effort for the next generation, not only for the parent.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Attachment theory, from Bowlby and Ainsworth, holds that consistent, responsive care helps children feel secure. Responsiveness matters more than perfection, which is hopeful for parents who missed time.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Grandparents and relatives may be raising members' children now. Frame allowing others' care as a parenting act in itself, which can ease shame and reduce conflict with caregivers.

ask: What parenting is possible from inside a facility, and how can it be strengthened?
How should prenatal substance exposure be discussed with members without heaping on shame?

terms.d: Early hardships like abuse, neglect, or a parent's incarceration, linked with later health and behavior problems.
The emotional bond between child and caregiver that shapes the child's sense of safety.

297.title: Who parented you, whom you parent
297.gist: Members define parenting in their own words, name the people who parented them, and describe their current role with any child. It links their own upbringing to the parent they are now.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Intergenerational transmission research shows parenting styles often pass down, but not inevitably. Main and colleagues' work on adult attachment suggests that parents who can tell a coherent story about their own hard childhood are less likely to repeat it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 2 may reveal many caregivers or none. Members raised by grandparents, the system, or the street need room to say so without the page's language making them feel deficient.

ask: Why might making sense of one's own childhood matter more than what that childhood contained?
How do you hold space for members who are not parents during a parenting unit?

terms.d: The passing of patterns, such as parenting styles or trauma, from one generation to the next.

298.title: Tired parents snap: the need for support
298.gist: The page widens who counts as a parent, explains that caregivers need both basic and social support, and warns that exhaustion and worry make normal child demands feel overwhelming. Members recall getting angry at a loved one because of stress.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Belsky's model of parenting holds that parenting quality depends on the parent's own resources, the child's traits, and outside support such as partners and work. Stress lowers patience; support buffers it.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The recovery acronym HALT, for hungry, angry, lonely, tired, names the same states that make parenting harder. One checklist serves both relapse prevention and patient parenting.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to trace a moment of snapping at a child back to what happened earlier that day. The chain from stress to anger is often clearer in hindsight and teaches early warning signs.

ask: How does the stress of reentry, such as parole requirements and job searching, set parents up for these moments?
Is snapping a skills problem, a resources problem, or both, and how would you tell?

terms.d: A recovery reminder to check if you are hungry, angry, lonely, or tired, which raise relapse risk.

299.title: What kids need, what parents need
299.gist: Members recall feeling overwhelmed by parenting, then list what children most need from parents and what parents most need to raise children. Answering both sides builds empathy for the role.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Pediatrician and analyst Donald Winnicott coined the good-enough parent, arguing children do not need perfection but reliable care with ordinary failures and repair. The idea eases the guilt of parents who feel they must make up for everything at once.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members often list material things for children first. Gently ask what they themselves wanted most as kids. Time and attention usually come up, which reframes what they can offer even with little money.

ask: How might overcompensating with gifts or leniency after release backfire with children?
What does good-enough parenting look like for a parent who is incarcerated?

terms.d: Winnicott's idea that reliable, imperfect care that repairs mistakes is what children need.

300.title: Nuclear, single, extended families
300.gist: The page describes nuclear, single-parent, and extended families, noting that households with grandparents, aunts, and cousins are widespread around the world. Members identify the type of family they grew up in and the type they are in now.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Historians note the isolated nuclear family is a relatively recent and Western norm. In much of Latin America, Africa, and Asia, grandparents and relatives share child-rearing, which can be a protective resource in reentry.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The page leaves out blended families, same-sex parents, and kinship care through child welfare, all common among members. Invite members to name their actual family form instead of fitting it into three boxes.

ask: How might an extended family both support and complicate a member's recovery?
Which family forms do child welfare and court systems tend to treat as default, and what are the effects?

terms.d: Children being raised by relatives or close family friends when parents cannot care for them.

301.title: Basic support and how craving crowds it out
301.gist: Members name the challenges their current family type brings, then learn that basic support means food, housing, clothing, and supplies, and that craving can push aside not only these needs but even the bond between parent and child.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Neuroscience research suggests chronic drug use can blunt the brain's response to natural rewards, including social ones, while heightening response to drug cues. That helps explain without excusing how a loving parent could neglect a child.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The line about craving overriding the parent-child bond can trigger deep shame. Present it as how the illness works, not who the person is, and pair it with the hope that the bond can recover.

ask: How does understanding addiction's effect on reward systems change moral judgments of neglect?
How can a member use this knowledge to explain past neglect to a child without excusing it?

terms.d: Reduced pleasure or interest in normal rewards, which can follow heavy, long-term drug use.

302.title: Facing neglect and using it
302.gist: Members are asked whether they ever neglected their own basic needs or a child's because of use, and how that experience might serve their recovery. It asks for painful honesty and points it toward growth.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Reporting obligations may apply if a member discloses ongoing child endangerment. Know your duty-to-report rules and explain limits of confidentiality before this exercise, not after a disclosure.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Question 3 invites post-traumatic growth, Tedeschi and Calhoun's term for positive change after struggle. Making meaning of harm done can fuel amends and motivation, as long as it does not skip accountability.

ask: How do you balance confidentiality, honesty, and mandatory reporting when parents disclose neglect in group?
When does turning past harm into motivation become a way to avoid feeling its weight?

terms.d: A professional legally required to report suspected child abuse or neglect.

303.title: The support network every parent needs
303.gist: The page lists sources of social support for parents: trusted friends, other parents, practical helpers, expert advisors, and community services. It explains that addiction erodes these networks through broken trust and exploitation, so recovery means rebuilding them deliberately.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on parenting consistently links social support with lower parenting stress and less harsh discipline. Support from partners and other adults buffers the effects of poverty on children, though it does not erase them.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members fill in each of the five categories with a real name or resource, leaving blanks honestly. The blanks become the reentry to-do list.

ask: Which of the five support types is hardest for formerly incarcerated parents to build, and why?
How can parents rebuild trust with people they exploited during active use?

terms.d: Help from others, emotional, practical, or informational, that eases stress and strengthens coping.

304.title: Who backs you up as a parent?
304.gist: Members check whether they have someone to talk with openly about parenting, someone who helps with parenting duties, and whether they help others. They also weigh how recovery makes parenting both harder and easier.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Reciprocity matters: supporting another parent builds the same network that will support you. It also restores a sense of competence for members whose parenting role has been suspended.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Recovery can make parenting harder because emotions once numbed now arrive full force, and children may test trust. Naming this prevents members from reading normal turbulence as failure.

ask: Why might children test a parent in early recovery, and how should a parent respond?
What does helping someone else parent look like from inside a facility?

305.title: Five kinds of parental needs
305.gist: The page outlines parents' biological, emotional, social, and spiritual needs, distinguishing immediate survival needs from long-term needs that help them thrive. It argues parents cannot care well for children while neglecting themselves.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The airline rule of putting on your own oxygen mask first captures the point. In care professions, the same idea appears as preventing burnout so helpers can keep helping.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The spiritual need described, searching for why we exist and why bad things happen to good people, echoes existential psychology, such as Irvin Yalom's themes of meaning, death, freedom, and isolation. Parenthood often sharpens these questions.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members may see self-care as selfish, especially after years of selfishness in addiction. Distinguish self-care that sustains caring for others from self-indulgence that replaces it.

ask: How do you separate necessary self-care from the self-centeredness Twelve Step programs warn about?
Why might parenthood intensify spiritual questions?

terms.d: Deliberate actions to maintain your own physical and emotional health.

306.title: Material needs and ranking your own
306.gist: The page adds material needs, things like cribs, diapers, school supplies, and transportation, separating genuine needs from wants. Members rank which parental needs matter most and least to them and consider how parents' needs differ from nonparents'.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ranking reveals values. A member who ranks material needs highest may carry a provider identity; one who ranks emotional needs highest may be focused on repair. Both are worth exploring, not judging.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Reentry barriers like criminal records, child support arrears, and limited job options make material needs hard to meet. Pair this page with concrete resource referrals so it does not become a reminder of what members cannot provide.

ask: How do child support arrears affect reentry, family relationships, and relapse risk?
Why might the provider role be both motivating and dangerous for a parent leaving prison?

terms.d: Unpaid child support that builds up, often during incarceration, creating debt after release.

307.title: What every child needs
307.gist: The page lists children's core needs: physical care, protection, love and attention, kind but firm limits without physical punishment, and a role model who teaches right and wrong. Members begin by reflecting on whether their own parents met their needs.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Diana Baumrind's research on parenting styles found authoritative parenting, warm with firm limits, linked with better child outcomes than authoritarian or permissive styles. Research broadly links physical punishment with more child behavior problems, supporting the page's stance.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Bandura's Bobo doll studies showed children imitate adults' aggression. Children learn more from what parents do than from what they say, which raises the stakes of a parent's recovery.

ask: Why might parents raised with physical punishment defend it, and how would you engage that belief?
How can an incarcerated parent be a role model from a distance?

terms.d: A style combining warmth and responsiveness with clear, consistent limits.

308.title: Babies who were fed but not held
308.gist: Members consider how unmet childhood needs affected them and whether their own children have unmet needs, then read about orphanage babies who wasted away despite good physical care because no one held, talked to, or played with them. Love turns out to be a survival need.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: René Spitz documented this pattern, called hospitalism, in institutional infants in the 1940s. The Bucharest Early Intervention Project later found Romanian orphans placed in foster families did better on development than those left in institutions, with earlier placement generally helping more.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Harry Harlow's monkey studies showed infant monkeys clung to a soft cloth mother over a wire one that gave milk. The studies are now seen as ethically troubling, but they shifted psychology toward seeing contact comfort as a core need.

ask: What does the orphanage story imply about solitary confinement and long isolation for adults?
How might a parent provide stimulation and affection through visits, calls, or letters?

terms.d: Spitz's term for the decline of infants in institutions who received physical care but little affection.

309.title: Fixing the orphanage
309.gist: Members identify which needs the orphans lacked, imagine how they would fix the orphanage as its manager, and describe what can happen to children who lack love, protection, or guidance. It asks them to think like a caregiver with power.

deeper.label: In the room
