deeper.text: The manager role is a smart move: it lets members design good care without first confronting their own failures. Once they have built a good plan, ask which parts they could do for their own kids.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Discussions of harm from unmet needs can sound deterministic. Emphasize that many children with hard starts grow into healthy adults, especially with at least one stable, caring adult. Outcomes are risks, not destinies.

ask: Why is it easier to design good care for strangers than to give it to our own children?
How do you discuss childhood harm without leaving members convinced they are permanently damaged?

310.title: Repair after addiction
310.gist: The page explains how addiction weakens parental bonding and responsibility and can harm babies exposed before birth, but stresses that children recover remarkably with consistent care. It steers parents from endless guilt toward building healthy relationships now, and asks how their addiction harmed their child.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Emmy Werner's long-term Kauai study and Ann Masten's research on resilience show many at-risk children do well, especially with one stable caring adult. Masten called resilience ordinary magic because it comes from everyday supports.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Recovery depends on the exposure. Babies with neonatal withdrawal can often do well with care, but fetal alcohol spectrum disorders involve lasting brain differences. Supportive care improves outcomes, but parents should not be told every effect fully reverses.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Ed Tronick's research on rupture and repair suggests that relationships are strengthened less by never failing than by repairing after failures. That gives parents a practical path forward.

ask: How would you correct the hopeful message about prenatal exposure without crushing a parent's motivation?
What makes repair believable to a child who has heard promises before?

terms.d: The ability to adapt well and develop healthily despite serious adversity.
The cycle of disconnection and reconnection in relationships, where repair builds trust.

311.title: Steps toward becoming a better parent
311.gist: Members describe what parents who harmed their children through addiction can do to move on and parent well. Asking in general terms lets them plan without being forced into personal confession.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to write a three-step plan in action verbs, such as listen, show up, keep promises small. Then ask which step they could start inside this week, for example a letter that asks questions instead of making promises.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Children may not want contact right away. Prepare members for this so that a cold response is not read as failure or used to justify relapse. Patience is part of repair.

ask: How does the Twelve Step idea of living amends differ from apologizing?
What should a parent do when the other caregiver blocks contact with the child?

terms.d: Making up for past harm through changed behavior over time, not only words.

312.title: Session 21 wrap-up
312.gist: The summary reviews human needs, how addiction rearranges priorities, the work of understanding and improving social relationships, and the introduction to parenting. It sets the stage for Family Matters next.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The session's arc, from survival needs up to meaning and parenting, follows a person's whole life outward from the body to the next generation. It is a reminder that recovery reaches beyond the individual.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Close by asking each member to name one need they will protect this week. A single concrete commitment helps the long session land.

ask: Which part of this session would you expect to matter most after release, needs, relationships, or parenting?
How might you adapt this session for members who are not parents and have little family contact?

313.title: Session 22: families under strain
313.gist: The introduction to Family Matters explains that the session examines families organized around a serious problem such as addiction, mental illness, or abuse. It previews the beliefs and roles such families produce and the work of overcoming hurt, anger, and fear through forgiveness.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Family systems theory treats the family as a unit that adapts to a problem. Each member's behavior makes sense as an adaptation, even when it hurts the person later. That lens reduces blame and invites understanding.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This session may stir trauma memories. Tell members ahead of time that they can share at their own pace and that individual follow-up is available. Predictability helps people feel safe enough to engage.

ask: Why might family dysfunction be both an explanation and an excuse, and how do you keep it from becoming the second?
How might this session land differently for members who are now the parent in a dysfunctional family?

terms.d: A family whose patterns of relating cause ongoing harm to its members.

314.title: What this session will ask of you
314.gist: The page lists objectives for each part and warns that reviewing one's family may bring painful memories. It argues that understanding the past helps members see their addiction and protect their sobriety.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Large adverse childhood experiences studies, beginning with Felitti and Anda, found strong links between childhood adversity, including household substance use, and later addiction. The relationship is dose-like: more adversity, higher risk on average.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Insight into the past does not by itself prevent relapse; behavioral skills do much of the work. Present family history as context that informs choices now rather than the key that unlocks recovery.

ask: What is the best evidence that understanding family history helps recovery, as opposed to feeling helpful?
How do you keep forgiveness from being pressured on members who were abused?

315.title: Fear of intimacy
315.gist: Part 1 restates the five marks of healthy interdependence and explains how addiction and poor family modeling make sharing feelings feel dangerous, feeding a fear of intimacy. Members reflect on why intimacy and interdependence matter in recovery.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Adult attachment research describes avoidant styles, where people keep distance to prevent rejection. Many people with addictions show insecure attachment patterns, and some theorists describe substances as a substitute attachment that feels safer than people.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Philip Flores developed the view of addiction as an attachment disorder, arguing that recovery requires learning to rely on people instead of substances. Group therapy then becomes practice in safe attachment.

ask: If addiction can work as a substitute attachment, what should treatment offer in its place?
How does fear of intimacy show up in group behavior, such as humor, silence, or hostility?

terms.d: A style of relating marked by discomfort with closeness and a strong push toward self-reliance.

316.title: Your family's feeling style
316.gist: Members describe how their family handled feelings and the style they developed, and the page introduces families with serious problems such as addiction, mental illness, or abuse. These problems strain everyone and create dysfunctional relationships and roles.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to finish the sentence: in my family, when someone was sad, we... Then angry, then scared. The answers map the family's emotional rules in under a minute.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will idealize their families or feel disloyal criticizing them, especially in cultures that value family loyalty. Frame it as understanding, not accusing: every family has strengths and blind spots.

ask: How does cultural loyalty to family affect a member's willingness to call it dysfunctional?
What feeling style would you expect most members to have learned, and how will it show up in your group?

317.title: Codependence and the family's unspoken rules
317.gist: The page defines dysfunction and trauma, then presents codependence as described by Sharon Wegscheider-Cruse and Claudia Black's family lessons: do not talk, trust, or feel. Unspoken rules keep families rigid, silent, in denial, and alone with their feelings.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Codependence is a popular clinical idea but has never been a formal diagnosis, and researchers have criticized its vague definition. Some feminist critics argue it pathologizes caregiving often expected of women. It works best as a descriptive lens, not a label.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Claudia Black's book It Will Never Happen to Me popularized the don't talk, don't trust, don't feel rules. They resemble what trauma researchers describe as adaptations that protect children in chaos but cost them as adults.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask which of the five lessons from Black's list members are still following now. Many will name not trusting, which also explains why group can feel hard.

ask: Is codependence a useful concept or a label that turns love into pathology?
How might a family's don't talk rule overlap with the prison code of not snitching?

terms.d: A pattern of focusing on an addicted person's needs and behavior at the expense of one's own identity and well-being.
The lasting emotional impact of a deeply distressing experience.

318.title: Rate the family you grew up in
318.gist: Members check which of two descriptions fits their childhood family on communication, decision making, cooperation, emotional trust, and caring. It turns the five healthy traits into a quick self-assessment.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Forced-choice items help members commit to a view rather than hedging. But real families fall between poles; use the checks as a starting point for discussion about where on a spectrum the family actually sat.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: After members check boxes, ask which item they would most want to change for their own children. The forward-looking question reduces defensiveness and links the past to present parenting.

ask: What are the limits of self-report about childhood, given memory and current mood?
How would siblings from the same family rate it differently, and why?

319.title: Healthy and unhealthy family systems
319.gist: The page contrasts healthy family systems, with open talk and flexible, fair rules, against dysfunctional ones, with closed talk and rigid, inconsistent rules that leave children ashamed and vulnerable to addiction. Members describe their family's rules about openness.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Salvador Minuchin's structural family therapy describes boundaries as too rigid, leaving members disconnected, or too diffuse, leaving them enmeshed. Healthy boundaries are clear but permeable, much like the flexible rules the page describes.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Inconsistent enforcement teaches unpredictability. Behavioral research shows intermittent reinforcement makes behaviors persistent, and children in such homes often stay hypervigilant, scanning for mood shifts. That vigilance can look like anxiety or aggression later.

ask: How might inconsistent rules at home prepare someone poorly for the rigid rules of prison or parole?
What does a flexible yet fair rule look like in a home with a parent in early recovery?

terms.d: Family closeness so intense that personal boundaries and individual identity are blurred.

320.title: Rule one: hold on tight
320.gist: Members judge whether family rules were fair and consistent and whether they felt safe and valued, then meet the first dysfunctional rule: act rigidly. Families cling to rules as a false anchor against an addicted member's chaos.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Rigidity is a control response to unpredictability. When one person is erratic, others tighten what they can control, such as routines, appearances, and roles. It reduces anxiety in the short run while preventing the family from adapting.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Organizations under threat do the same: psychologists call it threat rigidity, where stressed groups narrow their options and centralize control. The family is a small institution behaving the same way.

ask: Can rigidity be adaptive in a truly dangerous home, and when does it become harmful?
How might a member's own rigidity show up in recovery, for example in all-or-nothing rules?

terms.d: The tendency of people or groups under threat to narrow their thinking and cling to familiar responses.

321.title: When life is too serious
321.gist: The page contrasts healthy families that tolerate mistakes and experimentation with rigid ones that raise children to see life as deadly serious, though compromise-based relationships can repair this. Members describe how their family handles the unexpected and whether they overreact to what they cannot control.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Children raised amid unpredictable danger often develop hypervigilance, a nervous system tuned to scan for threat. As adults they may overreact to small surprises because their body learned that surprises meant harm.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to rate from one to ten how upset they get when plans change suddenly, then ask what happened at home when plans changed. The link between past and present reaction becomes visible.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prison schedules change constantly, so overreacting to change can lead to write-ups. Naming the childhood origin helps members respond with curiosity instead of shame.

ask: How might playfulness and humor be therapeutic for adults raised in rigid families?
What is the difference between being told you overreact and actually being hypervigilant?

terms.d: A heightened state of watching for danger, often developed in unsafe environments.

322.title: Unspoken rules and their penalties
322.gist: Members name their family's unspoken rules, what happened when someone broke them, and how the family responded to mistakes. It makes invisible norms visible.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Sociologist Harold Garfinkel showed the power of hidden social rules through breaching experiments, where students deliberately broke everyday norms and observed the strong reactions. Families enforce their own norms the same way, often without anyone stating them.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Common answers include never airing business outside, men do not cry, and do not upset Dad when he drinks. Write them on the board and ask which ones members still obey inside the facility.

ask: How can someone change a rule they never knew they were following?
Why might reactions to mistakes in childhood shape how members respond to slips in recovery?

323.title: Rule two: say nothing
323.gist: The second rule is silence: families avoid talking about the central problem, whether addiction, mental illness, abuse, or violence, with each other or outsiders. Feelings are bottled up and occasionally explode, and members recall times their family was clearly upset but silent.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Silence keeps a fragile peace and protects children from an unpredictable parent. But unspoken stress does not disappear; children read the tension without the words to make sense of it, which can feel more frightening than the truth.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The proverbial elephant in the room captures this. AA has a related saying: you are only as sick as your secrets. Both point to silence as a force that keeps problems alive.

ask: How might the rule of silence follow a child into adulthood as difficulty asking for help?
When is family privacy healthy, and when has it become harmful secrecy?

324.title: Guessing at what normal is
324.gist: Members examine how they react in a crisis, whether they have to guess what normal behavior is, and whether as children they sensed something was wrong without knowing what. These items capture the confusion silence creates.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Guessing at what normal is appears first on Janet Woititz's well-known list of traits among adult children of alcoholics. Many members raised in chaos never saw a model of ordinary family life to compare against.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members stay calm in crises and fall apart when things are quiet, because chaos feels familiar. Ask about this directly; it often explains why stable times in recovery feel strange or even risky.

ask: Why might calm and stability feel threatening to someone raised in chaos, and how does that relate to relapse?
How can members learn what normal looks like if they have never seen it?

terms.d: Adults raised with an alcoholic parent, a group with commonly described patterns of coping.

325.title: Rule three: nothing is wrong
325.gist: Members recall being punished for saying something obvious, then meet the third rule, denial: the family refuses to admit problems, sometimes telling children that all is well right after drunkenness or violence. Children learn to distrust their own perceptions.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Jennifer Freyd's betrayal trauma theory proposes that children may block awareness of harm from a caregiver they depend on, a pattern she called betrayal blindness. Not seeing is a survival strategy that later distorts how people read reality.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Being told reality is not what you saw resembles what is now called gaslighting, after the play and film in which a husband makes his wife doubt her perceptions. Over time, the child loses trust in their own eyes.

ask: How might growing up told that nothing was wrong make someone more vulnerable to denial about their own addiction?
What does rebuilding trust in one's own perceptions look like in treatment?

terms.d: Refusing to acknowledge a painful reality, as an individual or as a family.
Making someone doubt their own perceptions and memory, often to maintain control.

326.title: Told everything is okay
326.gist: The page notes that people taught to ignore pain may struggle to express it, and that groups help them learn. Members describe painful experiences they were told not to worry about and whether they tend to avoid problems, hoping they will vanish.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Alexithymia, difficulty identifying and describing one's own emotions, is more common among people with addictions. If feelings were never named at home, members may feel only vague distress, which substances once quieted.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Hand out a simple feelings vocabulary list. Ask members to circle three they felt this week. Expanding the emotional vocabulary is a concrete first step for those who never learned it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 2 links straight back to Session 19's avoidance pattern. Point out that hoping problems disappear may have been learned at home, not just from drug use.

ask: How strong is the link between alexithymia and addiction, and in which direction might it run?
How does naming an emotion help regulate it, as some affect labeling research suggests?

terms.d: Difficulty recognizing, naming, and describing one's own emotions.

327.title: How you handle pain now
327.gist: Members describe how they usually deal with painful experiences and whether they want to change it. It shifts the denial discussion from the family's past to the member's present choices.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect answers like using, sleeping, working, or fighting. Treat each as a coping strategy with a function, then ask what it costs. Members change faster when their methods are understood rather than condemned.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Khantzian's self-medication hypothesis suggests people often choose substances that soothe specific painful states. Asking how members handle pain can reveal which feelings their drug of choice once managed.

ask: If a member's coping method was using, what healthy replacement fits the same function?
Why might wanting to change something not be enough to change it?

terms.d: Khantzian's idea that people use substances to relieve specific painful emotional states.

328.title: Rule four: us against the world
328.gist: The fourth rule is isolation: rigid rules block honest talk inside and outside the family, which looks self-sufficient while fearing exposure or being broken up. Trust can still be learned as an adult, and members ask if their family felt like them against the world.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Social isolation is a known risk factor for child maltreatment, partly because isolated families have fewer outside eyes and supports. Community connection works as both support and safeguard.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: For many families, fear of outsiders was not irrational. Immigrant families fearing deportation, or Black families with historical reasons to distrust police and child welfare, may isolate for real protection. Distinguish dysfunction from justified wariness.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Us against the world loyalty can transfer to gangs or crews, which offer the same closed belonging. Ask members whether they found a second family like that and what it required.

ask: How do you separate a family's dysfunctional isolation from protective caution in a marginalized community?
Why might gangs feel familiar to people raised in isolated families?

329.title: Friends over and family secrets
329.gist: Members recall whether they could bring friends home and whether they were punished for sharing family secrets outside. These concrete memories test how closed their family really was.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Not bringing friends home is often a child's own choice, made from embarrassment or fear of what a parent might do. It shows how children enforce the family's isolation themselves, an early form of shame management.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to remember one friend's house where they felt comfortable as kids and what was different there. That memory often holds an early model of a healthier family they can draw on.

ask: How might keeping family secrets as a child shape a member's comfort with self-disclosure in group?
What separates loyalty from complicity when it comes to keeping family secrets?

330.title: Scoring your family's dysfunction
330.gist: Members check statements that fit their family, such as keeping secrets, rigid rules, guilt about leaving, crises, and denied conflicts, and total their score. It gives a rough sense of where their family falls from mild to severe.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: This checklist is a reflection tool, not a validated measure. A total does not diagnose a family, and members may score low out of loyalty or high from current anger. Use the items for discussion rather than treating the number as meaningful.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask which single statement felt truest rather than focusing on the total. A single strong item can shape a life more than several mild ones.

ask: What would a validated measure of family functioning need that this checklist lacks?
How might a member's score shift as their recovery deepens, and what would that mean?

terms.d: A questionnaire tested to show it reliably measures what it claims to measure.

331.title: Survival roles in an addicted home
331.gist: Opens Part 2 of Family Matters by arguing that children in chaotic, addicted homes adopt fixed roles that buy short-term stability. It introduces the four roles the following pages unpack: hero, placater, lost child and scapegoat.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is family systems thinking: the household behaves like a thermostat that resists change, and each child's role helps hold the temperature steady. The roles keep the secret (the drinking, the abuse) from ever becoming the topic.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Role typologies come from clinical observation, not controlled research. Studies of 'adult children of alcoholics' traits found many people from non-addicted homes endorse the same descriptions, a Barnum-like effect. Treat the roles as lenses for reflection, not diagnoses.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The hero, scapegoat, lost child and mascot set is often credited to Sharon Wegscheider-Cruse, while Claudia Black described related types. Erving Goffman's idea that we perform roles in everyday life gives the same insight a sociological frame.

ask: If a role is adaptive inside a dangerous home, at what point does it become a problem rather than a skill?
Which role do prisons and units quietly reward, and which do they punish?
How would you know whether a group member truly fits a role or is just borrowing a convenient story?

terms.d: Viewing the family as one interacting unit where each member's behavior affects and balances the others.
A system's tendency to resist change and return to its usual state, even an unhealthy one.

332.title: Noticing the roles you play
332.gist: Exercise 9 asks members whether they have acted a certain way because others expected it, and what someone loses by breaking out of a role. It warms the group up to the idea of roles before naming specific ones.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Start outside the family: the role someone plays on the yard, in a crew, or with an officer. Members admit to street or institutional roles more easily than family ones, and the bridge to childhood follows naturally.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Question 2 targets the hidden payoff. In MI terms you are surfacing the 'good things' about the old pattern, which must be acknowledged before ambivalence can tip toward change.

ask: Is a role something imposed on a person, something chosen, or both, and does the answer change accountability?
What does a person risk socially if they drop their role on a housing unit?

333.title: The hero: a child turned manager
333.gist: Describes the hero, the child who takes over adult duties as a parent's use worsens, gaining real competence but becoming serious and controlling. Exercise 10 begins by asking what the family gains from having a hero.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Clinicians call this parentification: a child carries parental duties, practical or emotional. Competence grows, but so does a belief that worth equals performance and that relaxing invites disaster.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Heroes in a prison group often look like model participants: tier reps, workers, the one who has all the answers. Gently ask who takes care of them, and watch whether the question lands as relief or threat.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The hero helps the family look healthy from the outside, which links to stigma research: image management can delay anyone outside noticing the addiction and offering help.

ask: Can someone be in the hero role and still be actively using? What would that look like?
How do you separate genuine leadership from compulsive control in a group member?

terms.d: When a child takes on adult or parental responsibilities, practical or emotional, for the family.

334.title: Cost of heroics; enter the placater
334.gist: Finishes Exercise 10 by weighing what the hero role gives and costs the child, then introduces the placater, the child who acts as the family's emotional caretaker and peacemaker.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have members list the hero's advantages and disadvantages in two columns on the board. The point to land is that the same trait sits in both columns: reliability becomes rigidity, responsibility becomes burnout.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The placater manages other people's moods to lower threat at home. It overlaps with what the recovery literature calls codependency and with the 'fawn' response some trauma clinicians describe: appeasing a threat instead of fighting or fleeing.

ask: Is 'fawn' a useful clinical idea or a popular label that outran the evidence?
Why might placaters be especially vulnerable to being pulled into others' drug use?

terms.d: A popular recovery term for organizing one's life around another person's needs or problems at one's own expense.

335.title: The placater grown up
335.gist: Shows the adult placater: agreeable, apologetic, a good listener whose own needs and feelings stay hidden. Exercise 11 asks what the family gains from someone filling that role.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to count how many times they say sorry in a day for things that are not theirs. Then practise swapping one apology for a plain statement of a need. It is a tiny assertiveness rep.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Warmth and sensitivity are strengths, and many cultures prize harmony and deference to elders. Frame the problem as never having a choice to disagree, not as being kind.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Carl Rogers argued that distress grows from a gap between who we are and who we present. The placater lives in that gap, showing a pleasing self while the real one goes unheard.

ask: How might a placater's people-pleasing show up as a relapse trigger, for example saying yes to a friend who is using?
When does empathy shade into self-erasure?

336.title: Placater's price; meet the lost child
336.gist: Completes Exercise 11 on the placater's gains and losses, then introduces the lost child, who copes with an unpredictable home by detaching emotionally, socially and physically.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Withdrawal is a classic way to cope when a child cannot change or escape the stressor. Learned helplessness research (Seligman) shows how repeated uncontrollable stress can teach a creature to stop trying, even later when trying would work.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Lost children are the quiet members who pass on every share. Rather than calling them out, give low-exposure ways in: writing first, pairs before the full group, or a rating from one to ten.

ask: How would you tell a lost-child style of detachment from depression or dissociation?
Is the placater's main problem low self-worth or a lack of skill in saying no?

terms.d: Giving up efforts to control outcomes after repeated experiences where nothing one did made a difference.

337.title: The lost child flies under radar
337.gist: Explains how the lost child survives by going unnoticed: compliant, average, avoiding leadership, steady through change but acting without much thought or feeling. Exercise 12 asks what the family gains from this child.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In a facility, invisibility can be smart: no write-ups, no attention. Respect that before challenging it, and ask where being unseen has cost them, such as needs never voiced to medical or a case manager.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Adult attachment research describes an avoidant style: valuing self-reliance and keeping distance from closeness. It is a useful parallel, though attachment styles are measured dimensions, not the same thing as family roles.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Neglect, the experience most linked to this role, is often overlooked because it leaves no visible marks, yet research on adverse childhood experiences counts it among the experiences tied to later health and substance problems.

ask: Why might the family find the lost child convenient, and what does that say about what the family needs?
Is the ability to ride out storms a strength worth keeping in reentry?

338.title: Lost child's cost; the scapegoat appears
338.gist: Finishes Exercise 12, then introduces the scapegoat, the one child who draws attention instead of avoiding it, becoming the visible sign that something is wrong at home.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Family therapists talk about the 'identified patient': the member labelled as the problem, whose symptoms carry the family's distress. Treating only that person often fails because the system keeps producing the symptom.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This role often resonates most with people in custody, many of whom were the 'bad kid'. Be ready for strong emotion, and stress that understanding the role explains behavior without erasing responsibility for it.

ask: What would it take for a family, or a justice system, to look past the scapegoat to the problem underneath?
Can the scapegoat role coexist with the hero role in one person over time?

terms.d: The family member treated as the problem, whose symptoms may express the whole family's dysfunction.

339.title: The scapegoat takes the blame
339.gist: Shows how the family focuses on the scapegoat's misbehavior, which pulls attention away from the parent's addiction or abuse; punishment follows and self-esteem drops. Exercise 13 asks what the family gains from this.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The word comes from the ancient ritual in Leviticus, where a goat was sent into the wilderness carrying the community's sins. René Girard built a whole theory of how groups find peace by uniting against one victim.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Social learning theory predicts what happens next: harsh, inconsistent punishment models aggression and teaches the child that attention comes through trouble. Gerald Patterson's work on coercive family cycles is a well-known example.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: There is a danger in telling incarcerated adults their offending was 'the result, not the cause'. Use it to reduce shame and open discussion, then pivot to choices now, which CBI would frame as thinking that can change.

ask: How do you hold both truths: the scapegoat was blamed unfairly, and the adult is responsible for current choices?
Where do you see scapegoating at work in institutions or communities?

terms.d: A pattern where child misbehavior and harsh parental responses escalate each other over time.

340.title: Scapegoat's cost and adult echoes
340.gist: Completes Exercise 13 on the scapegoat's gains and losses, then begins a section on adults from dysfunctional families, introducing a list of shared traits attributed to Janet Woititz.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what advantage a scapegoat gets. Answers like attention, freedom from expectations, or a tough identity reveal why the role is hard to give up; it is a status position, especially on the street.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Janet Woititz's book Adult Children of Alcoholics (1983) popularized the trait list on the next page and helped launch the ACoA self-help movement of the 1980s.

ask: What does someone have to grieve when they stop being the 'bad one'?
Why might a trait list feel validating even when it is not specific to addicted families?

341.title: Adult children: a self-check list
341.gist: Lists traits often seen in adults raised in dysfunctional families, such as harsh self-judgment, approval seeking and extreme loyalty. Exercise 14 asks members to circle those that fit and write a concrete example of one.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research is mixed: some studies find adult children of alcoholics at higher risk for substance problems and distress, but checklist traits like these are endorsed by many people with no addicted parent. The list is a mirror, not a test.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Insist on the specific example. A circled word is abstract; a story, like the time loyalty to a co-defendant cost them years, turns the insight into something the group can work with.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have each member pick one trait and name its opposite in action. Harsh self-judgment becomes one kind sentence they say to themselves today.

ask: Which of these traits might look like antisocial thinking to a correctional assessor but have a family origin?
How could a list like this increase hope, and how could it become an excuse?

342.title: How families process trauma, or don't
342.gist: Contrasts how healthy families talk through crises, support the injured and resolve feelings, with dysfunctional families where fear silences discussion. Unspoken feelings get suppressed and each new trauma hardens the roles.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Making meaning through talk is protective. Pennebaker's research on expressive writing found that putting difficult experiences into words was linked to better health in many studies, though effects vary.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Neuroscience offers a picture: naming an emotion (affect labeling) tends to dampen the brain's alarm response. Silence leaves the alarm running without a story to contain it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note the delayed reaction the page describes: feelings that surface long after an event, without a clear source. Many members will recognise this in the first weeks of sobriety, when numbed feelings return.

ask: What does a custody setting teach about talking through trauma, and how might it reinforce the old family rule?
Is it always healthy to talk about trauma right away? What does the research on debriefing suggest?

terms.d: Deliberately pushing feelings or thoughts out of awareness, which tends to keep them active rather than resolve them.

343.title: Crisis then and crisis now
343.gist: Exercise 15 asks how their family handled crises, whether they talked or ignored them, and whether members now respond the same way as adults. It tests whether the childhood pattern is still running.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The before and after format invites a self-generated contrast. When members notice a pattern on their own, it carries more weight than being told, which is the same logic behind MI's evocation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief with a recent crisis inside: a lockdown, a denied visit, bad news from home. Ask what the person did in the first hour. That is the current pattern, whatever they wrote.

ask: What separates healthy calm under pressure from the old shutdown pattern?
How would you help someone build a new crisis response without a safe family to practise in?

344.title: Hurt seeks an outlet
344.gist: Opens Part 3 on overcoming dysfunction: childhood hurt rarely fades alone and leaks out through drugs, as self-medication, or through hurting others. Exercise 16 asks about unresolved pain, its role in their addiction, and who they can tell.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Edward Khantzian's self-medication hypothesis holds that people often use substances to manage specific painful states, not only for pleasure. It is influential and clinically useful, though research gives it mixed support as a full explanation.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The claim that pain must be re-experienced to heal is not universal. Some people recover well through meaning-making, support and new routines, and pushing deep trauma work in a short group can destabilise.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Before this exercise, agree on limits: share the headline, not the details. Know your referral path for mental health staff in case someone is flooded.

ask: Why does the exercise ask whether they have someone to talk to, and what if the honest answer is no?
How would you tell self-medication from simple habit in a member's story?

terms.d: Using alcohol or drugs to ease emotional pain, anxiety or other distress.

345.title: Anger, loyalty and love together
345.gist: Finishes Exercise 16 with memories tied to the hurt, then turns to anger: often born from hurt, aimed outward or inward, and hard to express when the target is a loved parent. Loving someone and being angry at them can coexist.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Anger is often called a secondary emotion that protects a more vulnerable one, such as hurt or fear. This view is common in emotion-focused therapy, and it gives members a doorway from rage to what sits beneath it.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Freud described depression partly as anger turned against the self. The idea is debated today, but the page's link between inward anger and self-hatred echoes it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will defend a parent fiercely the moment anger is mentioned. Name ambivalence directly: two feelings about one person is normal, not betrayal.

ask: Is 'healthy expression of anger' about letting it out, or about understanding it? What does research on venting suggest?
How might loyalty to a parent block a member's honesty in group?

346.title: Mapping unresolved anger
346.gist: Exercise 17 asks members whether they carry unresolved anger from childhood, how it has fed their addiction, whether they can talk to anyone about it, and which memories it attaches to.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect anger to show up live, aimed at you, staff or the system. Treat it as data: ask what the anger in the room right now has in common with the anger on the page.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies on venting, such as Bushman's work, suggest that hitting pillows or rehearsing rage tends to keep anger going. Reappraisal and problem-focused talk tend to work better, which shapes how you debrief.

ask: What is the difference between expressing anger and acting it out, and where do your members draw that line?
How does anger connect to the criminal thinking patterns in CBI?

347.title: Fear of closeness after a hard home
347.gist: Explains that pain and anger from childhood leave fear of intimacy: fear of being hurt again, of hurting others, and of facing the feelings at all. Unfaced, it raises relapse risk. Exercise 18 asks about their own fear.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: In relapse prevention (Marlatt & Gordon), negative emotional states are among the most common high-risk situations. Unprocessed fear is a standing trigger that waits for the next stressful moment.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Bowlby's attachment theory describes children building working models of whether others are safe. Fear of intimacy is that model still running, expecting new people to act like old ones.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to complete one sentence: if I let someone close, I am afraid they will... Read a few aloud anonymously. Shared fears lose some power.

ask: How does the prison environment protect against intimacy fears and also deepen them?
Is it fair to say recovery cannot be completed without facing these feelings?

terms.d: Attachment theory term for a person's built-in expectations about whether others will be caring and dependable.

348.title: Forgiveness and making inner peace
348.gist: After the fear memories, the page argues recovery needs some resolution of old family conflicts, often through understanding and forgiveness, which may take years. Reconciliation is defined as reaching acceptance and peace, with others or inside.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Researchers such as Robert Enright and Everett Worthington developed forgiveness interventions, and reviews generally find they reduce anger and distress. Effects are modest and depend on the person choosing to forgive, not being pressured.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Forgiveness is not reconciliation, and reconciling with an unsafe person can be dangerous. Survivors of abuse may heal without forgiving. Make sure members hear that inner peace is the goal, not contact.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Hannah Arendt saw forgiveness as one way people release each other from the endless consequences of past acts, freeing them to start again.

ask: Should a counselor ever encourage a client to forgive? Whose goal is it?
How does forgiving others relate to the amends of Steps 8 and 9?

terms.d: Coming to terms with old hurts and reaching peace, with family members in person or within oneself.

349.title: Where are you on forgiveness?
349.gist: Exercise 19 asks whether members have forgiven others for hurtful childhood experiences, what forgiveness means for their recovery, and how they would like to reconcile, face to face or internally.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Give room for a 'not yet'. Some will feel pressure to say yes. Treat forgiveness as a process with stages, and ask what one small step would look like.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Worthington's REACH steps start with recalling the hurt honestly and empathising with the offender's situation, which does not excuse it. One stage at a time makes it doable in a group.

ask: What would reconciling 'inside yourself' look like in daily behavior, so you could tell it happened?
What happens to a member who reconciles with a family that is still using?

350.title: Session 22 in review
350.gist: Summarises the session: what makes a family dysfunctional, the beliefs and roles children develop, and ways to overcome hurt, anger and fear through forgiveness. It frames painful reflection as investment in present sobriety.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Close with a grounding check: each member names one feeling and one thing they will do tonight to take care of themselves. Family material stirs people up, and they return to a cell, not a home.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The session leans on the family as cause. Andrews and Bonta's RNR model would add that current factors like peers and thinking patterns drive reoffending more directly; balance insight about the past with skills for now.

ask: What would you want a member to do differently next week because of this session?
Which of these ideas is most likely to be misused as an excuse, and how would you prevent that?

351.title: Role-play: the family that won't talk
351.gist: Facilitator instructions for a role-play where Pat, abused by a stepfather, tries to raise it with a family whose signs read rigidity, silence, denial and isolation. In version one every attempt meets resistance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Heed the caution about trauma histories: do not cast someone in Pat's role who has a similar history unless they volunteer and you have checked in. Offer an observer role to anyone who wants it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Psychodrama, developed by Jacob Moreno, uses enactment so people feel a pattern rather than just discuss it. Physical cues, like the brother's chair facing outward, make the dynamic visible.

ask: How do you de-role actors so nobody leaves still carrying the part?
What is gained by playing the failure first and the repair second?

terms.d: A step after role-play where actors step out of character and return to themselves.

352.title: Breaking the silence, version two
352.gist: Version two of the role-play: family members start defensive, then drop their signs and talk honestly, the isolated brother turning his chair back in. Questions probe why people hide in roles and which topics are off-limits at home.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask the actor playing Pat what changed in their body between versions one and two. Felt experience often teaches more than the discussion questions.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Real families rarely open up within minutes. Name this so members do not expect a quick repair on their first call home; the scene shows a direction, not a timeline.

ask: The third question hints at timing: when is honesty in a family unsafe or unwise?
How might you adapt this role-play for a member whose family is still actively using?

353.title: Role-play: the four roles in action
353.gist: Facilitator setup where four members act out hero, placater, lost child and scapegoat after a drunk grandfather is arrested for wrong-way driving. A fifth tries to talk about his alcoholism and gets only resistance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Cast against type when you can: let the usual quiet member play the scapegoat. Playing an unfamiliar role helps people see roles as behavior, not identity.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Watching a pattern from outside is distancing, a known way to gain perspective. Ethan Kross's research on self-distancing suggests stepping back helps people reason more wisely about emotional situations.

ask: Why does the scenario make the scapegoat the target of the grandfather's anger?
What would the fifth person need to do differently to be heard?

354.title: Facing the grandfather's drinking
354.gist: Version two of the role play: after initial resistance, the family drops its roles and talks openly about getting help for the grandfather. Questions ask how families sidestep serious problems.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The scene echoes CRAFT (Community Reinforcement and Family Training), developed by Robert Meyers, which teaches families to encourage a loved one into treatment, and in studies did better than confrontational interventions.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members whether they have been the grandfather in a scene like this. It turns them from observers into people who can imagine their own family's side.

ask: What separates a family conversation that motivates change from one that triggers defensiveness?
Is intervening on an older relative different from intervening on a peer?

355.title: Session 23: you and your parents
355.gist: Introduces You and Your Parents, which covers parenting styles, the mother's role and the father's role, and how a parent's treatment of a child still shapes the adult. It lists the objectives for each of the three parts.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members had absent, incarcerated or deceased parents, or were raised by grandparents. Say early that 'mother' and 'father' can mean whoever filled those roles.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Dividing the session into mother and father reflects a two-parent model. Same-sex parents, single parents and kinship care are common, so invite members to adapt the frame.

ask: Which parenting style do you think dominated your members' childhoods, and how would you find out without assuming?
How might members' own parenting be shaped by what this session stirs up?

356.title: Unsent letters and who counts as parent
356.gist: Finishes the objectives, explains members will write unsent letters to mother and father, and defines parents as whoever raised them. A facilitator note suggests single-gender groups because parent material is raw, especially early in recovery.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The unsent letter is a long-standing therapy technique: writing to someone without the risk of their reaction frees honesty. It shares roots with Gestalt empty-chair work, which gives voice to unfinished business.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The single-gender suggestion matters in custody, where many women have histories of abuse by men and many men guard against looking weak in front of women. If groups are mixed, set extra safety agreements before Part 2.

ask: What risks come with asking someone to write deeply personal material in a setting where cells and property can be searched?
Why might the facilitator note single out early recovery as the hardest time for this?

terms.d: A written message to someone, never delivered, used to clarify and release feelings safely.

357.title: Parenting styles and family dysfunction
357.gist: Opens Part 1: approaches to raising children range from healthy to abusive, and many people with substance problems grew up with an addicted or mentally ill parent. It defines dysfunction and notes no family is truly normal. Exercise 1 asks about parental substance use.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Having a parent with a substance use disorder is a well-documented risk factor for a child's later substance problems. Twin and adoption studies show both genes and environment contribute, and many children of addicted parents never develop one.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The Adverse Childhood Experiences study (Felitti, Anda and colleagues, 1998) counted living with a substance-using household member as one of its core adversities, linked with many later health risks as adversities add up.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Saying there is no normal family lowers shame. It invites members to rate their family on a range instead of a pass or fail.

ask: If genes and environment both matter, how would you explain family risk to a member without sounding like fate?
What protective factors help some children of addicted parents avoid addiction?

terms.d: Something that raises the likelihood of a problem without guaranteeing it will happen.

358.title: Tracing addiction through the family tree
358.gist: Continues Exercise 1, asking about addiction in other relatives such as grandparents, aunts, uncles and adult siblings, and how a relative's addiction shaped members' feelings and choices.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members sketch a quick genogram: a three-generation family map, marking who used, who got sober and who stayed clear. Patterns across generations jump out visually in ways a list hides.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will discover they are the third or fourth generation. Pair that realization with hope: they may also be the first to break the chain, which is a powerful identity.

ask: What does a family map reveal that a single parent's story does not?
How would you respond if a member says addiction runs in the family, so there is no point?

terms.d: A family tree diagram showing relationships and patterns like addiction or illness across generations.

359.title: When rules are too tight
359.gist: Notes that research links overly strict, harsh, lenient or inconsistent parenting to later problems including substance use, then describes the too-strict parent who silences children and uses severe physical punishment. Exercise 2 asks what too strict means and whether it fits.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Diana Baumrind described authoritarian (high control, low warmth), permissive (warm but few limits) and authoritative (warm with firm limits) styles; Maccoby and Martin later added a neglectful one. Authoritative parenting is generally linked to the best outcomes.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Meta-analyses, including work by Elizabeth Gershoff, link spanking to more aggression and mental health problems in children and find little evidence of long-term benefit. Physical punishment is now widely discouraged by pediatric groups.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some research suggests the effect of strictness differs across cultures and communities, depending on whether it is read as care or rejection. Ask members how strictness felt, not just how much there was.

ask: How do members' views on physical discipline affect how they plan to raise their own kids?
Why might strict parenting produce both very shy and very aggressive children?

terms.d: Warm, responsive parenting with clear, firm and explained limits; linked to good child outcomes.

360.title: Harsh words and lost confidence
360.gist: Defines the too-harsh parent: not necessarily strict, but prone to screaming, shaming and criticizing in outbursts that erode a child's self-worth. Exercise 3 asks what harsh means to members and whether their parents fit.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on harsh verbal discipline, such as work by Ming-Te Wang, has linked yelling and insults to later behavior problems and low mood in teens, even when parents are otherwise warm. Words can wound like blows.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: In Beck's cognitive model, repeated criticism can become a core belief such as I am worthless. Later, that belief becomes the inner voice members hear when they fail, which feeds the guilt and shame cycle.

ask: How might a parent's harsh words show up in a member's self-talk today?
Is harshness from stress the same as harshness from contempt, from the child's side?

361.title: Too lenient: when no one leads
361.gist: Describes too-lenient parents who give in or offer no clear rules, leaving children without discipline. The page argues parents and children are not equals; parents must lead. Exercise 4 asks what lenient means and whether it fits.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Low monitoring, not knowing where kids are or who they are with, is one of the steadiest predictors of teen substance use and delinquency in prevention research. Leniency often equals low monitoring.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members with permissive parents may remember them fondly as the cool parent. Ask what they needed then that no one gave them, such as a curfew someone cared enough to enforce.

ask: Is neglect a form of leniency or something different, and does the distinction matter to the child?
Why might strict and lenient parenting both raise substance risk?

terms.d: A parent knowing and tracking a child's whereabouts, friends and activities.

362.title: Who raised you, and unseen pain
362.gist: Notes that one biological parent may be absent or unaware, and in single-parent homes the present parent's influence is greater. Exercise 5 asks members to name their authority figures. It then begins Childhood Pain, where stressed parents may take frustrations out on children.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Encourage broad answers: coaches, older siblings, gang elders, foster parents, officers. Who taught them the rules of life matters more than who held the legal title.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Parental incarceration is a major source of absence. Many members' own children are now living what members lived, which can make this page a turning point for motivation as parents.

ask: Which of your members' authority figures were positive, and how might those people be enlisted in reentry?
How does an absent parent shape a child differently from a present but harmful one?

363.title: Pain no one noticed
363.gist: Argues that unrecognized pain is among the worst things a child can suffer, often turning into anger aimed outward or inward. Exercise 6 asks whether members kept things from a parent, the gains and costs of that, and whom they confided in.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Developmental researchers call it emotional validation: a caregiver noticing and naming a child's feelings. Linehan's DBT theory holds that an invalidating environment helps produce later problems with regulating emotion.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 2 is clever: secrecy had advantages, like safety. Honour that, then ask whether the same secrecy is still protecting them or now hurting them, such as hiding cravings from a sponsor.

ask: Where does a group give members the validation they missed, and where does it risk repeating invalidation?
Is anger a signal of pain, a defence against it, or both?

terms.d: Having one's feelings dismissed, ignored or punished, teaching a person their inner experience is wrong.

364.title: Abandonment and the repeat pattern
364.gist: After asking whom members confided in, the page explores abandonment through divorce, death, neglect or a parent who fails to protect from abuse. Buried abandonment fear can fuel use and lead people into relationships that repeat the rejection.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Freud called this the repetition compulsion: unconsciously re-creating old painful situations. Modern attachment research describes something similar in more testable terms, with insecure expectations shaping partner choice and behavior.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A self-fulfilling prophecy is at work: expecting abandonment, a person may test, cling or push away, which makes leaving more likely and confirms the belief.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Incarceration itself is an abandonment, both of children left behind and of the member by friends who stop writing. Name it gently; it ties the page to the present.

ask: What would it look like for a member to choose a partner who breaks the pattern, and how would they recognise one?
Is failing to protect a child from abuse experienced as abandonment even if the parent was physically present?

terms.d: An unconscious tendency to re-create painful past experiences in new relationships.

365.title: Abandonment, then and now
365.gist: Exercise 7 asks whether members felt abandoned by a parental figure, how that felt, and whether later situations have seemed to replay that rejection.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Go slow: abandonment is often the deepest wound in a reentry group. Let members answer question 2 privately if needed, and invite only volunteers to share.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to draw a timeline of relationships and mark each ending. Then ask who left, how, and what they felt. Repetition can become visible in minutes.

ask: How might fear of abandonment show up as jealousy or control in members' relationships?
Which members might project abandonment onto you when the group ends or you go on leave?

366.title: Mother: the first relationship
366.gist: Finishes Exercise 7 with coping strategies for rejection, then opens Part 2, framing the parent bond as a person's first social relationship. Many members were raised mainly by a mother or female relative, a bond with lasting influence.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Attachment research from Bowlby and Ainsworth shows how early caregiving shapes a child's sense of safety. Ainsworth's Strange Situation studies sorted infants into secure and insecure patterns based on reunions with the caregiver.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Early attachment research focused on mothers, partly reflecting its era. Later work shows children form strong attachments to fathers, grandparents and other caregivers, so the mother focus should not imply only one bond counts.

ask: What might a member's coping with rejection tell you about their attachment pattern?
How does a mother's own trauma history pass through to a child, according to attachment theory?

terms.d: Confidence that a caregiver will respond reliably, letting a child explore and return for comfort.

367.title: The woman who raised you
367.gist: Exercise 8 asks members which female figure mattered most in childhood, whether there was more than one, and whether the bond with their mother was basically healthy or troubled.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In many groups 'mom' is sacred, and criticism of her draws heat. Normalize mixed feelings early, such as gratitude and disappointment both being true.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: In many Latino and Black families, grandmothers often raise children. Expect several mother figures and let members choose who they want to write about.

ask: Why might men in custody be quicker to defend their mothers than their fathers?
What do you lose by asking whether a relationship was healthy instead of what was good and hard in it?

368.title: The TV mother myth
368.gist: After asking about a mother's addiction, the page contrasts sitcom families with real ones, where a single working mother may struggle to provide. Real families face money, health and emotional strain; some solve problems, some create them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Comparing one's family to an ideal is a cognitive trap. Leon Festinger's social comparison theory shows we judge ourselves against others, and an unrealistic yardstick guarantees we come up short.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Winnicott coined the good-enough mother: a parent who meets needs reasonably, not perfectly, and whose small failures help the child grow. It offers members a kinder standard.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Invite members to compare not to TV but to what their mother faced. Many will see her struggles more clearly, which can soften blame without denying hurt.

ask: What media family shaped your members' idea of normal, and how did it distort expectations?
How does knowing a mother's hardships change forgiveness without changing the harm?

terms.d: Winnicott's idea that a caregiver who meets needs adequately, not perfectly, best supports a child.

369.title: Family strengths and weaknesses
369.gist: Exercise 9 asks members to name a serious family problem from childhood, how they wish things had been, and the family's strengths and weaknesses, balancing pain with resources.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking for strengths is a resilience move. Strengths-based approaches assume every family has assets, such as humour, faith or loyalty, that recovery can build on.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some will say the family had no strengths. Ask what helped them survive, which is always something, and trace it back to someone who taught it.

ask: How might you use members' family strengths in a reentry plan?
Why does wishing a family were different sometimes keep a person stuck?

370.title: Mood swings and a frightened inner voice
370.gist: Explains how a mother's unpredictable moods can make a child feel responsible, fearful and slow to trust; as adults that inner voice is anxious and may lash out. Exploring this is not about blame; grief and forgiveness may follow.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Young children are naturally egocentric in Piaget's sense: they explain events with themselves at the centre. Mom is sad, so I did something wrong. The guilt can survive long after the reasoning has matured.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Skinner found that rewards delivered unpredictably produce the most persistent behavior, harder to extinguish than steady rewards. Many clinicians see a parallel in unpredictable love, which can keep a child both hooked and anxious; that link is an analogy, not a direct finding.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Many therapies help people notice an inner critic and reply to it. CBT disputes its claims; compassion-focused therapy (Paul Gilbert) builds a kinder voice to soothe it.

ask: How would you help a member tell whether a feeling of being cornered is about now or about then?
Is forgiving because she did her best always true, and what if she did not?

terms.d: In Piaget's theory, a young child's tendency to see events only from their own point of view.

371.title: Acceptance and preparing the letter
371.gist: Exercise 10 asks what is hardest to accept about their mother, whether forgiveness is possible, and how those feelings may affect partners and children. It then explains why writing feelings down helps.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Acceptance does not mean approval. In acceptance and commitment therapy (Hayes), acceptance means making room for painful facts so energy goes to living by one's values rather than fighting the past.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 2 is the bridge to parenting: name the cycle. A member who sees their mother's pattern in how they treat their own child has found the strongest motive to change.

ask: What would acceptance look like for a member whose mother is still actively using?
Why might writing beat talking for members with limited literacy, and when might it not?

372.title: Prompts for a letter to Mother
372.gist: Invites members to write an unsent letter to their mother, even if she has died, and offers prompts: regrets, broken promises, resentments, ways she helped, secrets, and the wish to forgive or be forgiven.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Tell members to pick three or four prompts rather than all seventeen. A focused letter goes deeper; a long checklist becomes homework.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Grief therapists use letters to the dead as a way to finish conversations death cut short. For members whose mothers died while they were locked up, this may be the first chance they have had.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The prompts mix the member's wrongs with the mother's. That balance helps many, but survivors of maternal abuse may feel pushed to share blame. Let them skip the regret prompts.

ask: Why do the prompts include ways the mother helped, and what does it do to a resentment-heavy letter?
How would you keep the letter private if the facility searches property?

373.title: Writing the letter to Mother
373.gist: Exercise 11 provides space for members to write their unsent letter to their mother, using extra paper if needed.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Give quiet time and stay present. Some members will cry or freeze. A simple prompt, like start with the first word that comes, can unstick someone staring at the page.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Pennebaker's expressive writing studies often used several short sessions of writing about deep feelings. Benefits appeared across many studies but were modest, and some people feel worse at first.

ask: What would you do if a member writes something that suggests risk to self or others?
Should the group hear letters read aloud, or is the writing enough?

374.title: After the letter: debrief
374.gist: Exercise 12 asks how it felt to write the letter, the single most important message for their mother, and what change they want in the relationship and how to get there.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The move from feelings to action follows a recovery arc: insight is not enough without a plan. Question 3 turns emotion into a goal, like a single phone call or a visit request.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: If a mother is dead, reframe question 3 as how they want to carry her memory or change themselves. Avoid suggesting contact with a mother who is a danger or an active user.

ask: What makes a relationship goal realistic for someone still in custody?
How would you check in a week later without forcing a share?

375.title: The father's influence, present or absent
375.gist: Opens Part 3: fathers can deeply influence children for good or ill, even as mothers often have the more central role. Many members barely knew their fathers or had tense bonds with an addicted one. Exercise 13 asks if they were close to him or another man.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on father involvement, such as work by Michael Lamb, links engaged fathers with better child outcomes; quality of involvement matters more than mere presence. A harmful father in the home can do more damage than an absent one.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Father hunger is a phrase some clinicians use for the longing of children raised without a father. Gangs and older men on the street often fill that gap, so mentorship is a real reentry need.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect more anger toward fathers than mothers, and more silence. Allow both, and keep the second question alive: another man may have filled the role.

ask: If the male role model was a gang elder or dealer, what did he teach that was useful, and what was harmful?
How do changing family patterns over decades affect the claim that mothers are more central?

376.title: Your father today
376.gist: Continues Exercise 13: who the other close male was, how lacking one affected them, what the relationship with their father is like now, whether it is improving, and what they would keep or change.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 2 pulls the past into the present. Many members' fathers are also incarcerated, ill or recently released; their current status shapes what change is even possible, so ask before planning.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rate the relationship now and five years ago on a zero to ten scale, then ask what moved it. Scaling, borrowed from solution-focused therapy, finds forces of change fast.

ask: How would you work with a member who idolizes a father who harmed him?
What makes a father relationship repairable versus one to grieve?

377.title: Five styles of fathering
377.gist: Offers rough sketches of fathers: absent, distant, macho, buddy-type and unpredictable, each with its effect on children. The page cautions that no category captures a real man fully.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The styles map loosely onto Baumrind's dimensions of warmth and control. Macho is high control and low warmth; buddy is warmth without control; distant and absent are low on both, closer to neglectful.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The distant dad who is angry when unspoken needs go unmet echoes the mind-reading trap in CBT. Children learn to guess, often wrongly, and may grow into adults who expect partners to read them too.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: These are clinical sketches, not research categories. Many fathers move between styles over time, especially through addiction and recovery, and members may see their father in several at once.

ask: Which style is most common in the families your members describe, and what keeps it going across generations?
Can a macho father raise a son who becomes a buddy-type father, as a reaction? What does that say about breaking cycles?

378.title: The healthy father, and yours
378.gist: Describes the healthy father, who sees children as individuals, sets limits, puts their needs first and talks about feelings. Exercise 14 asks members to name their father's style, its effects, and whether illness or addiction made him unpredictable.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Before asking about their own father, ask who in the room is a father. Have them rate themselves against the healthy-father description privately. It reframes the page from grievance to growth.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Parenting programs for incarcerated fathers, such as InsideOut Dad, have been evaluated with generally encouraging but limited results, mostly on attitudes and knowledge rather than long-term outcomes.

ask: What does putting children's needs first look like for a father serving time?
Why might an unpredictable father leave deeper scars than a consistently distant one?

379.title: The ideal father and silent men
379.gist: After describing the impact of an unpredictable father, the page notes that fathers can be unprepared, trapped or struggling, and that men raised to be strong and silent often hide feelings. Exercise 15 asks what qualities make a good father.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Researchers on masculinity norms, such as Ronald Levant, describe restrictive emotionality: men being trained to hide vulnerable feelings. It is linked in studies to lower help-seeking and more substance use.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask the group to list good-father qualities on the board, then ask which of those the prison code punishes, such as showing softness. That tension is the real work.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have each man name one feeling his father never showed and one he wishes he had seen. It often unlocks talk about their own emotional range.

ask: How does the strong-and-silent norm differ across the cultures in your groups?
Is it fair to explain a father's silence by his upbringing without excusing it?

terms.d: A learned masculine norm of holding back vulnerable feelings like fear, sadness or tenderness.

380.title: Father wounds in new relationships
380.gist: After asking how their father compares to a good one, the page says feelings about a father, even an unknown one, persist and resurface with partners, friends and coworkers. Repair may not be possible; the inner child may need to grieve and forgive.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Psychodynamic therapists call it transference: feelings from an early relationship carried onto new people. A member who explodes at a male officer may be reacting partly to a father, not only to the officer.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Inner child is a popular recovery idea, spread by writers like John Bradshaw, rather than a research construct. It can be a useful metaphor, but some members may find it childish; offer plainer words like the younger you.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The page says the problem is what happened long ago, not now. Push gently: some fathers are still causing harm today, and members deserve permission to set boundaries, not only to forgive.

ask: How would you spot transference toward you in a group, and what would you do with it?
Is forgiving a father who did his best different from forgiving one who did not try?

terms.d: Unconsciously carrying feelings and expectations from early relationships onto people in the present.

381.title: Acceptance, then the father letter
381.gist: Exercise 16 asks what is hardest to accept about their father, whether they could forgive it, and how these feelings affect partners, children and friends. It then introduces the unsent letter to their father, echoing the mother section.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: By now members know the letter format. Use the familiarity: ask what they learned writing the first letter, and what they want to do differently in this one.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking about friends as well as family widens the frame. Father issues often show up with authority figures, bosses, officers, POs, so link to reentry risks like conflicts with supervisors.

ask: What is the difference between accepting what a father did and accepting the father?
How might feelings about a father affect how a member responds to his parole officer?

382.title: Prompts for a letter to Father
382.gist: Invites members to write an unsent letter to their father, even if he has died, using the same prompts as the mother letter: regrets, broken promises, resentments, help received, pride, secrets and forgiveness.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members never met their father. Suggest they write to the father they imagined or wanted, or to the man who filled in. The letter can hold questions as well as statements.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Literature is full of letters to fathers. Franz Kafka's Letter to His Father, never delivered, is a famous example of a son trying to explain a lifetime of fear. It can show the form has dignity.

ask: How would a letter to a never-met father differ in purpose from a letter to an abusive one?
Why repeat the same prompts for both parents? What does comparing the two letters reveal?

383.title: Writing the letter to Father
383.gist: Exercise 17 provides space for members to write their unsent letter to their father, adding pages as needed.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Men may write less than they did to their mothers. That is data, not failure. A short, honest line can be worth more than a full page; respect brevity.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: If someone is stuck, offer one opening line to complete: the thing I never got to tell you is... It narrows the task to a single door.

ask: What would you do with a letter full of rage: process it, contain it, or both?
How can you help a member who writes a letter that excuses everything?

384.title: After the father letter
