384.gist: Exercise 18 mirrors the mother debrief: how writing felt, the one thing they most want their father to know, and what change they want and how to reach it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Compare the two debriefs. Ask which letter was harder and why. The answer often points to the parent whose wound drives the member's current patterns.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Ending on what they would have to do shifts locus of control inward. Rotter's concept describes believing outcomes depend on one's own actions, linked with more effortful coping.

ask: What realistic step can a member take toward a father while still in custody?
How do you honor a decision to have no contact with a father?

385.title: Session 23 in review
385.gist: Summarises the session's look at parenting styles, the roles of mothers and fathers, and putting feelings about them into words. It warns this work can stir strong emotion and urges seeking a counselor, therapist or clergy, framing help-seeking as part of recovery.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The closing echoes the Serenity Prayer: accepting what cannot be changed (the past) and changing what can (the self). Members from Twelve Step groups will recognize the thread.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Check who might need a mental health referral after this session. Letters to parents can surface trauma; a quick private word with members who were quiet or shaken is good practice.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on post-traumatic growth (Tedeschi and Calhoun) suggests many people report positive change after hardship, matching the page's hope, though self-reports of growth do not always match measured change.

ask: What would tell you this session helped rather than just stirred things up?
How can members keep asking for help after release when services are thin?

terms.d: Positive psychological change some people report after struggling with major hardship.

386.title: Session 24: development and parenting
386.gist: Introduces Child Development and Parenting Skills, which covers five life stages with their emotional, intellectual and social tasks, plus practical parenting skills. It is aimed at parents but also invites members to examine their own growth.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Stage models in psychology go back to Freud, Piaget and Erik Erikson. Erikson's eight psychosocial stages, each built around a central conflict, underlie much of this session's language.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members have children they rarely see. Open by asking about the children in their lives, including nieces, nephews and stepchildren, so everyone has a reason to listen.

ask: Why might a session on child development help someone's own recovery, not just their parenting?
What does a stage model miss about real, messy development?

387.title: Five stages, three kinds of task
387.gist: Lists Part 2 objectives and asks members to consider unfinished developmental tasks of their own. Part 1 then sets out five stages, infancy to adulthood, each with emotional, social and intellectual tasks, such as a toddler learning to say what they need.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Recovery folk wisdom says emotional growth stalls when heavy use begins. That idea is not proven, but research shows adolescent substance use can disrupt learning and normal social development during critical years.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Tidy stage boundaries are a simplification. Modern developmental science sees growth as continuous and shaped by context, with large individual differences.

ask: What unfinished task do you see most often in your groups: trust, identity, or emotional expression?
How would you tell a member's unfinished task from a current skill gap that training can fix?

terms.d: A skill or achievement expected at a given life stage, like learning to talk or forming an identity.

388.title: Stages build on each other
388.gist: Explains that finishing a stage prepares the next, unfinished tasks cause later trouble, yet some tasks continue for years. Exercise 1 is a checklist quiz on these points and on why non-parents benefit too.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Use the quiz as a quick warm-up, not a test. The distractor about high school usually gets a laugh and opens discussion of what members never finished, from GEDs to emotional skills.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Neuroplasticity research supports the page's hope: the brain stays changeable into adulthood. Later learning is often slower but very much possible, which is the foundation of rehabilitation.

ask: Is it hopeful or discouraging to frame a member's struggles as unfinished childhood tasks?
Which developmental tasks are hardest to complete inside prison?

terms.d: The brain's ability to change its connections in response to learning and experience throughout life.

389.title: Infancy: bonding and trust
389.gist: Covers birth to about two: the infant bonds with caregivers, learns trust when needs are met reliably, explores and starts speaking. Parents help by meeting needs, allowing safe exploration and encouraging words over crying.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is Erikson's first stage, trust versus mistrust. A baby whose cries bring reliable care learns the world is safe enough; neglect teaches the reverse.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies of children raised in severely neglectful Romanian orphanages, such as the Bucharest Early Intervention Project, found lasting effects on development, and gains when children moved to foster families early. Timing mattered.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Harlow's monkey studies showed infant monkeys preferred a soft cloth mother to a wire one that gave milk. Comfort, not just food, builds attachment; the work is famous and ethically troubling.

ask: How might a mistrust learned in infancy show up in a member's response to staff kindness?
What does the orphanage research suggest about the value of early intervention for members' own infants?

terms.d: Erikson's first stage, where infants learn whether the world and caregivers are reliable.

390.title: Infant tasks and early recovery
390.gist: Exercise 2 asks how an infant's tasks resemble those of an adult in recovery, and what happens to adults who never learned to bond and trust, and how recovery can help.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The parallel is striking: early recovery means learning to rely on others, a sponsor or group, and to name needs instead of acting out. Recovery communities can work as a second chance at secure base experiences.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will bristle at being compared to babies. Frame it as starting over with new equipment, not being childish. Even strong people go back to basics.

ask: Can a group or counselor really serve as a secure base, or is that too much to ask?
What signs would show that a member is developing trust in the program?

391.title: Early childhood: feelings and curiosity
391.gist: Covers ages two to six: children learn to name and express feelings, relate to people outside the family, explore with curiosity, grasp cause and effect and process fears through play. Parents should answer questions, encourage socializing and allow mistakes.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Erikson's stages here, autonomy versus shame and initiative versus guilt, involve the child testing independence. Heavy shaming at this age can leave a lasting sense of being bad, which links to adult shame in addiction.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Vygotsky saw play as a leading activity of early childhood, where children practise rules and feelings. Symbolic play lets a child act out fears safely, as play therapists use today.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members what they did when their own kids asked endless why questions. Whether they answered or shut it down links neatly to how their own curiosity was treated.

ask: How might cause-and-effect learning in childhood relate to adult consequential thinking in CBI?
What does it mean for a child to learn feelings when the parent is high or absent?

392.title: Feelings and relationships missed
392.gist: Exercise 3 asks for more ways parents can support early childhood tasks and what happens to adults who never learned to understand and express feelings or form relationships, and how recovery helps.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Difficulty identifying and describing feelings is called alexithymia. It is more common among people with substance use disorders in many studies, and building an emotion vocabulary is a practical target.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Hand out a feelings wheel and ask each member to find the precise word for one feeling from today. Moving past angry or fine is a skill they can practise daily.

ask: Is alexithymia a cause of addiction, a consequence, or both?
How might group therapy itself teach early childhood social tasks?

terms.d: Difficulty recognizing, naming and describing one's own emotions.

393.title: Preadolescence: competence or inferiority
393.gist: Covers ages seven to eleven: school success builds a sense of adult capability while failure breeds inferiority, so effort deserves praise. Children form a self-image, healthier friendships and their own moral sense; parents support setbacks and activities like sports.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Erikson called this industry versus inferiority. Children learn whether their effort pays off, and many members say they first felt stupid or bad at this age.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Carol Dweck's research found that praising effort tends to help children persist more than praising intelligence. Later large studies of growth mindset interventions found smaller and more variable effects than early claims suggested.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Kohlberg described moral reasoning moving from avoiding punishment toward understanding rules and principles. The page's shift from doing as told to knowing right and wrong reflects that view.

ask: How does school failure and learning disability among your members link to this stage?
What does praise for effort look like for an adult learner in a prison GED class?

terms.d: Erikson's school-age stage where children develop a sense of competence or of falling short.

394.title: School years, then and now
394.gist: Exercise 4 asks about other key events and tasks for preadolescents, more ways parents can help, and what happens to adults who never built a sense of being able to succeed, and how recovery can help.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect stories of suspensions, special education and labels like troublemaker. Link them to self-efficacy: recovery is a new arena where members can rack up small wins.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Bandura's self-efficacy theory says mastery experiences, actually succeeding at something, build belief in one's abilities more than encouragement does. Setting small achievable goals in treatment uses this directly.

ask: What mastery experiences can you design inside a program for members who never had them?
When is a sense of inferiority rooted in real skill gaps, and when in what others said?

terms.d: Bandura's term for belief in one's ability to succeed at a specific task.

395.title: Adolescence: bodies, moods, identity
395.gist: Defines adolescence as roughly twelve to seventeen and explains puberty's hormonal and physical changes. It notes teen moodiness and the central social task of building one's own identity and tastes.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Brain research, such as work by Laurence Steinberg and B.J. Casey, suggests reward systems mature earlier than self-control systems, which keep developing into the twenties. This helps explain teen risk-taking, especially with peers present.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The same brain science influenced U.S. Supreme Court rulings like Roper v. Simmons (2005), which ended the death penalty for crimes committed under eighteen.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Erikson named this stage identity versus role confusion. Teens try on identities, and in some neighborhoods the most available identities are street ones.

ask: What does the late-maturing brain mean for how we judge members who offended as teens?
How might puberty timing, early or late, raise substance risk?

terms.d: Erikson's adolescent stage where young people work out who they are and what they value.

396.title: Parenting teens; your teen years
396.gist: Covers intellectual growth and advises parents to stay in touch with teens while letting them decide many things, watching for long, intense mood problems that need professional help. Exercise 5 asks members which teen tasks they struggled with.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Half of lifetime mental disorders begin by around the mid-teens in major surveys such as Kessler's work, so the page's warning about prolonged mood problems is well grounded.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 2 often brings out the age of first use. Map it: many members will notice their troubles accelerated at the same age as first use, a strong discussion point.

ask: How do you separate normal teen moodiness from early depression in a member's own story?
What does giving teens space look like in a dangerous neighborhood?

397.title: Breaking away to become oneself
397.gist: After asking about adults who never formed an identity, the page explains how children move from seeing parents as perfect to noticing their flaws, then distancing. Teens set and pursue goals and test limits, usually a healthy step.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: James Marcia expanded Erikson by describing identity statuses: foreclosure (adopting an identity without exploring), diffusion, moratorium (exploring) and achievement. Many members describe foreclosure on a street identity.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The page assumes individual independence is the goal. In many collectivist cultures, healthy development keeps teens closely tied to family duties, so rebellion is not a universal stage.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask who members rebelled against and how. Testing limits is normal; what changes outcomes is whether there was a safe adult to push against and whether drugs were part of the rebellion.

ask: What would healthy limit-testing look like in an adult in recovery, compared with criminal thinking?
Why might adolescents in chaotic homes skip rebellion entirely, or start far too early?

terms.d: Committing to an identity, often one given by others, without exploring alternatives.

398.title: Helping teens become themselves
398.gist: Notes that teens discover what makes them unique and different from family, and that missing this can bring hopelessness. Exercise 6 asks how parents can foster independence and a sense of uniqueness.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to list three things about themselves that are not shared with their family. Some will struggle; it reveals how much of identity came from the group they grew up in.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan) holds that autonomy, competence and relatedness are basic needs. Parents who support autonomy, offering choices with reasons, tend to raise more motivated teens.

ask: How can an incarcerated parent support a teen's independence from a distance?
What risks come when a teen finds uniqueness mainly through risky behavior?

399.title: Teens, meaning and first use
399.gist: After asking about adults who never learned to set goals, the page describes adolescence as the time of big questions about purpose and right and wrong. It notes this is often when alcohol and drug experimentation begins, and that lacking meaning can harm integrity.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Large surveys consistently show most adults with substance use disorders started using in adolescence, and earlier first use is associated with higher risk of later problems.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Viktor Frankl, writing after the Nazi camps in Man's Search for Meaning, argued that a sense of purpose helps people endure suffering. His logotherapy tradition fits the page's spiritual dimension.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The page ties lacking meaning to lacking integrity. Some members will hear that as a moral judgment; frame spirituality as broad, including purpose, values and connection, not only religion.

ask: How might drug use serve as a teen's answer to the meaning question?
What sources of meaning are realistically available to someone in prison?

terms.d: Viktor Frankl's therapy centered on helping people find meaning in life, even in suffering.

400.title: Big questions, then and in recovery
400.gist: Exercise 7 asks whether members wrestled with life, death and meaning as teens, what they saw in other teens, and how recovery has changed their sense of values and meaning.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members lost friends young to violence or overdose. Death questions may be concrete, not abstract. Make room for grief, and know your plan if someone discloses current suicidal thoughts.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to write one value they hold now that they would have laughed at as a teen. Contrasting the two selves makes growth visible.

ask: Is meaning something people find, build, or receive, and which view fits your practice?
How can recovery offer meaning without becoming a new rigid identity?

401.title: Teen intimacy and belonging
401.gist: After asking about adults who never found meaning, the page says adolescence is when people experiment with closeness, self-disclosure and sexuality. Good experiences build trust; repeated bad ones breed insecurity, distrust and disconnection.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Erikson placed intimacy versus isolation in young adulthood, built on a secure identity. The page folds early versions of it into the teen years, when friendships and first romances rehearse adult closeness.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Baumeister and Leary's belongingness hypothesis argues that the need to belong is a fundamental human motive. For many teens, a using crowd or gang answers that need when family and school do not.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Sexual development is a sensitive topic in custody, where many members experienced early sexual exploitation. Keep discussion general and be ready to refer privately.

ask: How might early intimate relationships with using partners shape a member's later recovery?
What is the line between healthy teen experimentation with closeness and exploitation?

terms.d: Sharing personal thoughts, feelings or information with another person, a building block of closeness.

402.title: Supporting teen relationships
402.gist: Exercise 8 asks parent members whether a teen's search for intimacy is hard to accept, how to help teens build relationships, and what happens to adults who never practised disclosure and closeness, and how recovery helps.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Parents in custody often fear their teens will repeat their mistakes, especially with sex and partners. Let that fear surface, then steer toward what they can do: stay curious, ask about friends, keep letters going.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Group therapy gives adults a second laboratory for disclosure. Irvin Yalom described the group as a social microcosm, where members' relationship patterns appear and can be practised differently.

ask: What makes disclosure in a prison group riskier than in the community, and how do you lower that risk?
How can a parent discuss dating with a teen when the parent's own history is a cautionary tale?

terms.d: Yalom's idea that a therapy group reproduces members' real-life relationship patterns in the room.

403.title: What sets childhood problems off
403.gist: Names what can spark problems in kids: developmental tasks left unmet that can become an identity crisis acted out through drugs, sex or crime; unbalanced parenting, from rejection to overprotection; and peers whose values, sometimes including drug use, clash with parents'.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Peer use is one of the strongest predictors of teen substance use. Research suggests it works both through influence and selection: teens pick friends who share their leanings, and friends then reinforce them.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Andrews and Bonta list antisocial associates among the central eight risk factors for criminal behavior. The page's peer section is a childhood version of a risk CBI targets directly.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Overprotection appears alongside neglect, a useful reminder that too much control can harm. Yet research on overprotection is less consistent than on harsh or neglectful parenting.

ask: Is a teen's identity crisis expressed through crime different from one expressed through drugs?
How would you help a member see his teen peer group as a risk factor without making him defensive about old friends?

terms.d: The tendency to choose friends who already share one's attitudes and behaviors.

404.title: Illness, crises and first use
404.gist: Adds two more triggers: psychiatric or medical illness in childhood and serious family crises such as divorce, job loss or housing problems, where explosive talk leads to guilt. Exercise 9 asks what led members to start using.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Co-occurring disorders are common: a large share of people with substance use disorders also have anxiety, depression or ADHD, often appearing first. Screening teens for mental illness is a recognised prevention strategy.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 1 offers friends, boredom, depression and inadequacy. Have members rank their own reasons. The answer guides relapse prevention, since the original job of the drug often still needs filling.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask: what did the first high give you that you did not have before? One word each. Common answers, like confidence, calm or belonging, become targets for healthier replacements.

ask: How does the reason someone started differ from the reason they kept using?
Why might family crises hit children harder than adults, even when the children are not the focus?

terms.d: Having a substance use disorder and another mental health condition at the same time.

405.title: Babies come without a manual
405.gist: Ends Exercise 9 by asking about childhood guilt and blame over things no one could control. Part 2 opens on parenting skills, noting children come with no instructions, and names three foundations: showing love, setting rules and being sensitive.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The three foundations line up with what parenting research calls warmth, structure and autonomy support. Programs from Triple P to Incredible Years teach versions of the same core.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The guilt question in the exercise can reveal a member who still believes he caused his parents' divorce or a sibling's removal. Naming that belief can lift something carried for decades.

ask: Which of the three foundations is hardest to deliver from a prison visiting room or a phone call?
Why do adults so often keep childhood guilt about events they could not control?

406.title: Love, clear rules and sensitivity
406.gist: Explains each foundation: express love and praise often, set simple, stable rules without yielding to whining, and respect children's needs and views, letting them voice feelings about rules. Exercise 10 asks how members show love to their children.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Parent training programs that combine warmth with consistent limits, such as Parent-Child Interaction Therapy developed by Sheila Eyberg, have strong research support for reducing children's behavior problems.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Not giving in to whining is basic learning theory. If tantrums sometimes work, they are rewarded on an unpredictable schedule, which makes them stronger and harder to stop.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members show love with money or gifts, especially after missing time. Explore other forms: undivided attention, keeping promises, remembering details from a child's life.

ask: How does an incarcerated parent express love consistently when contact is limited?
Is letting a child complain about rules different from letting them argue the rules away?

407.title: Were you loved? Balance in strictness
407.gist: Exercise 10 continues, asking whether members felt loved and how they wished to be, and what happens to adults who missed love, rules or sensitivity. The page then revisits strict, harsh and lenient parenting, now through a parent's eyes.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Session 23 asked how members were parented; this asks how they parent. Name the shift, and ask whether anyone finds themselves using the very style they resented.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to finish two sentences: I knew I was loved when... and I wish someone had... Their answers become their personal parenting guide.

ask: Why do people so often repeat a parenting style they hated, even knowing its cost?
What does balance between rules and flexibility look like for a toddler versus a teenager?

408.title: Inconsistency confuses children
408.gist: Reviews harsh and lenient parenting and adds inconsistency: rules enforced sometimes and not others leave children unsure of right and wrong and teach them rules do not matter. Exercise 11 asks members to rate their own consistency.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Gerald Patterson's research on family coercion showed how inconsistent discipline teaches children that escalating behavior eventually works. Consistency is what makes a rule real.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Addiction often drives inconsistency: rules enforced when sober, ignored when high or guilty. Children of using parents learn to read the parent's state rather than the rule.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask for honest examples of when they let rules slide because of guilt over absence. Overcompensation after release is common, and naming it in advance helps members plan.

ask: How can co-parents with different styles, one inside and one outside, stay consistent?
Is consistency ever a problem, for example when a rule no longer fits a growing child?

409.title: Physical punishment versus fitting consequences
409.gist: After asking what happens with too strict or lenient parents, the page states research finds physical punishment breeds fear, anxiety, depression and behavior problems. It introduces consequences that a child of a given age can understand, applied consistently.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The American Academy of Pediatrics issued a 2018 policy statement advising against spanking and harsh verbal punishment, citing links to aggression and later problems. Many countries have banned corporal punishment of children.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Many members grew up with physical discipline and say it made them who they are. Respect the experience; ask what else might have taught the same lessons without the fear, and what fear itself taught.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Physical punishment can stop a behavior in the moment but does not teach what to do instead, and it models hitting as a way to solve problems, which is Bandura's modeling at work.

ask: How would you respond to a member who says spanking is part of his culture and faith?
Why might punishment work for an adult supervisor but backfire with children?

410.title: Age-fit consequences and catching good
410.gist: Gives age-graded examples of consequences, from reassuring a toddler to grounding a teen, then says praise for good behavior works better than criticism, so parents must change their own habits. Praise effort, not just success. Exercise 12 asks for consequences that fit.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Behavior therapists call it catching them being good. Attention is powerful reinforcement; parents often give it mainly for misbehavior, accidentally strengthening what they dislike.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Labeled praise, naming the exact behavior praised, is a core skill in PCIT and similar programs, which show reductions in disruptive behavior. Specific praise teaches more than a general good job.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The same principle runs adult programs. Contingency management in addiction treatment rewards negative drug tests and is among the best-supported treatments for stimulant use.

ask: How might a parent's own recovery suffer if they only notice their failures, not their effort?
Why do people find criticism easier to give than praise?

terms.d: Praise that names the specific behavior being appreciated, such as thanks for putting your shoes away.

411.title: Listening as respect
411.gist: After asking members to recall praise and criticism that stuck, the page opens on communication: parent and child are not equals but must still talk openly. As children learn to speak, parents must shift from talking to them to listening.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Thomas Gordon's Parent Effectiveness Training (1970) applied Carl Rogers's client-centered listening to parenting. Its ideas, including active listening and I-messages, shaped many later programs.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to recall one sentence of praise or criticism from childhood, word for word. Most can. Use it to show how a parent's words echo for decades.

ask: Why does the criticism people remember from childhood often outlast the praise?
What does listening to a child communicate that talking cannot?

412.title: Invitations to speak and active listening
412.gist: Suggests special times when children can talk freely, and explains active listening: paraphrasing back what you heard so the child can confirm or correct it. Exercise 13 asks members to name their communication strengths and weaknesses.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is reflective listening, the core of Miller and Rollnick's motivational interviewing. The same skill a counselor uses with adult clients works with a five-year-old, just with shorter, simpler reflections.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Practise in pairs: one member describes a frustrating day for a minute, the other reflects it back without advice. Advice is the hardest habit to drop; let them notice the urge.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Phone calls from prison are short and monitored. Coach members to open with a question and reflect rather than lecture. Brief listening may be the most valuable parenting they can do inside.

ask: What is the difference between paraphrasing and parroting, and how would a child notice?
How might active listening change a member's relationship with his PO or partner?

terms.d: Restating what someone said in your own words so they know they were understood or can clarify.

413.title: When listening shuts down
413.gist: After asking whether members' parents listened, the page introduces roadblocks to listening: responses that make children unwilling to speak. The first is not letting the child talk, even when the parent is angry.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Gordon called these roadblocks to communication and listed a dozen common ones, such as ordering, warning, moralizing and ridiculing. Many parents use several in one sentence.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask who was told as a child to be quiet or to speak only when spoken to. The silence they learned often reappears as difficulty speaking up in group.

ask: Why might an angry parent cut a child off, and what does the child learn about anger from it?
Which roadblocks do staff in correctional settings use most?

414.title: Five more listening roadblocks
414.gist: Lists more roadblocks: focusing on blame, shaming and laughing at mistakes, long lectures, sweeping statements like you always, and forbidding disagreement. Each pushes children away from solving problems and thinking for themselves.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Overgeneralization is one of Beck's cognitive distortions. When a parent says you always, the child may adopt it as a belief about himself, and later as an adult habit of thought.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: June Tangney's research separates shame (I am bad) from guilt (I did something bad). Guilt tends to motivate repair, while shame is linked with hiding, anger and, in some studies, substance problems.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rewrite one shaming sentence into a problem-focused one, such as replacing you never listen with what got in the way of remembering? Then role-play both versions.

ask: Which roadblock is most likely to create a child who lies to avoid trouble?
Can disagreement be allowed while the parent still has the final word? How?

terms.d: Shame condemns the whole self; guilt focuses on a specific act and tends to prompt making amends.

415.title: Unlearning automatic responses
415.gist: Exercise 14 asks members whether their parents used these roadblocks, how that felt, and how a parent can stop a response that comes by instinct.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Question 2 is really about habit change. CBT approaches teach catching the trigger, pausing and choosing a planned response. The pause is the skill; insight alone rarely changes a reflex.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Link to CBI's thinking report: the situation, the automatic thought, the feeling, the action. Members can apply the same tool to parenting moments they want to handle differently.

ask: How long does it take to replace an automatic parenting response, and what helps it stick?
Why might stress and fatigue make old roadblocks return?

416.title: Solve problems, don't assign blame
416.gist: Asks what happens to adults raised with roadblocks, then argues blaming children for problems like bad grades or fights backfires, leaving them angry and feeling like failures. Parents should solve problems with children in four steps: define, brainstorm, choose, act.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: D'Zurilla and Goldfried's problem-solving model uses similar steps, and CBI teaches members a version of it. Teaching it to their children passes the same skill down a generation.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Ross Greene's Collaborative and Proactive Solutions approach, based on the idea that kids do well if they can, has shown promising results for children with explosive behavior in several studies.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Stress solving it together, rather than on the child's behalf. Many members, eager to fix things, will jump to solutions. The child's own ideas build their confidence.

ask: When is it right to find out who caused a problem, and when does it get in the way?
How does blame show up in criminal thinking, and how does problem solving counter it?

417.title: Fault-finding versus fixing
417.gist: Exercise 15 asks for an example where finding fault did no good and a better approach, why blame is easier than problem solving, and how problem solving can replace blame when members are held responsible for harm in recovery.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Blame is easier because it protects self-image and offers quick relief. Psychologists call one version the self-serving bias: crediting ourselves for success and blaming others or circumstance for failure.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 3 is sharp: members will be blamed by family. Coach them to hear blame without fighting it, then shift to what they can do now, which is the spirit of amends.

ask: Can problem solving ever become a way to dodge accountability?
How would you help a family stuck in blame after a member's release?

terms.d: The tendency to credit ourselves for successes while blaming others or circumstances for failures.

418.title: Structure: schedules and talk time
418.gist: Argues children cannot see how adults organize time unless shown. Families should post a written schedule for sleep, meals, homework and play, set aside at least fifteen minutes daily for relaxed family talk, and enforce fair rules consistently.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies link regular family routines and shared meals with better child outcomes, including lower teen substance use. The research is mostly correlational, so routines may partly reflect families that are already doing well.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Structure is also a relapse prevention tool. Unstructured time is a classic high-risk situation, so a family schedule protects the parent as well as the child.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members leaving prison know structure intimately, often too well. Explore what kind of structure feels supportive rather than like a cell count.

ask: What would a realistic schedule look like for a single parent working nights after release?
Why might children feel safer with structure even when they resist it?

419.title: Simple rules and a family schedule
419.gist: Urges rules that are simple, sensible and supported by the setting, like no TV during homework time. Exercise 16 asks how a family schedule would help members' families and their recovery.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Arranging the setting so the right behavior is easy is a form of stimulus control. Behavioral scientists find that changing the environment often beats relying on willpower.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members sketch one weekday schedule for their household after release, including a recovery meeting. Seeing where everything fits, or doesn't, prompts realistic planning.

ask: How can a family schedule support someone's recovery without making family life revolve around it?
What makes a rule easy to follow, beyond being simple?

terms.d: Shaping behavior by changing cues in the environment, such as removing distractions during homework.

420.title: Encourage, challenge, don't demand perfection
420.gist: After asking how family talk time helps recovery, the page says children want to succeed and make parents proud. Parents should set hard but achievable tasks, encourage rather than shame after failure, and reward effort over perfection.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Psychologists call this scaffolding: support a child just enough to master a task slightly beyond their current level, then step back. The term comes from Wood, Bruner and Ross's work on tutoring.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research by Hewitt and Flett and others links socially prescribed perfectionism, believing others demand perfection, with depression and anxiety. Asking for effort, not perfection, protects against it.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The advice applies to recovery itself. Expecting perfect sobriety can turn a slip into a full relapse, what Marlatt called the abstinence violation effect.

ask: How do you set a challenge that is hard but achievable for a child you rarely see?
Where in your own work could encouraging effort over perfection change outcomes?

terms.d: Giving just enough support for a learner to manage a task, then reducing it as skill grows.

421.title: Encouragement for kids and recovery
421.gist: Exercise 17 asks why effort should be praised over perfect results, how parents can motivate children through hard tasks, and how a focus on encouragement over criticism could help members' own recovery.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Question 3 turns parenting advice inward. Self-compassion research by Kristin Neff suggests treating one's own failures kindly is linked with more motivation to improve, not less, contrary to the belief that self-criticism drives change.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members how they talk to themselves after a mistake, then ask if they would speak that way to their child. The gap is often stark and memorable.

ask: What is the difference between encouragement and empty praise, and how do kids tell them apart?
Is harsh self-criticism ever useful in recovery?

terms.d: Treating oneself with the same kindness and understanding one would offer a friend who is struggling.

422.title: Acceptance plus guidance works
422.gist: Summarises research that acceptance and guidance raise well-behaved children while rejection and permissiveness do not. A side-by-side chart contrasts the accepting with the rejecting caregiver and the guiding with the permissive one.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The chart is two dials: warmth (accepting versus rejecting) and control (guiding versus permissive). Accepting plus guiding is the authoritative combination that decades of research tend to favor.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Children also shape parents. A temperamentally difficult child can pull a parent toward rejection or giving in, so outcomes reflect a two-way relationship, not parenting alone.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to mark where their own parents sat on each dial and where they sit now. Movement between the two marks is the session's story in one picture.

ask: Which side of the chart are parents most likely to slip toward under stress or during relapse?
How does a child's temperament affect which parenting style looks effective?

terms.d: A child's inborn tendencies, such as activity level or emotional intensity, that shape how they react.

423.title: Quick check, then homework help
423.gist: Exercise 18 is a true or false check on accepting and guiding caregivers plus a question on recovery. The page then opens a section on helping with homework, starting with children who struggle to remember assignments and feel shame as a result.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members struggled in school with undiagnosed learning problems or ADHD. Ask what would have helped them; their answers often equal the page's tips and personalize them.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Forgetting assignments is often an executive function problem, the brain's planning and memory system, not laziness. Reframing it changes how a parent responds.

ask: How can a parent help with homework when they themselves never finished school?
What does shame about school do to a child's later relationship with learning?

terms.d: Mental skills for planning, remembering instructions, organizing and controlling impulses.

424.title: Assignment notebooks and contracts
424.gist: Recommends a dedicated assignment notebook checked by child and parent, and a negotiated homework contract stating what each side expects and will do, used while grades are low. Exercise 19 asks for other ways to help with homework.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Behavior contracts work because they make expectations explicit and give the child a voice. Shared authorship tends to increase buy-in, much as collaborative goal-setting does in counseling.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Link to members' own contracts: treatment agreements, probation terms. Ask what makes a contract feel fair versus imposed, and use that to design one with a child.

ask: Why might a contract stop working once grades improve, and is that a feature or a flaw?
How can a parent in custody take part in a homework routine from a distance?

425.title: Sample homework contract
425.gist: A template contract: John agrees to record assignments, bring home books and work during set hours; Mom agrees to keep things quiet, review the work at a set time and allow an hour of play afterward.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The hour of play after homework uses the Premack principle: a preferred activity is used to reward a less preferred one. It is the grown-up rule that dessert follows dinner.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members draft a version for their own child, or for their own recovery: what I agree to, what my support person agrees to. Writing obligations for both sides feels balanced.

ask: What happens to a contract if the parent fails their part? What does the child learn?
Could this format work between a member and a sponsor or partner?

terms.d: Using a preferred activity as a reward for completing a less preferred one.

426.title: Session 24 in review
426.gist: Summarises the developmental stages and their tasks, notes that substance use or other problems may have left tasks unfinished but they can be learned as adults, and lists the parenting skills covered: communication and problem solving.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Close with a commitment: one parenting skill to practise on the next call or visit. Specific, small and soon beats a vague intention to be a better parent.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The session says it covered tasks for four of five stages; adulthood gets little attention. Adults face their own tasks, such as building intimacy, contributing to others and accepting aging, worth discussing in reentry.

ask: What evidence would show you a member actually uses these parenting skills after release?
How could you connect this session to family reunification services in the community?

427.title: Session 25: school and work goals
427.gist: Introduces Educational and Vocational Goals, which helps members choose an educational path and assess their job interests and skills, and teaches job searching, résumés, cover letters and interview behavior.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: A RAND review of correctional education studies found participants had substantially lower odds of returning to prison and better odds of employment. It remains one of the most cited cases for education behind bars.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Andrews and Bonta count school and work problems among the central eight risk factors for reoffending, so this session targets a criminogenic need, not just a life skill.

ask: Why might education reduce reoffending: skills, identity, social networks, or all three?
What barriers to work do your members face that a résumé cannot fix?

terms.d: A changeable risk factor directly linked to reoffending, such as unemployment or antisocial peers.

428.title: Education beyond the classroom
428.gist: Lists Part 2 objectives, including handling drug triggers at work, then opens Part 1: education includes lessons from life and work. Active addiction narrows learning to getting and using, and sobriety can revive forgotten interests.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Addiction narrows the behavioral repertoire. Researchers describe how drug cues come to dominate attention and motivation, crowding out other rewards. Rekindling old interests rebuilds competing sources of reward.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members are expert learners already: they mastered street economics, risk calculation and reading people. Name that intelligence, then ask where else it could go.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Programs like Defy Ventures, founded by Catherine Hoke, build on the idea that hustle skills can transfer to legitimate business. The idea is popular, but rigorous long-term evidence is still limited.

ask: What did members learn during addiction that could transfer to legitimate work?
How do you help someone rediscover interests when they cannot remember having any?

429.title: Strengths, gaps and goals
429.gist: Urges members to assess their educational and work goals, strengths, weaknesses and opportunities in recovery. Exercise 1 asks them to name their strengths and areas to improve in school and work.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Run a quick SWOT on the board: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats. Threats for members include a record, gaps in work history and drug-using coworkers; naming them early makes planning honest.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members often list only weaknesses. Require at least three strengths before any weakness, and accept skills like being reliable on work detail or teaching others in the unit.

ask: How do you help a member name strengths without it sounding like false praise?
What does an honest list of threats look like for someone with a felony?

430.title: School: why it went wrong
430.gist: Exercise 1 ends by asking about goals set aside during use and steps to reach them. The page then notes education means different things to people, and many did poorly or quit because they were unprepared, rebellious, or more focused on drugs or friends.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Researchers describe a school-to-prison pipeline: suspensions, expulsions and school policing are linked with higher odds of later justice involvement, with disproportionate impact on Black and Latino students.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The page frames school failure mostly as personal choice. For many members it also reflected poverty, unsafe schools, undiagnosed learning disabilities or homes in crisis. Both views deserve airtime.

ask: How do you hold members accountable for skipping school while acknowledging the forces against them?
Which goals did your members abandon earliest, and why those?

431.title: Why adults can succeed now
431.gist: Argues that age, new responsibilities and serious efforts at sobriety mean many who struggled in school can do well as adults. Exercise 2 asks how important school was, what competed with it and why.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Andragogy, the study of adult learning associated with Malcolm Knowles, holds that adults learn best when the material is relevant to their goals and draws on experience. That is a different design from teenage schooling.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Criminologists Sampson and Laub describe turning points: life events like stable work or marriage that redirect a criminal trajectory. Returning to school as an adult can be one such turning point.

ask: What makes adult education fail even when motivation is high?
Which of the three changes, age, responsibilities or sobriety, matters most for success in school?

terms.d: The theory and practice of teaching adults, stressing relevance, self-direction and use of experience.

432.title: Adult Basic Education explained
432.gist: After asking what is different now, the page defines Adult Basic Education for people sixteen and older without twelve years of school. It covers reading, job applications, employment resources, consumer and health information and workplace social skills, plus volunteer literacy tutors.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: National surveys of adult skills find people in prison have, on average, lower literacy and numeracy than the general adult population. That makes basic education a direct reentry need, not a remedial extra.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Low literacy is often hidden out of shame. Watch for members who avoid reading aloud or ask to take worksheets back to the cell, and offer help privately.

ask: How would you screen for low literacy in a group without embarrassing anyone?
Should social skills be taught alongside reading, as ABE does, or separately?

433.title: High school equivalency options
433.gist: Exercise 3 checks understanding of ABE. The page then describes equivalency tests such as the GED and HiSET, covering the four core academic subjects, whose credential opens doors to college and careers. Exercise 4 asks if members finished high school.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Economist James Heckman and colleagues found that GED holders, on average, do not match high school graduates in later earnings, partly because a diploma also reflects persistence. The GED still opens doors that are closed without it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Use the Heckman point as motivation, not discouragement: the credential is the door; persistence skills built in recovery are what carry someone through it.

ask: What does a high school equivalency credential signal to an employer, and what does it not?
Why might addiction be the reason some members dropped out, and why might it be the result?

terms.d: A high school equivalency test used in some states as an alternative to the GED.

434.title: What's stopping you from testing?
434.gist: Exercise 4 continues, asking whether members have considered an equivalency test, what blocks them, and its advantages. The page then advises preparing with study guides from libraries, bookstores or online, which include practice questions.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Learning research by Roediger and Karpicke shows that practising retrieval, by taking practice tests, improves memory more than rereading. Sample questions in study guides are the most powerful part.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking what is stopping you invites ambivalence into the open. In MI terms, barriers are the sustain talk you need to hear before helping a member build change talk.

ask: What practical barriers to testing exist in your facility, such as waitlists or transfers?
How might fear of failing again keep someone from even trying?

terms.d: Strengthening memory by actively recalling information, such as through practice quizzes, rather than rereading.

435.title: Preparing for test day
435.gist: Notes that adult education programs and libraries offer reviews and practice. Exercise 5 asks whether members plan to take an equivalency test, how they are preparing, and whether preparation could ease test nerves.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Test anxiety eases with mastery and familiarity. Practice under realistic conditions reduces uncertainty; this is mild exposure, the same principle used for other anxieties.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Teach a 60-second breathing reset, slow exhale longer than inhale, and have members practise it before a short quiz. The skill transfers to job interviews and court dates.

ask: How would you distinguish test anxiety from a learning disability in a struggling member?
What role can peers who passed the GED play in motivating others?

436.title: Apprenticeships: earn while learning
436.gist: Explains apprenticeships, which combine on-the-job training and classes for trades like plumbing, welding and electrical work, lasting one to five years under a signed contract. The page notes they carry no tuition. Exercise 6 asks about interest in trades.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Apprenticeship is ancient: medieval guilds trained young people for years under a master. Registered apprenticeships in the U.S. today usually pay a wage that rises as skills grow.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Licensing rules matter. Some states restrict certain licenses for people with records, so check before a member sinks years into a trade that may bar them.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Pre-apprenticeship programs inside prisons have grown, and early evaluations are encouraging, though rigorous long-term studies on recidivism remain limited.

ask: Which trades in your area hire people with records, and how would you find out?
Why might a structured, contract-based program suit someone in early recovery?

terms.d: A shorter program that prepares people with basic skills to enter a registered apprenticeship.

437.title: Vocational education explained
437.gist: Exercise 6 ends by asking whether members have looked into apprenticeships. The page then describes vocational education, which prepares people for jobs not needing a four-year degree, through general or job-specific programs that improve employment and wages.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Holland's theory of career interests sorts people and jobs into six types: realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising and conventional. Matching a person's type to a job tends to improve satisfaction.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what work members have actually enjoyed, including prison jobs. The kitchen, laundry or maintenance crew can hint at an interest area worth training in.

ask: Is it better to train for a job one enjoys or one that hires people with records?
How do changing technologies affect which vocational programs are worth the time?

terms.d: Six career interest types used to match people with suitable work, also called RIASEC.

438.title: Upgrading skills or starting fresh
438.gist: Exercise 7 continues: the benefits of learning new job skills or improving current ones, of extra training for a current job, and whether members know a vocational program and want to find one.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The yes/no question about knowing a program is a quiet call to action. Bring a short list of local programs and reentry job centers so a yes can turn into a name on the spot.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Hope theory (C.R. Snyder) frames hope as goals plus pathways plus agency. Knowing a specific program supplies the pathway, which is often what members lack.

ask: What information would make vocational training feel real rather than abstract to members?
How could you connect members to programs before release rather than after?

439.title: Self-examination and the employability plan
439.gist: Asks who might help members find a program and how ABE differs from vocational training. Part 2 then frames job planning as recovery's ongoing self-examination and introduces the employability plan, a written record of skills, interests and goals.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The self-examination language echoes Step 10's continued personal inventory. Applying it to work makes recovery practical: knowing strengths and gaps guides which jobs to chase.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Christopher Uggen's analysis of a large job program found that employment was linked with lower reoffending mainly for people in their late twenties and older. Readiness and age may shape how much a job helps.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Writing a plan makes goals concrete. Have members list one skill, one interest and one goal before the session ends, a starter plan they can grow.

ask: Why might work reduce reoffending more for older than younger people?
What belongs in an employability plan for someone with a long prison record?

terms.d: A written summary of one's job skills, interests and goals used to guide a job search.

440.title: Work, job loss and recovery
440.gist: Exercise 8 asks whether members are unemployed and whether addiction cost them a job directly or indirectly. Employed members are asked how recovery has changed their attitude toward work and whether they are thinking of a change.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Job loss is both a consequence and a trigger. Drug use can cost a job; unemployment then brings idle time, money stress and lowered self-worth, all relapse risks.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members lost jobs indirectly, through arrests or missed shifts. Ask them to trace the chain; seeing the links can strengthen motivation without heavy confrontation.

ask: How can work itself become a relapse risk, through stress, peers or paydays?
What does a healthy relationship with work look like in recovery, beyond simply having a job?

441.title: Disclosing a record, then naming interests
441.gist: The page closes the question of how to answer employers about arrests or drug use, then opens the job-search section by asking members to name their interests and talents (Exercise 9). It pivots from damage control to self-inventory.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Sampson and Laub's life-course work treats stable employment as a possible turning point away from crime, mostly because it restructures daily routines and social ties. Starting the search from interests rather than from the record frames work as identity-building, not just survival.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have members rehearse a 30-second disclosure script aloud: brief acknowledgment, what changed, what they offer now. Answers improvised under pressure tend to ramble into excuses or shame; a practiced script keeps it short and forward-facing.

ask: When does honest disclosure help an applicant, and when does it simply hand the employer a reason to reject?
Why might someone who has spent years in custody struggle to name any interests at all, and what does that say about identity loss?

terms.d: Policies (often called 'ban the box') that delay criminal-history questions until later in hiring, so applicants are judged on qualifications first.

442.title: Work skills versus job values
442.gist: Members list their general work skills and then their core job values, such as hours, location and responsibilities (Exercises 10-11). Separating what you can do from what you need keeps the search realistic and sustainable.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Person-environment fit theories, including Holland's interest types, predict that satisfaction and staying power rise when a job matches both abilities and values. A job that fits skills but violates values is a common setup for quitting or relapse.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to rank three values (pay, schedule, people, meaning) and then imagine a job that scores high on one and zero on another. Which loss would make them walk out first? That answer is their real non-negotiable.

ask: Do incarcerated adults have the luxury of job values, or does the reentry labor market force them to set values aside at first?
How would you help a member whose only stated value is fast cash, without moralizing?

terms.d: The features of work a person cares about most, such as pay, schedule, autonomy, purpose or setting.

443.title: Skills owned, skills wanted, worries
443.gist: Exercise 12 asks for the member's most useful skills, the skills they would like to gain, and their biggest worries about finding a job. It surfaces both strengths and the fears that may quietly stall a search.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Self-efficacy research from Bandura shows that belief in one's ability to perform a task predicts effort and persistence. Naming concrete skills is a small mastery experience that can lift job-search self-efficacy before any application is filed.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 3 is the gold. Worries like a record, no ID, or no transportation are practical barriers you can problem-solve in group; vague fears like 'nobody will want me' are cognitions worth gently challenging with evidence.

ask: Which worries on this page are distorted thinking and which are accurate readings of real discrimination? How do you tell the difference with a client?
What skills learned in custody or even in the street economy transfer legitimately to work?

444.title: Brainstorming interests from a menu
444.gist: A long menu of activities, from fixing cars to doing research, prompts members to list what they enjoy or would like to try (Exercise 13). The list lowers the bar for people who go blank when asked about themselves.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The list loosely mirrors John Holland's six interest types (realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising, conventional). Sorting a member's picks into those buckets can reveal a pattern they never noticed.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The menu leans toward a pre-internet economy (letters, files, TV-era tasks). Add current options like content creation, logistics, solar installation or commercial driving so the list feels like it belongs to members' actual futures.

ask: Is interest a stable trait or something that grows from exposure and competence? What does your answer imply for people with limited life experience?
How might early-recovery anhedonia make this exercise feel empty, and how would you name that for the group?

terms.d: Reduced ability to feel pleasure; common in early recovery as the brain's reward system readjusts after heavy substance use.

445.title: A catalog of hidden skill types
445.gist: The page lists sixteen skill families, from manual and numerical to persuasive and caretaking, to help members see abilities they overlook. It widens the definition of skill beyond formal job titles.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note that 'manipulating' and 'bargaining' sit under persuasive skills. Invite members to discuss how a hustle skill like reading people becomes legitimate in sales or conflict mediation, and where the ethical line falls.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is a strengths-based move, close to the Good Lives Model associated with Tony Ward, which argues rehabilitation works better when it builds capacities for a satisfying life rather than only managing risk.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pair members and have each interview the other about one ordinary day, then name five skills they heard. Others often spot strengths we discount in ourselves.

ask: Where is the line between redirecting a criminal skill and endorsing it?
Why do people with shame-heavy histories tend to underreport their own competencies?

terms.d: Abilities developed in one setting, like organizing or persuading, that can be applied in a different job or field.

446.title: Listing skills, then what work is for
446.gist: Exercise 14 has members write out their skills, then the text introduces job values: work as a source of purpose, whether pay, helping others, being outdoors, or hours that allow school. It shifts from what you can do to why you work.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Viktor Frankl argued that the search for meaning is a primary human drive, and he often cited Nietzsche's idea that a person with a reason to live can endure almost anything. A job tied to a purpose, even a modest one like supporting kids, can carry someone through hard shifts.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan) separates intrinsic from extrinsic motivation. Pay matters, but jobs that also offer some autonomy, competence or connection tend to sustain motivation longer.

ask: Is it fair to ask someone fresh out of prison what purpose their work should serve, or does need come first?
How might a sense of purpose at work act as a protective factor against relapse?

447.title: Trade-offs in what a job offers
447.gist: The page presents value pairs such as fixed versus flexible hours, small versus large company, safety versus challenge, then asks members what they seek in a job and why (Exercise 15). Framing values as trade-offs forces honest priorities.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push on 'constant challenge and risk.' Many members score high on sensation seeking; point out that legal high-stimulation work exists, like construction, emergency services or sales, which can meet that need without the old life.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Several options, like heavy business travel or high prestige, may be unrealistic for people on supervision with travel limits or license restrictions. Name those constraints openly so the exercise does not feel like a fantasy.

ask: How do supervision conditions (curfews, travel limits, check-ins) reshape the value choices on this page?
What does a member's preference for risk tell you about their relapse-prevention plan?

terms.d: A trait, studied by Marvin Zuckerman, describing a drive for novel, intense experiences and willingness to take risks for them.

448.title: Matching yourself to occupations
448.gist: Members are asked to combine interests, skills and values and match them to real jobs, using a sample list of fields from financial work to counseling. It is the synthesis step of the job-search inventory.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Many listed jobs face legal barriers for people with records: banking, nursing aide work and some licensed trades can require background clearance. Members deserve to know which doors are harder before they invest hope in them.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Counselor and peer-specialist roles appear on the list. Many states now certify peer recovery specialists, and lived experience can be an asset there. Mention it, but check local rules on records before promising anything.

ask: How should a counselor balance encouraging big goals with warning about occupational licensing barriers?
Which of these fields are growing or shrinking in today's economy, and how current is this list?

terms.d: State rules requiring a license for certain jobs; some exclude or restrict people with particular convictions.

449.title: Picking jobs and meeting the gatekeepers
449.gist: Exercise 16 asks members to name jobs that fit them and why, then the text introduces the cover letter and résumé as first contact with an employer. It explains that HR screens documents first, so appearance matters.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Devah Pager's audit study published in 2003 sent matched fake applicants to employers and found a criminal record sharply reduced callbacks, with an even larger penalty for Black applicants. Documents that get past screening really do matter for this population.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Today many employers use automated applicant tracking systems that scan résumés for keywords before a human ever looks. The 'screen out' step the page describes now often happens by software.

ask: If screening is the biggest hurdle, should reentry programs invest more in employer relationships than in résumé polish?
What would Pager's findings mean for how you prepare Black and Latino members versus white members?

terms.d: Software that collects and filters job applications, often ranking résumés by keyword matches before human review.

450.title: Three jobs of a cover letter
450.gist: The page stresses clean, error-free, typed documents and sets out three aims for a cover letter: address a real person and name the job, highlight a few matching skills, and say why you want this job. Interest signals the applicant will stay.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Signaling theory from economics (Michael Spence) holds that when employers cannot see quality directly, they read signals. A tidy, personalized letter is a cheap signal of care and follow-through, traits a record makes employers doubt.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members without typing skills or computer access can feel shut out. Line up the facility library, a reentry center or a mentor in advance, so the advice to 'ask a friend' is not a dead end.

ask: What would a letter that is honest about a gap without mentioning prison look like?
Is 'showing interest' a skill that can be taught, or does it depend on genuinely wanting the job?

451.title: Practicing cover-letter strategy
451.gist: Exercise 17 asks members how a cover letter can show real interest, be personal without running long, and spotlight their skills. It turns the previous page's rules into their own plans.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by writing one weak and one strong opening line on the board and letting the group vote and explain. Contrasting examples teach faster than rules, and critiquing a fictional letter feels safer than critiquing one's own.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have each member research one real local employer and write a single sentence on why that company, not just any job. Specificity is the hardest part and the most persuasive.

ask: Why do concrete details persuade more than general claims like 'hard worker'?
How could this exercise expose literacy gaps, and how would you protect members' dignity if it does?

452.title: Building a short, favorable résumé
452.gist: The page notes cover letters are usually three paragraphs and calls the résumé the more important document: accurate yet favorable, one or two pages. It introduces the sections, personal information, objective, education and qualifications, and says optional parts appear only when they show strengths.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Objective statements are widely seen as outdated; many current guides favor a brief summary of qualifications instead. Also add LinkedIn or a professional email, and warn against old nicknames in email addresses.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: 'Accurate but favorable' is an ethics question in miniature: selecting truthful emphasis versus misleading by omission. It mirrors how people in recovery learn to tell their story without either hiding or wallowing.

ask: Where exactly does favorable framing cross into deception on a résumé?
How would you list a GED, prison vocational certificate or in-custody course without flagging incarceration?

terms.d: A few lines at the top stating key strengths and experience; now often preferred over a stated objective.

453.title: Template for a three-paragraph letter
453.gist: A model cover letter lays out the header, the addressee, and three paragraphs: why you are writing and how you heard, one or two matching skills plus a reason for interest, and a specific request for an interview with follow-up. Enclosures note the résumé.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The closing paragraph asks for a concrete next step and promises a follow-up call. That is an implementation intention, a specific when-and-how plan, which Peter Gollwitzer's research links to higher follow-through than vague intentions.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members often skip the follow-up call out of fear of rejection. Role-play the call in pairs: introduce yourself, reference the letter, ask about next steps. Rehearsal shrinks the dread.

ask: Why does a template help low-confidence writers but risk producing identical letters employers ignore?
How does the fear of follow-up calls connect to the rejection sensitivity you see in group?

terms.d: A plan stating exactly when, where and how you will act, such as 'Monday at 10 I will call the manager.'

454.title: Employment history, gaps and affiliations
454.gist: The page advises listing significant jobs from the last ten years without dates, so unemployment gaps common in addiction are less visible, and adding relevant volunteer work or union membership. Exercise 18 checks understanding with true-or-false items.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Leaving off dates is the logic of the functional résumé, but many recruiters read missing dates as a red flag that something is hidden. A safer modern approach lists years only and fills gaps with training, treatment-program work assignments or certificates.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief item 3 (volunteer work for a nurse's aide job) to show relevance as the test for what goes in. Ask members what in-custody jobs, like kitchen, laundry or tutoring, could count as real experience.

ask: Is hiding gaps a short-term gain that sets up a credibility problem at the interview?
How would you coach someone to explain a five-year gap in one honest sentence?

terms.d: A résumé organized by skill areas rather than by dated job history; it hides gaps but some employers distrust it.

455.title: What stays off the résumé
455.gist: The page lists résumé don'ts: no salary, no unrelated hobbies or social and religious memberships, no legal, substance use or jail history, and no age, sex, marital status or family size. Exercise 19 tests these rules.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The rule against age, sex and family details echoes US anti-discrimination law: employers generally should not base hiring on those traits, so applicants have no reason to volunteer them.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Omitting a record from a résumé is fine, but members must not lie when an application directly asks about convictions. Background checks are routine, and a false answer discovered later can justify firing even years in.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Item 1 tempts some members to over-explain recovery. Reframe: recovery is something you can discuss when trust exists, but a résumé is a sales document, not a confession.

ask: What is the ethical difference between not volunteering information and denying it when asked?
Could listing a recovery-related volunteer role ever help rather than hurt?

456.title: Preparing for the application form
456.gist: The page explains that applications vary and are often online, then begins a practice form asking for legal name, contact details, birth date and work status. It advises memorizing the Social Security number rather than writing it down.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many people leaving prison lack ID, a Social Security card or a birth certificate. Treat document recovery as the first job-search task; without them, a perfect résumé goes nowhere.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members fill out the practice form under a time limit, then circle every item they could not answer from memory. That list becomes their homework before release.

ask: Why does the manual warn against writing a Social Security number on a worksheet, and what does that teach about identity theft risk in group settings?
How do online-only applications disadvantage people released after long sentences?

457.title: The felony question on the form
457.gist: The practice application continues with past employer contact, citizenship, and the key item: any felony conviction or prison release in the past seven years, plus a disability question. Members face the hardest question on paper before facing it live.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Fair-chance or 'ban the box' laws in many cities and states push conviction questions later in hiring. Research on their effects is mixed: some studies found employers then guessed at records using race, hurting young Black and Hispanic men who had none.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The disability question touches the Americans with Disabilities Act. Being in recovery from drug addiction (not currently using illegal drugs) can be protected under the ADA, though current illegal drug use is not.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Coach a short written answer for the 'describe' line: the offense category, time served, and what they have done since. Brief and factual beats long and emotional.

ask: If ban-the-box can backfire through statistical discrimination, what policy would actually help?
How do you hold both honesty and self-protection when coaching answers to this question?

terms.d: Judging an individual by assumed group averages when real information is missing, such as guessing who has a record by race.

458.title: Choosing three professional references
458.gist: The practice form asks for three non-relatives who know the applicant's qualifications, with full contact details and job titles. It pushes members to identify people who can vouch for them now.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Brainstorm legitimate references: a work supervisor inside, a teacher, a chaplain, a vocational instructor, a counselor where policy allows. Remind members to ask permission first and tell the reference what job they are seeking.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
