deeper.text: References are social capital, the resources that come through relationships. Incarceration erodes it, and rebuilding prosocial ties is itself a recognized desistance factor.

ask: What does it say about a member's social network if they can name no references, and how might that guide treatment goals?
Should staff ever serve as references for clients, and what boundaries apply?

terms.d: The benefits a person gains through relationships and networks, such as job leads, references or support.

459.title: Work history: duties and supervisors
459.gist: The form's work-history section asks for each job's title, employer, supervisor, pay, hours and duties, counting paid, military and relevant volunteer work, with the most recent first. Members learn to describe jobs in terms of skills shown.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Teach action verbs: turn 'worked in kitchen' into 'prepared meals for 300 people daily under food-safety rules.' Have members rewrite one past duty this way and read it aloud.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Most-recent-first exposes a gap immediately. Help members decide in advance how to list in-custody work assignments honestly, since leaving the most recent years blank invites questions anyway.

ask: How does writing duties as accomplishments change a person's view of their own past?
Should employers count unpaid in-custody labor as work experience?

460.title: Equipment and reasons for leaving
460.gist: The form continues with equipment used and reason for leaving, then repeats for a second job. 'Reason for leaving' is where incarceration or firing often has to be addressed.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Brainstorm honest, neutral phrasings for reason for leaving: 'relocated,' 'contract ended,' 'left to address personal matters.' Then discuss when neutral turns into misleading, and practice how to elaborate if asked.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Listing equipment and tools is concrete evidence of competence. Specific nouns like forklift, POS system or table saw are more believable than adjectives about work ethic.

ask: How would you respond to a member who says the honest reason for leaving was 'I got locked up' and refuses to soften it?
What does a pattern of 'reasons for leaving' reveal clinically about someone's work history?

461.title: Where jobs are found
461.gist: The page lists ways to find work: newspaper ads, schools, online job banks, private agencies that charge fees, government employment offices and company job listings, plus contacting businesses directly. Timing a direct contact well can open hidden openings.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Mark Granovetter's well-known 'strength of weak ties' research found that many people get jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends or ads. Networking and direct contact often matter more than listings.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Newspaper want ads are now a minor channel. Point members to state workforce centers (American Job Centers), reentry employment programs and second-chance employers, and warn against agencies charging applicants fees.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Warn that old acquaintances who are still using can also be 'weak ties' offering jobs. Ask members to sort their network into safe and risky contacts before release.

ask: If most jobs come through networks, how does incarceration's damage to networks compound disadvantage?
How do you help a member build weak ties that are also recovery-safe?

terms.d: Acquaintances rather than close friends; Granovetter showed they often bring new information such as job leads.

462.title: Online searches and the first interview
462.gist: The page suggests job websites, then explains the interview: often the first face-to-face meeting, sometimes preceded by forms or skills tests. It normalizes interview nerves and urges learning from a bad interview and trying again.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Normalizing anxiety is a core CBT move: labeling nerves as expected reduces the secondary fear of being anxious. Yerkes-Dodson style thinking suggests moderate arousal can even sharpen performance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The advice to go right back out after a failed interview is exposure in action. Frame repeated interviews as practice reps, and track attempts rather than outcomes so members get reinforcement for effort.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Rejection after rejection can trigger hopelessness and the 'why bother' thought that precedes relapse. Link the job search to the relapse-prevention plan explicitly.

ask: How might the abstinence violation effect show up after a failed interview rather than after a slip?
What makes a skills test feel humiliating for someone with limited schooling, and how would you prepare them?

463.title: Interview dos, don'ts and nerves
463.gist: Exercise 20 asks members what to do and avoid in interviews, whether they get anxious, and how they could ease that anxiety. It surfaces existing knowledge before the dos-and-don'ts list arrives.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Teach paced breathing with a longer exhale, about four counts in and six out, for the waiting room. Slow exhalation engages the parasympathetic system and is a quick, invisible coping skill.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Run mock interviews with a member playing the employer. Being on the other side of the table often teaches more about first impressions than any list.

ask: Why does generating answers before reading the list improve learning (the generation effect)?
Which interview anxieties come from the prison environment itself, like eye contact norms or posture?

464.title: Fourteen rules for the interview
464.gist: A checklist covers bringing a résumé, references and Social Security card, coming alone and early, dressing neatly, staying alert, no smoking or gum, honest brief answers, patience with tests, no arguing, no criticizing past bosses, and no personal problems.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prison survival habits can clash with these rules: a hard stare, guarded posture, or a quick defensive reply reads as hostility to an interviewer. Name this code-switching openly; it is skill, not fakeness.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The dress advice is gendered and dated. Update it to 'match the workplace, one step more formal,' and make sure members can get interview clothes through a clothing closet or reentry program.

ask: Is asking members to hide personal struggles in interviews in tension with the authenticity recovery asks for?
Which of these rules matters most for someone with a visible record, and why?

terms.d: Shifting language, posture and behavior to fit the norms of different settings.

465.title: Courtesy, then the workplace as family
465.gist: The checklist ends with staying polite and open to an interviewer's leads, followed by a true-false quiz. The coworkers section then compares a workplace to a family with parent-like bosses and sibling-like peers, and warns that early recovery brings irritability and conflict.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The family analogy is transference in plain clothes: people replay early relationship patterns with authority figures. A member who fought a harsh father may read a boss's correction as an attack.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Post-acute withdrawal is commonly described in recovery literature as lingering irritability, poor sleep and mood swings for weeks or months. Evidence for it as a distinct syndrome is debated, but the symptoms are real enough to plan for at work.

ask: When the workplace really is dysfunctional, how do you help a member tell legitimate grievance from old patterns?
What schemas about authority might your members bring to their first supervisor?

terms.d: Unconsciously redirecting feelings from past relationships, like with parents, onto present people such as bosses.

466.title: Coworker conflicts and using buddies
466.gist: The page urges a plan for cravings at work, then Exercise 22 asks how members handle coworker problems and whether they used with coworkers they still work with. Work can be both a stabilizer and a trigger.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt and Gordon's relapse prevention model treats people and places linked to past use as high-risk situations. Coworkers who used with you are cue-loaded; planned coping responses lower the chance a cue becomes a lapse.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Help members script a refusal for a coworker's invitation and decide whether they need to change shifts or jobs. Keep it practical: who to call on break, what to do after payday.

ask: When is staying in a job with using coworkers too high risk, even if quitting means losing income?
Why are paydays a classic high-risk moment, and how would you plan for them?

467.title: Work triggers and supervisor styles
467.gist: Exercise 22 closes with other work triggers and a plan to handle them; the text then describes supervisors as parent-like figures with very different skill and patience. It raises the fear that a boss learns of one's addiction history and begins to cite legal protection.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Leadership research often contrasts supportive, coaching supervisors with controlling or abusive ones. For someone with a history of harsh authority, a frustrated boss can activate old schemas of mistrust and defiance within seconds.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to describe the best and worst authority figure they ever had, then notice their body reaction to each memory. That bodily cue is an early warning they can use on the job.

ask: How might criminal thinking patterns about authority (the 'they're all out to get me' stance) show up with a new supervisor?
What part of a bad supervisor relationship is the worker's to change, and what part is not?

468.title: ADA protections and employee assistance
468.gist: The page explains that addiction in recovery is treated as a disability under the ADA, though active use can still get you fired, that disclosure is a personal choice, and that EAPs offer confidential help. Exercise 23 asks about trouble with supervisors and what sobriety changed.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The ADA picture is more nuanced than the page suggests. People in recovery who are not currently using illegal drugs can be protected, alcoholism has somewhat broader coverage, but employers may still enforce drug testing and conduct rules equally for everyone.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: EAP confidentiality is strong but not absolute: limits apply for safety threats and in mandated referrals, where the employer may learn whether the worker attended. Members should ask about those limits up front.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members will not have EAPs in entry-level jobs. Have a backup list ready: community clinics, mutual-help meetings, a reentry case manager.

ask: Is framing addiction as a disability empowering, stigmatizing, or both?
How does the 'sober today' condition in the law match or clash with a harm-reduction view of recovery?

terms.d: Employee assistance program: a workplace benefit offering confidential short-term counseling and referrals for personal, mental health or substance problems.

469.title: Improving the boss relationship, and disclosure
469.gist: Exercise 23 continues: what members want improved with their supervisor, what they can do to help, and how they would answer if asked directly about a drug or alcohol problem. It moves from blaming the boss to owning one's part.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This mirrors the locus of control idea (Rotter): people who see outcomes as partly under their control tend to act to change them. The question 'is there some way you can help' nudges toward an internal locus without excusing a bad boss.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Role-play question 3 three ways: denial, oversharing, and a calm boundary such as 'I'm in recovery and it's going well; it doesn't affect my work.' Let the group judge which protects both honesty and the job.

ask: Is it ever ethical to lie to an employer about past drug use? Where would you draw the line for a client?
How does the fear of being 'found out' itself become a relapse risk?

terms.d: A person's belief about whether life outcomes are driven mainly by their own actions (internal) or by outside forces (external).

470.title: Session 25 wrap-up
470.gist: The summary recaps the session: education and work goals, interests, skills and values matched to jobs, how to find and apply for work, and preparing for drug triggers on the job. It ties employment back to recovery.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Employment is one of the 'Central Eight' risk-need factors in Andrews and Bonta's RNR model, under school or work. Targeting it is part of evidence-based correctional practice, though a job alone rarely reduces reoffending without other changes.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Close the session with each member naming one concrete job-search action for the next seven days and one person who will hold them to it.

ask: Why do jobs alone show modest effects on reoffending, and what else must change for work to matter?
Which part of this session would your members find least realistic, and how would you adapt it?

terms.d: Andrews and Bonta's eight major risk-need factors for crime, including antisocial attitudes, associates, substance abuse and school or work.

471.title: Session 26 opens: money management
471.gist: The Money Management session introduction says addiction made money hard to manage and sobriety requires sorting it out. Two parts follow: setting financial goals across time frames and building monthly and yearly budgets.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Addiction research consistently finds steep delay discounting: future rewards lose value fast compared with immediate ones. Budgeting is a training ground for valuing the future self, the same muscle recovery needs.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: People leaving prison often carry court fines, fees, restitution and child support arrears that grew during incarceration. Money management here is not just thrift; it is navigating debt they may not even know the size of.

ask: Is poor money management a cause, a consequence, or a companion of addiction for most of your members?
What would a budget look like for someone whose income on release is zero?

terms.d: The tendency to value a reward less the longer you must wait for it; steeper in people with addictions.

472.title: Asking for help with money
472.gist: The page warns the session may feel personal and awkward, then argues that money skills are rarely taught and get rusty in addiction. It links recovery's habit of asking for help to finances, where shame often keeps people silent.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Behavioral finance describes an 'ostrich effect': people avoid checking finances when they fear bad news. Avoidance offers short relief but lets problems grow, a pattern that parallels avoidance in addiction.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Mullainathan and Shafir's book Scarcity argues that lacking money narrows mental bandwidth, so poor decisions often reflect pressure, not character. That reframe can reduce shame in group.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Talking about money in prison can raise real safety concerns about others knowing one's resources. Keep disclosures general and let members keep specific numbers private.

ask: If scarcity impairs judgment, how much responsibility for bad financial choices sits with the individual?
How is money shame similar to and different from substance-use shame?

terms.d: Avoiding financial information, like bank balances, when you expect it to be bad.

473.title: How drugs shaped your finances
473.gist: Exercise 1 asks how substances affected the member's money, whether money talk is uncomfortable, whether money is a family problem, and what skills they need. It builds the case for change through their own story.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is a motivational interviewing move: letting people tally costs themselves creates discrepancy between values and behavior, which Miller and Rollnick see as an engine of change.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to estimate what their use cost in one typical month, then multiply by a year and by years of use. Then ask what that amount could have bought. Keep it reflective, not punitive.

ask: Can a cost-tally exercise backfire by deepening shame rather than motivation? What signs would tell you?
How do you count costs that are not money, like lost custody or time?

474.title: Ranking what matters most
474.gist: Exercise 2 asks members to rate a long list of items, from religion and debt payoff to jewelry and partying, as very, somewhat or not important. Priorities come before goals.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Thorstein Veblen coined 'conspicuous consumption' for spending to display status. Items like nice jewelry, an expensive car or attracting partners often carry identity and respect needs, especially in street culture.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Do not shame status items. Ask what each provides (respect, safety, belonging) and whether a cheaper or prosocial path could meet the same need.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: After ranking, ask members to compare their list with where their money actually went last month. The gap between stated and lived values is the conversation.

ask: Why might values ranked in a classroom differ sharply from values shown on payday?
How does Maslow's hierarchy help or mislead in understanding these rankings?

terms.d: Buying goods mainly to display wealth or status, a term from economist Thorstein Veblen.

475.title: Three questions of money management
475.gist: The page reduces money management to three questions: what you have now (income and assets), what you want (common recovery goals like paying debts or saving), and how to get it (budgeting and saving, not luck). Exercise 3 sorts goals by time frame.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Goal-setting research from Locke and Latham finds specific, challenging but reachable goals improve performance over vague ones. Splitting goals into short, middle and long horizons makes distant goals feel attainable.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The lottery quip lands, but gambling problems often co-occur with substance use disorders. It is worth asking directly whether anyone sees gambling as their financial plan.

ask: Why do people in early recovery often struggle more with long-term goals than short-term ones?
What counts as an asset for someone who owns nothing but skills and relationships?

terms.d: Things of value you own, such as savings, a car or a house.

476.title: Short, middle and long-range goals
476.gist: The worksheet asks members to describe their most important family financial goals for within a year, one to five years, and more than five years. It turns wishes into a timeline.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to write each goal as a picture of a specific day when it is met: where they are, who is there. Vivid episodic future thinking has been shown in studies to reduce delay discounting.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will leave long-term blank because the future feels unreal after years inside. Treat that as information, not failure, and explore it gently.

ask: What role does hope play in whether people can plan five years ahead?
How do you balance realism with aspiration when a member writes 'buy a house' as a one-year goal?

terms.d: Vividly imagining specific future events; research links it to more patient choices.

477.title: Goals with price tags, then expenses
477.gist: Exercise 4 adds timing and total and monthly costs to each goal. Part 2 then begins budgeting by naming five expense types: fixed monthly, variable monthly, fixed yearly, seasonal and emergency, plus savings for future goals.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Dividing a goal's cost by months turns a dream into a monthly behavior. It is the financial version of 'one day at a time': a huge target becomes a small, repeatable action.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Richard Thaler's 'mental accounting' describes how people sort money into mental buckets. Used deliberately, like a labeled envelope for each goal, that bias can actually help saving.

ask: Why do people fear making a budget, and how is that like fearing a sober look at one's life?
Which expense type do your members most often forget, and what does that cost them?

terms.d: Treating money differently depending on its source or label; a concept from economist Richard Thaler.

478.title: Family financial goals grid
478.gist: A grid lets members enter three goals each for short-term, intermediate and long-term horizons, with when, total cost and monthly amount. It makes goals measurable and comparable.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have members check whether their monthly amounts across all goals fit inside a realistic first-job income. Seeing goals collide with income teaches prioritizing better than any lecture.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to star the one goal they would protect if money ran short. The starred column is their true priority.

ask: What happens to motivation when the monthly math shows a goal is years away?
How would you adapt this grid for someone with no family in the picture?

479.title: Fixed versus variable monthly costs
479.gist: The page defines fixed monthly expenses (rent, car payment, bus pass, child support) and variable ones (utilities, phone, food, clothing). Exercises 5 and 6 annualize fixed costs and average variable ones.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Variable expenses are where impulsive spending hides. Averaging them over a year exposes patterns a single month conceals, much like a craving diary reveals triggers over weeks.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Child support appears as a fixed cost here. Many members leave with arrears and wage garnishment; connect them with child support agencies about modification options rather than letting debt drive them back underground.

ask: Why might fixed costs feel safer psychologically than variable ones?
How does unpredictable shift work turn 'fixed' income into variable income, and how would you budget around that?

terms.d: A legal order requiring an employer to withhold part of a worker's pay for a debt, such as child support.

480.title: Fixed monthly expenses table
480.gist: A table lists common fixed costs, from rent and car insurance to child support and alimony, with columns for monthly and yearly totals. Members fill in their own baseline.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Add rows that matter for reentry: supervision fees, drug testing fees, court payments, restitution, phone plan. These are fixed costs the standard list misses and they surprise people after release.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: After totaling, ask members to compute how many hours at minimum wage it takes to cover just the fixed list. Concrete hours hit harder than dollar totals.

ask: How do supervision fees shape recidivism risk if people cannot pay them?
What does a member's emotional reaction to their total tell you clinically?

481.title: Variable monthly expenses table
481.gist: Members estimate a year of costs that change month to month, such as phone, utilities, groceries, clothes, fuel, child care and medical, then divide by twelve. The averaging smooths out spiky bills.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to circle the one variable line most tied to their old using life, like entertainment or eating out. That line is often where relapse spending first shows up again.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Few members will have real numbers yet. Offer typical local estimates for rent-free situations, transitional housing or living with family, so the table becomes a plausible draft rather than a blank.

ask: How could tracking variable spending serve as an early relapse warning signal?
Why are people generally poor at estimating small recurring costs?

482.title: Yearly and seasonal costs
482.gist: The page covers fixed yearly expenses, like taxes or annual insurance, and seasonal ones, like holiday gifts, school clothes and summer trips. Exercises 7 and 8 spread both across twelve months.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Spreading yearly costs into a monthly set-aside is what personal-finance writers call a sinking fund. It turns predictable shocks into routine, removing a common source of crisis and the stress that can feed cravings.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Holidays combine money pressure, family contact and emotional memories, a triple risk. Link seasonal budgeting to holiday relapse planning, and to guilt-driven overspending on children after time away.

ask: Why do parents returning from prison often overspend on gifts, and how would you address it without judgment?
Are seasonal financial stresses predictable enough to schedule extra support around them?

terms.d: Money set aside a little each month for a known future expense, like holidays or insurance.

483.title: Fixed yearly expenses table
483.gist: A table lists annual costs such as property tax, car registration and license fees, car insurance and a yearly car checkup, with room to add others and convert to monthly averages.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Add reentry-specific yearly items: driver's license reinstatement, ID renewals, probation or court annual fees, professional certificate renewals. Suspended licenses from unpaid fines are a common barrier to work.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Many states have suspended driver's licenses for unpaid court debt, a practice widely criticized for trapping people in a cycle of fines and job loss. Some states have reformed it.

ask: Which hidden yearly costs might push a newly released person into the informal economy?
How could you help a member find out what fines or fees they owe before release?

484.title: Seasonal expenses by month
484.gist: A month-by-month grid lets members place each seasonal expense in the month it lands, total them, and divide by twelve. It makes the calendar of money pressure visible.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Next to each month, have members also note any emotional anniversaries: a death, an arrest date, a holiday spent inside. Overlaying money stress and emotional stress shows which months need double support.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Seeing costs on a calendar exploits planning ahead rather than reacting, the basic logic of relapse prevention's attention to predictable high-risk situations.

ask: Why does visual layout, a calendar versus a list, change how people plan?
Which months are hardest for your members, and is that pattern consistent across people?

485.title: Planning for the unplanned
485.gist: The page defines emergency expenses, like medical bills, broken glasses, burglary or appliance repair, and suggests estimating them from last year's costs. Exercise 9 builds that estimate.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Household surveys in the US, such as the Federal Reserve's annual well-being survey, have repeatedly found many adults would struggle to cover a modest surprise expense with cash. Members are far from alone.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Using last year as a guide does not work for someone who spent last year in custody. Suggest a small fixed target, built slowly, instead of an estimate from history.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Unbudgeted emergencies are where payday loans and old contacts step in. Ask the group who they would turn to for a sudden need and whether that person is safe for their recovery.

ask: How does lack of an emergency cushion raise relapse and reoffense risk?
What does 'emergency' mean when your whole life is in transition?

terms.d: Savings kept for unexpected expenses so a crisis does not force borrowing.

486.title: Emergency expenses table
486.gist: Members list last year's surprise costs by category, from car and medical to legal, pet, home repair and parking tickets, then divide by twelve to find a monthly set-aside.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The 'legal emergency' line deserves attention: violations, warrants and court dates can carry costs. Encourage members to know their supervision terms precisely, since prevention is the cheapest legal plan.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name one emergency from their past that turned into a bigger crisis because there was no money. Then plan what the sober version would look like.

ask: Which 'emergencies' are actually predictable consequences of patterns, and how do you raise that without blaming?
How might a small emergency fund change someone's sense of control?

487.title: Adding up all expenses
487.gist: Exercise 10 combines the five expense types into one monthly and yearly total. Any income above that total can go to future goals or extras.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Totaling everything replaces vague anxiety with a single concrete number. In CBT terms, it trades catastrophizing for data; even a frightening number is usually easier to work with than a fog.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Watch for the member who stops halfway. Avoidance on this page is a clinical signal worth naming kindly, just as you would note avoidance of a hard topic in group.

ask: Why is a single summary number more motivating, or more frightening, than detailed lists?
What does it mean to define luxuries for someone who has lived with almost nothing?

488.title: Facing income against the bills
488.gist: The page names a habit learned in addiction, ignoring problems, and predicts members may want to skip comparing income and expenses. Exercise 11 asks them to total their own, a spouse's and other income.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: This is the money version of the First Step idea in 12-step programs: admitting a situation is unmanageable is a precondition for changing it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Avoidance is negatively reinforced: looking away removes anxiety right now, so the habit strengthens. Facing the numbers is a small exposure exercise, and anxiety tends to drop with repeated contact.

ask: Is the urge to avoid finances a learned addiction habit, a human universal, or both?
How do you encourage facing reality without overwhelming someone with no resources?

489.title: Surplus or deficit: the subtraction
489.gist: Exercise 12 subtracts total expenses from total income, with worked examples of a surplus and a shortfall. If expenses win, the only levers are cutting costs, raising income or both.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The page calls a shortfall 'debt,' but technically it is a deficit; debt is what accumulates if a deficit is covered by borrowing. The distinction helps members see where the danger starts.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For most members, the honest first-year result will be a deficit. Frame it as a starting map, not a verdict, and brainstorm legal income supports they may qualify for, like SNAP or workforce programs.

ask: What emotional story do people attach to a negative number, and how does that story affect what they do next?
Why might 'increase income' feel more hopeful than 'cut expenses' for your members?

terms.d: Spending more than you earn in a period; borrowing to cover it creates debt.

490.title: Using a surplus or closing a gap
490.gist: Exercise 13 asks members what to do with leftover money, or how to cut costs, raise income and reshape the monthly budget if there is a shortfall. It moves from numbers to decisions.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Behavioral economists have shown that making saving the default, such as automatic transfers on payday, works better than relying on willpower. A surplus spent by default rarely becomes savings.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to brainstorm ten ways to cut costs in two minutes, then rate each for pain and payoff. Pick the low-pain, high-payoff ones first.

ask: Why is willpower such an unreliable tool for saving, and what does that suggest for relapse prevention?
How can you help members tell needs from wants without imposing your own values?

491.title: Goals blocked by spending
491.gist: The exercise continues by asking which goals current expenses are blocking, how to reach them anyway, and what family spending changes to make first. It links daily spending to bigger hopes.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Family spending changes need family buy-in. Suggest members discuss the plan with whoever they will live with, instead of announcing it, to avoid power struggles after release.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: This echoes opportunity cost in economics: every dollar spent one way is a dollar not spent another. Naming the forgone goal makes the cost of a habit concrete.

ask: How does family conflict over money act as a relapse trigger?
Why is 'a good starting point' often more useful than a complete plan?

terms.d: The value of the best option you give up when you choose another.

492.title: Saving toward one or two goals
492.gist: Exercise 14 asks for the top one or two financial goals, their total cost, and the yearly and monthly savings needed. Narrowing to two keeps the plan doable.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Focusing on a couple of goals avoids overload; research on goal conflict suggests competing goals drain motivation. Small wins on one goal build the self-efficacy to take on the next.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: If paying debts is a goal, explain the two common payoff styles: smallest balance first for motivation, or highest interest first to save money. Let members choose the one they will actually stick with.

ask: Is paying off debt or building savings the smarter first goal for someone just released, and why?
How do you keep a member motivated when monthly savings look tiny compared to the goal?

493.title: Getting professional money help
493.gist: The page returns to asking for help, pointing to nonprofit consumer credit counseling, noting most agencies are trustworthy but some are not, and naming the National Foundation for Credit Counseling as a network of free or low-cost services.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some 'debt relief' or 'credit repair' companies charge large upfront fees and deliver little. Teach members warning signs: guarantees to erase debt, pressure to stop paying creditors, or fees before any service.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Update the contact details before sharing; addresses and phone numbers in manuals go stale. Also connect members to local reentry programs that may offer financial coaching.

ask: Why might people in recovery be especially vulnerable to financial scams?
How is seeking credit counseling psychologically similar to seeking treatment?

494.title: Session 26 wrap-up
494.gist: The summary recaps priorities, short to long-term goals, and monthly and yearly budgets that show how much can be saved. It closes the money session before credit and insurance.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: A budget is a statement of values written in numbers. That idea links this session back to recovery work on values: where the money goes shows what a person is living for.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: End by asking each member for one money habit to start and one to stop in their first month out, written on a card they keep.

ask: Did this session treat money mainly as a skill problem? What structural barriers did it leave out?
Which piece of budgeting do you think best transfers to emotional self-regulation?

495.title: Session 27 opens: insurance and credit
495.gist: The Insurance and Consumer Credit session introduction promises an overview of insurance types and of credit: when to use it, when not to, its pitfalls, and help for compulsive borrowing. Two parts cover insurance and credit.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Both insurance and credit are tools for moving money across time: insurance pays later for small premiums now, credit gives now for larger payments later. Addiction's present bias makes credit tempting and insurance easy to skip.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Behavioral economists like David Laibson modeled present bias with 'hyperbolic discounting,' which helps explain why people overborrow and underinsure even when they know better.

ask: Why would a recovery program include insurance and credit at all? What is the clinical rationale?
How might present bias show up in your members' choices beyond money?

terms.d: Overweighting immediate rewards compared to future ones, even against one's own long-term plans.

496.title: Owning past debts and insurance basics
496.gist: Objectives include spotting credit scams and compulsive borrowing; members are asked to own poor financial choices from active addiction and to repair credit. Part 1 defines insurance and notes some carriers restrict coverage for people in recovery.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Taking responsibility for old financial harm echoes the amends steps in 12-step programs. Repaying or arranging payments can be both practical repair and a moral act.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Under the Affordable Care Act, US health insurers generally cannot deny coverage for pre-existing conditions, including substance use disorders. The warning about carriers mainly applies now to life and some other insurance types.

ask: What is the difference between guilt and responsibility when facing old debts?
How should financial amends be balanced with meeting present basic needs?

terms.d: A health problem that existed before insurance coverage began; ACA health plans generally cannot deny coverage for it.

497.title: Your coverage now and auto basics
497.gist: Exercise 1 asks what insurance members have and whether they ever filed a claim. The text then explains that most states require auto insurance and describes no-fault policies, which pay your own damages regardless of fault in exchange for limits on suing.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Florida is one of the no-fault states, requiring personal injury protection (PIP) coverage. That is directly relevant for members returning to the Miami area who plan to drive.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Insurance is risk pooling: many people pay small premiums so the few who suffer losses are covered. It is a social contract in miniature, an interesting frame for people rebuilding trust in institutions.

ask: Why might people leaving prison see insurance as a scam rather than protection, and is that suspicion ever justified?
How does driving uninsured interact with supervision conditions and reoffense risk?

terms.d: Auto coverage where your own insurer pays your injuries up to a limit, whoever caused the crash.
The regular amount you pay to keep an insurance policy active.

498.title: Six kinds of auto coverage
498.gist: The page explains bodily injury liability, property damage liability, medical payments, uninsured motorist and collision coverage, defining liability as responsibility. Each covers a different person or object after a crash.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Give the group three crash scenarios (hit a pole, hit by an uninsured driver, injure a pedestrian) and have them name which coverage pays. Applying definitions to cases sticks far better than reading them.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note that liability coverage protects other people from you. For members who caused harm in the past, this can open a conversation about responsibility as something you plan for, not just something you feel.

ask: Why does the law require liability coverage but usually not collision?
How does the concept of liability here compare with moral responsibility in recovery?

terms.d: Legal responsibility for harm or damage you cause to others.
Pays to repair your own car after a crash with another vehicle or object.

499.title: Comprehensive coverage and crash history
499.gist: The page defines comprehensive coverage for non-crash damage such as theft, fire, hail and animals, then Exercise 2 asks whether members insured their car, know their coverage, and what happened after any past accident.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will recall accidents while impaired. Treat that disclosure carefully: it can be a turning-point story, but keep the focus on what was learned, and be clear about confidentiality limits in your setting.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking what actually happened after an accident turns abstract coverage types into lived consequences, an experiential learning approach that adults retain better than lectures.

ask: How might a DUI history affect insurance costs, and how long can that effect last?
What does not knowing your own coverage reveal about how people handle risk generally?

terms.d: Auto insurance for damage not caused by a crash, such as theft, storms, fire or hitting an animal.

500.title: Shopping for auto, home and renter coverage
500.gist: The page offers tips for buying auto insurance: know state requirements, compare quotes, ask about discounts, bundle vehicles, choose deductibles, buy enough liability, check health coverage and resist pressure. It then introduces homeowner's and renter's insurance.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A deductible trades a lower premium for taking on small losses yourself. It only makes sense if you can actually pay the deductible, which links back to the emergency fund from the money session.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Minimum required liability is often too low to cover a serious crash. Choosing state minimums saves money now but can leave a driver personally on the hook for large damages.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Renter's insurance is often cheap and can protect the few possessions someone rebuilds after release. It may also be required by some landlords.

ask: Why do salespeople pressure buyers, and what recovery skills help resist sales pressure?
How should someone with very little income weigh a higher deductible?

terms.d: The amount you pay yourself on a claim before insurance starts paying.

501.title: Inventory, liability and your home
501.gist: The page advises listing possessions with serial numbers and photos for claims and explains personal liability coverage for injuries or damage at home. Exercise 3 asks about owning or renting and the risk of theft or injury without insurance.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Suggest members use a phone to video each room of their future home, narrating what they own. A two-minute video is a simple inventory that most insurers accept as evidence.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Recording what you own is also a quiet measure of progress. For someone who left prison with a bag, a growing inventory can be a concrete marker of rebuilt stability.

ask: Why might people who have lost everything before resist insuring what they have now?
How does having something to lose change risk-taking behavior?

502.title: Uninsured losses and health coverage
502.gist: Exercise 3 continues with stories of uninsured theft or disaster. Personal insurance is then introduced, starting with health and hospital plans that may cover substance use treatment, newer options for the uninsured, and Medicare for older adults.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Federal parity law (the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act) generally requires covered health plans to treat substance use and mental health benefits no more restrictively than medical ones, though enforcement has been uneven.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Medicaid eligibility rules vary by state, and Florida has not adopted the ACA Medicaid expansion as of recent years. Help members check their real options early, since a coverage gap after release falls in a known high-risk period for overdose.

ask: Why is the first weeks after release such a dangerous period for overdose, and how does health coverage fit into prevention?
What are the ethics of a system where treatment access depends on insurance status?

terms.d: The legal principle that insurance must cover mental health and addiction treatment on terms comparable to physical health care.

503.title: Disability, life coverage and job benefits
503.gist: The page explains disability insurance replacing income during illness, whole versus term life insurance, and employer benefit packages often deducted pre-tax. Exercise 4 asks about health insurance for the member's family.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Whole life policies are often sold aggressively and carry high fees; many independent financial educators suggest term life is the better fit for people on tight budgets. Members should know that pressure here is common.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Benefits are a reason to prefer a job with slightly lower pay but coverage. Revisit the job-values exercise from Session 25 and ask whether benefits now rank higher.

ask: Why might life insurance matter more emotionally to a parent who has been absent?
How would you explain the difference between term and whole life in one sentence to a group?

terms.d: Pays a death benefit only if you die within a set number of years; cheaper than whole life.
Lifelong coverage that also builds a cash value; costs considerably more.

504.title: Unexpected illness and buying on credit
504.gist: Exercise 4 asks what would happen financially after a medical emergency or long disability. Part 2 then begins: credit can ease life but become a big problem, and debt equals what you borrowed plus interest and fees.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Credit and drugs share a structure: pleasure now, cost later, and the cost can grow faster than expected. Pointing out this parallel can help members spot the same reward pattern in a new place.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Medical debt is one of the most common kinds of debt collections in the US. A health crisis without coverage can wreck a fresh financial start quickly.

ask: Is credit inherently risky for people in early recovery, or only when misused?
How could you test whether the credit-drug parallel resonates or feels preachy to your group?

terms.d: The extra cost charged for borrowing money, usually a yearly percentage of what you owe.

505.title: Credit history, bureaus and repair
505.gist: The page explains that three bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, track payment behavior, that most negative items fall off after about seven years, and that consumers can request reports and demand correction of errors.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Federal law now entitles everyone to free credit reports from each bureau through an official central site, so the fee mentioned is outdated. Bankruptcies can stay longer than seven years, up to ten.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Many landlords, and some employers with written consent, check credit. A damaged credit report can become a second hidden record alongside the criminal one.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members list every debt they think they owe, then compare against an actual report after release. The gap is usually surprising and is the start of a real repair plan.

ask: Is a credit score a fair measure of responsibility, or does it penalize poverty itself?
How does the seven-year fall-off rule offer a model of redemption that criminal records usually lack?

terms.d: A company that collects people's borrowing and payment records and sells reports to lenders.
A number summarizing creditworthiness; common scores range roughly from 300 to 850.

506.title: Denied credit and checking your report
506.gist: Exercise 5 asks whether members were ever refused credit, how they could fix it, whether they have reviewed a credit report, and whether they would want to. It surfaces both history and avoidance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Identity theft is a real risk while someone is incarcerated, sometimes by people they know. A report check can reveal accounts opened in their name; explain how fraud reporting and credit freezes work.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The 'why or why not' question invites ambivalence. In MI terms, listening for both sides lets members argue themselves toward looking, instead of being told to.

ask: What feelings might stop someone from looking at their own credit report?
How would you respond if a member discovers family members used their identity while they were locked up?

terms.d: A free lock on your credit file that blocks new accounts from being opened in your name.

507.title: Store cards and the interest trap
507.gist: The page describes retail and gas-station credit as the easiest to get, explains interest on unpaid balances, and advises paying in full and avoiding too many cards. Exercise 6 asks how many cards members have and use.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Minimum payments exploit present bias: paying a little now feels manageable while interest compounds quietly. Seeing a balance grow despite payments resembles how tolerance grows despite 'just a little.'

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Advice on number of cards is more nuanced today. Scoring models weigh utilization and history heavily; closing old cards can sometimes lower a score. Opening many new cards quickly is the clearer risk.

ask: Why are store cards easiest to get, and who benefits from that ease?
How would you teach compound interest without math anxiety taking over the group?

terms.d: How much of your available credit you are using; lower is better for credit scores.

508.title: Major cards and secured cards
508.gist: Exercise 6 asks whether stores prefer full payment, then the page explains bank-issued major cards with limits and interest, how to repair bad credit by paying debts, and secured cards backed by a deposit to build credit from scratch.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 2 is a good critical-thinking prompt: companies profit from unpaid balances. Let members reason it out; recognizing a business model is a defense against being exploited by it.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Walk through a secured card plan: deposit, charge one small recurring bill, pay it in full on autopay, check progress after six months. Simple, boring, effective, a reliable recovery formula too.

ask: How might a secured card serve as a structured 'practice' of trustworthiness?
Who profits most from people who carry balances, and what does that suggest about marketing to people in reentry?

terms.d: A card backed by your own deposit, which usually sets the limit; used to build or rebuild credit.

509.title: Debit cards, overdrafts and card use
509.gist: The page explains debit cards drawn from checking and overdraft lines that carry fees and interest. Exercise 7 asks members how they use any credit card, how it helped or hurt, and its pros and cons.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Overdraft fees have been a major source of bank revenue and hit low-balance customers hardest. Members can usually opt out of overdraft coverage on debit purchases, letting a card decline instead of triggering a fee.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members have never had a bank account. Many banks and credit unions offer low-cost 'second chance' or basic accounts; prefer these to check-cashing stores with high fees.

ask: Why might being unbanked keep people tied to cash economies that overlap with crime?
What are the advantages of a card that declines rather than overdrafts for someone in early recovery?

terms.d: Spending more than your account holds; the bank covers it but usually charges a fee.

510.title: Two kinds of credit card scams
510.gist: The page warns that ads guaranteeing credit to people with bad credit are usually scams, either selling worthless services, like lists of secured-card banks for a fee, or catalog-only 'gold cards' tied to overpriced merchandise.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: These scams work like a con game, exploiting hope and shame. Members who know street hustles can analyze the pitch from the hustler's side, which builds immunity better than warnings.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Today's versions are mostly online and by text: fake loan apps, upfront-fee 'approvals,' and impersonated lenders. Update examples so the lesson matches what members will actually see.

ask: Why does a guarantee in an ad signal fraud almost by definition?
How is the psychology of being scammed similar to the psychology of relapse rationalizations?

511.title: What credit ads promise
511.gist: Exercise 8 asks members whether they have seen bad-credit-OK ads, which fears and hopes those ads target, and whether they have been pressured into credit. It builds media literacy about financial marketing.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Robert Cialdini's work on persuasion describes levers like scarcity, urgency and social proof. Spotting 'limited time' or 'approved today' language trains members to slow down before deciding.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Bring in or describe a real ad and have the group dissect it line by line: what emotion each line targets, what is left out. Cognitive distance from a pitch reduces its pull.

ask: Which persuasion levers in these ads also appear in drug-using social situations?
How can slowing down a decision protect people across many risky choices?

512.title: Legitimate debt counseling
512.gist: The page explains that real credit counseling agencies, often nonprofit NFCC members, are free or low cost, do not sell cards, and often have clients stop using cards until debt is cleared. Exercise 9 asks how current debt problems feel.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Destroying cards is a stimulus-control strategy, removing access to a cue, the same logic as clearing paraphernalia from home. Making the unwanted behavior harder works better than relying on resolve.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 1 asks how debt feels. Debt shame can be intense and is linked with depression; listen for hopelessness and connect the financial plan to mood and relapse risk.

ask: Why does stimulus control often beat willpower, in money and in drug use?
How would you help someone who feels that old debts make recovery pointless?

terms.d: Changing your environment to remove or limit cues that trigger an unwanted behavior.

513.title: Debt plans and installment loans
513.gist: Exercise 9 closes with what members have tried about debts and why good credit helps. The text then introduces installment loans for big purchases like cars, homes and school, and explains that lenders profit through finance charges.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking what a member has already tried before suggesting solutions is a classic solution-focused and MI move. It honors their effort and often surfaces strategies that partly worked.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Federal student aid rules have been loosened for people with drug convictions in recent years, and Pell Grant access for incarcerated students was restored. Check current rules before advising, since education loans may be more reachable than members assume.

ask: Why is 'it costs money to borrow money' so easy to forget at the moment of borrowing?
How might good credit open doors that matter for desistance, like stable housing?

terms.d: A loan repaid in fixed regular payments over a set term, such as a car loan or mortgage.
The total cost of borrowing, including interest and fees.

514.title: What a loan really costs
514.gist: The page notes private finance companies often charge very high rates and late penalties, and names three cost drivers: amount, interest rate and length of repayment, with longer loans costing more. Exercise 10 asks for good and poor reasons to borrow.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has noted that a typical two-week payday loan fee works out to an annual rate near 400 percent. Short-term lenders cluster in low-income neighborhoods and near reentry populations.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by sorting reasons into 'builds the future' (a reliable car for work, a training course) and 'feeds the present' (a party, a status item). Ask where borrowing to pay a dealer's debt falls, and why.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Show the same car loan over three years and over six. Members are usually startled that the lower monthly payment costs far more overall.

ask: Why do lenders advertise monthly payments rather than total cost?
Is borrowing to escape an unsafe situation ever a good reason, even at high cost?

terms.d: Annual percentage rate: the yearly cost of a loan including interest and certain fees.

515.title: Building credit from zero
515.gist: The page explains that landlords and lenders check credit, and suggests building it through checking and savings accounts, layaway plans that may lead to store credit, paying bills on time, and calling creditors early when trouble hits.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Bank accounts and layaway do not usually appear on credit reports by themselves. Today, secured cards, credit-builder loans and rent-reporting services are more direct ways to build a file.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Calling a creditor before missing a payment is assertive communication under stress. It is the same skill as telling a sponsor about a craving before acting on it: early disclosure widens options.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For many members, the fear behind avoidance is being shamed on the phone. Role-play a hardship call with a calm, scripted request for a payment arrangement.

ask: Why does early disclosure of a problem tend to protect relationships, financial or personal?
What does a credit file represent socially: trust, conformity, or both?

terms.d: A small loan held in savings while you make payments; it reports your on-time payments to credit bureaus.

516.title: Quiz: accounts, layaway, late bills
516.gist: Exercise 11 checks understanding with multiple-choice items: why accounts help credit, which statement is not a layaway benefit, and what to do when you cannot pay a bill on time. It reinforces contact over avoidance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief the wrong options, not just the right ones. Ask who has ever ignored a bill or threatened a company, and what happened. Wrong answers often mirror real habits and make the lesson personal.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Retrieval practice, testing yourself after learning, is one of the best-supported learning techniques in cognitive psychology. A short quiz consolidates more than rereading would.

ask: Why might 'borrow from somewhere else to pay it' feel like a solution while actually deepening the problem?
How do you design quiz items that teach rather than just test?

terms.d: Learning by recalling information from memory, such as quizzing, which strengthens long-term retention.

517.title: Rules for when credit makes sense
517.gist: The page proposes a personal monthly credit limit set by the budget and three rules: buy only true needs, clear the full balance once the statement comes, and use credit for planned sale items if interest does not erase the savings. Exercise 12 asks about impulse buying.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking 'do I really need this' inserts a pause between urge and action. That pause is the heart of many interventions, from DBT's STOP skill to urge surfing in mindfulness-based relapse prevention.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Teach a 24-hour rule: any unplanned purchase over a set amount waits a day. Have members predict how many urges survive the wait; most fade, which is a lesson about cravings too.

ask: Why do urges to buy and urges to use often fade with time if not acted on?
How would you adapt the 'do I need this' question for someone who has gone without for years?

terms.d: A mindfulness technique of observing a craving rise, peak and fall without acting on it.

518.title: Guilt after buying
518.gist: Exercise 12 continues: is impulse buying a problem, and do members buy things they later feel guilty about, why, and what they would change. It ties purchases to emotion.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Emotion-driven buying fits Gross's emotion regulation model: shopping can be a quick way to change a bad feeling, but it is a response-focused strategy that brings guilt later. Earlier strategies, like reappraisal, avoid the backlash.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Listen for whether guilt leads to more buying, a shame cycle that mirrors use after a slip. Naming the loop helps members see one pattern across several behaviors.

ask: Is guilt after a purchase useful information or just punishment?
How is post-purchase guilt like the abstinence violation effect Marlatt described?

terms.d: The ways people influence which emotions they have, when, and how they experience and express them.

519.title: When to keep the card away
519.gist: The page warns against treating credit as free money and lists three don'ts: impulse purchases, unnecessary items, and going deep into debt. The test is whether you would pay cash. Exercise 13 asks about buying on credit what you would not buy with cash.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies by Drazen Prelec and Duncan Simester found people willing to pay more for the same item with a credit card than with cash. Card payment reduces the felt 'pain of paying,' which encourages spending.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Discussing big purchases with family is good advice but can be loaded for members whose families were harmed by their past. Frame it as rebuilding trust through transparency, not asking permission.

ask: Why does physical cash feel more 'real' than a card, and how could members use that?
What does 'free money' thinking have in common with entitlement-style criminal thinking?

520.title: Spending, gambling and the high
520.gist: Exercise 13 ends with end-of-month overwhelm. The text then distinguishes occasional splurges from losing control and describes compulsive spending and gambling as giving a high that relieves depression, anxiety or low self-esteem, followed by guilt.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Gambling disorder is classified in DSM-5 alongside substance use disorders, the only behavioral addiction given that status. Compulsive buying is not an official DSM diagnosis, though it is widely studied.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Gambling works on variable-ratio reinforcement, the unpredictable reward schedule that B.F. Skinner showed produces the most persistent behavior. Near-misses and occasional wins keep people playing.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Sports betting apps have made gambling constant and pocket-sized. Ask members whether betting was part of their life before, and screen for it as a possible substitute addiction.

ask: Why might someone in recovery from drugs be at risk of switching to gambling or shopping?
Is calling a behavior an 'addiction' clinically useful, or does it stretch the term too far?

terms.d: Rewards delivered after an unpredictable number of actions; it produces strong, persistent behavior.
Shifting from one compulsive behavior or substance to another.

521.title: Screening for compulsive debt
521.gist: The page describes compulsive borrowing despite harm and draws parallels to drug addiction: rushes, crashes and withdrawal-like depression for gamblers. Exercise 14 starts a yes-no checklist on debt beliefs and behaviors.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The first item, believing you will always be broke, captures learned helplessness, Seligman's term for giving up after repeated uncontrollable failure. That belief can make reckless spending feel logical: why save if it never works?

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: This checklist is a discussion tool, not a validated screening instrument. For gambling, recognized tools exist; use the checklist to open conversation and refer for proper assessment if concerns appear.

ask: How does learned helplessness about money connect to hopelessness about recovery?
Which items on this list reflect poverty rather than compulsion, and how would you tell the difference?

terms.d: Giving up trying after repeated experiences of failure that felt uncontrollable; described by Martin Seligman.

522.title: Secrets, risky lenders, maxed cards
522.gist: The checklist continues with secret debts, constant money thoughts, borrowing from disreputable sources, maxed-out cards, and chasing new cards. Four or more yes answers suggests a possible compulsive debt problem.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The item about lenders with a bad reputation is a safety issue in this population: debts to dealers or street lenders can carry threats. Treat a yes as a risk to address in the release plan, not just a money habit.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Secrecy is a recurring marker across addictions. In 12-step thinking, secrets keep people sick; disclosure to a safe person is often the first real break in a cycle.

ask: Why is secrecy such a reliable warning sign across many addictive behaviors?
How should a cutoff score like 'four or more' be used responsibly in a group setting?

523.title: Session 27 wrap-up
523.gist: The summary recaps insurance types, credit and its risks, when to use credit, and each member's own spending and borrowing patterns, including possible compulsive borrowing.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Insurance and credit both rest on trust over time: you trust an insurer to pay later, a lender trusts you to repay. Recovery is, in part, rebuilding a track record that lets others extend trust again.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Close by asking each member which of three moves they would take first after release: get ID and a bank account, check their credit report, or call about an old debt.

ask: What did this session assume about members' access to banks, cars and homes, and how accurate is that for your group?
How would you measure whether the session changed anyone's behavior?

524.title: Help for debt and gambling problems
524.gist: A resource page lists Debtors Anonymous, a 12-step program built on AA principles that asks members to stop new unsecured borrowing and offers Pressure Relief meetings for spending plans, and begins the Gamblers Anonymous listing.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Verify contact details before sharing; printed phone numbers and addresses age quickly. Many of these groups now run online and phone meetings, which can help members in areas without local meetings.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on mutual-help groups is strongest for AA and alcohol; evidence for DA specifically is limited. Present these as useful supports with peer accountability rather than proven treatments.

ask: How might the 12-step model fit or clash with money problems that stem mostly from poverty?
What would make a member willing to attend a DA meeting on top of other requirements?

terms.d: A 12-step fellowship for people with compulsive debting, focused on not taking on new unsecured debt.

525.title: GA, Gam-Anon and credit counseling
525.gist: The resources continue: Gamblers Anonymous with Pressure Groups for repayment, courts and family issues; Gam-Anon for families, focused on self-care and not rescuing the gambler; and NFCC credit counseling.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Gam-Anon's refusal to rescue the gambler from debts reflects a family-systems insight: bailing someone out can unintentionally reinforce the behavior by removing its consequences.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: CRAFT, a family approach developed by Robert Meyers, offers an alternative to both rescuing and detaching, teaching families to reward non-use and let natural consequences happen. It has good evidence for getting loved ones into treatment.

ask: Where is the line between support and enabling for families of people in reentry?
Why might families resist the idea of not rescuing someone they love?

terms.d: Actions by others, often well-meant, that shield a person from consequences and make a problem easier to continue.

526.title: National problem gambling helpline
526.gist: The final resource lists the National Council on Problem Gambling, a nonprofit that publishes information, certifies counselors, runs a 24-hour confidential helpline, and refers to treatment, GA and Gam-Anon.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Gambling problems often stay hidden in substance use treatment because nobody asks. Consider adding one or two gambling screening questions to intake or group check-ins.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The helpline model, anonymous and available at any hour, fits the timing of cravings, which rarely arrive during office hours.

ask: Why are behavioral addictions often missed in substance use treatment settings?
What role should certified gambling counselors play in a reentry program?

527.title: Session 28 opens: sexual abuse
527.gist: The Sexual Abuse session introduction names rape, other sexual assault, and abuse in childhood as its painful focus. Part 1 covers mixed cultural messages about sex, legal definitions and support for victims; Part 2 covers childhood abuse.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The Adverse Childhood Experiences study by Felitti, Anda and colleagues found that childhood abuse, including sexual abuse, is linked with much higher rates of later substance use problems. Trauma is a central thread in addiction for many members.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect that your group may include both survivors and people who have caused sexual harm, sometimes the same person. Set ground rules and a plan for distress before you begin.

ask: How do you hold a trauma-informed stance in a room where survivors and perpetrators may sit together?
Why might this session come late in the curriculum rather than early?

terms.d: Adverse childhood experiences: abuse, neglect and household problems before 18 that raise risk for later health and addiction problems.

528.title: What the session asks, and gender groups
528.gist: Members will examine their attitudes and behavior around sex during addiction and sobriety, respond to abuse scenarios, and seek help if they are survivors. A facilitator note recommends separate male and female groups because the material is so personal.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Trauma-informed care, as described by SAMHSA, emphasizes safety, choice, trustworthiness and collaboration. Same-gender groups and the right to pass are ways of building those conditions.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In prisons, sexual abuse can be a present danger, not only a past event. Know your facility's PREA procedures and reporting duties, and tell members clearly what you must report before anyone discloses.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A male-female split assumes a binary that does not fit every member; transgender and nonbinary participants need a thoughtful, individual plan.

ask: What are your mandated reporting obligations if a member discloses recent abuse inside the facility?
How might male survivors' shame differ from female survivors', and what does that mean for facilitation?

terms.d: The Prison Rape Elimination Act of 2003, a US law setting standards to prevent, detect and respond to sexual abuse in custody.

529.title: Mixed messages and sex in advertising
529.gist: Part 1 defines sexual assault as a family of crimes, including rape, statutory rape, sexual battery and some harassment, and notes that conflicting cultural messages about sex breed confusion. Exercise 1 asks members to dissect an ad that uses sex to sell.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Media analysis is a gentle on-ramp to a heavy session. Starting with ads lets members practice critical thinking about sex at a safe distance before turning to personal history.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Sexual scripts theory (Gagnon and Simon) proposes that people learn culturally shaped 'scripts' for how sex should unfold. Ads, porn and peer talk all write those scripts, sometimes including coercive ones.

ask: How might media scripts about sex differ from the scripts members learned on the street or inside?
Why start a sexual abuse session with advertising rather than with definitions?

terms.d: Sexual contact with someone below the age of consent set by state law, even if they appeared to agree.
Culturally learned expectations about who does what, and when, in sexual situations.

530.title: Reading ads between the lines
530.gist: Exercise 1 continues: what hidden promise does the ad make, is that promise unrealistic, and how could such messages harm recovery. Members learn to spot implied claims.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push past 'sex sells' to how alcohol ads in particular pair drinking with sex appeal and confidence. Those pairings feed expectancies that drinking makes you more attractive or bold, a common relapse rationalization.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Alcohol expectancy research shows that what people believe a drink will do, like increase sexual confidence, shapes how they behave after drinking, sometimes even with a placebo.

ask: How do expectancies about sex and substances reinforce each other?
What harm can come from images of conflict-free relationships for people rebuilding relationships after prison?

terms.d: Beliefs about the effects alcohol will have, which influence drinking and behavior regardless of actual intoxication.

531.title: Shame-based messages about sex
531.gist: The page contrasts media's push for sex with messages that sex is dirty or sinful, often passed from uninformed parents, and notes abuse survivors may fear intimacy. Some people fake comfort, some panic, and some use sex to bargain or hurt. Exercise 2 begins.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Brené Brown's popular work, and older psychology, distinguish shame (I am bad) from guilt (I did something bad). Sexual shame learned in childhood tends to be global and hidden, which makes it a fertile ground for secret behavior.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Religious backgrounds in your group will vary widely. Avoid implying faith teaches harm; focus on messages that left a member feeling dirty or confused, whatever the source.

ask: How might sexual shame and substance use form a cycle: shame, use to numb, behavior, more shame?
What are the cultural differences among your members in how sex is discussed, for example in Latino or religious families?

terms.d: A deep sense of being bad or dirty about one's sexuality, often learned early.

532.title: Sex, addiction and recovery triggers
532.gist: Exercise 2 continues: how contradictory sex messages played into addiction, whether the member's attitude is healthy, whether they can talk openly with a partner, and whether sex could be a recovery trigger.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Many substances, especially methamphetamine and cocaine, become tightly paired with sex. Through classical conditioning, sexual arousal itself can become a craving cue, so sex in early recovery may carry unexpected risk.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: These questions invite very private answers. Offer the option to answer privately in writing rather than aloud, and debrief themes, not individual disclosures.

ask: Why might sober sex feel frightening for someone who has only had sex while high?
How do you talk about sexual triggers without shaming or sensationalizing?

terms.d: Using drugs, often stimulants, specifically to enhance or prolong sex; linked with strong cue-craving pairing.

533.title: Defining rape and sexual battery
533.gist: The page suggests a specialist referral where sexual issues affect recovery, then defines rape as forced sex without consent, a felony everywhere, and sexual battery as unwanted sexual touching. It notes state differences, marital rape, and broader gender-neutral definitions.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Marital rape was legally exempt in many US states until the 1970s and 1980s; all states now criminalize it in some form. That history shows how definitions of consent have changed.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The page's list of who can rape whom is awkward and dated. Current law in most states is gender-neutral and centers on consent and capacity, including incapacity from intoxication.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Florida law uses the term sexual battery for what other states call rape. Members returning here should know that term carries the full weight of a serious felony.

ask: Why do legal definitions of rape differ from many people's personal definitions?
How does incapacity due to alcohol or drugs complicate consent in the lives your members describe?

terms.d: A clear, freely given, ongoing agreement to sexual activity by someone with the capacity to give it.
Unwanted sexual touching; in Florida law, also the term covering what other states call rape.

534.title: Whose definition of rape?
534.gist: Exercise 3 asks whether the session's definition of rape differs from the member's own, and what problems arise when people define rape differently. It brings hidden beliefs into the open.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Rape myth acceptance, a construct studied since Martha Burt's work around 1980, measures beliefs like 'she asked for it.' Higher acceptance is associated with greater likelihood of sexual aggression and victim blaming.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect some members to voice myths. Respond with curiosity and Socratic questions rather than lectures, but do not let harmful statements stand unchallenged; others in the room may be survivors.

ask: How do you challenge rape myths in a group without shutting down honest discussion?
What cognitive distortions from CBI or criminal thinking work resemble rape myths?

terms.d: False but common beliefs that excuse sexual assault or blame victims.

535.title: Anger, control and substances
535.gist: The page frames rape as violence driven by domination rather than desire, notes it often occurs between acquaintances, and links alcohol and drugs to lowered inhibitions, increased hostility and reduced ability to resist, including date-rape drugs. Exercise 4 begins.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The 'power not sex' framing, popularized in the 1970s, was a vital corrective to victim blaming. Many researchers now see mixed motives, with power, hostility and sexual gratification combined differently across offenders.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research consistently finds alcohol is the substance most often involved in drug-facilitated sexual assault, far more often than Rohypnol or other sedatives slipped into drinks.

deeper.label: In the room
