611.gist: The page says major losses can bring renewal, a healthier reordering of life, and lists shared features with recovery: new self-awareness, focusing on real needs over money or status, doing without things that are wants, and accepting responsibility instead of blaming.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Tedeschi and Calhoun coined post-traumatic growth for positive change after struggle, such as new priorities and deeper relationships. Research finds it is real for many, though self-reports can overstate it, and growth does not erase suffering.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Viktor Frankl, writing after the Nazi camps, argued that people can find meaning even in unavoidable suffering, and that meaning sustains them.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Material needs are real for men leaving prison with nothing. Do not let a needs-versus-wants message shame them for wanting stability or nice things.

ask: Can loss be turned into growth on purpose, or does growth only come unplanned?
Where is the line between accepting responsibility and blaming oneself for everything?

terms.d: Positive psychological change reported after struggling with major hardship or trauma.

612.title: Helping others heals the helper
612.gist: The page adds helping others as the last feature of renewal, since supporting people boosts self-esteem. Exercise 14 asks for other life-changing experiences and the difference between needs and wants.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Frank Riessman's helper therapy principle holds that helping others benefits the helper. AA's twelfth step builds this in.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies of AA members, including work by Maria Pagano, suggest that helping others in recovery is associated with lower relapse rates, though cause and effect are hard to separate.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Find real helping roles inside: peer mentor, tutor, orientation buddy. The principle works only if the help is real.

ask: Can helping others become a way to avoid one's own work?
How could helping roles be built into a prison program safely?

terms.d: The finding that those who help others with a problem often benefit themselves.

613.title: Summing up loss and regain
613.gist: The summary recaps the session: how losses happen, how judgment eroded until friends, family and jobs were traded for the high, renewal in recovery, what is lost and gained by getting sober, and where to find support.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Close with balance: ask each member for one thing lost and one thing gained or regained. Ending on a gain protects hope.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Japanese kintsugi repairs broken pottery with gold, treating the break as part of the object's story. It is a vivid image for regaining what was lost.

ask: Which losses in this session might never be regained, and how should a program handle that?
How does this session prepare members for the grief session that follows?

614.title: Opening the grief session
614.gist: Session 31 introduces grief as the response to loss, covering normal and complicated reactions, what makes a loss hit harder, coping strategies, and the stages people move through toward resolution. Two parts: understanding grief and stages of grief.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Grief and addiction are tightly linked: unresolved grief is a common relapse trigger, and many people started using to numb a loss.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Stage models of grief are widely taught but poorly supported as fixed sequences. Many researchers now prefer models like Stroebe and Schut's dual process model, which describes moving back and forth.

ask: What grief might be hiding behind a member's anger?
How would you introduce stages without making members feel they are grieving wrong?

terms.d: Stroebe and Schut's model in which grievers alternate between facing the loss and rebuilding daily life.

615.title: Grief that drugs kept frozen
615.gist: After the part 2 objectives, the page defines grief as the feeling of losing something important and argues that drugs mute it, so losses pass with little reaction. It notes that many people began using to escape early losses, like a parent's death, that they never safely mourned.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Avoidance keeps grief stuck: numbing blocks the emotional processing that normally softens loss over time. When sobriety removes the numbing, old grief can arrive as if fresh.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Kenneth Doka's term disenfranchised grief names losses society does not recognize, such as grieving a fellow user or a relationship ended by incarceration. Unrecognized grief is harder to process.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Warn members early that grief may surface weeks into sobriety, unexpectedly. Knowing it is coming helps them see it as a normal sign of recovery.

ask: Which of your members' losses would society refuse to recognize as worth grieving?
How would you tell old grief returning from new depression?

terms.d: Kenneth Doka's term for grief that is not openly acknowledged or socially supported.

616.title: What drugs did to feelings
616.gist: The page compares emotional pain to physical pain as a warning that does not leave if ignored. Exercise 1 asks what drugs did to members' feelings, whether sobriety changed them, and what unresolved grief they carry.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Emotion regulation research, notably James Gross's model, finds that suppressing feelings tends to backfire, raising physical stress while doing little to reduce the feeling. Substances are a chemical form of suppression.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name a feeling they barely felt while using and rate how strong it is now, from 0 to 10. The gap shows how much numbing was happening.

ask: Why is unresolved grief easier to see in others than in ourselves?
Can emotional pain ever be ignored safely, and when is waiting healthy?

617.title: Losses that never registered
617.gist: Exercise 1 asks how grief threatens sobriety. The text then explains that in active addiction people may not notice losses, or minimize them, blame something else, or hide the feeling, though grief is an emotional process that takes time.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Minimizing and externalizing protect self-esteem, a pattern CBT calls cognitive distortion and criminal-thinking curricula often target directly. Here the cost is that grief stays unprocessed.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: William Worden described tasks of mourning, starting with accepting the reality of the loss. Minimizing skips the first task, so the rest cannot begin.

ask: How does minimizing a loss resemble minimizing harm done to victims?
What would a member gain by finally admitting a loss mattered?

terms.d: Worden's model: accept the loss, work through the pain, adjust to life without it, find an enduring connection.

618.title: Missed losses, muted reactions
618.gist: Exercise 2 asks members whether drugs ever cost them something important without their noticing at the time, and whether they had an unusually flat reaction to a loss. It invites members to spot their numbed grief.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: These questions can surface a funeral missed while high or in custody. Make room for that: it is often a heavy, unspoken shame among incarcerated men.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Invite members to write one sentence to a loss they never acknowledged. Reading aloud is optional.

ask: What makes a reaction to loss normal, and who decides?
How might a flat reaction be adaptive in the street or in prison?

619.title: When others grieved and you didn't
619.gist: Exercise 2 continues by asking whether others were angry that members seemed unaffected by a loss they felt deeply, and how covering up emotional reactions threatens sobriety. It looks at the relational cost of numbness.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Families grieve together, and a member who does not join in can look uncaring. That mismatch damages trust long after the loss itself.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Men are often socialized to hide grief, and prison culture rewards it. Not showing grief is not the same as not feeling it; avoid labeling stoicism as coldness.

ask: How would you help a member repair a rift caused by his absence during a family loss?
Where is the line between healthy composure and harmful emotional cover-up?

620.title: Normal grief versus stuck grief
620.gist: The page describes normal grief: shock, deep sadness, withdrawal, angry protest and gradual acceptance. Abnormal grief shows as long-lasting physical problems, years of preoccupation, overwhelming guilt and isolation, while normal grievers still find warmth in others.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Prolonged grief disorder was added to the ICD-11 and to the DSM-5-TR in 2022, for grief that stays intense and disabling well beyond the usual period. Most grievers do not develop it.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: George Bonanno's research found that many bereaved people show resilience, with relatively stable functioning, challenging the idea that everyone must go through intense grief work.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Abnormal is a harsh word. Clinicians now prefer terms like complicated or prolonged grief, and what counts as normal varies across cultures.

ask: How might traumatic losses common among your members, like murder, raise the risk of prolonged grief?
When does guilt in grief serve repair, and when does it become self-punishment?

terms.d: A diagnosis for intense, persistent longing or preoccupation with the deceased that impairs life long after the loss.

621.title: Your grief history, high and sober
621.gist: Exercise 3 asks members when they felt grief, whether they were using then, and what drugs did to that grief, plus examples of smaller losses with milder grief. It helps them map their own grief range.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Small losses are practice for big ones. Noticing mild grief, such as a cancelled visit, trains people to recognize the feeling before it builds.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prison produces a steady drip of losses: transfers, missed holidays, a visit cancelled. Use these as safe, shared examples for question 2.

ask: How might many small losses add up to something as heavy as one large one?
What happens to grief that is delayed until release?

622.title: Some people break, others grow
622.gist: Exercise 3 ends with the sobriety risk of abnormal grief. The text notes that some people are crushed by loss while others grow, and that growth comes from evaluating the loss's meaning, which requires self-assessment and looking at changed relationships.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Spouses do show increased risk of death shortly after bereavement, sometimes called the widowhood effect. The heart condition takotsubo cardiomyopathy, nicknamed broken heart syndrome, can follow severe emotional stress.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Robert Neimeyer argues that grief is largely a process of meaning reconstruction: rebuilding a life story that the loss broke.

ask: What helps some people grow after a loss while others stall?
Why does living crisis to crisis prevent meaning-making?

terms.d: Neimeyer's view that grieving involves rebuilding a sense of meaning and identity after a loss.

623.title: Mapping roles and routines after loss
623.gist: The page says healing a relationship requires describing what it was and what it is now, including changed roles, and that major losses disrupt routines that must be rebuilt. Exercise 4 asks why personal assessment matters after loss and how routines change.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Routine is a quiet stabilizer: sleep, meals and activity regulate mood. Behavioral activation, an evidence-based depression treatment, works partly by restoring meaningful routines.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Incarceration changes family roles: a child becomes the man of the house, a partner becomes sole provider. Help members describe role changes before they walk back in expecting the old ones.

ask: What role changes will your members face at home, and how can they prepare?
Why might routine be the first thing a grieving person loses and the last thing they think to fix?

terms.d: A therapy that lifts mood by scheduling meaningful, rewarding activities and rebuilding routines.

624.title: How grief shows in body and mind
624.gist: After asking how loss self-assessments help relapse prevention, the page explains that grief intensity depends on the loss's importance, drug use and prior health. It lists emotional symptoms like despair and guilt, and physical ones like insomnia and fatigue. Exercise 5 asks about physical symptoms.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Grief activates the body's stress response, and studies link bereavement with temporary changes in immune function and sleep. Mind and body grieve together.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many men describe grief as headaches, back pain or insomnia rather than sadness. Asking about the body can open a door that asking about feelings closes.

ask: Why might men be more likely to express grief physically?
How would you distinguish grief symptoms from withdrawal symptoms in early sobriety?

625.title: Grief symptoms as relapse risks
625.gist: Exercise 5 continues by asking what physical and emotional symptoms of grief members have had, and how those symptoms could threaten sobriety and be planned for. It links grief directly to relapse prevention.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt and Gordon's relapse prevention research found negative emotional states to be among the most common precipitants of relapse. Grief is a negative emotional state that can last months.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members write a grief plan: three warning signs, two people to call, one activity that helps. Treat it like any other relapse prevention plan.

ask: Why might insomnia during grief be especially dangerous for sobriety?
How would you prepare a member for an anniversary of a death?

626.title: What makes grief heavier or lighter
626.gist: The page lists factors shaping grief: prior coping experience, how important the loss is, violent or sudden circumstances, practical problems with courts, hospitals or money, cultural and religious rituals, emotional support, and how quickly routines return.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research consistently finds violent, sudden losses such as homicide, suicide and overdose raise the risk of complicated grief and PTSD. Many members have lost people this way.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Anthropologists note that mourning rituals across cultures give grief a shape and a community. Latin American traditions like novenas or Day of the Dead keep a bond with the dead in public view.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Prior losses can build coping, but repeated losses can also accumulate into grief overload. Experience does not always protect.

ask: Which of these factors can incarceration make worse, and how?
How could a facility allow meaningful mourning rituals for inmates?

terms.d: Strain from facing several losses close together, without time to grieve each one.

627.title: Quick check on grief factors
627.gist: The page adds resuming enjoyable activities as a healing factor, then Exercise 6 offers multiple-choice items: which option does not influence grief, and which loss would hurt an average person most. It checks comprehension of the factors.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 2 has an obvious answer, but use it to discuss ranking grief. Someone may grieve a pet more than a grandparent, and that is valid.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The suicide example could hit hard if a member has lost a child or someone close that way. Scan the room and be ready to slow down.

ask: Is ranking losses useful, or does it invalidate personal grief?
Why might enjoying something again trigger guilt in a griever?

628.title: Stages as a map, not a script
628.gist: Part 2 introduces the stages of grief, noting people move in and out of them rather than in strict order. Knowing them helps people see grief as natural and temporary and seek help. Exercise 7 asks whether knowing what to expect helps.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's five stages came from interviews with dying patients in On Death and Dying (1969), not bereaved people, and research has not confirmed a fixed sequence. They work best as a vocabulary.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Klass, Silverman and Nickman's work on continuing bonds argued that healthy grief often keeps a connection with the dead rather than letting go completely.

ask: What is the risk if a member thinks he is grieving wrong because he skipped a stage?
Does knowing what to expect really reduce pain, or just fear of the pain?

terms.d: The idea that grievers can keep a healthy ongoing connection with the deceased.

629.title: Stage one: shock and numbness
629.gist: The first stage of grief is emotional shock: numbness and disbelief lasting from moments to weeks, sometimes with panic or sudden rage, and often little memory of the time afterward. Exercise 8 asks members to describe a time they felt numb and disoriented.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Shock works like an emotional circuit breaker, limiting how much pain arrives at once. Dissociation during overwhelming events is a well-documented protective response.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members received devastating news by phone, through a chaplain or from an officer, then had to return to the unit. Ask how they managed that moment; it often has never been spoken about.

ask: Why might rage, not tears, be the shock response most visible in a prison?
How would you support someone who receives death news during your group?

terms.d: A detachment from thoughts, feelings, surroundings or sense of self, often during overwhelming stress.

630.title: Why the mind goes numb
630.gist: Exercise 8 continues by asking why people go numb after a major loss and how emotional shock could threaten sobriety. It asks members to think about the purpose of numbness, not just its feel.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Numbness can feel familiar to people who used drugs to feel nothing, and that resemblance is the danger: the urge to extend the numbness chemically.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Teach a simple grounding drill for shock moments: feet on the floor, five slow breaths, name three things you can see. Practice it before it is needed.

ask: When does numbness protect and when does it trap?
How could a crisis plan address the first 48 hours after bad news?

631.title: Stage two: the storm of feelings
631.gist: Once shock fades, the full pain arrives in emotional disorganization: rumination, idealizing or demonizing the lost person, bitterness, guilt, self-pity and fear about coping, with a temporary drop in self-esteem. The page stresses this confusion fades over time.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Rumination, repetitively dwelling on distress, is linked with longer and deeper depression in Susan Nolen-Hoeksema's research. Brief, focused reflection tends to help more than endless replaying.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: C. S. Lewis wrote A Grief Observed after his wife's death, describing grief as feeling like fear. It captures the disorientation of this stage in plain, honest prose.

ask: How do you help someone hold both the good and bad memories of a person who hurt them?
What separates healthy reflection from rumination?

terms.d: Repetitive, passive focus on distress and its causes, without moving toward solutions.

632.title: Feelings that seem endless
632.gist: Exercise 9 asks members whether they ever had a powerful emotional experience they thought would never stop, how it felt, and how emotional disorganization might threaten sobriety. It aims to show that intense feelings pass.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Dialectical behavior therapy, developed by Marsha Linehan, teaches distress tolerance: surviving intense emotion without making it worse. A core lesson is that emotions rise and fall like waves.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: After members share, ask: and did it stop? Every person in the room survived the feeling they thought would never end. That evidence is persuasive.

ask: Why does the belief that a feeling will last forever increase relapse risk?
Which distress tolerance skills work in a cell with no privacy?

terms.d: A DBT skill set for getting through intense emotional pain without acting in harmful ways.

633.title: Stage three: denial in disguise
633.gist: The page describes denial as an unconscious shield against loss, much like denial in addiction. It often appears as substitute feelings: jealousy of people who still have what was lost, anger at helpers, or overwhelming shame about things said or left undone.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Anna Freud and later psychodynamic thinkers described defense mechanisms like displacement, aiming a feeling at a safer target. Anger at helpers is often grief displaced.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When a member snaps at someone offering support, try naming it gently: I wonder if this is about the loss more than about him. Offer it as a guess, not a diagnosis.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Calling all anger denial can invalidate real injustice. Some anger after a loss, such as one caused by violence or neglect, is a fitting response.

ask: How do you tell displaced grief-anger from anger at a genuine wrong?
Why might shame be easier to feel than loss?

terms.d: A defense in which feelings toward one target are redirected to a safer one.

634.title: Grief denial versus lying
634.gist: Exercise 10 asks how denial in grief resembles denial in addiction, how unconscious denial differs from deliberate lying, and how denial of loss could threaten sobriety. It sharpens the concept of denial.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Unconscious denial protects the self, while lying protects an outcome. Treating denial as lying makes people defensive; treating it as protection makes it easier to lower.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Confrontational approaches to denial in addiction treatment have generally performed poorly in research. Miller and Rollnick's motivational interviewing grew partly out of that finding.

ask: How does this distinction change how you respond to a member who minimizes his use?
Can a person be in denial and lying at the same moment?

635.title: Stage four: exhaustion as recharge
635.gist: The page explains that grief drains energy and disrupts sleep and eating, leading to fatigue, withdrawal, loneliness and sometimes hopelessness or suicidal thoughts. It frames exhaustion as a time to rest and recharge for the grieving still ahead.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Suicidal thoughts appear on this list, so screen for them. Ask directly and calmly; asking about suicide does not plant the idea, and know your facility's protocol and the 988 crisis line for after release.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Calling hopelessness a recharge phase risks minimizing depression. When exhaustion persists or includes suicidal thinking, it needs clinical attention, not just rest.

ask: How would you distinguish grief exhaustion from major depression?
Why is the period after a loss a high-risk time for overdose?

636.title: What to do when you're drained
636.gist: Exercise 11 asks members whether they have felt emotionally exhausted, how they should respond when drained in body and mind, and how post-loss exhaustion could threaten sobriety. It encourages planning self-care.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: HALT, a recovery reminder to check if you are Hungry, Angry, Lonely or Tired, captures why exhaustion matters: depleted states weaken self-control and make old coping feel tempting.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members write their minimum self-care list for bad days: one meal, one call, one walk, sleep time. Low bars get met.

ask: Why do people in recovery often ignore tiredness until it becomes a crisis?
What does rest look like for someone who equates stopping with weakness?

terms.d: Recovery slogan: watch out when Hungry, Angry, Lonely or Tired, since these raise relapse risk.

637.title: Stage five: healing takes work
637.gist: Emotional healing requires effort: resuming control by returning to routines, giving up roles that ended with the loss, such as a widower becoming a single parent, and searching for meaning as bitterness gives way, sometimes through spiritual awakening or renewed family bonds.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Worden's tasks of mourning include adjusting to a world without the lost person, internally, externally and spiritually. The role-change example is that adjustment.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on meaning-making after loss suggests that finding some sense in the loss, or benefit in its aftermath, is often linked with better adjustment, though many people adapt well without ever finding a reason.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members what role they lost when they went to prison: father present at dinner, son who visits mom, worker. Abandoning old roles is not abandoning people.

ask: Must a loss have meaning for someone to heal from it?
How does incarceration force role loss without a death?

638.title: New priorities after loss
638.gist: The page says losses can reveal what truly matters, such as families setting aside quarrels and people taking life a day at a time and saying out loud that they care. Exercise 12 asks whether a loss changed members' roles or priorities.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Laura Carstensen's socioemotional selectivity theory finds that when people sense limited time, they prioritize close, meaningful relationships. Loss can produce the same shift at any age.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to list their top three priorities before their last loss and now. Discuss any item that moved up or vanished.

ask: Why does it often take loss to clarify priorities, and could it happen without loss?
How long do priority shifts last after a crisis?

639.title: Letting go without forgetting
639.gist: After asking how healing helps relapse prevention, the page explores second-guessing and replaying what might have changed the outcome, which usually fades. Letting go happens through funerals, new jobs and routines, and means the loss no longer dominates, not forgetting.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Psychologists call what-if replay counterfactual thinking. Upward counterfactuals, if only I had, can motivate future change but also feed guilt when nothing could have been done.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Incarcerated members often miss funerals. Offer a substitute ritual: a written goodbye, a moment of silence in group, or a plan to visit the grave after release.

ask: When is a what-if useful learning and when is it self-torture?
What substitute rituals could help someone grieving inside?

terms.d: Imagining how things might have turned out differently, such as if only I had acted otherwise.

640.title: Ways to let go
640.gist: Exercise 13 asks whether members struggled to let go of something emotionally, what people can do to help themselves let go, and how letting go strengthens relapse prevention. It moves from story to strategy.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Buddhist teaching treats clinging to what is changing as a root of suffering. Acceptance and commitment therapy borrows a similar idea: accept what cannot change, and act on what matters.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will hear letting go as betrayal of the dead. Emphasize that the bond can continue; what changes is how much the pain controls them.

ask: Is letting go a decision, a process, or something that just happens?
How would you respond to a member who says letting go means he did not love them?

641.title: Anger as a substitute for grief
641.gist: The page argues that difficulty forgiving keeps grief stuck: staying angry and assigning blame feels active and easier than feeling loss. Letting go means forgiving others, oneself, or even the dead for harm they caused. Exercise 14 asks why bitterness is easier than forgiveness.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Forgiveness interventions developed by Robert Enright and Everett Worthington have shown benefits for anger, anxiety and depression in controlled studies. Forgiveness here means releasing resentment, not excusing harm.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Pressure to forgive can harm survivors of abuse. Forgiveness is a choice, separate from reconciliation; a person can forgive and still keep distance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members carry anger at parents who died while still harmful. Ask what the anger is protecting; often it shields hurt or longing.

ask: Why might anger feel like loyalty to the dead or to oneself?
How do you encourage forgiveness without implying the harm was acceptable?

terms.d: Choosing to release resentment and the wish for revenge, without necessarily excusing harm or reconciling.

642.title: Who you have struggled to forgive
642.gist: Exercise 14 continues by asking whether members found it hard to forgive someone who wronged them, what happened, and how forgiveness after loss could strengthen their recovery. It makes forgiveness personal.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Introduce Worthington's REACH steps briefly: recall the hurt, empathize with the offender, offer forgiveness as a gift, commit to it, hold on when doubts return. Let members pick one step to try.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will name people they harmed who have not forgiven them. Use it to explore both sides of forgiveness, receiving and giving.

ask: Is self-forgiveness different in kind from forgiving others?
How might forgiveness change risk of violence after release?

terms.d: Everett Worthington's five-step forgiveness model: Recall, Empathize, Altruistic gift, Commit, Hold on.

643.title: Unfinished grief and next steps
643.gist: The final question asks members what they can do about grief they have just noticed is unresolved and whom they can talk to. The summary reviews normal and complicated grief, intensity factors, and the stages, calling grief knowledge a relapse prevention tool.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: End with a concrete next step, not a summary. Have each member name one person or time to talk about the grief that surfaced, and schedule check-ins for the ones who opened up most.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Mary Oliver's poem In Blackwater Woods ends on three tasks: to love what is mortal, to hold it close, and to let it go when the time comes. It is a quiet companion to this session.

ask: How would you track whether grief work in group affected relapse after release?
What support should exist for facilitators who absorb this much grief?

644.title: Spirituality as a route to change
644.gist: Session 32 introduces spirituality as a driver of personality change in recovery, covering surrender, commitment, acceptance and restitution, then meditation. Its three parts are spirituality and personality change, how change happens, and meditation.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: William James, in The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), studied sudden and gradual conversions as real psychological transformations. AA's founders drew on his ideas.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Spirituality framed through a Higher Power can alienate atheist, agnostic or Muslim members if it sounds Christian. Courts in the United States have ruled that mandating religious twelve-step participation can raise constitutional problems.

ask: Can personality change happen without anything you would call spirituality?
How would you make this session work for a member who rejects all religion?

645.title: Looking at who you were and are
645.gist: The page lists goals for parts 2 and 3, on how personality change happens and how meditation supports spiritual growth. Members will compare their traits in addiction and recovery, consider tasks for change, and try a simple meditation on words they choose.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Longitudinal research by Brent Roberts and others shows that personality traits do change across adulthood, often toward more conscientiousness and emotional stability. Recent studies suggest therapy can also shift traits.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members believe people never change. Ask them to name someone they knew who did, and what changed first: behavior, friends, or beliefs.

ask: What would count as evidence that a member's personality, not just his behavior, has changed?
Can a facilitator's belief that people can change affect outcomes?

646.title: Drugs stunted or warped personality
646.gist: Part 1 claims addiction either made a healthy personality unhealthy or kept a young one from forming, since many began using early and never knew their sober adult selves. Personality reflects spiritual life, and recovery shifts values. Members are asked to assess their traits.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Using during adolescence overlaps with brain development, especially of the prefrontal cortex, which matures into the mid-twenties. That supports the claim that early use can disrupt emotional and social development.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For men who started using at twelve, sobriety can feel like meeting a stranger. Frame it as an adventure: you get to find out who you are.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Linking personality to spiritual life is a value claim, not a scientific one. Present it as the program's perspective, open to members' own interpretations.

ask: What might a man meeting his sober personality at thirty-five need from a counselor?
Is personality the cause of addiction, a casualty of it, or both?

647.title: Who you were while using
647.gist: Exercise 1 gives paired opposites, such as agitation versus serenity, blame versus forgiveness, slavery versus freedom, and asks members to check which described them during active use. It builds a snapshot of their addicted self.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Forced-choice pairs make abstract traits concrete and quick to rate. The opposites also quietly name a destination for each trait.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some pairs are tricky: guilt versus innocence, or shame versus pride. Discuss them, since healthy pride and owning guilt can both be signs of recovery.

ask: Which pair on this list do you find most debatable, and why?
What does it reveal that solitude is paired against sharing?

648.title: Who you are now in recovery
648.gist: Exercise 2 repeats the same list of paired opposites and asks members to check what describes them now in recovery. Comparing it with Exercise 1 shows how far they have moved.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members count shifts between the two lists and circle the one change they are proudest of and one they still want. Shifts made in custody count as real progress.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: In a structured setting without access to drugs, some traits may look better because temptations are absent. Ask which changes they expect to hold after release.

ask: How would you check whether self-reported change matches observed behavior?
Which trait is hardest to change inside a prison and why?

649.title: Values you want to live by
649.gist: The page notes drug use pushes aside what matters most and lists values like honesty, loyalty, fairness and self-discipline. Exercise 3 asks members to pick their top three, say whether they live them daily, and plan how to live them more.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Values clarification is a core part of acceptance and commitment therapy, developed by Steven Hayes. Brief values affirmation exercises have shown some benefits in studies, though effects vary.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Loyalty is a powerful value inside, but it can bind members to codes of silence or gangs. Ask: loyal to whom, and does that loyalty serve your recovery?

ask: What happens when two of a member's values, like loyalty and honesty, collide?
How would you turn a value into one observable action this week?

terms.d: Chosen life directions that guide action, such as honesty or care, as opposed to goals that can be completed.

650.title: Surrender as the start of humility
650.gist: Part 2 says sobriety alone brings some personality change, but lasting change takes effort. The first step is surrender: dropping rigid defenses built to protect use, admitting your instincts may lead to relapse, and accepting guidance from a group, program or Higher Power.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Psychiatrist Harry Tiebout, an early AA supporter, wrote about surrender as the collapse of a defiant, grandiose ego, distinguishing true surrender from mere compliance.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: In prison, surrender can sound like submission to authority, something members resist for good reason. Distinguish surrendering to a recovery process from obeying power.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members about a time they took advice and it saved them. Real examples make surrender feel like wisdom, not defeat.

ask: How is surrender different from compliance, and how could you tell which a member is doing?
Can surrender coexist with building self-efficacy?

651.title: Letting go of the drug as relationship
651.gist: Exercise 4 asks what is gained by surrendering control over use and why the illusion of control is attractive. The text introduces letting go: replacing addiction with healthier things, noting the drug once seemed like a companion that never rejected you.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Describing the drug as a loyal companion fits attachment views of addiction, such as those of Philip Flores, in which substances substitute for unreliable human bonds.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Invite members to write a breakup letter to their drug, listing what it gave and what it cost, and saying goodbye. It is often surprisingly emotional.

ask: What does the never-rejected-me feeling tell you about a member's relationship history?
Why does the illusion of control persist despite repeated evidence against it?

652.title: Stop fighting, walk away
652.gist: The page argues that trying to control an addiction makes it fight back, so the way out is to walk away, and that manipulating and controlling people, learned while using, must also go. Exercise 5 asks about progress in letting go and the cost of holding on.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Daniel Wegner's ironic process research found that trying not to think of something, like a white bear, can make the thought come back more. Fighting cravings head-on can work the same way.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Manipulation is a survival skill on the street and inside. Acknowledge that, then ask what it costs in relationships they want to keep.

ask: Is walking away from the fight a cognitive skill, a spiritual stance, or both?
How do you help someone unlearn manipulation without shaming the survival behind it?

terms.d: Wegner's finding that deliberately suppressing a thought can make it come back more often.

653.title: Commitment through setbacks
653.gist: Exercise 5 ends by asking why letting go is hard and how holding on hurts. The text says each person must find their own recovery path and commit to it, returning after setbacks or relapse with courage and continuous effort, since sobriety is never finished.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Prochaska and DiClemente's stages of change model treats relapse as a common part of change, with people often cycling through stages several times. Commitment means returning, not never falling.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies of commitment language in motivational interviewing suggest that clients' own statements of intention, especially late in a session, are linked with later behavior change.

ask: How do you encourage commitment without setting up shame after a lapse?
What does it mean for each person to find their own path when a program is mandated?

terms.d: In motivational interviewing, a client's own statements favoring change, such as desire, reasons or commitment.

654.title: Commitment needs help and faith
654.gist: The page says commitment is not a solo act: groups, counselors, family and a Higher Power can help. It requires faith that doing the work will pay off, whether in oneself, others or a Higher Power. Exercise 6 asks what commitment members made and what blocks it.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: C. R. Snyder's hope theory defines hope as having both pathways to a goal and the agency to use them. Faith that things will improve is the agency part.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask who or what members have faith in right now, even if it is only one person or their kids. Start building from whatever faith exists.

ask: Can faith be borrowed from others until one's own develops, and is that honest?
What obstacles to commitment come from the system rather than the person?

terms.d: Snyder's model: hope combines pathways thinking, ways to reach goals, with agency, the motivation to use them.

655.title: Faith and the risks of commitment
655.gist: Exercise 6 continues by asking whether members have faith in themselves, others or a Higher Power, what could strengthen it, and how commitment could both hurt and help recovery. It invites a nuanced look at commitment.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Commitment can hurt when it becomes rigid: an all-or-nothing vow can collapse after one slip, feeding the abstinence violation effect. Flexible commitment survives setbacks.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members write a commitment with a built-in plan for lapses: If I slip, I will call this person within 24 hours.

ask: What separates a resilient commitment from a brittle one?
How would you discuss faith with a member whose prayers seemed to go unanswered?

656.title: Accepting what you cannot change
656.gist: The page says change also requires accepting what cannot change: first, having a substance use disorder and being unable to use safely, then responsibility for past acts without excuses. Acceptance also means doing the work without obsessing over outcomes. Exercise 7 asks what role acceptance plays.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Acceptance and commitment therapy pairs acceptance of what cannot change with committed action toward values. The page's pairing of acceptance and effort echoes that balance.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The Bhagavad Gita teaches acting without attachment to the fruits of action, an ancient version of doing what you must without obsessing over outcome.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Accepting that you can never use any substance is the abstinence view. Some evidence supports moderation for some people with milder problems, so this is a program stance rather than universal fact.

ask: How do you hold both suffering from addiction and being responsible for one's actions?
When might acceptance become passivity?

657.title: What not-accepting gets you
657.gist: Exercise 7 continues by asking what members find especially hard to accept, how not accepting it helps them, and how resisting acceptance could hurt recovery. It looks for the hidden payoff of resistance.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking how not accepting helps is a motivational interviewing move: exploring the benefits of the status quo honestly makes the costs more believable.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Common answers include a sentence, a parent's choices, or a lost child custody case. Validate how unfair some losses are before talking about acceptance.

ask: Is there something a member should not accept, such as injustice?
How might resisting acceptance protect a person's sense of dignity?

658.title: Making amends and giving back
658.gist: The page defines restitution as doing, saying or giving something to repair harm, which shows others you have changed and eases guilt. Since not every wrong can be fixed, service to others in recovery is another way to give back. Exercise 8 asks which harms seem hardest to repair.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Restorative justice, associated with Howard Zehr, focuses on repairing harm to victims and communities rather than only punishment. Amends work fits naturally with it.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Gratitude research by Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough found that regularly noting things you are grateful for is linked with modest improvements in wellbeing.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Remind members that some amends could harm victims or break no-contact orders. Indirect or living amends may be the right path; check with staff before reaching out.

ask: When is direct amends harmful, and what should replace it?
Can service ever become a way to avoid facing a specific harm?

terms.d: Making up for past harm by consistently living differently, when direct repair is impossible or unwise.

659.title: When repair is impossible
659.gist: Exercise 8 continues by asking what members should do if restitution cannot be made, what benefits they have found from amends, and what they gained from service to other recovering people, or what has held them back.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: When the harmed person is dead or unreachable, symbolic amends, such as a letter never sent or service in their name, can still reduce guilt and reinforce change.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name one small service they could do this week inside, like helping someone with paperwork or reading. Small acts still count.

ask: How would you counsel a member who caused a death and cannot make restitution?
What keeps people from doing service even when it would help them?

660.title: Meditation as listening
660.gist: After asking how failing to make restitution hurts recovery, Part 3 introduces meditation, tied to Step Eleven, as quieting the mind and stopping the flow of thoughts. Some describe prayer as asking and meditation as listening, bringing inner peace and new perspective.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Mindfulness-based relapse prevention, developed by Sarah Bowen, Neha Chawla and Alan Marlatt, has shown some reduction in drug use and heavy drinking compared with usual care in trials, though evidence quality varies.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Stopping the flow of thoughts is a hard goal that sets beginners up to feel they failed. Most mindfulness teachers instead teach noticing thoughts and returning to the breath.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prison units are loud. Start with one minute of breath counting, eyes open if members feel unsafe closing them, and normalize a busy mind.

ask: Is meditation in a recovery group a spiritual practice, a clinical skill, or both?
How would you adapt meditation for trauma survivors for whom stillness feels threatening?

terms.d: Paying attention to the present moment on purpose, without judgment, including thoughts and sensations.

661.title: First contact with meditation
661.gist: Exercise 9 asks members whether they have tried meditation, what it might offer even without belief in God, and how it could fit recovery. It opens a secular door into a spirituality session.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many men hear meditation as soft or religious. Reframe it as attention training used by athletes, snipers and surgeons; then ask who has ever stayed calm on purpose during a count or a cell search. They have meditated already, informally.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Mindfulness-based relapse prevention (Bowen, Chawla and Marlatt) showed promising reductions in craving and use in trials, though effects vary and many studies are small. Honest framing: a useful tool, not a cure.

ask: Why might question 2 matter more than question 1 for a group of skeptical or non-religious members?
What would count as evidence that meditation is helping a member, beyond his saying it feels good?

terms.d: Deliberate training of attention, usually by resting it on an anchor and returning to it when the mind wanders.

662.title: Two roads to a quiet mind
662.gist: The page contrasts concentration meditation, fixing attention on one object such as a word or the breath, with mindful meditation, open awareness of whatever arises without judging it. It shows the practice belongs to many faiths and gives practical setup tips.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Concentration builds the muscle of returning attention; open awareness teaches that thoughts and urges are passing events, not orders. That second insight is the core of urge surfing: watching a craving rise, crest and fade without acting.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Christian lectio divina and the Jesus Prayer, Hindu mantra repetition, and Buddhist vipassana arrived at similar techniques independently. Neuroscience studies link practice to changes in attention networks, though claims about lasting brain change are often overstated.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prison is noisy, so the quiet-place advice may sound impossible. Offer short anchors that work anywhere: five breaths before a phone call, feeling the feet during count.

ask: Which type better suits someone with intrusive trauma memories, and why might open awareness be risky for him at first?
Is non-judgmental awareness compatible with the moral inventory work elsewhere in this program?

terms.d: Holding attention on a single object, such as a word, candle or the breath.
Open, non-judging awareness of present thoughts, feelings and sensations as they come and go.

663.title: Fitting meditation to your life
663.gist: Exercise 10 asks members how they feel about daily meditation, where they could practice, and which style suits them. It notes that movement practices like yoga, Tai Chi and walking can also be meditative.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Habits stick when they are tied to a fixed cue and place. Asking where and which type turns a vague intention into an implementation plan, which research on if-then planning (Gollwitzer) suggests raises follow-through.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For restless or hyperactive members, start with walking meditation in the yard: counting steps and feeling each footfall. Movement lowers the bar for people who find stillness agitating.

ask: How would you adapt question 2 for someone who will spend years in a facility with no lake or park?
What is lost, and what is gained, when meditation is reduced to a stress tool cut off from its spiritual roots?

664.title: Trying a word-based meditation
664.gist: The page walks members through meditating on a meaningful word or passage for half an hour, warning against texts tied to using, then starts Exercise 11 on how it felt. It is the session's hands-on experiment.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Thirty minutes is a big first ask; beginners often quit after a frustrating session. Many programs start with three to ten minutes and build up, since early success predicts continued practice.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pick one line a member chooses, perhaps a lyric or a verse. Breathe in on the first half, out on the second, for two minutes. Then ask how many times the mind wandered and how it found its way back.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Repeating a phrase until it opens new meaning is close to how poets read: slow repetition reveals layers a quick read misses.

ask: Why might choosing one's own passage produce more buy-in than using an assigned prayer?
How would you tell the difference between a member meditating and a member ruminating?

665.title: Debriefing meditation and closing session
665.gist: Exercise 11 closes by asking what thoughts surfaced during meditation, then the session summary restates that spirituality can reshape personality through simple but demanding principles like surrender and commitment.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Normalize a bad first try: a busy mind is the practice, not a failure at it. Ask members to report the content of thoughts that came up; resentments and cravings that surface are rich material for later sessions.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The claim that personality changes through spiritual practice is plausible but loosely defined here. Personality research shows traits do shift in adulthood, especially conscientiousness, but slowly and through repeated behavior.

ask: What does surrender mean to someone whose survival in prison has depended on never appearing weak?
If personality really changes in recovery, what would you measure to show it?

666.title: Role-play: amends without guaranteed forgiveness
666.gist: Three volunteers act out a man making amends to two sisters for money he spent on cocaine; one forgives, one stays angry. The questions push members to separate making amends from earning forgiveness.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Step Nine teaches that amends are about the giver taking responsibility, not about controlling the response. That shifts locus of control inward, protecting recovery from someone else's anger.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Cast someone known for resentment as the forgiving sister and a calm member as the angry one. Playing the other side builds perspective-taking, and debrief what each actor felt in role.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Restorative justice frameworks distinguish accountability from reconciliation in much the same way: the harm-doer owes repair, the harmed person owes nothing.

ask: Is Joan's refusal unhealthy, or a legitimate boundary the program should respect?
How would amends differ when the harmed person is a victim of the member's crime and contact is legally restricted?

terms.d: Acknowledging specific harm done and acting to repair it, beyond simply apologizing.
A mutual-help fellowship for family and friends affected by someone else's drinking or drug use.

667.title: Just for Today: one-day living
667.gist: A sample meditation listing daily resolutions: live only today, choose happiness, study, do secret kindnesses, avoid hurry and indecision, take a quiet half hour. It offers ready text for the session's meditation practice.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Shrinking the time frame makes abstinence manageable: a lifetime of never is overwhelming, twelve hours is doable. This mirrors goal-setting research favoring proximal goals for building self-efficacy (Bandura).

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The Lincoln line is widely considered misattributed, with no reliable source. And hiding hurt feelings sits uneasily with emotion-regulation work that values naming feelings over suppression (Gross).

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The text dates to the early twentieth century, often credited to Sibyl Partridge, and later spread through Al-Anon. Stoics like Seneca urged living each day as a complete life.

ask: Which line would you cut or rewrite for men in custody, and why?
Is doing two things you don't want to do a sound idea, from a behavioral activation standpoint?

668.title: Footprints and the Serenity Prayer
668.gist: Two classic recovery texts: a parable about being carried during the hardest times, and the prayer asking for acceptance, courage and the wisdom to tell them apart. Both offer meditation material on support and control.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The Serenity Prayer is a compact sorting tool for control: problem-focused coping for what can change, acceptance for what can't. Lazarus and Folkman's coping research makes a similar split.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The prayer is usually credited to theologian Reinhold Niebuhr; authorship of Footprints is disputed among several claimants. Epictetus opened the Enchiridion with the same control distinction.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members list five current stressors, then sort them into change, accept, and not sure. The third column is where the wisdom part of the prayer lives.

ask: How does Footprints land for a member who felt truly abandoned, by family or by God, in his worst times?
Can acceptance slide into passivity about injustice in the system? Where is the line?

669.title: Prayer of St. Francis
669.gist: A sample meditation text asking to bring peace, love, pardon and hope where their opposites are, and to seek to console and understand rather than be consoled and understood. It reframes recovery around giving.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Despite its name, the prayer was not written by Francis of Assisi; it first appeared in France in the early 1910s. Its power comes from its structure of paired reversals, a rhetorical form called antithesis.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Helping others is linked to better recovery outcomes; research on AA service (for example by Pagano) found members who help others tend to stay sober more often. Giving pulls people out of self-focus.

ask: What risks does a self-giving ideal pose for members with histories of being exploited or people-pleasing?
How would you offer this text to a Muslim or atheist member without making it feel like pressure?

670.title: Advanced Relapse Prevention: session map
670.gist: The session opener outlines three parts: triggers and how to defuse them, building a mental wall against relapse, and trusting others in recovery. Part 1 objectives include identifying triggers and using thought-stopping.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The structure follows Marlatt and Gordon's relapse prevention model: identify high-risk situations, build coping responses, and strengthen lifestyle balance so fewer situations become high-risk.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Thought-stopping is dated. Wegner's white bear studies showed trying to suppress a thought can make it rebound, and newer approaches favor defusion or urge surfing. Teach it with that caveat.

ask: Why might the program place trust in others last rather than first?
What would an advanced version of relapse prevention add that a basic one lacks?

terms.d: A person, place, feeling or situation that sets off cravings or the urge to use.

671.title: What the session will ask
671.gist: The page lists objectives for parts 2 and 3: strengthening physical, emotional, relational and spiritual well-being, naming weaknesses, and examining trust. It warns that reviewing personal triggers can be emotionally hard.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Since the page admits trigger work is emotional, set a ground rule early: describe triggers, don't narrate using stories in vivid detail. War stories can themselves trigger craving in listeners.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The four domains resemble the biopsychosocial-spiritual model used in addiction medicine, which treats recovery as rebuilding several life areas rather than removing one substance.

ask: Which of the four domains is most neglected inside a facility, and how could you partly compensate?
How do you assess trust in someone whose distrust is an accurate reading of his environment?

672.title: Why triggers win and brakes help
672.gist: The page lists many triggers, from stress to celebrations, and likens craving to a train without brakes that relapse prevention skills can stop. It warns that symptom-free weeks don't mean addiction is gone.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Cue reactivity is classical conditioning: places, people and moods paired with use come to trigger craving on their own. These links fade with extinction but can return suddenly in old contexts, which is why release is so risky.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The addictive personality idea lacks solid research support as a single type. Traits like impulsivity and negative emotionality raise risk, but most researchers reject one personality that causes addiction.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Highlight that success and celebration are triggers. Members expect danger in bad days; good news after release, like a first paycheck, catches many off guard.

ask: If cravings return when context changes, what does that imply about relapse risk on the day of release?
How would you explain the brakes metaphor to someone who says he simply chooses whether to use?

terms.d: Craving and body arousal triggered by reminders that were repeatedly paired with past drug use.

673.title: Today's biggest relapse risks
673.gist: Exercise 1 has members name what is most likely to make them relapse now, what they already do to prevent it, and what more they could do. It anchors the session in current, personal risk.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking about today, not the past, matters: high-risk situations shift with context. Inside a facility the risk may be boredom or contraband; after release it may be a payday or an old block. Plans built for one setting can fail in the other.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members often answer with nothing, I'm locked up. Ask instead what would put them at risk on day one out, then work backward. Future-facing questions dodge the defensiveness.

ask: What does it say about a member if he can list risks easily but no prevention steps?
How might your answers to this worksheet differ from a member's, and what does that teach about writing relapse plans for others?

674.title: Three kinds of triggers
674.gist: The page defines triggers as people, places, things and feelings linked with past use, and sorts them into internal (moods), external (places, people, paydays) and sensory (sights, songs, smells). It sets out the chain from trigger to thought to craving to relapse.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Smell is an especially strong cue because olfactory signals reach memory and emotion regions such as the amygdala and hippocampus very directly. That is why a scent can pull someone back faster than a picture.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Calling the chain automatic can sound fatalistic. Triggers raise the odds of craving, but people vary, and many encounter cues without craving. Stress that the links are learned and can weaken.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Draw three columns on the board: inside me, around me, my senses. Each member adds one trigger per column on a sticky note. Patterns across the group reveal shared risks worth planning for.

ask: Is a feeling like joy really a trigger in the same sense as a dealer's apartment? What differs in how you'd handle each?
How could the facility itself contain sensory triggers staff never notice?

terms.d: A mood or body state, such as anxiety or elation, that has become linked with using.
A sight, sound, smell, taste or touch that recalls past use and sparks craving.

675.title: Mapping my current triggers
675.gist: Exercise 2 asks members which triggers have been hardest recently and to sort their own into internal and external examples. It moves the definitions on the previous page into personal inventory.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members often list only external triggers because naming feelings feels exposing. Model by offering an internal trigger of a hypothetical client, such as feeling disrespected, to give permission.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Sorting triggers by type guides strategy: external ones can often be avoided, internal ones cannot and need coping skills. The worksheet quietly sets up that distinction for the next page.

ask: Why might recent triggers be harder to name than old ones?
What follow-up question would reveal the trigger behind a trigger?

676.title: Five steps to defuse triggers
676.gist: The page lays out a five-step method: identify, avoid, interrupt with healthy activities, talk about triggers, and stop obsessive thoughts with relaxation and visualization. It insists silence keeps triggers powerful.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Talking about triggers works partly through affect labeling: research by Lieberman and colleagues found that putting feelings into words can dampen amygdala responses. Shame-driven secrecy blocks that relief.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For interrupting unavoidable triggers, help members schedule a replacement for each known danger time, such as Friday at 5 or the hour after a hard phone call. Vague plans to stay busy rarely survive the moment.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Total avoidance has limits in reentry, where housing, family and work may sit inside old neighborhoods. Pair avoidance with coping practice so members aren't helpless when they can't escape a cue.

ask: Which of the five steps does the most work for someone returning to the same neighborhood?
When does talking about triggers help, and when could it feed craving?

677.title: Small decisions lead to danger
677.gist: Exercise 3 asks what has helped members avoid and interrupt triggers, then introduces a visualization built on one insight: people rarely stumble into high-risk situations by accident but through chains of small choices.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt called these seemingly irrelevant decisions: choices like taking the long route home that look harmless but steer someone toward relapse. Spotting them early is easier than resisting a craving later.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The same pattern appears in criminal thinking work: offenses usually follow a sequence of permission-giving choices, not one sudden act. Members can map their crimes and their relapses on the same timeline.

ask: Why do people so often deny the small decisions, insisting it just happened?
How could you help a member see decision chains without making him feel blamed for every misfortune?

terms.d: Minor choices that seem unrelated to using but gradually move a person toward a high-risk situation.

678.title: Visualization: the trigger movie
678.gist: Exercise 4 guides members into relaxation and asks them to recall a recent high-risk situation as a movie they can play, pause and rewind. It sets up safe distance from which to examine a trigger.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Watching yourself on a screen creates psychological distance. Kross and Ayduk's research on self-distancing shows viewing a memory from an observer's angle reduces emotional reactivity and helps reflection.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Guided imagery of using scenes can provoke craving or trauma memories. Let members keep eyes open if they prefer, offer an exit signal, and avoid this exercise right before members return to housing units unsupervised.

ask: Is relaxation before imagining a trigger a form of mild exposure, and what would make it therapeutic rather than risky?
How would you adapt this exercise for someone with PTSD?

679.title: Rewinding the choices that led there
679.gist: The visualization continues: members pause before the risky scene, weigh consequences, rewind to find earlier choices, and adopt the question of whether a decision helps or hurts recovery. It closes with a check-in for any craving stirred up.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Pausing to imagine consequences engages slower, deliberate thinking, the kind Kahneman calls System 2, against the quick, habitual pull of the cue. Rehearsing the pause makes it more available later.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Give members a one-line filter card: good for my recovery or bad for it? Ask them to use it on three decisions before the next group and report one surprise.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The rewind mirrors chain analysis in Linehan's DBT, which traces a problem behavior link by link to find where a different response was possible.

ask: Is imagining heartbreak a reliable motivator, or can fear-based images lose force with repetition?
Where is the most practical rewind point in a typical relapse chain: hours before, the day before, or earlier?

680.title: Debrief: the trigger I imagined
680.gist: Exercise 5 asks members to name the trigger they visualized, the small decisions leading to it, and how different choices could avoid it. It converts imagery into a concrete written plan.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief in pairs before the full group; it is easier to admit a small decision to one peer. Then collect common early-decision points on the board, like skipping a meeting or answering an old number.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Writing after imagery consolidates what was rehearsed. Concrete alternatives turn insight into an if-then plan the person can recall under stress.

ask: Which small decisions are visible to staff or family, and could they be used as early warning signs?
How specific must an alternative decision be before it's actually usable?

681.title: Four steps from trigger to relapse
681.gist: The page breaks relapse into four steps: trigger, thoughts, cravings, relapse, and says the earlier the chain is broken the better. Triggers come automatically, but whether to keep thinking about using is a choice.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The page draws a useful line: the first thought is not chosen, but dwelling on it is. Cognitive therapy distinguishes automatic thoughts from the elaboration that follows, which is where skills can act.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Elaborated intrusion theory (Kavanagh, Andrade and May) describes craving the same way: a spontaneous thought becomes craving when the mind builds vivid imagery around it, which is why competing imagery can help.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will hear that thoughts can be interrupted as proof they are weak when they fail. Frame each step as a new exit, so catching it late still counts.

ask: If the first thought isn't chosen, where does moral responsibility begin in this model?
Does a linear four-step chain fit relapses that seem to happen in seconds?

682.title: Craving and the blackboard of goals
682.gist: The page warns that uninterrupted obsessive thoughts can grow into physical and mental craving, offers fallback moves like leaving or talking, and begins Exercise 6, a visualization of writing life goals on a blackboard.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Cravings typically rise and then subside within minutes if not acted on, which is the basis of urge surfing. Telling members a craving is a wave, not a wall, can make staying with it bearable.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Replacing drug imagery with vivid goal imagery competes for the same limited mental workspace. Studies on visual tasks, even simple games, suggest they can reduce craving intensity, supporting the blackboard approach.

ask: What makes a goal vivid enough to compete with a craving?
Why does the page say thoughts are easier to interrupt than cravings, and what does that imply for practice timing?

terms.d: A strong desire to use, with mental urges and physical signs like tension, restlessness or a racing heart.

683.title: Goals that outshine cravings
683.gist: The blackboard visualization continues: members recall how use wrecked past goals, picture small next steps, affirm their determination, and leave with a mental image to summon when drug thoughts start.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Upbeat affirmations can backfire for people with low self-esteem; Wood and colleagues found positive self-statements made some low-esteem participants feel worse. Small, believable steps matter more than declarations of conquest.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to write one goal and its very next step on an index card he can carry. A physical card is easier to recall under stress than an imagined blackboard.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Oettingen's mental contrasting research shows pairing a desired future with the obstacles in the way works better than positive fantasy alone. Add obstacles to the blackboard.

ask: How would you rewrite one line of this script so it stays honest for someone facing a long sentence?
What happens to this technique when a member's goals feel impossible to him?

684.title: Applying thought-stopping to my urge
684.gist: Exercise 7 asks members to describe a recent urge to use, how they handled it, and how a thought-stopping technique could have helped. It ties the visualization back to real experience.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Accept any honest answer about how they handled it, including using. Praise the specific moment they noticed the urge; noticing is the skill this session is building.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Expect some members to report that pushing thoughts away made them louder. Validate that and offer alternatives: redirecting attention to a task, or naming the urge and riding it out.

ask: What is the difference between stopping a thought and redirecting attention, and does it matter in practice?
Which member profiles would benefit most and least from this technique?

685.title: Stopping a lapse, then building walls
685.gist: After a final goals question, the page says relapse is common, should be stopped quickly without self-condemnation, and may require treatment. Part 2 then begins: building a protective wall after early abstinence.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt named the abstinence violation effect: after one slip, guilt and an I've-blown-it belief fuel a full binge. The page's advice not to beat yourself up targets exactly that spiral.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Telling members to take responsibility and stop without naming medical risk can be dangerous. After a period of abstinence, tolerance drops, so a return to former opioid doses carries high overdose risk. Say this plainly.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to plan their first call after a slip now, while calm: a name, a number, a place. Lapse plans written in advance cut the time between slip and help.

ask: How do you hold both accountability and self-compassion after a relapse without one cancelling the other?
Should a correctional program openly plan for lapses, or does that seem to give permission?

terms.d: The guilt and self-blame after a slip that lead a person to give up and keep using.
A single episode of use after abstinence, as distinct from a full return to old patterns.

686.title: A five-level wall against relapse
686.gist: The page introduces a psychological wall built in five levels: bodily health, emotional balance, stable relationships, spiritual growth and awareness of one's weak points. It will always have weak spots and may become unnecessary once life is full.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The layered structure echoes Maslow's hierarchy, with bodily needs at the base. Maslow's model is a teaching image, not a tested law, and research suggests needs are pursued in parallel more than strictly in order.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The promise that the wall may fade aligns with recovery capital research (Granfield and Cloud): as people gain resources like work, relationships and meaning, the need for constant vigilance shrinks.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members draw their wall and shade each level from strong to crumbling. The weakest level, not the strongest, is where next week's goal should go.

ask: Is a wall the right metaphor, or does it suggest defending against life instead of building one?
Why might knowing your weaknesses sit at the top rather than the base?

terms.d: The personal, social and community resources a person can draw on to start and sustain recovery.

687.title: Level 1: the body first
687.gist: The base level covers nutrition, exercise, sleep, hygiene and medical and dental care, and must be solid to support the rest. Exercise 8 asks members what they need for physical health and their next step.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Sleep loss impairs the prefrontal control that resists impulses and raises stress reactivity, and poor sleep is linked to relapse risk across substances. Exercise has modest but encouraging evidence for reducing craving.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Teach HALT: hungry, angry, lonely, tired. It links the body level to relapse moments in a phrase members remember, and two of its four letters are physical.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Inside a facility, food, sleep schedule and medical access are largely outside members' control. Focus the worksheet on what they can control, such as movement, hygiene and requesting care, and plan the rest for release.

ask: What evidence would convince a skeptical member that sleep affects craving?
How does neglected dental pain connect to relapse risk, especially for opioids?

688.title: Level 2: managing, not erasing, emotions
688.gist: Emotional well-being is defined as managing feelings, not constant happiness: talking about problems without being ruled by them, making sound choices while upset, and seeking professional help for serious problems.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Gross's process model of emotion regulation shows options at several points: choosing situations, shifting attention, reappraising meaning, or modulating the response. Reappraisal generally has better outcomes than suppression.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Aristotle argued virtue is feeling the right emotion, at the right time, toward the right person, in the right amount. That is close to this page's balance, rather than emotional numbness.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many men equate managing emotions with hiding them, which prison culture rewards. Draw a line between choosing when to express a feeling and pretending it doesn't exist.

ask: How does emotional numbing from long-term use complicate building this level in early recovery?
When should you refer a member for psychiatric evaluation rather than coaching coping skills?

terms.d: The ways people influence which emotions they have, when, and how they experience and express them.

689.title: Planning emotional well-being steps
689.gist: Exercise 9 asks members what they need to do to keep emotional balance and the next step to strengthen this level of their wall.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push for specifics: rather than staying calm, ask what he will do in the first sixty seconds after bad news. Concrete actions such as leaving the dayroom or breathing slowly are what survive stress.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rate their emotional level on a 1-10 thermometer for a week, noting the trigger at each spike. Patterns found this way usually beat guesses written in a single session.

ask: Can someone have emotional well-being while living in an environment that is genuinely threatening?
How would you measure progress on this level over a twelve-week group?
