690.title: Level 3: steady people, slow romance
690.gist: The page urges stable, trustworthy relationships, advises delaying new romance in early recovery because it can mimic drug highs and trigger craving, and suggests distance from people who keep conflict going. Exercise 10 begins.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Brain imaging studies of early romantic love, such as those by Helen Fisher and colleagues, show activity in dopamine reward regions also involved in drug reward. That supports the analogy, though it does not prove romance causes relapse.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The usual one-year rule comes from recovery tradition, not controlled research. And distancing from family can backfire for reentry, where family support is one of the strongest predictors of success. Encourage repair where safe.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect pushback: many members plan to return to a partner. Shift from forbidding romance to examining it: is this relationship calm or chaotic, and does the partner use?

ask: Where is the line between protective distance and isolating someone from support?
How would you discuss this page with a member whose release plan depends on living with a partner?

691.title: Level 4: something bigger than you
691.gist: Spiritual growth is defined broadly: anything meaningful beyond the self, from religion to nature, art, music or sport. Addiction is framed as self-centered and spirituality as other-centered and lifelong.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Viktor Frankl argued in Man's Search for Meaning that people endure almost anything with a why to live for; he wrote from the camps. His idea of self-transcendence matches the page's other-centered view.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Calling television a lesser addiction is a loose use of the word. Better to ask whether an activity is chosen and enriching or numbing and compulsive, a test that fits screens, sport or even religion.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-centeredness here is not selfishness but tunnel vision: addiction narrows attention to the next use. Meaning-centered activity widens the field again.

ask: Can a purely secular pursuit like chess or music do the same work as faith in recovery? What would it need to have?
Is it fair to call addiction self-centered, given how often it begins as self-medication for pain?

692.title: Planning spiritual growth steps
692.gist: Exercise 11 asks members what they need to do to maintain spiritual growth and their next concrete step for this level of the wall.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will say they have no spirituality. Ask instead what moments made them feel part of something larger, a game, a song, holding a child. Start from experience, not belief.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to name one value he would want his kids or a younger person to say he lived by, then one action this week that expresses it. Values work is a secular entry point.

ask: Is it possible to set measurable steps for spiritual growth without reducing it to a checklist?
How does a facility's chaplaincy access shape what you can realistically ask here?

693.title: Level 5: knowing your weak spots
693.gist: The top level asks members to know their personal big triggers and vulnerabilities and have plans ready, including a short-term plan for conflicts that will take years to resolve. Exercise 12 begins.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is the high-risk situation analysis at the heart of Marlatt's relapse prevention. Marlatt's research found negative emotions, interpersonal conflict and social pressure are among the most common relapse situations.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Unresolved conflicts may include trauma, a custody battle or a victim's family. Help members split these into a long-term route, like therapy or legal aid, and a this-week holding plan.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to finish one sentence privately: the one thing that could knock my wall down in a single day is... Then write who they would call within an hour.

ask: Why does the program put knowing weaknesses last, after the stronger supporting levels?
What weaknesses might members be unable to see in themselves, and how could peers help?

terms.d: Any circumstance that threatens a person's sense of control and raises the chance of using.

694.title: Wall maintenance and depending wisely
694.gist: The page says the wall needs ongoing rebuilding until its levels become a lived balance, then opens Part 3: overcoming one dependency may mean temporarily depending on people, but only on those who earn trust.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Attachment theory (Bowlby) holds that a secure base lets people explore and take risks. Healthy reliance on others is not weakness but the platform for independence, a reframing that suits men taught that needing help is shameful.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Highlight the page's judgment questions about whether a person deserves trust. In a prison setting, blanket trust is unsafe; teaching discernment respects members' experience instead of dismissing it.

ask: Is swapping a drug dependency for a dependency on a group a real cure or a substitution? Does it matter?
What signs tell you a helper is exploiting rather than supporting someone?

terms.d: A trusted relationship that gives a person enough safety to explore, take risks and grow.

695.title: Why trusting help feels risky
695.gist: The page explains why trust is hard after abuse or betrayal, including fear of judgment and shame, and notes people may fake trust without honesty. Exercise 13 asks whether members trust others and what blocks them.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: In custody, distrust is often an accurate adaptation, not a defect. Treat it as a skill to be tuned, not removed: trusting the right people a bit more and the wrong ones not at all.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Shame differs from guilt: guilt says I did a bad thing, shame says I am bad. Tangney's research links shame to hiding and blaming, guilt to repair, which explains why shame blocks honest help-seeking.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members may answer yes to trust to look good. Ask a sharper follow-up: who knows the worst thing you've done and still talks to you?

ask: How do you build trust with members when you are also part of a system that can sanction them?
What does pretending to trust look like in a group, and how would you spot it?

696.title: The blindfolded trust walk
696.gist: After a last question on building trust, Exercise 14 sets up the trust walk: one partner leads another who is blindfolded. The page notes it is a prompt for reflection, not a real measure of trust, and can be fun.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Check facility security rules first; blindfolds may be banned. A workable substitute is eyes closed while the partner guides only by voice. Also let anyone opt out, since being unable to see can be frightening for trauma survivors.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Experiential exercises work because the body learns faster than a lecture: feeling the urge to peek or grab is direct evidence of one's trust pattern, which members then put into words.

ask: What is the ethical difference between a trust exercise that challenges people and one that coerces them?
How would you debrief a member who refused to participate?

697.title: Leading and being led
697.gist: The page gives trust walk instructions, fifteen minutes each way with agreed limits and a hand on the leader's shoulder, then Exercise 15 asks how it felt to be led and what fears came up.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief the leaders too: many members find guiding someone carefully harder than following. Responsibility for another person's safety is a rehearsal for sponsorship and fatherhood.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: After the walk, ask each follower to rate trust at the start and end on a 0-10 scale. Most rise as the walk goes on, a small, felt demonstration that trust grows through repeated safe experience.

ask: What does it reveal if a member trusts a peer more easily than staff during this exercise?
How could the exercise unintentionally reinforce distrust, and how would you repair that?

698.title: Trust is earned over time
698.gist: The last trust walk question links the exercise to sharing feelings, then the page notes trusting someone with secrets is far harder than walking blindfolded: trust builds slowly through respectful treatment.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The therapeutic alliance, the working bond and agreement between client and counselor, is one of the most consistent predictors of treatment outcomes across therapies. This page is quietly describing how that alliance forms.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Game theory offers a parallel: in repeated interactions, cooperation emerges through consistent reciprocal behavior, as Axelrod showed with tit-for-tat. Trust is a track record, not a decision.

ask: What specific counselor behaviors signal respect and dignity to someone who has rarely received them?
Can trust be rebuilt with people who broke it, or only built with new people?

terms.d: The collaborative bond between client and helper, including shared goals and agreement on how to reach them.

699.title: Session 33 in review
699.gist: The summary recaps the session's three threads: triggers and how to defuse them, the five-level wall against relapse, and the role of trust in recovery.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Close with a one-word go-around: each member names the single tool from today he is most likely to use in the next week. Public commitments, even small ones, raise follow-through.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The session moves from inner skills to outer supports, mirroring a common shift in recovery science from individual willpower toward environment and relationships as the stronger long-term protectors.

ask: Which of the three parts would you cut if you had only one hour, and why?
How would you check a week later whether any of this transferred to behavior?

700.title: Role-play: a payday errand gone risky
700.gist: Three volunteers act out a woman in early recovery who, on a Friday payday, chooses a pharmacy in her old using neighborhood, meets a using friend, and refuses alcohol and crack. Members identify her triggers and how she could avoid them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The scene is a textbook string of seemingly irrelevant decisions: volunteering for the errand, choosing the far pharmacy, saying it's cheaper. Each choice sounds reasonable, which is the point.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask the group to replay the scene with Annette spotting the risk at three different points: on the phone, at the door, and with Sheila. Then compare how much willpower each version required.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Annette refuses successfully, so the scene could teach that exposure is survivable. Discuss how close the pause after the rock offer came to a different ending.

ask: Which of Annette's statements is the clearest rationalization, and how would you gently challenge it?
How does her mother's warning function, and why might Annette dismiss it?

701.title: Role-play: dropping the tough mask
701.gist: Two volunteers play old friends from a rough street, both former prisoners; one is in recovery, the other still using. At dinner the recovering one hides his feelings, then later calls to share his story openly.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The tough front is a learned survival strategy that once worked. In social learning terms (Bandura), it was reinforced by safety; recovery requires discriminating where it still helps and where it blocks connection.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Sociologist Elijah Anderson's Code of the Street describes how projecting toughness becomes protective in high-violence neighborhoods, a useful frame for discussing the mask without shaming it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask the actor playing Donnell what stopped him at dinner, in character. Answers like not wanting to seem better than Ray reveal loyalty dilemmas many members face at reentry.

ask: Is Donnell's call a healthy act of carrying the message or a risky return to a using contact?
How would you help a member decide when to keep the mask on in prison and when to drop it?

702.title: Debriefing the tough mask
702.gist: The suggested questions ask why Donnell hid his feelings, the pros and cons of a tough street front, and the risks of revealing real feelings to another person.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 2 invites honest credit for the mask. Let members list its advantages first; once its value is acknowledged, they are more willing to name its costs, a classic decisional balance move from motivational interviewing.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Hand out a quick two-column card: where the mask protects me, where it costs me. Ask each member to fill in one honest entry per column.

ask: Why might acknowledging the benefits of a behavior make people more open to changing it?
What is the risk for a counselor who pushes a member to be vulnerable in a setting that punishes vulnerability?

terms.d: Weighing the pros and cons of changing versus staying the same, used to explore ambivalence.

703.title: MAT meets Twelve Step recovery
703.gist: The session opener introduces medication-assisted treatment for alcohol and opioid addiction within a biopsychosocial-spiritual model, and notes that some groups disapprove of medication, so members should find supportive sponsors and groups.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Methadone and buprenorphine are strongly supported for opioid use disorder and are associated with markedly lower overdose death risk. Many guidelines now favor the term medications for opioid use disorder, MOUD.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Stigma inside recovery culture, the idea that someone on buprenorphine is not truly clean, has kept people off life-saving treatment. The page's honesty about disapproval is a strength worth emphasizing.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect strong opinions from members who see MAT as trading one drug for another. Ask what they would say to a diabetic told insulin is a crutch; then discuss where the analogy holds and where it fails.

ask: Why would a recovery program that sees addiction as a disease resist medication for it?
How does release from custody change the urgency of MAT for someone with opioid use disorder?

terms.d: Medication-assisted treatment: prescribed medications combined with counseling and support to treat substance use disorders.

704.title: Session goals and medication glossary
704.gist: The page lists objectives on medications and active Twelve Step participation, including locating MAT-friendly meetings, and previews the glossary: acamprosate, buprenorphine, disulfiram, methadone, naltrexone and Vivitrol.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Narcotics Anonymous has historically been more cautious about MAT than AA, and local meetings vary widely. Groups such as MARA, Medication-Assisted Recovery Anonymous, emerged partly to fill that gap.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to sort the glossary drugs into three bins: replaces the drug, blocks the drug, makes drinking unpleasant. It builds a mental map before the details arrive.

ask: What do members need to know about these medications before release that the program could easily skip?
How should a counselor talk about medications without straying outside the scope of practice?

terms.d: A medication that blocks opioid receptors, used for both alcohol and opioid use disorders; Vivitrol is its monthly injectable form.

705.title: How medications support recovery
705.gist: The page defines MAT as medication for withdrawal, craving and relapse prevention, explains addiction as a brain disease per NIDA, and says medication frees attention for lifestyle change while doctors plan eventual discontinuation.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Long-term use alters reward and stress circuits, which is why choice feels impaired. Medications act on these systems directly, quieting craving or blocking reward, so counseling has a calmer brain to work with.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The brain disease model is debated. Critics such as Marc Lewis argue addiction is better seen as deeply learned behavior, and that the disease label can undercut agency. Many clinicians hold both views at once.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: For opioids, stopping maintenance medication raises relapse and overdose risk, and many experts see long-term or indefinite treatment as reasonable. The page's framing of planned discontinuation is not universal.

ask: If addiction is a brain disease, what remains for counseling to do?
How would you explain the disease model to a member who finds it an excuse, and to one who finds it a relief?

terms.d: The medically supervised process of clearing a substance from the body while managing withdrawal symptoms.

706.title: My view of medication in recovery
706.gist: Exercise 1 asks members how MAT helps people with substance use disorders and what concerns they have about using medication in their own recovery.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 2 surfaces myths: getting high on bupe, failing drug tests, being judged at meetings. Collect them on the board without arguing, then address each with facts later in the session.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Eliciting concerns before informing respects autonomy, a core MI principle (Miller and Rollnick): ask, then provide information, then ask again what the person makes of it.

ask: Which concerns reflect real risks and which reflect stigma, and how would you tell them apart in the room?
How might a member's legal situation, like probation conditions, shape his answer?

707.title: Medication is one piece
707.gist: The page stresses that medication alone isn't full treatment; because addiction affects biological, psychological, social and spiritual life, MAT works best paired with counseling, relapse prevention skills and peer groups.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Combined treatment is the standard recommendation, but evidence also shows buprenorphine and methadone save lives even with minimal counseling. Lack of counseling should not be a reason to deny medication.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: George Engel proposed the biopsychosocial model in 1977 as a challenge to purely biomedical medicine; the spiritual dimension was added later by addiction and palliative care fields.

ask: If medication works without counseling for some outcomes, what is counseling's distinctive contribution?
Which of the four domains do jail and prison programs tend to neglect most?

terms.d: The view that health and illness result from interacting biological, psychological and social factors.

708.title: Mapping damage and medication's role
708.gist: Exercise 2 asks which life areas addiction hit hardest and whether MAT alone is enough treatment, then the page begins listing benefits: craving control, safe withdrawal, and long-term maintenance for stability.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Draw four quadrants labeled body, mind, people, meaning. Members place a dot where addiction did the most damage. Point out that medication mostly reaches one quadrant, which is why the others need work.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Maintenance can sound like lifelong dependence. Frame it as stabilization, the way a cast holds a bone while it heals, and note some people need it longer than others.

ask: Why might the most damaged domain differ between a member's own view and his family's?
Is maintenance medication a step toward recovery, a form of recovery, or both?

709.title: What medications can do
709.gist: The page lists MAT benefits such as easing withdrawal, cutting craving, blocking alcohol or opioid effects and restoring health, has members check how medication can help in Exercise 3, and introduces alcohol medications disulfiram and acamprosate.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Naltrexone is also FDA-approved for alcohol use disorder and is often a first-line option; the glossary lists it. Among alcohol medications, effects are generally modest, helping some people substantially and others little.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Exercise 3's answer is all of the above; use it as a quick quiz to build confidence, then ask which option a member would actually want and why.

ask: Why might modest-effect medications still be worth offering?
What does it mean for a medication to be non-addictive, and why does that matter to members?

710.title: Disulfiram, acamprosate and post-acute withdrawal
710.gist: The page explains disulfiram, which makes drinking cause a sickening reaction, and acamprosate, which eases post-acute withdrawal: the mood, sleep and energy problems that can recur long after acute withdrawal ends.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Disulfiram blocks an enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde, a toxic alcohol byproduct; the buildup causes the reaction. It works mainly through deterrence, so it helps most when someone else supervises dosing.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Post-acute withdrawal syndrome is widely used in treatment settings but its definition and timeline are less settled in research. Still, naming it helps members not mistake months-later irritability for failure.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Warn that alcohol hidden in mouthwash, cough syrup or some sauces can trigger the disulfiram reaction. Practical details like this build trust in the information.

ask: Is a medication that works through fear of sickness ethically different from one that reduces craving?
How would you explain post-acute withdrawal to a member six months sober who feels worse than at month one?

terms.d: Antabuse; makes a person sick if they drink alcohol, discouraging drinking.
Lingering mood, sleep and energy symptoms that can come and go for months after stopping.

711.title: Quiz, then naltrexone
711.gist: Exercise 4 checks understanding of disulfiram and acamprosate, then the page introduces naltrexone, a non-addictive medication that blocks opioid receptors and dampens alcohol's reward for both alcohol and opioid addiction.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Watch for a printing error: the page calls naltrexone an opioid receptor agonist, but it is an antagonist, a blocker. Correct this in the room; agonist and antagonist mean opposite things.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Naltrexone works through extinction: if drinking no longer delivers the expected reward, the learned link weakens over time. Sinclair's work on taking it before drinking builds on exactly this idea.

ask: Why does a mislabel like agonist versus antagonist matter for client trust and safety?
Which members would naltrexone suit poorly, given that it blocks opioid pain relief?

terms.d: A drug that occupies a receptor and blocks it, preventing other drugs from activating it.
A drug that activates a receptor, producing effects like the natural chemical or drug it mimics.

712.title: Naltrexone's track record and Vivitrol
712.gist: The page summarizes naltrexone's benefits, fewer drinking days and less craving for alcohol, better abstinence for opioids, and introduces monthly injectable Vivitrol to improve adherence. Exercise 5 quizzes its uses.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Oral naltrexone for opioids has struggled because people stop taking it; the monthly injection addresses that. Trials comparing injectable naltrexone with buprenorphine found similar outcomes once started, but starting is harder.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Vivitrol requires being opioid-free for about a week to ten days first, or it triggers withdrawal. That makes release from custody a natural starting window, which is why many jail programs offer it before discharge.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: After stopping naltrexone, tolerance is low, so using former doses of opioids can be fatal. Members must hear this explicitly.

ask: Why might correctional systems prefer naltrexone over methadone or buprenorphine, and is that preference clinical or political?
How would you explain loss of tolerance to someone sure he knows his dose?

terms.d: Extended-release naltrexone given as a monthly injection, removing the need for daily pills.

713.title: Methadone and buprenorphine explained
713.gist: The page defines agonists, partial agonists and antagonists, then describes methadone, a slow, long-acting agonist with strong outcome research, and buprenorphine, a partial agonist that is safer in overdose, combined with naloxone in Suboxone to deter injection.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Buprenorphine has a ceiling effect: past a certain dose its opioid effect stops rising, so breathing suppression is limited, though mixing with benzodiazepines or alcohol remains risky.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The brand Subtex is likely a misprint for Subutex. Also, methadone does produce opioid effects in people without tolerance; it feels non-euphoric mainly to tolerant patients on stable doses.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Dole and Nyswander pioneered methadone maintenance in New York in the 1960s, framing addiction as a medical condition decades before this became mainstream.

ask: Why does a slower route to the brain reduce euphoria and abuse potential?
What should members know about precipitated withdrawal when starting buprenorphine?

terms.d: A drug that activates a receptor only partway, giving milder effects with a ceiling.
A point beyond which higher doses produce no further effect.

714.title: Checking knowledge of opioid medications
714.gist: Exercise 6 quizzes why methadone and buprenorphine are used: easing withdrawal and craving, blunting other opioids, and reducing injection, with all of the above as the intended answer.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some options, like no mood change, are true at stable maintenance doses but not universally. Use the quiz to teach nuance: the answer depends on dose and tolerance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Turn the multiple choice into a debate: assign half the group to argue all of the above, half to find the weakest option. Members retain more when they argue than when they check boxes.

ask: Do quiz formats like this teach understanding or just recognition?
How would you rewrite one option to make it more accurate without losing simplicity?

715.title: Active participation, not just attendance
715.gist: Part 2 presents Twelve Step groups as central to recovery and says research links active participation, not mere attendance, to better outcomes. It lists what active means: regular meetings, sharing, working steps, reading, and a sponsor.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: A 2020 Cochrane review (Kelly and colleagues) found AA and Twelve Step facilitation produced abstinence outcomes as good as or better than other established treatments like CBT. Engagement measures predict outcome better than counting meetings.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Researchers think AA works largely through social mechanisms: changing friendship networks toward sober people, and building self-efficacy through role models, which echoes Bandura.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Court-mandated attendance raises legal and ethical issues; several U.S. courts have ruled that coerced attendance at religiously grounded meetings violates the Establishment Clause, so secular options should be offered.

ask: Why would speaking at a meeting predict better outcomes than listening?
What alternatives would you offer a member who rejects Twelve Step groups, such as SMART Recovery?

terms.d: An experienced member who guides a newer member through the steps and offers support.

716.title: Surrender and speaking up
716.gist: The page explains the Twelve Step view of recovery as spiritual awakening, often gradual, beginning with Step One's admission of powerlessness, and urges honest sharing at meetings. Exercise 7 asks if a group would help.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: William James, whose Varieties of Religious Experience influenced AA's founders, distinguished sudden conversion from gradual educational change. The Big Book later stressed the gradual kind as most common.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Powerlessness can clash with criminal justice messages of personal responsibility and with empowerment needs of trauma survivors. Some feminist critics, like Charlotte Kasl, rewrote the steps for this reason.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Reframe powerlessness as accuracy rather than weakness: admitting that willpower alone lost every round. Many members find that reframe less humiliating.

ask: Can someone be powerless over a substance and fully responsible for his actions at the same time?
How would you help a member whose prior meeting experience was in a court-ordered, crowded room?

terms.d: The first Twelve Step: admitting powerlessness over the substance and that life became unmanageable.

717.title: Meetings differ on medication
717.gist: After asking what members could share at a meeting, the page explains that local AA and NA groups vary widely in their attitudes toward MAT; some members view it as still using, others see its value.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: AA's own literature has long said members should not play doctor and that properly prescribed medication is between a person and their physician. Local culture often lags behind this official stance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Role-play a moment where a meeting member says you're not really clean. Let members practice a calm response that keeps them in the room without debating.

ask: Where does stigma toward MAT in recovery groups come from historically?
How should a counselor respond if a sponsor tells a client to stop prescribed medication?

718.title: Welcoming, partial, or closed doors
718.gist: The page sorts Twelve Step groups into welcoming ones that let MAT patients fully take part, partially welcoming ones that restrict speaking or service, and non-welcoming ones focused on strict abstinence, and urges finding a supportive meeting.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Restricting MAT members to making coffee is a form of tiered membership; it signals lesser status. Belonging is a key active ingredient in mutual help, so exclusion may undercut the very mechanism that helps.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to imagine walking into each group type and rate the likelihood they'd return. Then ask how a person might feel who has no other group in his town.

ask: Does NA's tradition of group autonomy justify excluding MAT patients, or does it conflict with its own primary purpose?
How could someone tell what type of group it is before disclosing his medication?

719.title: Finding a home group
719.gist: Exercise 8 asks members which kinds of meetings they have attended, whether any felt non-welcoming and why, and whether they have found a home group that supports their medication.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members who have only attended meetings inside a facility may have no comparison. Ask them to describe the facility meeting's culture, then imagine what they'd want in a community one.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A home group gives continuity, the same faces week to week, which builds the accountability and attachment that sporadic attendance cannot.

ask: What makes a group feel like home rather than just tolerable?
Is it healthier to stay and change a non-welcoming group or to leave for a better fit?

terms.d: The meeting a member attends regularly and commits to, often taking on service roles there.

720.title: Many kinds of meetings
720.gist: The page surveys meeting types: speaker, Big Book, step study, discussion; open and closed; men's, women's, young people's and LGBT groups; large or small; and notes groups reflect their neighborhoods. Exercise 9 asks what fits each member.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research suggests people tend to stay engaged when they identify with group members, sharing age, background or experience. Matching meetings to identity, like a men's or Spanish-language meeting, can improve retention.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Mention Spanish-speaking and ex-offender-friendly meetings where relevant. For reentry clients, meetings with others who have done time can lower the shame barrier.

ask: What are the risks of choosing a meeting purely for comfort?
How might racial or cultural mismatch in a meeting affect engagement, and what can a counselor do?

terms.d: A meeting limited to people who want to stop drinking or using; open meetings welcome anyone.

721.title: How to find MAT-friendly meetings
721.gist: After asking whether members disclosed their medications to a sponsor, the page suggests finding MAT-friendly meetings through counselors, onsite treatment program meetings, alumni groups, and online or phone searches.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Before release, build a short list with members: two or three specific meetings near their release address with times. A named meeting is far more likely to be attended than a general plan to find one.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Online boards can contain strong anti-MAT opinions and misinformation. Teach members to seek specific meeting suggestions there, not medical advice.

ask: What does it say about recovery culture that people must strategize about disclosing a prescribed medication?
How could you, as a counselor, keep an up-to-date list of welcoming meetings?

722.title: Planning for an unwelcoming meeting
722.gist: Exercise 10 asks members how they will find a MAT-friendly meeting and what they would do if a group criticized their medication: quit meetings or look for a better one.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Question 2 is a coping rehearsal: anticipating a social rejection and planning a response prevents an all-or-nothing reaction where one bad meeting ends all support.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to also plan the opposite case: what if a meeting pressures them to stop medication? Rehearse a sentence like my doctor and I decide that, which ends the debate politely.

ask: Why might someone stop medication rather than switch meetings, and what does that reveal about belonging needs?
How does all-or-nothing thinking show up here, and in relapse generally?

723.title: Friends, sponsors and step work
723.gist: The page advises making friends by arriving early and staying late, finding a MAT-supportive sponsor with solid sobriety, or a temporary one, and working the steps through step study meetings and recovery literature.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Having a sponsor early in AA participation is associated with better abstinence in several studies, and changing social networks toward sober friends is among AA's best-supported mechanisms of change.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Sponsorship resembles apprenticeship, one of the oldest ways humans pass on skill: learning by working beside someone further along, not from manuals alone.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members have been warned never to share phone numbers inside, and parole rules may restrict contact with people who have records. Help them check those conditions before planning sponsor contacts.

ask: What makes the fellowship before and after a meeting as important as the meeting itself?
How would you help a member evaluate whether a prospective sponsor is healthy?

724.title: My plan for meetings and sponsorship
724.gist: Exercise 11 asks members how they will befriend people who support MAT recovery, how to find and judge a potential sponsor, and what working the steps means to them.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For question 2, brainstorm red flags in a sponsor: pushing to stop medication, romantic interest, asking for money, demanding control. Then green flags. A clear list protects vulnerable newcomers.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have each member write the opening line he would use to ask someone to be his sponsor. Practicing the words lowers the dread of an awkward ask.

ask: How should a member handle a sponsor whose advice conflicts with his counselor's?
What does working the steps look like for someone who will be incarcerated for many more years?

725.title: Show up, speak up, disclose slowly
725.gist: The page urges active involvement: arrive early, help set up, start with speaker meetings, share at discussion meetings, and disclose MAT only when trust feels right. Exercise 12 asks for concrete steps toward participation.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Gradual self-disclosure follows social penetration theory (Altman and Taylor): relationships deepen as people share progressively more personal information as trust grows. Timing disclosure is a skill, not secrecy.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Setting up chairs is a low-stakes first service role. For members uneasy speaking, a job gives them a reason to be there and a way to meet people without talking about themselves yet.

ask: When does choosing not to disclose MAT become harmful hiding rather than healthy caution?
Why might helping others, like setting up chairs, benefit the helper's recovery?

726.title: Lingering after and facing criticism
726.gist: Exercise 12 continues, asking whether members linger after meetings and when they'd share their MAT, then the page advises focusing on one's own recovery rather than convincing others, and accepting differing views, likening MAT to insulin.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The insulin analogy helps reduce stigma but has limits: insulin replaces a missing hormone, while opioid agonists act on circuits shaped by drug use. A fairer comparison is long-term blood pressure medication, managing a chronic condition.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask who leaves meetings the moment they end. For many members, staying feels exposed; suggest one modest goal: one handshake and one name before leaving.

ask: Is it better to defend MAT in meetings or to stay silent and focused? What does each cost?
How would you improve the insulin analogy for a skeptical group?

727.title: Others' opinions are their recovery
727.gist: The page frames others' anti-medication views as part of their own recovery efforts, says medication advice belongs with counselors and doctors, not meetings, and Exercise 13 asks how members might reply to criticism.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Seeing criticism as about the critic, not oneself, is a cognitive reappraisal that reduces the sting and the urge to retaliate, central to anger management in CBI programs too.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Calling such opinions neither right nor wrong is a diplomatic stance, but medically, telling someone to quit buprenorphine can raise overdose risk. Members can respect a person while recognizing the advice as unsafe.

ask: Can you be tolerant of a view while firmly rejecting it as dangerous? How would you model that?
Where else in members' lives would reframing criticism this way be useful?

728.title: Calm responses and final advice
728.gist: Exercise 13 asks for three responses to MAT criticism that avoid both anger and shame, then the page lists closing advice: avoid triggers, arrive early, get a sponsor and home group, call when in trouble, try ninety meetings in ninety days.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pairs practice a 30-second exchange: one voices a common criticism, the other replies with a calm, non-defensive line, then they swap. Saying it out loud once makes it available later.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Ninety in ninety reflects front-loading support when relapse risk is highest, in the first months. It parallels intensive outpatient structures that taper over time.

ask: Is ninety meetings in ninety days realistic for someone juggling parole, work and family? What is the core principle behind it?
Why might shame be a riskier reaction to criticism than anger?

729.title: Session 34 in review
729.gist: The summary recaps MAT's role within a multi-component treatment plan, the value of active Twelve Step participation, and how to find meetings that support medication.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The session tries to reconcile two traditions often seen as rivals: medical treatment and mutual-help recovery. Integration of this kind is a growing trend in addiction care.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to state one fact about medication he didn't know before today and one meeting step he'll take. A two-part close checks both halves of the session.

ask: What tension between MAT and Twelve Step culture did the session leave unresolved?
How would you measure whether members left more open to MAT than they arrived?

730.title: Session 34 medication glossary
730.gist: The glossary defines acamprosate, buprenorphine, disulfiram, MAT, methadone, naltrexone and Vivitrol, summarizing each medication's purpose.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The buprenorphine entry blends descriptions: it is a partial agonist that activates receptors partway, not a blocker in the way naltrexone is. And Subtex is likely a misprint for Subutex. Worth correcting for members.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Make flashcards with the drug on one side and its action, replaces, blocks or deters, on the other. Quizzing in pairs strengthens memory through retrieval practice.

ask: Which single fact from this glossary could save a member's life after release?
Why might simplified descriptions of medications cause confusion later?

terms.d: Campral; helps people stay alcohol-free by easing lingering withdrawal symptoms.
A partial opioid agonist that eases withdrawal and craving with lower overdose risk.

731.title: MAT resources list
731.gist: The page lists organizations offering information and support on medication-assisted treatment, including AA, NA, Methadone Anonymous, a buprenorphine advocacy group and medication-assisted recovery services.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Web links are useless inside most facilities. Before release, help members write down names and phone numbers of local resources instead, and verify they still exist; resource lists age quickly.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Groups like Methadone Anonymous exist because mainstream fellowships didn't always welcome medication users, an example of communities forming around exclusion.

ask: How would you keep a resource list current for your facility?
Which resources would matter most to a Spanish-speaking member returning to Miami?

732.title: Chronic Pain and Opioids: session map
732.gist: The opener presents four parts: effects of chronic pain, working with health professionals, pain treatment options in recovery, and using opioids for intense pain without harming recovery. Part 1 covers the stress response and pain-addiction cycle.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Chronic pain and addiction share brain circuits for reward, motivation and emotion. Pain can drive drug use, and long-term opioid use can sometimes increase pain sensitivity, a phenomenon called opioid-induced hyperalgesia.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will feel accused of drug-seeking when they mention pain. Open by validating that pain is real, and that this session is about getting it treated safely, not dismissed.

ask: Why is pain treatment for people with addiction histories so often either too restrictive or too permissive?
How does incarceration affect access to good pain care?

terms.d: Increased sensitivity to pain that can develop with long-term opioid use.

733.title: What Session 35 covers
733.gist: The page lists objectives: describing pain's psychosocial harm and talking openly with providers, using physical therapy, CBT, non-opioid medicines and hypnosis, and handling opioid use, MAT adjustments and treatment agreements during intense pain.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Multi-component pain programs combining exercise, psychological therapy and education generally outperform single treatments for function, though pain reduction is often modest. Improved function is a realistic goal.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Hypnosis has a long, real research base for pain; brain imaging studies by Rainville and colleagues showed hypnotic suggestion altering how unpleasant pain feels.

ask: Why might function, not pain score, be the better target in chronic pain care?
Which of these options are actually available to members inside your facility?

734.title: Pain as a biopsychosocial process
734.gist: The page explains what members will be asked to do: rate pain and explore how it affects body, mind and relationships, then begins Part 1 by treating chronic pain, like addiction, as a changing biopsychosocial process.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Melzack and Wall's gate control theory (1965) showed the spinal cord and brain modulate pain signals, so mood, attention and beliefs genuinely change how much something hurts. Pain is not just damage reporting.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Avoid any hint that pain is in the head. Say it the other way: the brain helps produce all pain, which is why brain-based tools can lower real pain.

ask: How does seeing pain as a process change what treatment success looks like?
Why might people with trauma histories experience pain more intensely?

terms.d: Something shaped by body, mind and social life, changing over time rather than fixed.

735.title: Chronic pain can be managed
735.gist: The page defines chronic pain as lasting over six months, notes it is common and manageable though rarely eliminated, and shows how pain and addiction both fluctuate, with one's treatment sometimes helping or harming the other.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Chronic pain is more common among people with substance use disorders than in the general population, and pain is a frequent reason given for misusing opioids. Treating both together is the recommended approach.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Definitions vary; many current sources, including the international pain classification, define chronic pain as lasting beyond three months, not six. The six-month mark reflects older usage.

ask: What does managing rather than eliminating pain ask of a patient psychologically?
How do you help a member accept chronic pain without resignation?

terms.d: Pain persisting beyond normal healing time, usually over three to six months.

736.title: Seeing addiction and pain as processes
736.gist: Exercise 1 asks members how their addiction and their chronic pain have each unfolded over time rather than as single events.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members draw two timelines, one for pain and one for use, on the same sheet. Points where pain peaks and use rises together often reveal self-medication patterns in seconds.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members without chronic pain can answer the pain question about any long-term health issue or emotional pain. Keep everyone engaged.

ask: What insight does a process view offer that an event view hides?
How might a member's injury history connect to his drug history in ways he hasn't noticed?

737.title: Pain, stress and a worn-out body
737.gist: The page lists shared features of pain and addiction: nervous system effects, genetic and environmental roots, behavior change, serious untreated consequences. It then explains how repeated pain triggers the stress response, leading to exhaustion, insomnia, anxiety and depression that worsen pain.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Repeated activation of the stress system, called allostatic load (McEwen), wears down sleep, mood and immune function. Sleep loss in turn lowers pain thresholds, creating a feedback loop.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Teach slow breathing with longer exhales for two minutes. Extended exhalation engages the parasympathetic system, a direct counter to the fight-or-flight response the page describes.

ask: Where in the pain-stress loop is the easiest place to intervene for someone in custody?
How does this loop resemble the one between stress and craving?

terms.d: The fight-or-flight reaction: faster heart and breathing, sweating, and a surge of energy.
The cumulative wear on the body from repeated or chronic stress.

738.title: My stress signs and the pain cycle
738.gist: Exercise 2 has members check their stress response symptoms and how they feel after repeated stress, then the page describes the pain-addiction cycle: untreated pain leads to exhaustion and using to numb it, which worsens both.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Self-medication models (Khantzian) propose that people use substances to ease specific suffering. Support is mixed overall, but pain is one area where the pattern is commonly observed.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Normalize the cycle without excusing it: using to numb pain made sense in the moment, and now there are better tools. That stance lowers shame and raises openness.

ask: Why might alcohol, which numbs pain briefly, worsen chronic pain over time?
How would you help someone break the cycle when legitimate pain care is hard to get?

739.title: Tolerance traps and the pain team
739.gist: The page explains how tolerance, dependence and withdrawal turn pain relief into more pain, then starts Part 2: tell providers about pain, name a point person on the care team, and expect a pain assessment whose answers members should save.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Withdrawal itself heightens pain sensitivity, so the return of pain after a dose wears off is partly withdrawal. That confusion fuels the cycle: the drug seems to treat pain it is partly causing.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Physical dependence is not the same as addiction; patients on long-term medication can be dependent without compulsive use. Blurring the two can make members fear any necessary medication.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Encourage members to request a point person for pain. Fragmented care is where people fall through cracks or get mixed messages about opioids.

ask: How would you explain the difference between dependence and addiction to a member on a long-term prescription?
What gets lost when pain care and addiction care are handled by separate providers?

terms.d: Needing more of a substance to get the same effect after repeated use.
The body's adaptation to a drug, causing withdrawal when it stops; not the same as addiction.

740.title: Describing and rating my pain
740.gist: Exercise 3 begins a pain self-assessment: when pain started, words describing its quality like aching or shooting, and an average-day rating on a 0-10 scale.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Pain quality words carry clinical clues: burning, tingling and shooting often suggest nerve pain, while aching and throbbing point to muscle, joint or inflammation. That steers treatment choices.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Numeric scales are anchored differently by each person; a tough member may call severe pain a 4. Ask what a 10 would mean to him so the number has a reference point.

ask: Why might a single number underrepresent the impact of pain?
How could cultural norms around toughness distort pain ratings in a men's facility?

terms.d: A structured set of questions about pain's onset, quality, severity and effects on daily life.

741.title: Pain patterns and what helps
741.gist: The assessment continues with a current pain rating and pain pattern (intermittent, constant with flares, or unrelenting), then the page stresses telling providers what worsens and eases pain. Exercise 4 begins.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Pain pattern matters: constant pain with flares suggests planning both a baseline strategy and a flare plan. Intense flares are exactly where relapse risk spikes.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to keep a three-day pain log: time, rating, activity, mood. Patterns from a log beat memory, which tends to recall the worst moments.

ask: Why might past attempts that failed be just as useful to a provider as what worked?
How does recall bias affect a pain history given in a ten-minute appointment?

742.title: What worsens and eases my pain
742.gist: Exercise 4 continues: members rate how well they manage pain and list the things that make it worse and the things that make it less intense.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect drug use to appear on the eases list. Welcome it as honest data, then ask what it cost afterward. This keeps the worksheet truthful rather than performed.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Rating management separately from pain separates the problem from coping capacity. Someone with high pain but good management is doing well; that reframe builds self-efficacy.

ask: Why might emotional factors like conflict appear on the worsens list, and what does that say about pain?
How would you use these lists to build a non-drug pain plan?

743.title: Pain's toll on daily life
743.gist: After asking what members have tried and what worked, the page explains how chronic pain disrupts mood, sleep, eating, sex and relationships, and leads people to drop activities they enjoy.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Dropping activities because of pain is a form of avoidance that the fear-avoidance model (Vlaeyen) links to deconditioning, low mood and more disability. Gradual return to valued activities is a core treatment.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The shrinking world of chronic pain mirrors the narrowing of life in addiction: both crowd out pleasures and people until one thing dominates.

ask: How can someone tell the difference between protective rest and harmful avoidance?
Which lost activity would be worth restoring first, and why?

terms.d: Avoiding movement or activity out of fear of pain, which can make disability and pain worse over time.

744.title: Mood, sleep and relationships in pain
744.gist: Exercise 5 asks members to describe their mood and whether pain affects sleep, appetite, sex life and relationships with others.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The sex question may meet laughter or silence in a men's group. Name it matter-of-factly as a common medical topic; it also matters for opioids, which can lower testosterone and libido.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Depression and chronic pain commonly occur together and each worsens the other; treating depression often improves pain outcomes too.

ask: Why might members find it easier to report pain than low mood?
How would you follow up if a member's answers suggest depression?

745.title: Lost activities and psychological roots
745.gist: Exercise 5 ends asking what members gave up or wish they could do, then the page explains that anxiety, depression, past abuse, trauma and brain injury can cause or worsen pain. Exercise 6 begins with mental health history.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Adverse childhood experiences are linked in large studies to higher rates of chronic pain and substance use in adulthood. Traumatic brain injury is notably common among incarcerated people, by many estimates.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Linking trauma to pain is valid but can feel like the pain is being blamed on the person's psyche. Frame it as the nervous system staying on high alert, a physical process.

ask: How does a trauma history change the way you'd approach pain in group?
What might a wish list of lost activities reveal about a member's values?

terms.d: Brain damage from a blow or jolt to the head, which can affect thinking, mood and pain.

746.title: Trauma, head injury and sleep
746.gist: Exercise 6 continues with sensitive history questions: past abuse or trauma, head injuries, PTSD diagnosis, and sleep problems.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: These are screening questions; in a group setting, members should answer privately and not share aloud. Make clear what you will do with disclosures and your duty-to-report limits before they write.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: PTSD, poor sleep and chronic pain often feed each other: hyperarousal disturbs sleep, poor sleep lowers pain tolerance, pain disrupts sleep. Treating one strand can loosen the others.

ask: What are the ethical risks of asking trauma questions in a correctional group?
Why might head injury be underreported, and how would you ask about it more effectively?

terms.d: Post-traumatic stress disorder: lasting intrusive memories, avoidance, and hyperarousal after a traumatic event.

747.title: Telling providers about addiction
747.gist: The page urges sharing substance use history and recovery plans with care providers, especially any methadone, buprenorphine or naltrexone, since these change how pain medicines work, and notes legal confidentiality. Exercise 7 begins.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Naltrexone blocks opioid pain relief, and people on methadone or buprenorphine often need different pain strategies, sometimes higher opioid doses. Hiding these medications risks undertreated pain or dangerous interactions.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: U.S. federal confidentiality rules (42 CFR Part 2) give substance use treatment records stronger protection than most health records, a response to the stigma and legal risks clients face.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members may fear that disclosing addiction means doctors will refuse pain care. Acknowledge that stigma is real, and coach a way of stating it: I'm in recovery and want a plan that protects it.

ask: How would you advise a member who fears his addiction history will make doctors dismiss his pain?
Why does family history of addiction matter for pain treatment decisions?

748.title: Recent use and recovery supports
748.gist: Exercise 7 continues: last use and substance, over-the-counter medications, recovery group attendance, and whether the member has a sponsor and sober friends.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Over-the-counter use matters more than members think: high doses of acetaminophen can harm the liver, and mixing several products can stack up the same ingredient without realizing it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking about supports tells a provider how much risk a pain plan can carry. Someone with a sponsor and sober friends can more safely handle a short opioid course than someone isolated.

ask: Why might honesty about last use be harder with a medical provider than with a counselor?
How would supports change what pain medication a doctor is willing to prescribe?

749.title: Ask questions, build the plan together
749.gist: The page coaches members to bring written questions, a family member, and notes to appointments, offers sample questions on diagnosis, non-mood-altering options, risks and relapse, and stresses co-creating a pain plan they will actually follow.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Patients forget much of what they're told in medical visits, and the teach-back method, repeating instructions in your own words, is widely recommended to improve understanding and adherence.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Shared decision-making respects autonomy and raises follow-through, consistent with MI: people commit to plans they helped choose. Saying no to an option they won't do is honesty, not defiance.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rehearse a two-minute appointment: one plays the doctor, the other asks three questions from the list. Practice beats freezing in a real exam room.

ask: Why might members who distrust authority struggle to ask doctors questions, and how would you coach them?
Which sample question on the page matters most for someone with an opioid history?

terms.d: Patient and provider choose treatment together, weighing evidence alongside the patient's values and preferences.

750.title: Following through on the plan
750.gist: The page urges following through on referrals and recommendations right away, enlisting family for rides and support, staying in touch with providers, and adjusting the plan over time. Exercise 8 asks how members might fail to follow through.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking how you might not follow through is anticipatory problem-solving, close to a premortem: imagining failure in advance surfaces barriers like transport, cost or fear that can be planned around.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Reentry barriers are concrete: no ID, no insurance, no ride. Help members list one practical obstacle and one fix per item; Medicaid enrollment before release can matter as much as any skill.

ask: Why does the page treat pain care follow-through like recovery work, and is that a fair parallel?
Which barriers to follow-through are within a member's control and which are system failures?

751.title: Why pain care works best stacked
751.gist: Closes a follow-through question, then opens Part 3 on ways to treat pain for people recovering from addiction. It argues that several treatments combined beat any single one, starting with exercise and its mood benefits.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Pain is not just a signal from tissue; the brain amplifies or dampens it depending on mood, fear and attention. That is why lifting depression or anxiety can genuinely lower felt pain, and why a bundle of treatments hits more of the dials at once.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Melzack and Wall's gate control theory (1965) proposed that the spinal cord and brain can 'close a gate' on pain signals. It helped move pain science away from a pure wiring model toward the biopsychosocial view this session is built on.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Men who used opioids for an injury may hear 'exercise' as dismissive. Frame the multi-part plan as a toolkit a serious athlete or soldier would use, not a consolation prize for being denied pills.

ask: If mood changes how much pain hurts, where is the line between 'real' pain and 'psychological' pain, and is that line even useful?
What makes a person stick to a plan with five parts when a pill promised one easy step?

terms.d: A plan that combines several methods (movement, therapy, non-addictive medication) so each covers what the others miss.

752.title: Exercise as medicine, and its barriers
752.gist: Finishes the case for exercise (heart, blood pressure, mood, weight) and suggests a physical therapist to start safely. Exercise 9 has members recall past exercise and name and dismantle their barriers to moving regularly.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Reviews broadly support exercise for chronic low back pain and fibromyalgia, though effects are moderate and depend on sticking with it. For substance use, exercise looks promising as an add-on, but the evidence is less settled than for pain or mood.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Inside a facility, barriers are concrete: yard time, lockdowns, no equipment. Debrief by turning each barrier into a cell-sized option (bodyweight sets, walking laps, stretching before count) and plan for reentry barriers like shift work.

ask: Is 'it works if you work it' motivating or quietly blaming for someone whose pain makes movement frightening?
How would you use a decisional balance from MI to explore exercise instead of just recommending it?

terms.d: A licensed clinician who teaches targeted exercises and movement to restore strength, range and function.

753.title: Physical therapy and lost abilities
753.gist: Explains what physical and occupational therapists do: targeted exercises, hands-on work, and less painful ways to handle daily tasks. Exercise 10 asks members about past PT and which lost abilities they want back.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Chronic pain often traps people in fear-avoidance: they stop moving to avoid hurting, lose strength, and then hurt more. Graded activity under a therapist breaks the loop by proving movement is safe in small doses.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to name one specific thing pain has taken (lifting a child, playing ball, kneeling to pray) and say it aloud. A concrete lost ability is a far stronger motivator than a vague goal of getting healthier.

ask: How is fear-avoidance in pain similar to avoidance in anxiety or in early recovery?
What does losing a physical ability do to a man's identity, and how might that feed using?

terms.d: A clinician who helps people do everyday activities (work, self-care, chores) in ways that suit their body and limits.

754.title: Thinking tools and hypnosis for pain
754.gist: Presents cognitive-behavioral therapy and clinical hypnosis as pain treatments. CBT builds coping, relaxation, flare plans and a problem-solving stance; hypnosis uses focused attention to lower pain intensity and restore a sense of control.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Pain catastrophizing (magnifying, ruminating, feeling helpless) predicts worse pain and disability. CBT targets those thoughts directly, which is why the same skills members use against cravings transfer to pain.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: CBT for chronic pain shows consistent but modest benefits on pain and distress, with larger effects on mood and disability than on pain itself. Hypnosis has supportive trials too, though responsiveness varies a lot between people.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: 'Hypnosis' may sound like a stage trick or mind control to some members, and in custody that can raise trust issues. Present it as trained focused attention, close to guided imagery, and respect anyone who opts out.

ask: If CBT reduces suffering more than pain intensity, what exactly is it changing?
Why might a sense of control matter so much for people whose daily lives are tightly controlled by others?

terms.d: A guided state of deep focus used by trained clinicians to shift perception, such as how strongly pain is felt.
A pattern of magnifying pain, dwelling on it, and feeling helpless about it.

755.title: Borrowing recovery skills for pain
755.gist: Exercise 11 asks members how group therapy has helped their addiction recovery, then which pain-related problems they want techniques for, such as sleep, stress or helplessness.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Make the bridge explicit: the thought record they use for a craving can be used for a pain spike. Members gain confidence when they learn they already own the toolkit rather than needing to start over.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Transfer of learning rarely happens on its own; people tend to file skills under the context they learned them in. Naming the overlap and rehearsing it in the new context is what makes the skill portable.

ask: Which CBI or LIB skill do you think transfers most naturally to pain, and which one least?
What signs would tell you a member is using 'coping skills' talk to avoid seeing a doctor?

756.title: Non-addictive pain medicines and their limits
756.gist: Surveys mood-neutral pain medicines suitable in recovery: NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and antidepressants such as SNRIs and tricyclics used for nerve and widespread pain. It flags stomach bleeding with NSAIDs and liver risk with acetaminophen overdose.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: NSAIDs block enzymes that make inflammatory prostaglandins, so they suit inflammatory and dental pain. SNRIs and tricyclics act on pain-dampening pathways running from brain to spinal cord, which helps explain why they work for nerve pain at doses unrelated to their antidepressant effect.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect jokes that Tylenol does nothing. Validate that it is weaker than opioids, then stress that combining a modest medicine with movement and skills can match more than people expect, without the relapse cost.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: 'Not addicting' does not mean harmless; people with heavy drinking histories face added liver and stomach risks with these drugs. Members should never self-dose to make up for the lack of opioids.

ask: Why might an antidepressant prescribed for pain carry stigma for a man in custody, and how would you address it?
What makes a drug 'mood-changing' enough to threaten recovery, and where do medicines like gabapentin sit in that debate?

terms.d: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, like ibuprofen or naproxen, which eases pain by reducing inflammation.
An antidepressant class that boosts serotonin and norepinephrine and also eases some chronic pain.

757.title: When opioids are on the table
757.gist: Repeats that combined treatments beat single ones, then opens Part 4: for people with addiction and chronic pain, opioids are sometimes appropriate, only when benefit outweighs risk and with firm limits. It names dependence, relapse and withdrawal-driven pain as the risks.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The page uses a risk-benefit frame instead of an abstinence absolute. That is a harm-reduction stance inside a Twelve Step-friendly curriculum, and it mirrors how modern pain medicine treats addiction history as a risk factor rather than an automatic ban.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Medical ethics weighs beneficence against nonmaleficence: relieving suffering versus avoiding harm. Undertreated pain is itself a relapse risk, so refusing all opioids is not automatically the safe choice.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will hear 'sometimes' as a loophole. Ask them to describe what honest, limited, supervised use would look like, and who in their life would notice if it drifted.

ask: Is 'sometimes' the most honest answer, and what would it take for you to trust a member's judgment about it?
How do Twelve Step views of 'clean time' fit with a supervised, prescribed opioid after surgery?

terms.d: The body's adaptation to a drug so that stopping it causes withdrawal; different from addiction, which involves compulsive use despite harm.

758.title: Weighing opioid benefits against risks
758.gist: Notes that opioids only partly relieve pain, lose effect with tolerance, and bring sedation, confusion, constipation and overdose risk when mixed. Exercise 12 has members picture a situation where benefits might win and list their personal risks.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Trials of long-term opioids for chronic non-cancer pain have generally shown small benefits and real harms, which shifted guidelines toward caution. Some patients also develop opioid-induced hyperalgesia, where the drug seems to increase pain sensitivity.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by separating 'risk to anyone' from 'risk to me': overdose history, mixing with benzodiazepines or alcohol, who supplies refills. Personal risk lists change behavior more than generic warnings do.

ask: How would you tell genuine pain needs apart from drug-seeking without becoming cynical toward everyone?
Why does tolerance make opioids especially tricky for a disease defined by escalation?

terms.d: Needing more of a drug over time to get the same effect.
A state where long-term opioid use makes a person more sensitive to pain.

759.title: Pain care while on MAT
759.gist: Explains that pain and addiction doctors should coordinate for people on MAT: buprenorphine doses may be split for relief, methadone patients may get a short added opioid, and naltrexone blocks opioid pain relief. Exercise 13 checks MAT status and comfort talking about pain.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist that binds tightly to opioid receptors; methadone is a full agonist; naltrexone is an antagonist that blocks them. Those three mechanisms explain each pain strategy on the page.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members fear being labeled drug-seeking if they mention pain to a doctor. Role-play a short, specific script: where it hurts, how long, what has been tried, and that they are in recovery and want a safe plan.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Access is the real-world gap: jails and prisons vary widely in offering MAT, and people often lose it at release. Planning around MAT and pain must include the handoff to community care.

ask: What does a person on naltrexone need to know before an emergency surgery?
How might shame about MAT keep someone silent about pain, and how does that link to stigma within some recovery groups?

terms.d: A drug that activates a receptor only partly, giving a capped effect; buprenorphine works this way.

760.title: The opioid treatment agreement
760.gist: Describes opioid treatment agreements: written expectations between patient and provider covering drug screens, one pharmacy, refill limits, pill counts and permission to talk with others. It presents them as tools for clarity, accountability and safety.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Critics note these agreements can feel like contracts of suspicion and their effect on misuse is not well proven. For people coming out of custody, urine tests and counts may echo surveillance more than partnership.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Behavioral contracting in psychology works best when both sides commit to something. An agreement that only lists patient duties is compliance monitoring; one that also lists provider duties is a working alliance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Reframe the rules as guardrails a person chooses in advance, like Ulysses tied to the mast so he could hear the Sirens safely. Pre-commitment is a strength, not a sign of being distrusted.

ask: What would make an agreement feel collaborative rather than punitive to someone on probation?
How is a treatment agreement like or unlike a relapse prevention plan a member writes for himself?

terms.d: A written plan stating what patient and prescriber each commit to while opioids are used for pain.
Choosing limits ahead of time to protect yourself from future impulses.

761.title: Drafting both sides of an agreement
761.gist: Exercise 14 asks members what they would want from a provider and what the provider would want from them. The page then begins on stopping opioids, which are usually prescribed only for short periods in this population.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Split the group into 'patients' and 'prescribers' to draft the agreement, then swap. Seeing the provider's fears (diversion, overdose, liability) often softens members' resentment of the rules.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking what they want from the provider is an empowerment move: it treats members as consumers with rights, not just people to monitor. That fits the shared decision-making model in modern medicine.

ask: What would a fair agreement include about how the provider treats a slip?
Why might people with incarceration histories struggle to ask a professional for anything at all?

762.title: Tapering safely and flare planning
762.gist: Lists reasons to stop opioids (pain eased, no longer working, side effects, cravings) and warns against stopping alone. It then teaches a written plan for intense pain episodes, and Exercise 15 asks which episodes members expect.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Abrupt opioid discontinuation has been linked to withdrawal, uncontrolled pain, and in some cases a turn to illicit drugs and overdose. That is why guidance now favors gradual, supported tapers.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to write the plan on a card while calm, because pain and panic shrink thinking. Include doctor's number, the non-opioid steps, and one person to call who knows they are in recovery.

ask: What predictable pain episodes (dental work, surgery, old injuries) would your members face after release?
How is a flare plan like a 'coping card' for cravings, and why do both work better when written in advance?

terms.d: Pain that is intense but short-lived, often after injury or surgery.
Gradually lowering a medication dose to reduce withdrawal and rebound pain.

763.title: When pain treatment stirs cravings
763.gist: Finishes the flare-planning question, then shows what to do if short-term opioids awaken cravings: tell the provider and counselor, call a sponsor, attend meetings, and lean harder on the non-drug pain plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt and Gordon's relapse prevention model treats a lapse as a moment of choice, not destiny. Cravings after a prescribed dose are a high-risk situation that calls for coping, not proof that recovery has failed.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Neuroscience calls this cue-induced craving: the drug itself re-primes reward circuits shaped by past use. That helps explain why even legitimate medical exposure can feel like a trigger.

ask: How would you help a member avoid the abstinence violation effect if a prescribed opioid sparked cravings?
Who should be told first about craving: the doctor, the sponsor, or the counselor, and why?

terms.d: A strong urge or craving to use a substance.

764.title: Past cravings, future defenses
764.gist: Exercise 16 asks members to describe a craving they had while in recovery, its cause and their response, then list what they can do when cravings appear.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Mine the past example for what worked, not just what went wrong. A member who once survived a craving by calling his brother already has evidence of self-efficacy, a core idea in Bandura's work.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Teach urge surfing: notice the craving, rate it, breathe, and watch it rise and fall like a wave over a few minutes. It pairs well with pain, which also tends to come in waves.

ask: What makes a craving story useful for learning instead of just stirring shame?
How could you tell if a member's plan is realistic for life after release rather than tailored to the facility?

terms.d: A mindfulness skill of riding out a craving by watching it build and fade without acting on it.

765.title: Session 35 wrap-up
765.gist: Summarizes the chronic pain session: rating pain, seeing its biological, psychological and social effects, working with providers, treatment options, and handling opioids for intense pain without endangering recovery.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Close by asking each member for one sentence: the single pain tool they will try this week. A spoken commitment in front of peers tends to stick better than a silent one.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The session assumes access to physical therapy, CBT and coordinated providers. For many returning citizens on Medicaid or uninsured, the realistic plan may start with a free clinic and self-guided exercise.

ask: Which part of this session would change most if you taught it to women, or to older adults?
What would a member need on day one after release to keep this plan alive?

766.title: Session 35 key terms
