766.gist: Defines acute and chronic pain, biopsychosocial processes, opioid treatment agreements, the stress response, and tolerance for the chronic pain session.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: George Engel proposed the biopsychosocial model in 1977 as a challenge to purely biomedical thinking. It now shapes pain medicine, addiction treatment and counseling psychology alike.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The six-month cutoff for chronic pain is a convention; many clinicians use three months. Tell members the label matters less than the pattern: pain that outlasts healing needs a different approach.

ask: Why is calling something a 'process' rather than an 'event' a clinical choice with consequences?
How does the stress response connect pain, anxiety and craving in one body system?

terms.d: Looking at a problem through body, mind and social life together.

767.title: Opening the chronic diseases session
767.gist: Introduces Session 36 on chronic diseases alongside substance use disorders, in two parts: understanding chronic and comorbid disorders, and living in balance with them. It lists learning goals for each part.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Addiction is often described as a chronic, relapsing condition, much like diabetes or hypertension. This session quietly uses that parallel: the habits that manage one chronic illness also manage the other.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: People leaving prison have higher rates of chronic conditions like hypertension, hepatitis C and asthma than the general population, and the first weeks after release carry elevated risk of death, especially from overdose.

ask: What do you gain and lose by calling addiction a chronic disease like diabetes?
Which chronic diseases are most common among your members, and how often are they diagnosed?

768.title: What this session will ask
768.gist: Finishes the objectives (diet, exercise, support groups, health journals, apps) and explains that members will examine how a chronic disease and addiction affect each other. It warns the work is personal and lists glossary terms.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A new diagnosis inside a facility can feel like another sentence. Open by normalizing fear and asking what members already know about their own conditions, so the session starts from their knowledge rather than a lecture.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Susan Sontag's 'Illness as Metaphor' argued that we load diseases with moral meaning. Members may see illness as punishment for past use; untangling blame from responsibility is part of this work.

ask: Why might a health journal or app be harder to use after release than the session assumes?
How does guilt about past use shape how someone cares for a disease that use may have worsened?

769.title: What makes a disease chronic
769.gist: Defines chronic diseases: slow to develop, long-lasting, multi-causal, disabling, not self-resolving, manageable but rarely curable. It notes they are very common and rise with age, listing examples like diabetes, heart disease and hepatitis.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The shift from curing to managing changes the goal from 'fix it' to 'live well with it.' That is the same mental shift recovery asks for: daily maintenance rather than a single victory.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Epidemiologists call the 20th-century move from infections to chronic illness as main killers the epidemiologic transition. Longer lives and changing lifestyles turned slow diseases into the main battleground of health.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask who knows someone with diabetes or high blood pressure who 'did everything right' and someone who ignored it. Contrasting the two outcomes makes 'manageable' concrete.

ask: What is psychologically harder: a disease you can cure once, or one you must manage forever?
How could you use the idea of management to soften all-or-nothing thinking about recovery?

terms.d: A long-lasting health condition that usually can be managed but not fully cured.

770.title: Naming your own chronic conditions
770.gist: Exercise 1 asks members whether they have a diagnosed chronic disease and whether such diseases run in their family.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members may suspect a condition but never had a diagnosis due to no insurance or avoiding doctors. Treat 'I don't know' as a valid answer that leads to a screening request, not a failure.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A family history is a map of inherited risk mixed with shared habits and environment. Seeing both strands helps members see what they can change and what they need to monitor.

ask: How would you respond if a member disclosed a serious condition like hepatitis C for the first time in group?
What confidentiality limits apply when health information is shared in a correctional group?

771.title: Four habits behind most chronic disease
771.gist: Shows that chronic diseases lead US deaths and disability, with heart disease and cancer accounting for a large share. It names four changeable risk behaviors (inactivity, poor diet, tobacco, heavy drinking), and Exercise 2 asks which apply to members.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Calling these behaviors the cause can hide social causes: poverty, food deserts, stress, and prison diets. Individual choice matters, but members' options were often shaped by circumstance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Tobacco is still common in recovery circles and sometimes treated as the 'last vice.' Note that research suggests quitting smoking during addiction treatment does not harm, and may support, sobriety.

ask: How do you hold personal responsibility and structural causes together without letting either erase the other?
Why are the same four behaviors so often clustered in people with substance use disorders?

terms.d: A changeable habit, like smoking or inactivity, that raises the chance of disease.

772.title: Prevention and the recovery bonus
772.gist: Says the most common and costly chronic diseases are largely preventable and manageable through healthy eating, activity, avoiding tobacco and limiting alcohol. It adds that the same habits strengthen addiction recovery.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is the logic of 'keystone habits': one healthy routine tends to pull others along. Regular exercise, for example, often improves sleep and eating, which in turn steadies mood.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Aristotle described virtue as built through repeated action until it becomes character. Recovery and disease management both run on that idea: who you become is what you practice.

ask: Which single healthy behavior would give your members the biggest double benefit for health and sobriety?
Why does 'preventable' sometimes increase shame instead of motivation?

terms.d: A routine that sets off a chain of other positive changes.

773.title: Healthy habits now and next
773.gist: Exercise 3 asks which healthy behaviors members already practice, which they want to add, and how such habits could improve their lives.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Start with what they already do; it builds self-efficacy before asking for change. Then use a 1-to-10 confidence ruler from motivational interviewing on the new habit they choose.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have each member write an implementation intention: 'When X happens, I will do Y.' Specific if-then plans tend to beat vague goals in follow-through.

ask: What separates a habit a member wants from one he thinks the counselor wants to hear?
How would the answers change between life inside and the first month home?

terms.d: A specific if-then plan linking a situation to a chosen action.

774.title: Comorbid: two conditions, one person
774.gist: Explains that 'co-occurring' usually means addiction plus a mental disorder in treatment settings, while medicine uses 'comorbid' for any two or more conditions, including addiction plus a physical disease. Exercise 4 asks members to describe their own.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Co-occurring mental and substance use disorders are common, and integrated treatment that addresses both at once generally outperforms sequential or separate care.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The term comorbidity is credited to physician Alvan Feinstein around 1970. It reminds clinicians that the 'other' illness changes prognosis and treatment of the main one.

ask: How should your treatment plan change when a member has addiction, PTSD and diabetes at once?
Is 'comorbid' a useful label for members, or mostly a clinician's word?

terms.d: Two or more health conditions present in the same person at the same time.
In addiction treatment, usually a substance use disorder plus a mental health disorder.

775.title: How two conditions shape a life
775.gist: Continues Exercise 4, asking how members' comorbid conditions affect their lives and how healthy behaviors could help.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Listen for the vicious cycles: pain or illness leads to using, which worsens the illness. Draw the loop on the board with a member's permission and look for the easiest point to break it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Systems thinking sees feedback loops rather than single causes. Small changes at one point in the loop can ripple through the whole cycle.

ask: Where in a typical illness-and-use cycle is intervention easiest for your members?
How would you avoid repeating the earlier healthy-behaviors question so it feels fresh?

776.title: Each disorder runs its own course
776.gist: Teaches that comorbid disorders are independent: neither causes the other, and each has its own symptoms, untreated course, treatment plan and recovery. Exercise 5 asks members to explain this idea in their own words.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Strict independence is a simplification. Alcohol can cause liver disease, injection drug use can transmit hepatitis, and depression can feed drinking; conditions often interact or share causes even while each needs its own care.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Use the independence idea practically: getting sober does not cure diabetes, and controlling blood sugar does not cure addiction. Each needs its own daily attention.

ask: When is it helpful to treat disorders as independent, and when does it mislead?
How does this idea challenge the belief that 'once I'm clean, everything else will fix itself'?

777.title: Symptoms rise and fall independently
777.gist: Closes Exercise 5 with a personal example, then explains that each comorbid condition varies in severity on its own timeline. Cravings flare with triggers and ease with skills, just as asthma flares with mold or stress and diabetes quiets with good care.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Asthma is a sharp teaching analogy: a hidden vulnerability, quiet stretches, and attacks set off by triggers. Members who know asthma from family life can map their own craving pattern onto it without feeling judged.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Seeing symptoms as waves rather than a fixed state undercuts all-or-nothing thinking. A bad week of cravings becomes information about triggers instead of proof of failure.

ask: How might the asthma analogy reduce moral blame around cravings, and where does it fall short?
What would a member need to track to notice that both conditions flare together?

778.title: Charting two sets of symptoms
778.gist: Exercise 6 asks members to list the main symptoms of their chronic disease and of their substance use disorder, and when each is strongest or weakest.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members sketch two lines on one timeline, one per condition, across a typical week. Overlapping peaks (Friday night stress, pay day, poor sleep) often reveal a shared trigger worth targeting.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some men will only list physical cravings. Prompt for the quieter symptoms: irritability, boredom, isolation, sleep loss. Naming them widens the early-warning system.

ask: What does it tell you clinically when a member can describe disease symptoms well but not addiction symptoms, or the reverse?
How could this chart feed into a written relapse prevention plan?

779.title: Both conditions need a real diagnosis
779.gist: Stresses that untreated comorbid disorders worsen and can kill, so both need professional screening, assessment and diagnosis. It urges members who have not seen a doctor to talk with their counselor now, and Exercise 7 asks about the benefits of testing.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Avoiding doctors is often tied to past mistreatment, fear of bad news, or distrust of institutions. Explore those reasons with curiosity before pushing a referral, the way MI explores ambivalence.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Ethicists discuss a 'right not to know,' but for treatable conditions like hepatitis C or hypertension, early diagnosis changes outcomes dramatically. Knowledge here is a tool for control, not just a burden.

ask: What stops your members from getting screened, and which of those barriers can a counselor actually influence?
How do you respond when a member says he would rather not know?

780.title: Two conditions, two treatment plans
780.gist: Asks whether members have discussed their disease with a clinician, then explains that each disorder needs its own specialized care: a primary care doctor and specialists for the disease, and the addiction team for the substance use disorder, producing two plans to follow.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Two separate plans can conflict or leave gaps, for example a doctor prescribing a benzodiazepine unaware of addiction history. Integrated or coordinated care, with consent to share information, usually works better than parallel tracks.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Encourage members to be the bridge: carry a one-page list of both diagnoses, all medications and their recovery status to every appointment.

ask: Who is responsible for coordinating two plans when the providers never talk to each other?
How does reentry disrupt continuity of medical care, and what could you build into discharge planning?

terms.d: The main doctor who screens, treats common conditions and refers to specialists.

781.title: When one illness feeds the other
781.gist: Exercise 8 asks the dos and don'ts of a disease plan and how it resembles a recovery plan. The page then shows how comorbid conditions can worsen each other, using cocaine's strain on a diseased heart as the example.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Cocaine is a stimulant that raises heart rate and blood pressure and narrows coronary arteries, so it can trigger heart attacks and dangerous rhythms even in young people. For someone with heart disease, the risk is amplified.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The similarity question invites members to see that a medical plan and a recovery plan share a structure: daily routines, avoid triggers, monitor warning signs, know when to get help. That shared structure is relapse prevention by another name.

ask: Why might a vivid medical consequence like a heart attack motivate some members and leave others unmoved?
Which other drug-disease pairs (alcohol and liver, smoking and asthma) would land best with your group?

terms.d: An abnormal heart rhythm, which can be life-threatening.

782.title: The loop runs both directions
782.gist: Shows the reverse path: neglecting heart care brings fatigue, stress, poor sleep and low mood, which are classic cocaine triggers. Exercise 9 asks members how their disease affects their substance use and vice versa.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The HALT reminder (hungry, angry, lonely, tired) from recovery culture captures this: body states lower self-control and raise craving. Poor disease care creates those states every day.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by drawing a figure-eight on the board, one loop per condition, crossing at shared triggers like sleep and stress. Ask members to mark one crossing point they could change this week.

ask: Is low mood a symptom of neglected illness, a trigger for use, or both, and does the distinction matter for treatment?
How would you adapt this example for a member with diabetes rather than heart disease?

terms.d: A recovery reminder to check if you are Hungry, Angry, Lonely or Tired before acting on urges.

783.title: Healing one helps heal the other
783.gist: Turns the cycle positive: treating one condition with exercise, healthy eating and avoiding tobacco and alcohol lifts energy, sleep, mood and thinking, which supports the other condition's recovery. Exercise 10 asks how disease recovery improves well-being.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is the upward spiral idea from positive psychology, linked to Barbara Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory: small gains in well-being widen people's options and build resources, making the next gain easier.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name one 'small win' from the past month in either area, then trace what it made easier next. Seeing their own chain makes the spiral believable.

ask: Why do vicious cycles feel more natural to people than virtuous ones?
Where might a member hit a plateau in the upward spiral, and how would you keep him going?

784.title: Partnering with two care teams
784.gist: Finishes Exercise 10, then opens Part 2 on living with comorbid disorders. Members are coached to treat both care teams as resources, keep regular appointments, use a question worksheet with the doctor, and tell addiction staff about their disease.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Patient activation research links being informed, confident and engaged in one's care with better self-management and outcomes in chronic illness. Engagement is a skill that can be taught.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members learned to be passive or guarded with authority figures. Practice how to ask a doctor a question and how to say 'I didn't understand, can you explain again' without feeling small.

ask: How do power dynamics between a formerly incarcerated patient and a physician affect what he will disclose?
What would 'activated patient' look like for someone with low health literacy?

terms.d: A person's knowledge, skill and confidence in managing their own health.

785.title: Rating what you know about your illness
785.gist: Exercise 11 asks members to rate their knowledge of their chronic disease and of how to manage it as strong, medium or weak, say where they learned it, and list what they still want to know.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-rating builds metacognition: knowing what you know and what you don't. People often overrate knowledge of familiar topics, so asking for sources tests whether confidence is earned.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect street knowledge and myths (for example, that hepatitis C means certain death, though modern antivirals usually cure it). Treat myths as the starting point for education, not as foolishness.

ask: How does the Dunning-Kruger pattern show up in health beliefs among your members?
Which sources of health information do your members trust most, and why?

786.title: Questions to bring the doctor
786.gist: Presents the Physician Question Worksheet, a two-column form covering diagnosis, causes, treatment options, diet, exercise, medications and doses, substances to avoid, visit frequency, and when to seek emergency care.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Stress the 'substances to avoid' line: it is where members can safely disclose addiction history and ask about interactions. Practice asking it out loud until it feels routine.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Medicine's 'teach-back' method has patients repeat instructions in their own words to confirm understanding. Members can flip it: summarize the doctor's answer back to check they got it right.

ask: Which question on this list would your members be least likely to ask, and why?
What would you add for someone with both an addiction and a chronic disease?

terms.d: Repeating health instructions in your own words to confirm you understood them.

787.title: Tracking symptoms and side effects
787.gist: Explains that symptoms of both conditions shift with stress and events, so members should log them and learn their medications. It warns that quitting meds over side effects can backfire, and Exercise 12 starts a symptom checklist.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Poor medication adherence is common in chronic illness, often estimated at around half of patients not taking medicines as prescribed. Side effects, cost and forgetting are frequent reasons.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Writing side effects down turns a vague complaint into data the doctor can act on, often by changing dose or drug. It replaces a silent, risky decision to quit with a collaborative one.

ask: How is stopping a medication over side effects like stopping recovery work when it feels uncomfortable?
What makes a symptom log stick for someone who has never journaled?

terms.d: Taking treatment as agreed with your provider.

788.title: Symptom log and trusted sources
788.gist: Offers a Symptom Checklist grid for each symptom, when it appears, its strength and its discomfort on 1-10 scales. It then urges self-education through national disease associations and federal health websites.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Fill one row together using a common example, like knee pain rated 6 in the morning and 3 after walking. Modeling one row removes the confusion of a blank grid.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Sending members to websites assumes internet access and reading level that many returning citizens lack. Offer library computers, printed fact sheets or a clinic nurse as alternatives.

ask: How would you teach members to tell a trustworthy health website from a sales page or rumor?
Why does separating 'strength' from 'discomfort' on the grid matter?

789.title: Staying informed and eating well
789.gist: Describes what disease associations offer (fact sheets, support groups, patient navigators, help with insurance) and urges staying current as treatments evolve. It then gives general healthy diet guidelines, to be tailored with a physician.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Patient navigators can be gold for reentry: they help with insurance and finding clinics. Make finding one a concrete reentry task, not just reading.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Recovery often brings sugar cravings as the brain seeks quick reward, and some people swap alcohol for sweets. A diet plan that expects this is more realistic than one that ignores it.

ask: What would a healthy diet realistically look like on a tight budget in a neighborhood with few grocery stores?
How does staying informed protect patients from outdated treatment?

terms.d: A helper who guides patients through care, appointments and insurance.

790.title: Is your diet helping or hurting?
790.gist: Exercise 13 asks whether members' current diet supports recovery and disease management and how it could improve. The page then introduces federal exercise guidelines, advising members to check their exercise plan with a physician.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Commissary and institutional food limit choices. Debrief on small swaps available now, then plan the bigger changes for after release, so the exercise doesn't feel pointless.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Heavy drinking and drug use commonly leave nutrient deficiencies, such as low thiamine in long-term drinkers. Nutrition repair is part of early recovery, not a luxury.

ask: How do food and mood interact in early recovery?
What would make a diet change feel like self-respect rather than another rule?

791.title: How much movement counts
791.gist: Lays out the guidelines: any activity beats none, about 150 minutes of moderate or 75 of vigorous aerobic exercise weekly, and strength training twice a week. Short bouts count, and it lists aerobic activities from walking to tennis.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The biggest health gains come from moving from no activity to some activity; benefits keep rising with more but with diminishing returns. That makes 'any is better than none' good science, not just encouragement.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Do a two-minute brisk march in place with the group, then ask how heart rate and mood changed. Feeling the effect beats hearing about it.

ask: How would you translate 150 minutes into a weekly plan that fits a member's shift job after release?
Why might vigorous exercise feel risky to someone with heart disease, and what would you advise?

terms.d: Activity that raises breathing and heart rate but still lets you talk, like brisk walking.

792.title: Choosing activities that fit
792.gist: Lists strength activities (bands, weights, bodyweight, gardening, carrying, yoga, Tai Chi). Exercise 14 asks which members do now, which would suit their recovery and disease, and how to remove barriers.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Tai Chi and yoga blend movement with breath and attention, close cousins of mindfulness. They may train the same calm focus that helps people ride out cravings.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some men may see yoga as unmasculine. Mention that athletes and military programs use it for flexibility and stress, and offer calisthenics as an equal choice.

ask: What activity would give a member both exercise and sober social contact?
How do identity and culture shape which exercises people will try?

terms.d: Exercises that use your own body weight for resistance, like push-ups and squats.

793.title: Peers who share the diagnosis
793.gist: Reports that peer support helps people with many chronic diseases adjust, manage and feel less depressed and isolated. It describes online, phone and face-to-face formats and lists benefits from shared experience to better communication with doctors.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Peer support works partly through modeling, as in Bandura's social learning theory: seeing someone like you succeed raises your belief that you can too. It is the same engine that powers Twelve Step sponsorship.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Peer groups vary in quality; some spread misinformation or discourage medication. Members should treat peer advice as experience to discuss with a clinician, not a substitute for treatment.

ask: What makes a peer more persuasive than a professional in some situations?
How could a member who already attends AA or NA build on that habit for a disease support group?

terms.d: Help from people who share the same condition or experience.

794.title: Finding a disease support group
794.gist: Exercise 15 names associations for arthritis, Alzheimer's, lung disease and diabetes, notes groups meet in community spaces or online, and asks members to find a group and record when and how it meets.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Turn research into action: help each member leave with one real group name and meeting time near the address they will return to. A plan with a place and time is far more likely to happen.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members practice a 20-second introduction they could say at a first meeting. Rehearsal lowers the social fear that keeps people from walking in.

ask: How would you help a member with no internet access complete this exercise?
Which barriers to attending a first meeting are emotional rather than practical?

795.title: Goals for support and journaling
795.gist: Finishes Exercise 15 by asking what members want from a group and its contact details. It then introduces health journaling, claiming research links it to better physical and emotional outcomes across several chronic illnesses.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: James Pennebaker's expressive writing research found benefits from writing about emotional experiences, and some trials in asthma and arthritis showed improvements. Later reviews suggest effects are real but often small and inconsistent, so the page's claims are stronger than the evidence.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Expressive writing can briefly stir distress, especially for trauma survivors. In a prison setting, also consider privacy: a journal can be read during searches.

ask: How would you present journaling honestly given mixed evidence?
What should a member do if journaling brings up trauma memories?

terms.d: Writing about deep thoughts and feelings around a difficult experience.

796.title: How to keep a health journal
796.gist: Explains that writing about comorbid disorders can help understand and manage emotions, then gives tips: a dedicated notebook, fifteen minutes daily, thoughts, feelings, life impact, recent changes and symptoms. Exercise 16 starts a practice entry.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Putting feelings into words, called affect labeling, has been shown in brain imaging studies to lower activity in the amygdala. Naming an emotion helps tame it, which links journaling to emotion regulation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For members who struggle with writing, allow bullet points, drawings, or a feelings word list. The habit of noticing matters more than the prose.

ask: What's the difference between journaling that processes emotion and journaling that feeds rumination?
How could a journal also serve as an early warning system for relapse?

terms.d: Putting a feeling into words, which can lessen its intensity.

797.title: Practice journal entry
797.gist: Completes Exercise 16 with prompts for current feelings, how the comorbid disorders affect life, family and work, and recent changes and symptoms.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: After writing, ask members to circle one word that surprised them. Reflecting on the surprise builds insight faster than rereading the whole entry.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Invite sharing but never require it; read-aloud pressure can make men write for the group rather than for themselves.

ask: How would you debrief this exercise without turning private writing into public performance?
What patterns across a week of entries would be most clinically useful?

798.title: Health apps for illness and recovery
798.gist: Describes health apps for chronic diseases (an asthma tracker example), finding AA or NA meetings, and mental well-being tools like breathing, meditation and biofeedback. Exercise 17 starts an app store search.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Most health apps have never been rigorously tested, though a few digital therapeutics for substance use have trial support. Quality, privacy and data sharing vary widely.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Members in custody usually have no smartphones, and some on supervision face phone monitoring. Treat this as reentry planning rather than an immediate task.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Apps work by prompts and tracking, the self-monitoring principle from behavior therapy: what gets measured tends to change, at least while people keep measuring.

ask: How would you judge whether a recovery app is helpful or just engaging?
What privacy risks do health apps pose for people on parole?

terms.d: Using a device to see body signals like heart rate so you can learn to control them.

799.title: Picking three apps to try
799.gist: Continues Exercise 17, asking members to find three apps tied to their chronic disease, describe what they do, and explain how they might help.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: If devices are unavailable, bring printed screenshots or descriptions of a few well-known free apps and let members compare features. The judgment skill transfers even without a phone.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rank their three apps by the one feature they would really use. Most people use one function; picking it guards against downloading and forgetting.

ask: What feature in a health app is most likely to keep someone using it after the novelty wears off?
Could an app replace human contact in recovery, or only support it?

800.title: Five pillars of living in balance
800.gist: Pulls the session together: understand your disorders, stay informed and ask if treatment is current, take charge of both recovery plans with an emergency plan, eat well, and exercise to manage disease and reduce anxiety and depression.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan) holds that autonomy, competence and relatedness fuel lasting motivation. 'Take charge,' learning, and support groups map neatly onto those three needs.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to define a medical emergency and an addiction emergency for themselves, such as chest pain or a strong urge with drugs within reach, and who they would call for each.

ask: Which pillar is hardest for your members, and why?
How does 'take charge of your recovery' sit with the Twelve Step idea of admitting powerlessness?

801.title: Taking charge of both recoveries
801.gist: Urges joining disease support groups the way one joins Twelve Step groups. Exercise 18 asks how well members understand their disease, how to learn more, and how to take charge of their disease recovery.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The Twelve Step tradition grew partly from the Oxford Group and influenced later self-help groups for other conditions. Members already fluent in meeting culture have a ready template for disease groups.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push for one concrete action per question. 'Learn more' becomes 'ask the nurse about my A1C at next visit.'

ask: Is there a risk in treating every condition through a Twelve Step lens?
How specific does a 'take charge' plan need to be before you trust it?

802.title: Picturing a healthier future self
802.gist: Finishes Exercise 18 on addiction recovery, then Exercise 19 leads a guided visualization: relax, recall the harm from illness and use, imagine the future self, name goals, and treat reaching them as a source of purpose and meaning.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Viktor Frankl argued that people can endure much when they have a 'why.' This exercise borrows that logotherapy idea: purpose as a protective factor.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Pure positive fantasy can sap effort, Gabriele Oettingen found; pairing the wished-for future with obstacles and an if-then plan (her WOOP method) works better. Consider adding an obstacle step.

ask: How would you adapt this visualization for a member who has trouble imagining any future?
What risks come with guided imagery for trauma survivors, and how would you set it up safely?

terms.d: Imagining a goal, then the obstacles in the way, to boost follow-through.

803.title: Session 36 wrap-up
803.gist: Summarizes the chronic disease session: how a chronic disease and addiction interact, the two treatment plans, and healthy behaviors and tools for managing both. It acknowledges the courage the session required.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to name the one link between his illness and his use that he hadn't seen before. A single insight is easier to carry out of the room than a summary.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The session leans on individual behavior and gives less weight to health care access, insurance and housing, which shape outcomes after release. Pair it with concrete reentry health linkage.

ask: What evidence would show you this session changed behavior, not just knowledge?
How would you follow up with a member who disclosed a new diagnosis here?

804.title: Session 36 key terms
804.gist: Defines chronic diseases, comorbid, comorbid diseases, co-occurring disorders, and the four health risk behaviors behind most chronic illness.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Clarify that 'co-occurring' and 'comorbid' are mostly a matter of field vocabulary; members will hear both in treatment and medical settings and should know they overlap.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The 'four behaviors' framing comes from public health research on preventable death. It is powerful for prevention but simplifies how genes, environment and stress also contribute.

ask: Why do different professions develop different words for the same thing, and what does it cost patients?
How would you explain 'comorbid' to a member in one plain sentence?

805.title: Opening the older adults session
805.gist: Introduces Session 37 for adults sixty and over, noting rising alcohol and prescription drug use among seniors. It previews low-risk drinking limits, alcohol-medication dangers, and how losses in later life (work, health, people, routine) feed use.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Later life piles up losses while removing the roles that once gave structure. Many models of late-onset drinking see it as a coping response to that squeeze, which is why this session leans on meaning and connection.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Erik Erikson's last stage, integrity versus despair, frames old age as a time to make peace with the life lived. Addiction can tip the balance toward despair; recovery can reopen integrity.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In a prison population, 'older' often starts earlier: people aging behind bars tend to show health problems sooner than their age suggests. Many corrections systems treat 50 or 55 as the older-adult threshold.

ask: How does incarceration change what 'loss of work and routine' means for an older member?
Which of Erikson's stages do you see most often in your groups, and how does addiction distort it?

806.title: Goals and demands of this session
806.gist: Lists the objectives for both parts, from identifying the main substance used by older adults and reviewing past and present use, to examining losses, retirement, meaning, recreation and spirituality. It asks members to look honestly at use and medications.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Older members may feel lumped in or patronized by a session aimed at seniors. Invite them to act as the experts on aging in the room and let younger members listen.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: References to grandchildren and retirement assume a conventional life course. Many incarcerated older adults have broken family ties or no work history to retire from, so adapt examples.

ask: What does respect look like when facilitating with someone decades older than you?
How might ageism inside treatment programs shape what older members disclose?

807.title: Alcohol leads; boomers changed the picture
807.gist: Previews a medication inventory and the role of losses in addiction, lists glossary terms, then opens Part 1: alcohol problems dominate among adults sixty and over, while illicit drug use among those fifty and up has risen as baby boomers age.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is a cohort effect: habits formed in youth travel with a generation. Boomers grew up during the 1960s and 1970s drug culture, so their later-life substance profile differs from earlier generations'.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Older adults are often under-screened for substance problems because symptoms like falls, confusion or low mood get blamed on aging. Missed diagnosis is a recurring theme in geriatric addiction research.

ask: Which symptoms of addiction in an older person could easily be mistaken for normal aging?
What cohort effects might your own generation carry into old age?

terms.d: A pattern shared by people born in the same era because of the times they grew up in.

808.title: Your generation's drug history
808.gist: Notes that people 65 and older use a large share of prescription drugs, often many at once, and cognitive decline can lead to mistakes. Exercise 1 asks members if they are boomers and what and how they used as teens and young adults.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Life-history questions can open a long story. Give a time frame and invite members to name one substance and one era, so others get space and the group can spot shared patterns.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Polypharmacy, often defined as taking five or more medications, is a major cause of falls and hospital visits in older adults. Adding alcohol or illicit drugs multiplies the danger.

ask: How does an early start with substances shape risk decades later?
Why might older adults hide prescription misuse more easily than younger people?

terms.d: Taking many medications at once, which raises the risk of interactions and side effects.

809.title: Drinking limits and the DSM-5 checklist
809.gist: Gives the NIH low-risk limit for those over 65 (about one drink a day, no more than three at once), warns medications make any drinking riskier, and calls for abstinence after an SUD diagnosis. Exercise 2 begins the eleven DSM-5 criteria as a self-check.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Older bodies hold less water and process alcohol more slowly, so the same drink produces a higher blood alcohol level than it did decades earlier. That is the biology behind lower limits.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Self-checking diagnostic criteria can help insight but is not a diagnosis. Some members will under-check out of denial, others over-check out of shame; a clinician should interpret the result.

ask: Why does DSM-5 avoid the word 'addiction' as a formal category, and what was gained or lost?
How would you handle a member who checks no criteria despite a long criminal record tied to use?

terms.d: The American Psychiatric Association's diagnostic manual, which rates substance use disorders from mild to severe.

810.title: Counting criteria, gauging severity
810.gist: Completes the DSM-5 checklist, including role failure, danger, tolerance and withdrawal. It explains that four or five criteria indicate moderate severity, and asks members whether they meet at least moderate criteria.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Under DSM-5, two or three criteria indicate mild, four or five moderate, and six or more severe. Tolerance and withdrawal from medicines taken as prescribed do not count toward the diagnosis.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Seeing a severity label can provoke defensiveness. Use it as a mirror, not a verdict: ask which criterion was the hardest to check honestly, and why.

ask: How do the DSM-5 criteria fit older adults whose roles (work, school) have already ended?
Is a severity scale more useful for the clinician or the client?

811.title: What counts as medication misuse
811.gist: Defines medication misuse as taking a prescribed or store-bought medicine other than as directed, including too little or off schedule. It warns that alcohol and sedating drugs mix dangerously even hours apart, and Exercise 3 starts a medication list.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Alcohol and drugs like benzodiazepines, opioids and sleep medicines all depress the central nervous system. Combined, their effects can add up or multiply, slowing breathing and raising fall risk.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Taking too little is misuse too, which surprises people. Older members may ration pills to save money; ask gently about cost before assuming carelessness.

ask: How does financial strain contribute to medication misuse in older adults?
Why do herbal remedies feel safe to people even when they interact with drugs?

terms.d: Using a medicine in any way other than prescribed: wrong amount, wrong timing, or with risky substances.

812.title: Aging bodies, risky combinations
812.gist: Asks whether members have checked alcohol interactions with a doctor, then explains that aging changes how the body handles drugs and alcohol. It lists dangers: aspirin and bleeding, drowsy cold medicines, acetaminophen and liver damage, alcohol-containing syrups, and deadly sedative mixes.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Geriatric medicine uses the Beers Criteria, a list maintained by the American Geriatrics Society of drugs that are often risky for older adults, including many sedatives. It shows how seriously medicine takes age-related drug sensitivity.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to guess which household products contain alcohol (some mouthwashes, cough syrups, tinctures), then reveal. It is a vivid way to show hidden exposure in recovery.

ask: Why might older adults trust over-the-counter products more than prescriptions?
How would you help a member with low literacy read medication warning labels?

terms.d: When one substance changes how another works, sometimes dangerously.

813.title: Warning signs and too many doctors
813.gist: Exercise 4 is a checklist of warning signs like memory lapses, falls, bruises, sleep and appetite changes, isolation, poor hygiene and lost interest. The page then warns that older adults often see several specialists who prescribe without knowing each other's orders.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many of these signs overlap with depression, dementia and substance problems. Teach members that the checklist points to 'get checked,' not to a specific cause.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Fragmented care is a system problem, not only a patient one. Expecting a confused or isolated elder to coordinate several doctors places the burden on the person least able to carry it.

ask: How would you tell whether memory problems come from alcohol, medication, or dementia?
Which warning sign on this list might staff in a facility be likely to miss?

814.title: One doctor who sees every pill
814.gist: Urges having one physician who knows all medications: bring every bottle to the primary care doctor for review, allow doctors to talk, and ask why each drug is taken, its side effects, and interactions with other drugs, alcohol and herbs.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Medication reconciliation, often done as a 'brown bag' review where patients bring all their pills, is widely used to catch duplications and dangerous combinations, especially after hospital stays.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: At release, people may get prescriptions from the facility, a community clinic and an ER. Help members build a one-page medication list to carry, updated at every visit.

ask: What would stop a member from giving permission for doctors to share information, and how would you address it?
How does medication reconciliation relate to honesty in recovery?

terms.d: Comparing all a person's medicines to catch duplicates, conflicts and errors.

815.title: Losing a spouse or loved one
815.gist: Opens Part 2: losing a partner or close person brings numbness, anger, sadness and trouble with sleep and decisions. Heavy drinking is more common among widowed and divorced older adults and can raise suicide risk. Exercise 5 asks about such a loss.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Older men, especially after losing a spouse, are among the highest-risk groups for suicide, and alcohol raises that risk further. Screening for suicidal thinking belongs in any grief conversation with this group.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Older men may struggle to name grief and show it as irritability or drinking instead. Use plain words like 'missing,' 'empty' or 'lost' rather than clinical terms.

ask: How would you assess suicide risk sensitively in a group setting when grief comes up?
What makes grief from inside prison, missing a funeral, especially hard to process?

terms.d: The period of grief and adjustment after someone close dies.

816.title: Other losses that come with age
816.gist: Continues Exercise 5 on how a loss affects members now, their use, and whether to work on it. It then starts on other losses: deaths, separations, adult children moving away, and leaving a long-time home.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Kenneth Doka's idea of disenfranchised grief describes losses others don't recognize, like a home, a pet, or a role. Unrecognized grief can go underground and find its outlet in drinking.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to draw a simple timeline of losses over the past ten years. Seeing them all at once often explains a rise in use better than any single event.

ask: Which losses of incarcerated older adults are least likely to be acknowledged by others?
How do you help someone grieve a loss that his own use helped cause?

terms.d: Grief that is not openly recognized or supported by others.

817.title: Lost mobility, lost trust
817.gist: Lists losses of mobility, hearing, sight and self-care, then losses caused by drinking: a license after drunk driving, unsupervised time with grandchildren, and family trust after broken promises. Exercise 6 asks about personal losses.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Separate losses that came with age from losses that came from use, without shaming. The first call for grief and adaptation; the second also open a path to amends.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Trust research suggests it is rebuilt slowly through consistent small actions rather than big promises. That fits the Twelve Step idea of 'living amends,' changing behavior over time.

ask: How would you respond to a member who blames all his losses on aging and none on drinking?
What is the difference between guilt that motivates change and shame that fuels use?

818.title: When retirement hurts
818.gist: Finishes Exercise 6, then explains that retirement can be chosen or forced, and that about one-third of retirees struggle with the change. Losses include income, workplace friends, daily structure, social role and pride in work.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Work supplies more than money: time structure, social contact, purpose, status and activity. Marie Jahoda's work on unemployment named these hidden benefits, and losing them all at once can feel like losing a self.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For members leaving long sentences, release can mimic forced retirement: no job waiting, no routine. Planning a daily schedule is a relapse prevention tool, not just time management.

ask: What 'hidden benefits' of work could a recovery routine provide instead?
How does a forced transition differ psychologically from a chosen one?

819.title: Free time as a risk factor
819.gist: Notes that sudden free time without hobbies or social ties can lead to boredom, loneliness, depression and problem drinking. Exercise 7 asks whether members are retired and how retirement affects them and their use.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Boredom is commonly reported as a relapse trigger and loneliness is linked to worse health in older adults. Structured activity and social ties are protective in both areas.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members map an empty Tuesday hour by hour, then fill the riskiest hour with one specific activity and person. The riskiest hour is often late afternoon.

ask: Why is unstructured time risky in recovery even for people who are not retired?
How would you adapt this exercise for members who never had steady work?

820.title: Searching for meaning, late and sober
820.gist: Asks the big questions of why we are here, notes meaning often comes from spiritual, social and service activities, and says intoxication can become life's main purpose. Recovery can renew the search, and looking back can find meaning even in mistakes. Exercise 8 begins.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Robert Butler's life review therapy encourages older adults to revisit their past to find coherence. It echoes Frankl's view that meaning can be found even in suffering, which suits people with painful histories.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Life review can stir regret and unresolved trauma. It works best with support and a forward step, so it doesn't become rumination about wasted years.

ask: What does meaning-making look like for someone who has spent much of adult life incarcerated?
How do you hold space for regret without letting it become despair?

terms.d: Looking back over one's life to make sense of it, often used with older adults.

821.title: Shrinking social circles with age
821.gist: Finishes Exercise 8, then describes how aging narrows social networks: deaths, losing the ability to drive, resentment about depending on others, and disability or relocation.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Loneliness and social isolation in older adults have been linked to higher risks of heart disease, dementia and early death in large studies. Connection is a health issue, not just a comfort.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking for help may feel like weakness to older men who prized self-reliance. Reframe interdependence as strength, the same shift asked of newcomers in Twelve Step groups.

ask: How does pride about independence interact with the need for support in recovery?
What would rebuilding a social network look like for someone returning home after decades?

terms.d: Having few social contacts; different from loneliness, which is the painful feeling of being disconnected.

822.title: Repairing relationships use damaged
822.gist: Explains how addiction harms ties with family, friends and coworkers, leaving anger, shame and distrust, and that some people may resist a member's recovery. Treatment teaches feelings, communication and amends to rebuild trust. Exercise 9 asks how aging hurt relationships.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Family systems theory sees a household adapting around the addiction; when the person changes, the system can push back. That explains why some relatives seem unsupportive of recovery.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Warn members that family may not trust them quickly. Rehearse how to respond calmly to suspicion, since frustration at being doubted is a common early relapse trigger.

ask: Why might someone in a member's life feel threatened by his recovery?
When could making amends do more harm than good, as the Ninth Step itself cautions?

823.title: Aging and the body's new demands
823.gist: Finishes Exercise 9 on how substance use harmed relationships. It then turns to physical health: older adults face more arthritis, heart disease and, with poor diet, diabetes.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Avoid repeating the chronic disease session wholesale. Focus on what is specific to age: slower healing, more medications and greater fall risk.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Gerontologists distinguish chronological age from biological age. Heavy substance use and incarceration can speed biological aging, which is why some 50-year-olds have the health of much older people.

ask: How might earlier sessions on pain and chronic disease be woven into work with older members?
Which health issue do your older members talk about least?

824.title: Alcohol's toll on older bodies
824.gist: Lists other age-related conditions (cataracts, dementia, glaucoma, sleep problems, incontinence) and how alcohol worsens blood pressure, stroke, immunity, liver and bleeding risks, plus falls and hip fractures. Treatment is an opportunity for full medical, dental and vision checks.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Falls are a leading cause of injury in older adults, and alcohol use raises fall risk, especially combined with sedating medicines. A hip fracture can sharply reduce independence.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members when they last had a dental, vision or hearing check. Turning the gap into a concrete request to medical staff is a small, winnable step.

ask: Why do people often put off dental and vision care, and how does that link to self-worth?
How would you explain fall risk to a member who feels invincible?

825.title: Mental health risks in later life
825.gist: Asks how use affected physical health, then reports older adults face memory loss, depression, loneliness and feeling a burden. About one in five have a mental health problem, depression being most common, with risk tied to bereavement, illness, disability and heavy drinking.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Feeling like a burden is a key element in Thomas Joiner's interpersonal theory of suicide, alongside feeling that one doesn't belong. Both are common in isolated older adults.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Older members may see depression as weakness or normal aging. Present it as a treatable medical condition, like high blood pressure.

ask: How would you notice 'burdensomeness' thinking in a member's talk?
Why might depression in older men be missed by staff and family?

terms.d: Depression that appears for the first time in later life.

826.title: Screening the mind in recovery
826.gist: Stresses that depression is very treatable and that substance use worsens memory, sleep, mood, anxiety, confusion and dementia. Treatment offers questionnaire-based screening and evaluation. Exercise 11 asks how aging and use affected psychological health.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Heavy, long-term drinking can cause cognitive problems, and some of this improves with sustained abstinence. Alcohol-related brain damage is often more reversible than dementia from other causes.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Short screening tools like the PHQ-9 for depression are quick to give and help flag who needs a fuller evaluation. They screen; they don't diagnose.

ask: How would hope that some memory problems may improve with sobriety affect a member's motivation?
What can a screening questionnaire miss that a conversation would catch?

827.title: Others see what we don't
827.gist: Finishes Exercise 11 by asking whether others have noticed memory problems, confusion or sadness the member doesn't see. It then introduces leisure as free time for rest and enjoyment, recreation as the activities filling it, and research linking both to well-being.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Lack of insight into one's own cognitive or mood changes (anosognosia in its stronger forms) is common. Outside observers often notice changes first, which is why family reports matter in assessment.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Aristotle saw leisure not as idleness but as time for the activities that make life worthwhile. Recovery invites reclaiming leisure from intoxication.

ask: How do you respond respectfully when a member rejects family concerns about his memory?
What separates leisure that supports recovery from leisure that drifts toward use?

terms.d: Free time away from obligations, used for rest and enjoyment.
Active, enjoyable pursuits done in free time, like sports, music or crafts.

828.title: A menu of meaningful activities
828.gist: Notes barriers like transportation can be eased by senior centers and local programs. Exercise 12 offers a checklist of activities: walks, library events, senior centers, classes, hobbies, volunteering, docent work, collecting and travel.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Volunteering among older adults is associated with better well-being and lower mortality in observational studies. Purposeful roles seem to matter more than activity alone.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For members with records, some volunteer roles involve background checks. Help them pick options realistically open to them so the plan doesn't stall.

ask: Which activities on the list build sober relationships, not just fill time?
How might a criminal record shape which recreational paths are open?

829.title: Barriers, first steps, spiritual drift
829.gist: Finishes Exercise 12 with barriers and first steps like making a call. It then explains that older adults may lose spiritual and religious ties as isolation and depression turn focus inward and drinking replaces connection with a Higher Power.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Carl Jung's letter to Bill W. described alcohol craving as a misplaced thirst for wholeness, captured as 'spiritus contra spiritum.' This page draws on that same idea: drinking fills a space spirituality once held.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name one thing larger than themselves they once felt connected to: faith, nature, family, a cause. Spirituality need not be religious to count.

ask: How can you discuss spirituality with members of different faiths, or none, without imposing your own?
Why does depression often look like a spiritual emptiness?

830.title: Paths back to a spiritual life
830.gist: Calls spiritual growth central to recovery, through meditation, prayer, religious life and service, with Twelve Step groups as the most common path. It suggests older adults seek AA meetings with peers their age. Exercise 13 asks how age and use affected spirituality.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on AA, including a large Cochrane review, suggests it can be as effective as or more effective than some other approaches for staying abstinent. Spirituality is one proposed mechanism, along with social support.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Calling Twelve Step groups the most powerful path can sideline members who are non-religious or prefer secular groups like SMART Recovery. Offer options so spirituality isn't a gate to recovery.

ask: What role does service to others play in recovery, and why might it work for older adults especially?
How would you support an older member who wants recovery but rejects the Higher Power concept?

831.title: Turning insight into action
831.gist: Finishes Exercise 13, recaps the session's paths (meaning, relationships, physical, mental and spiritual health), then starts Exercise 14: a checklist of actions like counseling, Twelve Step groups and meeting people, with space for concrete examples.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push for specifics: not 'meet new people' but 'go to the Wednesday meeting at the senior center and talk to one person.' Vague plans tend to fade.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Behavioral activation, an evidence-based depression treatment, works by scheduling meaningful activity before motivation arrives. This checklist is essentially an activation plan.

ask: How do you know whether a member's action plan is realistic?
What would you check at follow-up to see if the plan took hold?

terms.d: A therapy approach that schedules meaningful activity to lift mood, rather than waiting to feel motivated.

832.title: The rest of the action list
832.gist: Completes Exercise 14's checklist with joining a religious group, hobbies, recreation, leisure, volunteering, medical and dental exams, and courses or therapy on social life.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have each member star the one item he will do within seven days of release and name who will help. A single near-term commitment is more likely to happen than a long list.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members which item feels most out of reach and why. The answer often reveals a barrier (shame, transportation, money) worth problem-solving now.

ask: Which item on this list would most protect an older member from relapse?
How do you balance offering many options with the risk of overwhelming someone?

833.title: Session 37 wrap-up
833.gist: Summarizes the older adults session: generational use patterns, the dangers of mixing medications with alcohol, applying misuse categories to oneself, and later-life issues like retirement, disability and isolation that recovery can help heal.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The hopeful tone that losses 'can be healed' may oversell what recovery can do about permanent losses like death or disability. Healing here means adapting and finding meaning, not reversal.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask older members what advice they would give their younger selves about substances, and let younger members respond. It turns the group into an intergenerational exchange.

ask: What would a version of this session designed for aging adults in prison look like?
How does honoring loss differ from trying to fix it?

834.title: Session 37 key terms
834.gist: Defines depression in later life, medication misuse, older adult, the older adult drinking guideline, problem drinking, and substance use disorder for the older adults session.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Highlight that problem drinking can occur even below the guideline limits in older adults, especially with medications. Limits are ceilings, not safe zones.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The shift from 'abuse' and 'dependence' in DSM-IV to a single severity spectrum in DSM-5 reflected research showing the old categories overlapped. Members may still hear the older terms.

ask: Why might a single severity spectrum be more useful than separate categories?
How would you explain 'problem drinking at low amounts' to a skeptical older member?
